text: --- Top Stories The US Military Buildup Against Iran: Largest Since 2003 The Trump administration has assembled what military analysts are now describing as the most concentrated display of US military force in the Middle East since the 2003 invasion of Iraq. Four American carrier strike groups are either in the region or converging on it: the USS Gerald R. Ford arrived at Souda Bay on the island of Crete on Monday and is expected off the coast of Israel within days; the USS Abraham Lincoln carrier strike group is operating in the Arabian Sea. More than 40,000 US military personnel are now stationed across bases and naval assets in the region. Robert Pape, professor of political science at the University of Chicago and a leading analyst of American air power, wrote Saturday: "This represents 40-50% of the deployable US air power in the world. Think air power on the order of the 1991 and 2003 Iraq war. And growing. Never has the US deployed this much force against a potential enemy and not launched strikes." Col. Richard Kemp, former commander of British forces in Afghanistan, told the Media Line that the current scale already exceeds the June 2025 "12-day war" (Operation Midnight Hammer) and "could run into weeks." The State Department on Monday ordered the evacuation of non-essential personnel and family members from the US Embassy in Beirut — 32 to 50 staff and family members flew out of Beirut airport. The State Department updated its travel advisory for Lebanon, warning US citizens not to travel to the country. The WSWS's Andre Damon noted that this evacuation follows the identical pattern established before Operation Midnight Hammer in June 2025, when US presence was similarly reduced at embassies in Baghdad, Kuwait, and Bahrain in the days before B-2 bombers struck Iran's nuclear facilities. The Washington Post reported separately that the Joint Chiefs of Staff Chairman, Gen. Dan Caine, has privately warned the president that a US attack on Iran carries "acute risks" — including a lack of munitions and allied support — that differ sharply from Trump's public boasting that Caine had told him an attack would be an "easy victory." This contradiction between Trump's public claims and military reality is itself a dangerous indicator: it suggests the president is building a public justification for war that has been deliberately detached from the military's own risk assessments. From the WSWS's perspective, the bourgeois media's framing — the Financial Times headline "Crisis of his own making" is typical — obscures the bipartisan character of the war drive. The Democrats' objections to Trump on Iran are tactical, not principled. The NYT analysis noting that Tehran views concessions on uranium enrichment as riskier than war should be understood not as Iranian intransigence but as the rational response of a state that has watched how the United States treated Libya and Iraq after they gave up their weapons programs. The fourth anniversary of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine (February 24, 2022) falls today. Four years in, the UN reports more than 15,000 civilians killed, including 763 children. Russia holds approximately 20 percent of Ukrainian territory, and front lines are largely frozen. Ukraine's Zelenskyy told the FT that the war is at "the beginning of the end" — but what that end looks like remains contested. Negotiations are now under way, with the NYT reporting that a major sticking point is the fate of Ukrainian citizens in Russian-controlled Donetsk, who face an "agonizing choice" about their political future. Hungary is blocking both the latest EU sanctions package on Russia and a $106 billion financial aid package to Kyiv, a pressure point that significantly weakens the Western position going into any talks. The BBC published a striking report today: four Russian soldiers testify that they witnessed fellow troops executed by commanders for refusing orders. This is not simply a human interest story. It is evidence of the coercive, non-voluntary character of Russia's own war effort — a point that connects to the WSWS's analysis of the war as driven by competing ruling class interests, with the working class on both sides bearing the catastrophic costs. Trump's State of the Union: Reeling from Supreme Court, Falling Polls Tonight's State of the Union address is being delivered under conditions the White House itself acknowledges are difficult. The NYT reports Trump is "bruised and unpopular," reeling from the 6-3 Supreme Court decision last Friday invalidating his "reciprocal tariffs" under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA). His approval ratings are declining. The paper notes that "cracks appear in Trump coalition" in bellwether regions like Northeastern Pennsylvania, where working-class discontent is growing. The circumstances around tonight's speech are significant beyond the speech itself. The WSWS Perspectives published today — "The real state of Trump's America" — provides the counter-narrative that the speech will attempt to bury. Key facts that Trump will not mention: the national debt stands at $38.4 trillion ($113,000 per person), growing at $8 billion per day; cumulative price increases since 2020 include food up 25%, housing still climbing 3% annually; the top 1% control 31.7% of all wealth — the highest share since the Fed began tracking in 1989; Elon Musk's fortune has ballooned to $726 billion; CEO pay is 285 times average worker pay; 2025 was the deadliest year for ICE detention on record, with 66,000 people currently held. The Democrats have selected Virginia Governor Abigail Spanberger — a CIA veteran — to deliver the party's response, just as they chose Senator Elissa Slotkin (also a CIA veteran) last year. The WSWS Perspectives correctly identifies this as a deliberate signal to the ruling class that the Democratic Party will uphold the military-intelligence apparatus regardless of the electoral outcome. Bernie Sanders and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez will offer their customary "left"-sounding rhetoric; in practice, the Democrats collaborate with Trump on the core class interests of the financial oligarchy. The "Angel Families" staging at the White House on Monday — families of people killed by undocumented immigrants — is the latest in Trump's cynical exploitation of victims to normalize the immigration crackdown. The NYT notes that public support for Trump's immigration approach is "softening." Hanging over the proceedings is the Jeffrey Epstein scandal. The WSWS Editorial Board's Perspectives makes this explicit: "The Justice Department's release of nearly 3 million pages has shaken the upper tiers of corporate America." Billionaire Leslie Wexner was identified as a co-conspirator in 2019 FBI documents yet faces no charges. The arrest in London of former UK Ambassador to the US Peter Mandelson on suspicion of "misconduct in public office" — tied to Epstein revelations — is a separate but connected story that reveals how far the rot extends into the transatlantic ruling class. Supreme Court Strikes Down Trump Tariffs — Trump Escalates Immediately Last Friday's 6-3 Supreme Court ruling in Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump struck down the "reciprocal tariffs" Trump had imposed under the IEEPA — a ruling that voided approximately $160 billion in tariffs collected over the past year. The decision was written by Chief Justice John Roberts, with Justices Gorsuch and Amy Coney Barrett joining the three liberals in the majority. Trump's response was immediate and revealing. At a hastily convened press conference, he attacked the three conservative justices who voted against him as "fools and lapdogs of the radical left," called the entire majority "major sleazebags" and "foreign country-centric," and compared himself to a Mafia don warning foreign countries that they would stop "dancing in the streets." The Wall Street Journal editorialized that "Trump owes the Supreme Court an apology." But the more significant story is what Trump did immediately after the ruling. He invoked Section 122 of the 1974 Trade Act — a provision never previously used at this scale by any president — to impose a 10-15% tariff on all imported goods for 150 days, after which Congressional approval is required for extension. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent described this as temporary. In the meantime, Trump has directed his legal team to pursue longer-term tariff authority under Section 301 of the same act. The Guardian is covering a related development: the 10% tariffs that came into effect Tuesday — the "replacement" tariffs following the Supreme Court ruling — are being greeted with anger by trading partners globally. China has simultaneously imposed export restrictions on 20 Japanese companies with defense ties, escalating the US-China confrontation in a different theater. The WSWS Perspectives by John Burton correctly identifies the Supreme Court ruling not as a restoration of constitutional norms but as an expression of deepening divisions within the ruling class over the strategic direction of US capitalism. Trump's willingness to attack three of his own appointees exposes how far the presidency has moved from any conventional understanding of institutional loyalty. Mexico: El Mencho Killed — US Intelligence Decisive — Violence Erupts On Sunday, Mexican security forces, with decisive assistance from US Northern Command intelligence, killed Nemesio Oseguera Cervantes — "El Mencho" — leader of the Jalisco New Generation Cartel (CJNG), in a compound in Tapalpa, Jalisco. El Mencho was tracked after surveillance of a romantic partner he traveled to visit. Defense Secretary Ricardo Trevilla acknowledged that "the exchange of information and data" with US Northern Command was "how we arrived at this specific case." The operation killed 25 soldiers, 30 alleged CJNG members, and 3 civilians, including a pregnant woman. 70 arrests were made across seven states. The Mexican government immediately deployed 10,000 additional troops nationwide. In the days since, violence has erupted across western Mexico: schools shut in several states, businesses closed, US citizens were warned to shelter in place in Puerto Vallarta and Cancún. Guadalajara — a 2026 World Cup host city — descended into chaos. The WSWS's Andrea Lobo provides the essential class analysis: the "war on drugs" is not a humanitarian project but a mechanism for deepening US imperialist control over Mexico and justifying the militarization of the country's internal security apparatus — directed ultimately against the Mexican working class. The killing of El Mencho does not end the cartel; it will likely trigger a violent succession struggle within CJNG and provoke inter-cartel warfare, which will in turn be used as a pretext for expanded military deployment. The broader context is the Trump administration's ongoing coercion of the Mexican government. Trump has continued to demand that Mexico "step up" its anti-cartel efforts even after this major operation, signaling that no level of compliance will satisfy Washington's demands. The CIA's role (reported by WaPo) in tracking El Mencho further underscores that this is a US intelligence operation conducted on Mexican soil with the acquiescence of a government under severe imperial pressure. Kaiser Strike and NewYork-Presbyterian Nurses: Twin Betrayals in One Day Two major healthcare worker strikes were brought to anticlimactic ends within the past 48 hours, exposing the systematic function of the union bureaucracy as a mechanism for demobilizing workers rather than representing them. **Kaiser Permanente:** On Monday, UNAC/UHCP officials ordered an abrupt end to the four-week strike of 31,000 healthcare workers — nurses, pharmacists, and clinicians in California and Hawaii. Workers were told to return by 7:00 AM Tuesday. No contract was ratified. No membership vote was held. The union described "significant movement at the bargaining table" without disclosing any specifics. By calling the action "suspended" rather than ending it through ratification, the leadership bypassed democratic procedures entirely and used its own discretionary authority to demobilize the strike. The WSWS's Marc Wells correctly identifies this as "a flagrant violation of members' basic democratic rights." **NewYork-Presbyterian:** On Saturday, NYSNA officials announced the ratification of a contract ending a six-week strike by 4,000 nurses — the last of four facilities still on strike. The key facts: nurses had overwhelmingly rejected the previous tentative agreement just over a week before; the new ratification vote was conducted hours after the deal was announced, with no time for workers to read or discuss the contract; the vote was conducted online under conditions that NYSNA itself had already acknowledged as insecure (the previous vote was on SurveyMonkey); and the union had isolated nurses in below-freezing temperatures while withholding strike pay to coerce ratification. The contract does not adequately address safe staffing. These two betrayals on the same day, combined with the WGA West staff strike — in which 115 administrative workers are striking against their own union — reveal the trade union apparatus as an instrument of class collaboration, not class struggle. The developing strike wave is real; the question is whether workers can build the rank-and-file organizations necessary to wage it independently of the bureaucracy. --- International Developments Ukraine War: Year Five — Stalemate, Atrocities, and Deteriorating Western Position The fourth anniversary of Russia's February 24, 2022 full-scale invasion brings no resolution. The NYT reports that Ukraine faces an "agonizing choice" over the fate of residents in Russian-controlled Donetsk — people who have lived under occupation and may face a peace deal that leaves them formally under Russian sovereignty. The BBC published testimony from four Russian soldiers claiming they witnessed their own comrades executed for refusing to advance. Russia's war economy is increasingly strained. A major NYT analysis reveals that approximately half of Russia's federal budget now goes to the Ukraine war — spending that "does little to support its long-term development" while enriching defense contractors and a narrow military-industrial stratum. The ruble has been partially stabilized through capital controls and commodity exports, but Russia's long-term productive capacity is being hollowed out. Meanwhile, the Western coalition supporting Ukraine is fracturing. Hungary — under the Orban government — is blocking both the latest EU sanctions package against Russia and a €96 billion ($106 billion) financial aid package to Kyiv, according to the NYT. This gives Russia a diplomatic opening and significantly weakens the position of the NATO bloc going into any ceasefire talks. The EU's ability to sustain Ukraine economically is a political, not just a financial, question. Ukraine's President Zelenskyy told the Financial Times that the war is "at the beginning of the end" — a formulation that is diplomatically significant because it signals Kyiv's openness to negotiations while trying to manage expectations. The actual negotiating positions remain far apart: Russia's demands for territorial concessions and Ukrainian neutrality remain unacceptable to Kyiv, and the social base for a compromise peace in Ukraine itself is narrow, as the NYT's reporting from Donetsk makes clear. France: Fascist Mobilization and the Macron Government's Complicity The death of Quentin Deranque — a young supporter of the far-right organization Lyon Populaire who died following a confrontation after a lecture by France Unbowed's Palestinian-origin Euro-MP Rima Hassan — has been seized upon by the entire French political establishment to launch a coordinated offensive against the left. The WSWS's Anthony Torres identifies the key political fact: a political front spanning fascist groups, the Socialist Party, the National Rally (Marine Le Pen and Jordan Bardella), and President Macron's own government has formed around the Deranque death to criminalize left-wing political activity. Macron explicitly blessed the far-right demonstration in Deranque's honor at the opening of the Agricultural Fair. The French government has refused to ban the fascist mobilization while simultaneously using the event to attack France Unbowed and the broader left. The WSWS draws the parallel with the United States, where the death of fascist agitator Charlie Kirk was similarly exploited to mobilize the right and delegitimize opposition. The objective in France, as Torres writes, is to clear the way for either Le Pen or Bardella to assume power after the forthcoming local elections and 2027 presidential election. The US ambassador to France, Charles Kushner (son of Jared Kushner's father), further inflamed the situation by citing "violent radical leftism" in the Deranque death — a formulation the French government found unacceptable and formally protested, summoning Kushner twice. He declined to appear on both occasions, sending a junior official in his place. Australia: Democratic Rights Under Labor Attack on Multiple Fronts The Albanese Labor government's assault on democratic rights is accelerating on several fronts simultaneously, all of which the WSWS's Australian correspondents are documenting: **The Bondi terrorist attack cover-up:** More than two months after the December 14 attack in which IS-linked father-son pair Sajid and Naveed Akram killed 15 people at a Jewish gathering at Bondi Beach, Oscar Grenfell reports that the central political question — how known-to-ASIO perpetrators were able to plan, arm, and execute the attack without interception — remains entirely unanswered. The attack is being invoked to justify sweeping new powers (protest bans, political party proscription) without any scrutiny of the intelligence and security failures that allowed it to occur. **Banning Hizb-ut Tahrir:** Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke has initiated the banning of Hizb-ut Tahrir under new legislation that does not require any terrorism link — only political speech deemed to promote "hate speech." Burke explicitly boasted that this is "the first time we have been able to ban a group which falls short of a terrorist listing." The legislation, as the WSWS has previously reported, is structured in a way that could be used to ban political parties. **Police raid on anti-fascist artwork:** On February 18, three ACT Policing officers entered the Dissent Cafe and Bar in Canberra after an anonymous Crime Stoppers complaint about satirical posters depicting Trump, Musk, Netanyahu, Vance, and Putin in Nazi-style uniforms, produced by British protest collective Grow Up Art. When the owner refused to surrender the posters, police declared the premises a crime scene for more than two hours. Detectives from the Major Crimes Unit were later dispatched to seize the posters. The action is being treated as a test case under the Combatting Antisemitism, Hate and Extremism Act 2026. **Healthcare and education strikes betrayed:** The ANMFSA (South Australian nurses' union) suspended all industrial action after a backroom deal with the Labor state government that fell far short of workers' 21% pay demand. In Victoria, early childhood educators are striking Thursday — but the AEU is keeping them separated from the March 24 school teacher stoppage to prevent unified action against the Labor government. Israel-Palestine: Settlers, Annexation, and the Berlinale Protests Twenty countries issued a joint statement condemning Israel's "de facto annexation" drive in the occupied West Bank, calling it a "deliberate and direct attack on the viability of a Palestinian state." The statement represents a significant diplomatic development but carries no enforcement mechanism. The NYT published a detailed report by Azam Ahmed on the systematic dispossession of Palestinian families in the West Bank through settler violence. The Rezeq Abu Naim family, after two years of continuous attacks on their land at all hours and in all forms, finally abandoned their home after another violent incursion over the weekend. This is not exceptional; it is the operational method of what twenty countries are now officially calling annexation. At the Berlin International Film Festival (Berlinale), award-winning filmmakers used the closing ceremony to denounce German government complicity in Gaza genocide. Stefan Steinberg's WSWS report describes how festival management — including director Tricia Tuttle and jury head Wim Wenders — deliberately sought to prevent any political discussion of Palestine, with Wenders initially declaring artists should "stay out of politics." The protest from filmmakers was so sustained and forceful that it dominated the closing ceremony despite these attempts at suppression. The political character of the German cultural establishment's silence on genocide is itself a story. UK: Mandelson Arrest, Epstein Fallout, and the Crisis of Starmerism The arrest on Monday of Peter Mandelson — former UK Ambassador to the United States, key architect of Blairite "New Labour," and longtime central figure in the Labour establishment — on suspicion of "misconduct in public office" has sent shockwaves through British politics. The arrest followed revelations about Mandelson's dealings with Jeffrey Epstein. This is the deepest penetration of the Epstein scandal into the British political establishment since the arrest of Prince Andrew earlier this month. The NYT reports that the Mandelson arrest "deepens a scandal that has led to calls for Prime Minister Keir Starmer's resignation." Starmer's Labour government, which came to power in 2024 promising a break from the corruption of the Conservative years, is now implicated through its most senior figures in the Epstein network's exposure. The political implications extend beyond Labour's domestic difficulties. Mandelson is a figure who has operated at the intersection of transatlantic ruling class networks for decades. His arrest, combined with the UK's move to back Australia on removing Prince Andrew from the line of succession, suggests that the Epstein exposure is beginning to consume figures previously considered untouchable. China-Japan Economic Confrontation Escalates China placed export restrictions on 20 Japanese companies with defense industry ties — the latest escalation in an ongoing economic confrontation between Beijing and Tokyo that has developed alongside Japan's rearmament drive. The NYT frames this as a "monthslong feud." The broader context is China's role in the global economic restructuring driven by the end of the post-Cold War liberal order: Beijing is now explicitly using export controls on critical materials (rare earths, semiconductor components) as a geopolitical weapon in the same way the US uses financial sanctions. The WSWS has not yet covered this specific development. It connects directly to: the Taiwan semiconductor scenario (NYT published a major analysis today of the vulnerability of US tech industry if China cuts off Taiwan chip exports); the broader US-China military confrontation; and the Japanese government's decision to dramatically increase defense spending under US pressure. --- United States Georgia Concentration Camp: 10,000-Bed Detention Complex The Trump administration's plans for a 10,000-bed immigrant detention complex in Social Circle, Georgia — detailed in Jacob Crosse's WSWS report — represent the largest planned civilian mass detention facility since the Japanese American internment of World War II. Utility filings project more than one million gallons per day in wastewater demand, consistent with permanent large-scale operation. The broader development plan encompasses more than 2.3 million square feet. This is not a "surge" measure. It is infrastructure for indefinite mass incarceration on a scale that would make the United States the world's leading incarcerator of a targeted ethnic and political group. The plan is provoking outrage — which the bourgeois press covers — but without the class analysis: this concentration camp network is not simply an immigration enforcement tool. It is, as the WSWS Perspectives notes, the infrastructure of a police state directed ultimately against the entire working class, beginning with its most vulnerable sector. Congress has already allocated $45 billion for detention expansion, with projected capacity of 135,000 — double the current record level of 66,000. Quakertown, Pennsylvania: Students Jailed, Police Cover-Up At least five high school students from Quakertown Community High School in Bucks County, Pennsylvania remain in police custody more than 72 hours after being arrested during an anti-ICE walkout on Friday, February 20. The incident began when Police Chief Scott McElree — not in uniform — physically grabbed students during the protest, with video widely circulated showing him choking a young female student. Another officer was filmed throwing a student into a planter. Five students and one adult were arrested. As of this writing, no charging documents have been released, no body camera footage has been shared, and the department has issued no public statement explaining McElree's use of force. A Change.org petition demanding McElree's resignation has exceeded 7,800 signatures; a GoFundMe for legal and medical costs has raised nearly $33,000. The IYSSE statement published today correctly frames this not as an isolated incident of police misconduct but as part of a "broader campaign to intimidate youth, criminalize political opposition and normalize police-state methods." Student walkouts against ICE have now occurred in more than 36 states. Will Lehman, the Mack Trucks worker and UAW presidential candidate, issued a statement calling the Quakertown assault "police brutality against children" and demanding working class solidarity with the students. The 323-student suspension at Woodbridge Senior High School in Prince William County, Virginia — for participating in an anti-ICE walkout — is documented in the IYSSE statement. Administrative punishment is being used alongside police violence as a two-pronged strategy to suppress the youth movement. Pentagon, Iran, and the Military-Industrial Budget The Pentagon is racing to spend $153 billion in added funds — money Republicans pushed through in their "sweeping domestic policy bill" — while having ignored Congress's demands for a spending plan for months. This is the militarization of the US economy in real time, directed toward war preparations rather than social needs. The Anthropic-Pentagon confrontation is a significant development: the Defense Department summoned Anthropic's CEO after the AI company demanded guardrails be maintained in a major defense contract. This reveals how AI is being conscripted into the military apparatus, and the pressure being placed on tech companies to remove safety restrictions for military applications. The Pentagon separately pulled its support for an air safety bill — legislation written in response to the January 2025 D.C. helicopter-plane collision — just as the House was expected to vote on it. This means the safety improvements prompted by a disaster that killed dozens of people are being blocked by the military. The Epstein Files and the Decomposition of the American Ruling Class The WSWS Perspectives today weaves the Epstein scandal into its analysis of the State of the Union — and rightly so. The Justice Department's release of nearly 3 million pages has now resulted in: Attorney General Pam Bondi deflecting questions by citing the Dow Jones index; FBI documents showing billionaire Leslie Wexner identified as a co-conspirator in 2019 with no charges brought; and email evidence of Epstein's own clinical dehumanization of the girls he trafficked. Trump himself is deeply implicated. The British dimension — Mandelson's arrest, Andrew's earlier arrest — reveals that this is not an American aberration but a feature of the transatlantic ruling class as a social formation. David North's characterization, cited in the Perspectives, of the Epstein revelations as revealing "the social physiognomy of a degenerate ruling class and oligarchical society in an advanced state of decomposition" is the correct political-historical framework for understanding what the files expose: not the crimes of bad individuals, but the systematic character of a social class that has detached itself from any restraining legal or moral framework. --- Science and Public Health Bhattacharya Controls NIH and CDC — Measles Surges — Public Health Infrastructure Being Demolished The Trump administration confirmed last week that NIH Director Jay Bhattacharya — best known as the Stanford health economist who co-authored the Great Barrington Declaration advocating for COVID-19 "herd immunity" — will simultaneously serve as acting director of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Benjamin Mateus's WSWS analysis is essential reading. Bhattacharya has no formal training in public health administration and no experience directing infectious disease response. His "primary qualification," as Mateus correctly writes, "stems from his role during the COVID-19 pandemic as a leading propagandist for the mass infection policies demanded by Wall Street." The Great Barrington Declaration was written at the American Institute for Economic Research, a libertarian think tank tied to Charles Koch, and advocated "herd immunity" — a position that the WSWS's Global Workers' Inquest into the COVID-19 Pandemic has extensively documented as a deliberate policy of mass death in the service of capitalist profit. Now the same person controls both the NIH — the US government's primary biomedical research agency — and the CDC — its leading disease surveillance institution. This is occurring while measles cases are surging across the United States: a preventable disease returning in the context of RFK Jr.'s anti-vaccination campaign (Kennedy last week defended Trump's order ramping up glyphosate production before angry "MAHA Moms" who had not anticipated he would take that position on pesticides). The dismantling of public health is not a policy failure; it is a policy success from the standpoint of the financial interests who want to remove regulatory obstacles to profit. The Supreme Court's agreement to consider whether states can sue fossil fuel companies over greenhouse gas emissions is a separate development but part of the same pattern: the systematic weakening of regulatory constraints on capital. Dozens of municipalities are seeking billions in damages; a positive ruling for plaintiffs could have significant financial implications for the oil and gas industry. --- WSWS Coverage — Last 24 Hours "The real state of Trump's America: Social misery, dictatorship, war — and an upsurge of class struggle" — by WSWS Editorial Board **[FULL TEXT — Perspectives article published February 24, 2026]** US President Donald Trump will deliver the annual State of the Union address Tuesday night before a joint session of Congress. Were it honestly titled, the speech would be called "The State of the Rich"—a demagogic exercise in self-congratulation, burying the catastrophic reality of American life beneath a mountain of lies. The speech is being delivered in the year that the United States is to celebrate the 250th anniversary of the Declaration of Independence. On July 4, 2026, the nation will commemorate the issuing of the document that proclaimed "all men are created equal" and asserted the inalienable rights of "Life, Liberty and the pursuit of Happiness." The founders fought a revolution against King George III. Two hundred and fifty years later, Trump's America offers its own answer to the Declaration's ideals: a government of the billionaires, by the billionaires and for the billionaires, presiding over armed raids on immigrant communities, a network of concentration camps spreading across the country, children torn from their parents, and the gunning down of unarmed civilians by federal agents on the streets of Minneapolis. Hanging over the proceedings is the stench of Jeffrey Epstein. The Justice Department's release of nearly 3 million pages has shaken the upper tiers of corporate America, exposing connections of billionaires, chief executives and senior political figures to a convicted child sex trafficker. The files, as WSWS Chairman David North recently wrote, "reveal the social physiognomy of a degenerate ruling class and oligarchical society in an advanced state of decomposition. Their offenses are rank; they smell to heaven." Trump himself is deeply implicated. Attorney General Pam Bondi responded to questions about the ongoing cover-up by boasting that the Dow had hit 50,000. FBI documents reveal that billionaire Leslie Wexner was identified as a co-conspirator in 2019, yet no charges have been brought. Emails show Epstein comparing the girls he trafficked to "shrimp—you throw away the head and keep the body." This is the ruling class that governs America. Consider the facts that will be buried beneath Trump's demagogy. The national debt stands at $38.4 trillion, or $113,000 for every person in the country, and is increasing at $8 billion per day. The Congressional Budget Office (CBO) projects the deficit at $1.9 trillion this year, growing to $3.1 trillion by 2036, with debt reaching 120 percent of GDP, which is higher than at any point in the nation's history. The dollar fell more than 9 percent in 2025, its worst annual performance since 2017, and remains in bear market territory as BRICS nations increase local currency trade settlements from 35 to 50 percent. Cumulative price increases since 2020 have been devastating: food up more than 25 percent, housing costs still climbing at 3 percent annually, natural gas up nearly 10 percent. The level of social inequality is historically unprecedented. The top 1 percent of households now control 31.7 percent of all wealth, the highest share since the Fed began tracking such data in 1989. They hold $55 trillion, nearly as much as the bottom 90 percent combined. The combined wealth of 935 American billionaires surged to $8.1 trillion at the end of 2025. Elon Musk, Trump's partner in dismantling the federal government through DOGE, has seen his fortune balloon to $726 billion. CEO compensation at S&P 500 companies averaged $18.9 million—285 times the typical worker's pay, up from 21-to-1 in 1965. CEO pay has risen 1,094 percent since 1978, while worker pay has increased just 26 percent. Tesla has proposed a $1 trillion pay package for Musk, exceeding the total annual compensation of the entire federal workforce. The stock market is not a measure of national prosperity. It is a barometer of ruling class enrichment. But the most sinister dimension of the real state of the union is the deployment of armed federal agents against the population. In December 2025, the administration launched Operation Metro Surge, deploying 3,000 masked ICE and Border Patrol agents into the Twin Cities, Minnesota, in what the DHS itself called the largest immigration operation in American history. On January 7, ICE shot and killed Renée Good, a 37-year-old American citizen and mother of three. On January 24, Border Patrol agents shot and killed Alex Pretti, a 37-year-old ICU nurse, firing as many as 10 rounds into him as he lay on the ground. The administration has built a network of detention camps across the country, holding nearly 66,000 people—a 75 percent increase, the highest level in history. Congress has allocated $45 billion for still more facilities, with capacity projected at 135,000. Children are separated from their parents at a record rate. A tent camp at Fort Bliss, Texas, holds 5,000 people on the same ground that served as an internment camp for Japanese Americans during World War II. 2025 was the deadliest year for ICE detention on record. The Democrats will offer no genuine opposition. Whatever gestures they make Tuesday night will be meaningless stunts. In actual practice, they collaborate with Trump on the issues that matter most to the ruling class. Where their differences with Trump exist, they are centered on tactical questions of imperialist strategy—above all, dissatisfaction with his insufficient support for the US-NATO proxy war against Russia in Ukraine. But on the drive toward war with Iran, the two parties are in essential agreement. The Democrats' selection of CIA veterans—Senator Elissa Slotkin last year, Virginia Governor Abigail Spanberger this year—to deliver the party's response to Trump's State of the Union is itself an assurance to the ruling class that they will uphold the military-intelligence apparatus while using "left"-sounding demagogy from Bernie Sanders and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez to block the emergence of a mass movement from below. This is the real state of Trump's America in the 250th year since the Declaration of Independence: a society riven by class antagonism on a scale not seen since the Gilded Age, ruled by a criminal oligarchy that has dispensed with even the pretense of democratic governance, lurching toward war abroad and dictatorship at home. But there is another side to the equation, and it is the decisive one. The same crisis driving the ruling class toward fascism and war is propelling the working class into struggle. A developing strike wave, the mass anti-ICE protests, last year's "No Kings" marches, the ongoing walkouts by high school students—these are the initial expressions of a social force that neither party of big business can contain. The critical question is one of political program, perspective and organization. The opposition to the Trump administration cannot be entrusted to the Democrats, who are complicit in everything he does. It must be based on the independent mobilization of the working class. Workers must form rank-and-file committees in every workplace, school and neighborhood to coordinate resistance, demand an end to the ICE terror, defend immigrants, and prepare for a general strike against the government's program of war, austerity and dictatorship. The building of such committees, organized on the basis of a socialist and internationalist program, is the only realistic strategy for defeating the fascistic conspiracy of the American oligarchy. --- "US begins pulling staff from Beirut embassy amid Iran attack buildup" — by Andre Damon Published February 24, 2026. Trump's State of the Union: 108 minutes of demagogy, Iran war threats, and Democratic complicity Donald Trump delivered the longest State of the Union address in modern history on the night of February 24 — approximately 108 minutes of belligerent demagogy that centered the drive toward war with Iran, doubled down on the immigration crackdown, and buried the catastrophic social reality of American life beneath transparently false economic claims. --- Pseudo-left press review - [Jacobin / DSA](#jacobin--dsa) — defends Mamdani's collaboration with Trump as "trying a fresh tactic"; attacks the Iran war as Trump's personal failure without class analysis of imperialism - [Left Voice (PTS/FT)](#left-voice-ptsft) — opposes both the Iranian regime and US imperialism but promotes a nationalist-reformist framework for "who decides Iran's future" - [Socialist Alternative (ISA/CWI)](#socialist-alternative-isacwi) — calls for a May 1 "general strike" as an abstract slogan divorced from any political program or party-building perspective - [SWP UK (IST)](#swp-uk-ist) — moralistic anti-war stance without class analysis; articles on Iranian student protests objectively align with regime-change framing - [Socialist Appeal / RCP (IMT)](#socialist-appeal--rcp-imt) — focuses on UK by-election as an opportunity for Labour left; continues to promote entry into the Labour Party Jacobin / DSA The Iran war dominates Jacobin's output, but the tendency's response reveals its fundamental incapacity to provide a Marxist analysis of imperialism. Branko Marcetic's "Donald Trump, Warmonger-in-Chief" attacks the Iran war as driven by Trump's personal decision "to drag us into war" without coherent strategic logic. While criticizing neoconservatism, the article frames the war as the product of Trump's individual psychology and neoconservative ideology rather than the systemic crisis of US capitalism and the imperialist system as a whole. There is no call for independent working class action, no analysis of the bipartisan character of US imperialism, and no acknowledgment that the Democratic Party voted overwhelmingly for every previous Middle Eastern war. Arron Reza Merat's "There Is No Pretext or Plan for the US-Israel War on Iran" argues the attack has no legitimate pretext, framing it as driven primarily by Israel's agenda. While the article contains useful factual material about the absence of congressional authorization, Jacobin characteristically fails to connect the Iran war to the broader crisis of US imperialism, the internal class war against the American working class, or the need for an international socialist opposition. Most revealing is Meagan Day's defense of Mamdani's second White House meeting: "Zohran Mamdani Is Trying a Fresh Tactic With Trump." Day explicitly defends class collaboration with an authoritarian government, writing: "Governing entails cooperation and compromise, even with a noxious authoritarian president." She characterizes Mamdani as "trying to thread the needle of obtaining concessions from Donald Trump without abandoning his core socialist principles." This is the purest expression of the DSA's political orientation: the defense of collaboration with fascism under the guise of pragmatism. Day implicitly dismisses the principled opposition of the WSWS as impractical "purism." **Overall orientation:** Jacobin's Iran war coverage is moralistic opposition to the war that locates responsibility in Trump's personality and neoconservative ideology, never in the capitalist system. Its defense of Mamdani-Trump collaboration demonstrates that the DSA's real political function is to provide a left cover for the integration of "progressive" politicians into the fascist state apparatus.

This formulation implicitly promotes a nationalist-reformist program of regime change from within Iran rather than building international working class solidarity against imperialism. It fails to connect the Iran war to the international crisis of capitalism or to call for socialist opposition in the US. Iran war Day 3: Hezbollah enters the conflict, RAF Akrotiri struck, three F-15s downed by friendly fire The US-Israeli war on Iran escalated dramatically on Day 3 as the conflict spread beyond Iran's borders into Lebanon, Cyprus, Iraq, and Kuwait. Hezbollah broke the 15-month ceasefire that had been in place since November 2024, launching what it called "a barrage of precision missiles and a swarm of drones" at a military base near Haifa in northern Israel. Hezbollah framed its attack as "revenge for the blood of the Supreme Leader of the Muslims, Ali Khamenei." Israel responded with what IDF Chief Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir said would be a multi-day "offensive campaign" against Hezbollah targets in Lebanon, striking Beirut's southern suburbs and killing at least 31 people and wounding 149, according to Lebanon's Health Ministry. Iran struck the British RAF Akrotiri base in Cyprus with Shahed-type kamikaze drones overnight, marking the first attack on a British military installation since 1986. Two drones hit the runway; no casualties were reported. The UK is evacuating families and non-essential staff. Home Secretary Yvette Cooper confirmed the strike involved "Iranian kamikaze drones," while insisting Britain is "not at war." The attack followed PM Starmer's statement that UK bases could be used for US "defensive strikes" on Iranian missiles. In a separate incident, three US F-15E Strike Eagles were shot down by Kuwaiti air defense in a friendly fire incident while flying support for Operation Epic Fury during an Iranian missile and drone barrage. All six aircrew ejected safely. The Pentagon separately confirmed three US service members killed and five seriously wounded in an earlier Iranian missile strike on a Kuwait base. Iraq's Iran-backed militias also entered the conflict, firing on a US base in Erbil and claiming a drone attack on Baghdad airport. Trump told the New York Times the operation would last "four to five weeks," adding: "Unfortunately there will be more casualties. That's how it is." Netanyahu said Israel "will strike thousands of targets in the coming days." Iran reported strikes across 24 of its 31 provinces. Iran's ambassador to the IAEA confirmed the Natanz nuclear facility was struck on March 1; a monument to Islamic Republic founder Khomeini was toppled by crowds in southern Iran the same day. Key facts: - **Lebanon:** 31 dead, 149 injured in Beirut (Lebanon Health Ministry); IDF offensive expected to last "several days" - **RAF Akrotiri:** First attack on British military base since 1986; two Shahed drones hit runway; no casualties - **Friendly fire:** Three US F-15Es shot down by Kuwaiti air defense; six aircrew safe - **US casualties:** Three US service members killed, five seriously wounded in separate Iranian missile strike - **Iran:** 24 of 31 provinces struck; Natanz nuclear facility confirmed hit - **Trump timeline:** "Four to five weeks" for the operation (NYT interview)

IAEA emergency session: Natanz nuclear strike risks radiological catastrophe The IAEA Board of Governors convened an emergency special session on March 2 after Iran's ambassador Reza Najafi confirmed that Natanz — Iran's primary uranium enrichment site with deep underground centrifuge halls — was struck on March 1. IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi stated the agency currently has "no indication" of structural damage to nuclear installations and radiation levels remain at normal background in neighboring countries. However, Grossi issued an explicit warning: if attacks on nuclear sites continue, a radiological release "cannot be excluded," and the fallout could require evacuations of areas "as large or larger than major cities." Iran's ambassador condemned the strikes as deliberate attacks on facilities under IAEA safeguards, constituting war crimes under international law. The strike on Natanz represents one of the most serious nuclear security crises since Chernobyl in terms of potential risk — the deliberate military targeting of active nuclear facilities under international safeguards is virtually unprecedented. The irony is glaring: Operation Epic Fury was ostensibly launched to eliminate Iran's nuclear "threat," yet the bombing of nuclear facilities creates precisely the radiological catastrophe it claimed to prevent. As the SEP National Committee statement noted, Trump himself had previously declared Iran's nuclear capacity "obliterated" following June 2025 strikes, while Defense Intelligence Agency assessments showed Iran was "years, if not a decade" from intercontinental missile capability. 4. Congress challenges Iran war powers with bipartisan resolutions Operation Epic Fury was launched without congressional authorization. The White House notified top lawmakers shortly before strikes began but did not seek approval. Bipartisan war powers resolutions have now been introduced in both chambers: Senator Tim Kaine (D-VA) and Senator Rand Paul (R-KY) introduced a Senate resolution requiring explicit congressional authorization before further hostilities; Representatives Thomas Massie (R-KY) and Ro Khanna (D-CA) introduced a parallel House resolution to compel a halt to unauthorized military action. Public opinion is strongly against the war. A University of Maryland poll found only 21% favor the attacks, with 49% opposed. A CBS/YouGov poll found 74% said Trump needed congressional approval. Rep. Jim Himes (D-CT) said: "We have not heard articulated a single good reason for why now is the moment to launch yet another war in the Middle East." From a technical standpoint, the risks are severe. Natanz's underground centrifuge halls contain cascades of spinning centrifuges enriching uranium hexafluoride (UF6) — a compound that, if released by structural damage, reacts with moisture to produce hydrofluoric acid and uranyl fluoride, both acutely toxic. A breach of containment would not produce a nuclear explosion but could create a chemical-radiological contamination zone requiring mass evacuation. The IAEA's monitoring capacity is itself under threat: inspector access depends on physical presence at facilities now under active bombardment. If IAEA personnel are evacuated — a real possibility — the international community loses its only independent verification of what is happening inside Iran's nuclear infrastructure. The precedent is dangerous: no state has deliberately targeted active, safeguarded nuclear facilities on this scale since Israel's 1981 strike on Iraq's Osirak reactor, which was still under construction and contained no enriched material. Frederick Wiseman, chronicler of American institutional life, dies at 96 Frederick Wiseman, whose 45 observational documentaries over six decades constituted the most sustained cinematic examination of American institutional life ever undertaken, died at 96 at his Cambridge, Massachusetts home. Working without narration, formal interviews, or musical scores, Wiseman turned his camera on the institutions that constitute the actual fabric of social life: schools ("High School," 1968), hospitals ("Hospital," 1970; "Near Death," 1989), welfare offices ("Welfare," 1975), courts ("Juvenile Court," 1973), police departments ("Law and Order," 1969), and public libraries ("Ex Libris," 2017). His 1967 debut "Titicut Follies" — exposing conditions at Bridgewater State Hospital for the criminally insane in Massachusetts — was banned from public screening for 25 years, a nearly unprecedented act of government censorship of an American film. He received an Honorary Academy Award in 2016. His death coincides with the destruction of the very public institutions he spent his life documenting — libraries defunded, hospitals privatized, schools stripped of resources — under the regime now launching war abroad.

The tragedy exposed a systemic practice: approximately 93% of Chinese schools operated commercial enterprises to address budget shortfalls caused by the restoration of capitalism. The school's children — some as young as nine — assembled explosive fireworks for a local manufacturer, their labor treated as a subsidy for an educational system hollowed out by market reforms. Five workers were killed and over 150 wounded. The massacre triggered solidarity strikes involving more than 500,000 workers across Spain — one of the largest strike waves in modern European history. Iran operates multiple nuclear facilities that process or store hazardous materials: the Natanz enrichment plant (confirmed struck by Iran's IAEA ambassador), the Bushehr nuclear power plant on the Persian Gulf coast, the Tehran Research Reactor in the capital, and several uranium fuel storage sites. The critical substance at risk is uranium hexafluoride (UF6), used in the enrichment process. If released by an explosion or fire, UF6 reacts with moisture in the air to produce hydrofluoric acid — an extremely corrosive and toxic compound that can cause severe burns, organ damage, and death at relatively low concentrations. A significant release at Natanz would require evacuation of surrounding population centers. At Bushehr, a reactor breach would release fission products with contamination patterns depending on wind and weather — analogous to the scenarios modeled after Fukushima. The silence from Iran's nuclear regulatory authority is itself a major concern. It could indicate communications infrastructure damage, personnel casualties, deliberate information suppression, or some combination. Without independent monitoring, the international community is effectively blind to conditions at these facilities. This week in history: March 2-8 **March 2, 1919 — Founding of the Communist International (Comintern).** The First Congress of the Communist International opened in Moscow, attended by 52 delegates from 34 parties and organizations across 22 countries. The founding represented the organizational culmination of Lenin and the Bolsheviks' struggle against the betrayal of the Second International, which had collapsed into national chauvinism at the outbreak of World War I in 1914. The Comintern's founding manifesto, drafted by Trotsky, declared: "We who have assembled in Moscow, Communists, representatives of the revolutionary proletariat of Europe, America and Asia, feel and consider ourselves the followers and fulfillers of the programme whose banner was unfurled 72 years ago." The congress established the organizational framework for world revolution — a framework that would later be destroyed by the Stalinist bureaucracy's nationalist degeneration. **March 5, 1953 — Death of Joseph Stalin.** Stalin's death at age 74 triggered a succession crisis in the Soviet bureaucracy and opened a period of political instability that culminated in Khrushchev's "secret speech" three years later. The ICFI has analyzed Stalin's rule as the political expression of the bureaucratic caste that usurped power from the Soviet working class, betraying the program of world socialist revolution in favor of the nationalist doctrine of "socialism in one country." **March 7, 1965 — "Bloody Sunday" in Selma, Alabama.** Alabama state troopers attacked 600 civil rights marchers attempting to cross the Edmund Pettus Bridge. The televised brutality — troopers on horseback beating unarmed marchers with clubs and firing tear gas — galvanized national opposition and accelerated passage of the Voting Rights Act of 1965. The event demonstrated both the courage of the civil rights movement and the violent resistance of the Southern ruling class to even minimal democratic reform. **March 8, 1917 — International Women's Day triggers February Revolution.** Women textile workers in Petrograd walked off the job on International Women's Day, demanding bread and an end to the war. Within five days, the strike had spread to 200,000 workers and the tsarist autocracy — which had ruled Russia for over 300 years — was overthrown. The February Revolution confirmed the Marxist understanding that wars create revolutionary crises, as the mass suffering inflicted by World War I found expression in working-class action that no amount of repression could contain.

Lam himself articulated his project in explicitly revolutionary terms: "I could act as a Trojan horse that would spew forth hallucinating figures with the power to surprise, to disturb the dreams of the exploiters." Lam's masterwork "The Jungle" (1943), housed in MoMA's permanent collection, remains one of the defining images of twentieth-century art — a dense thicket of hybrid human-plant forms that evokes the violence of colonialism, the sugar plantation, and the persistence of resistance. The retrospective provides an opportunity to assess his full trajectory, from his early academic training in Havana and Madrid through his wartime exile in Marseille (where he was among the intellectuals aided by Varian Fry) to his later work engaging with the Cuban Revolution. The curatorial framing is part of a broader pattern in major museums of assimilating radical artists into identity-based categories that strip away their political commitments. When Lam is presented primarily as an artist of the African diaspora rather than as a revolutionary who happened to be of African descent, the challenge his work poses to bourgeois society is domesticated.

Landmark study reveals tropical insects far less resilient to warming than assumed A sweeping new study of more than 2,000 insect species, published in Nature, reveals that many insects may be far less capable of coping with rising temperatures than previously assumed. The survey of tropical insect populations and thermal tolerance limits indicates that species from lowland areas have particularly low capacity to survive increased temperatures, with thermal tolerance constrained by fundamental properties of protein architecture — suggesting a hard biological limit rather than a gap that evolution can bridge on relevant timescales. The findings have major implications for biodiversity projections. Tropical lowlands host the majority of the planet's insect species and are the engine of terrestrial ecosystem function. If lowland species cannot survive even modest warming, the cascading effects on pollination, decomposition, and food webs could be catastrophic. The study adds to growing evidence that climate change projections have been systematically underestimating biological impacts. --- Pseudo-left press review - [Jacobin / DSA](#jacobin--dsa) — channels antiwar sentiment into Democratic Party proceduralism and AIPAC-focused lobbying; avoids class analysis of war's origins in capitalist crisis - [Left Voice](#left-voice) — takes more radical anti-imperialist positions than Jacobin but still lacks a Trotskyist program for working-class power; notable polemic against Eric Blanc's reformism on military spending - [PSL / Liberation News](#psl--liberation-news) — Stalinist-oriented war opposition that defends the Iranian regime as anti-imperialist without class analysis - [Socialist Alternative](#socialist-alternative) — reformist framework channels opposition through abstract "movement" building rather than revolutionary party construction Jacobin / DSA Jacobin's war coverage reveals the fundamental limitations of Democratic Socialist politics when confronted with imperialist war. Four significant pieces published in the past 24 hours: "US, Israel Target Civilians as Iran Escalates War to Survive" covers civilian casualties but frames the conflict through the lens of Iranian "survival" — as though the war were a conflict between two belligerents rather than an imperialist assault on a semi-colonial nation. The article avoids any class analysis of the war's origins in the crisis of American capitalism. "Trump's War on Iran Makes a Mockery of American Democracy" channels opposition through concern for democratic procedure — noting that only 21% of the public supports the war — but proposes no path beyond Congressional mechanisms. The implied solution is better Congressional oversight, not independent working-class action. Most revealing is "The Iran War Shows Why It's Time for Chuck Schumer to Go," which channels genuine antiwar sentiment into an internal Democratic Party leadership fight. The argument that replacing Schumer with a more "progressive" Senate leader would change the trajectory of US imperialism exposes Jacobin's essential function: keeping working-class opposition trapped within the two-party system. "AIPAC Is Influencing Trump's War in Iran" focuses on the Israel lobby's influence — a framework that implies removing AIPAC's money from politics would alter the war's trajectory, obscuring the fact that the war serves fundamental US imperialist interests regardless of any individual lobby's influence. **Overall orientation:** Jacobin is performing its characteristic function during wartime — expressing limited opposition while channeling it into safe Democratic Party proceduralism and single-issue lobbying frameworks. The class character of the war and the need for independent working-class action are entirely absent.
Sources Jacobin US, Israel target civilians as Iran escalates war to survive · Jacobin Trump's war on Iran makes a mockery of American democracy · Jacobin The Iran war shows why it's time for Chuck Schumer to go · Jacobin AIPAC is influencing Trump's war in Iran

--- Arts and culture The cultural landscape this week is dominated by the reverberations of the US-Israeli war on Iran, which has created both a crisis of censorship and an uneasy cultural silence in Western capitals — a silence broken in part by artistic and literary production that attempts to reckon with the social catastrophe unfolding in real time. Roy Medvedev (1925–2026): death of a Soviet dissident historian The death of Roy Medvedev at 100 marks the passing of one of the most significant figures in Soviet dissident historiography. His landmark work *Let History Judge* (1971), smuggled to the West and published while he remained in the Soviet Union, was the first systematic documentation by an insider of the crimes of the Stalin era — the purges, the show trials, the destruction of an entire generation of Bolsheviks. The book was a genuine contribution to historical truth at a moment when Stalinist falsification was still official state policy. Yet Medvedev's political trajectory illustrates the limitations of opposition that remains within the framework of Stalinism. He never broke organizationally with the Communist Party, never developed a Trotskyist analysis of the degeneration of the Soviet state, and in the Gorbachev era accommodated himself to "reform" currents that ultimately liquidated the Soviet Union. His importance lies in what he documented rather than in the political conclusions he drew — a distinction that the WSWS's critical assessment, published today by M. Schönman, develops in substantial detail. His death invites renewed attention to the question of how historical truth and political program relate to one another. *The Best American Essays 2025* and American literary culture in crisis The WSWS published a literary review by James McDonald of *The Best American Essays 2025*, assessing how contemporary American nonfiction prose engages with the period's social upheavals — anti-war sentiment, labor militancy, political polarization, and the deepening crisis of democratic forms. McDonald evaluates individual essays for depth of social insight and aesthetic quality, and draws broader conclusions about the state of American literary culture at a moment when the gap between what writers know and what they are willing to say has never been wider. The best nonfiction writing of the period reflects an awareness that the old frameworks — identity-based personal essays, memoir-as-politics, the confessional mode that dominated the 2010s — are inadequate to the scale of what is happening. The question is whether literary culture can develop forms adequate to the historical moment, or whether it will continue to retreat into private experience as the world burns. The cultural cost of Iran's internet blackout Iran's 240-hour internet shutdown has severed 90 million people not only from news and communication but from the entire infrastructure of modern cultural life — streaming music and film, digital publishing, social media as a space for artistic community, and the diaspora networks that connect Iranian artists to global audiences. The blackout has effectively erased Iranian cultural production from the digital sphere for the duration of the war. Independent filmmakers, musicians, and writers inside Iran are unable to share work, receive payments, or communicate with international collaborators. The shutdown represents a form of cultural destruction that compounds the physical destruction of aerial bombardment. Death of Jürgen Habermas Jürgen Habermas, the German philosopher and last surviving member of the Frankfurt School, died on March 14 in Starnberg at age 96. Blanc, a Rutgers professor and DSA Bread and Roses caucus member, acknowledges the war's historic unpopularity but identifies the main obstacle as "sectarianism" — meaning activists who use "alienating, excessively radical rhetoric and slogans" and tie antiwar demands to "romanticization of 'anti-imperialist' forces." His solution is to build toward the March 28 and May 1 protests "not as one-off protests but as mechanisms to recruit, onboard, and train as many people as possible into ongoing campaigns." As the WSWS responded on March 12, this is not an explanation for the absence of an antiwar movement — it is propaganda aimed at blocking one. Blanc's framework channels opposition away from independent working-class action and toward the Democratic Party orbit, with "sectarianism" serving as a codeword for any politics that breaks with bourgeois respectability. Jacobin's **"A Post-Order World"** (March 2026) examines declining US global hegemony without identifying it as a crisis of the capitalist system. The analysis is presented as a geopolitical observation rather than the expression of the terminal crisis of the nation-state system. A piece on **Hasan Piker** describes "imperial end times" and a "quagmire in Iran" — adopting a left-populist vocabulary that substitutes media commentary for political program. These were Anderson's first career Oscar wins. Ryan Coogler's *Sinners* also made history with four wins, including Michael B. Jordan for Best Actor and Autumn Durald becoming the first woman to win Best Cinematography. The ceremony's most politically significant moment came when Javier Bardem declared "No to war. Free Palestine" before an audience of roughly 20 million viewers. Palestinian actor Motaz Malhees, barred from attending due to his citizenship, sent a statement read aloud: "You can block a passport. You cannot block a voice." These interventions represented rare instances of direct political speech at a ceremony that has increasingly policed such expression. As WSWS arts editor David Walsh noted, the ceremony reflects a tentative but significant shift in cultural consciousness away from identity politics toward broader opposition to state violence and imperial war — though he cautioned against overstating the depth of this shift. Anderson's choice of subject matter — the machinery of immigration enforcement as a system of state terror — represents a noteworthy departure from the safely biographical or nostalgic films that have dominated recent Best Picture winners.

The analysis is conducted entirely within a geopolitical-realist framework — the question of working-class opposition to the war is never raised. Jacobin treats the conflict as a matter of strategic miscalculation rather than the organic product of imperialism. Separately, Juliano Fiori's "A post-order world" argues US hegemony has collapsed into a period of "zonal geopolitics" — unstable competition across regions with no replacement hegemon. While correctly identifying the erosion of American dominance, the article's framework is purely academic, offering no political perspective for the working class. Max Sawicky's "Socialists need a distinctive economic policy agenda" proposes five "pillars" of socialist economic policy (labor power, industrial policy, social insurance, public ownership, reduced federalism) explicitly designed to be "neither revolutionary nor frightening" — a reformist program that amounts to a left-Keynesian wish list positioned within the existing capitalist state. Jacobin's overall orientation remains that of a left-liberal publication adapting socialist vocabulary to Democratic Party-adjacent politics. Its Iran coverage avoids any call for independent working-class mobilization against the war.

Jürgen Habermas (1929–2026): death of the last Frankfurt School philosopher Jürgen Habermas died on March 14 in Starnberg, Germany at the age of 96. The most cited humanities scholar of the postwar era and the last surviving representative of the Frankfurt School, Habermas is best known for his two-volume *Theory of Communicative Action* and his theories of the public sphere and deliberative democracy. Born in Düsseldorf in 1929, he was drafted into the German military in 1944 and later recalled the Nazi atrocities as a formative moment that guided him toward philosophy. Habermas's relationship to Marxism was complex: the Frankfurt School was critical of capitalism but also of orthodox Marxism, and Habermas's later work on communicative rationality explicitly departed from the class-struggle framework of historical materialism. His theory of the public sphere, while influential, idealized bourgeois democratic discourse in a manner that obscured the class character of the institutions he studied. Jacobin published a sympathetic obituary praising his "profound critique of irrationality" — a framing that elides his distance from revolutionary politics. His ideas shaped constitutional law scholarship and debates over European integration, but the fundamental contradictions of bourgeois democracy that he sought to resolve rationally remain unresolvable within the capitalist framework.

--- Arts and culture The past 24 hours in arts and culture have been dominated by the intersection of war, institutional power, and the contested meaning of cultural production. From the closure of America's premier performing arts center to the postponement of the Gulf's flagship art fair, the Iran war's shockwaves are reshaping the cultural landscape — while significant new works and revelations open questions about art's relationship to society. New Museum reopens with OMA expansion in New York The New Museum on Manhattan's Bowery reopened to the public on March 21 after a two-year closure, unveiling a $82 million expansion designed by OMA (Rem Koolhaas and Shohei Shigematsu) with executive architect Cooper Robertson. The project, a decade in the making, doubles the museum's gallery space to 11,148 square meters and creates what is one of the few cultural institutions worldwide to unite the work of two living Pritzker Prize–winning practices (OMA alongside the original 2007 SANAA building). The reopening exhibition, *New Humans: Memories of the Future*, brings together more than 200 artists, writers, scientists, and filmmakers — including Hito Steyerl, Anicka Yi, Francis Bacon, and Salvador Dalí — to explore how technological and societal changes have redefined what it means to be human. Opening weekend offers free admission. The question of who has access to such institutions remains pertinent: standard adult admission is $25, though visitors under 18 and SNAP/EBT recipients enter free. Art Dubai postponed to May amid Iran war Art Dubai has postponed its 20th anniversary edition from mid-April to May 14–17 in response to the Iran war, transforming the event from a full-scale commercial fair into a "more focused, curated, and flexible" cultural gathering. Several international galleries had already pulled out, art shipments had halted, and airlines suspended Dubai routes after the UAE was forced to temporarily close its airspace due to Iranian retaliatory strikes. The postponement joins a growing list of Gulf cultural events disrupted by the conflict — ISEA2026 in Dubai, the annual March Meeting in Sharjah, and the Arabian Travel Market have all been rescheduled. The disruption lays bare the fragility of the Gulf's cultural infrastructure, built on petrodollar wealth now directly threatened by the war whose energy consequences drive the very crisis. Banksy identified as Robin Gunningham in Reuters investigation A major Reuters investigation published March 13 identified the world's most famous anonymous street artist, Banksy, as Robin Gunningham, 51, from Bristol. The evidence includes handwritten police confessions from a 2000 arrest in New York, court documents, and immigration records showing Gunningham (who changed his name to David Jones in 2008) crossed into Ukraine in 2022 just days before new Banksy murals appeared in Horenka. Banksy's lawyer, Mark Stephens, stated his client "does not accept that many of the details contained within the enquiry are correct," while Pest Control, Banksy's company, said the artist "has decided to say nothing." Reuters argued the public interest justified publication given Banksy's "profound and enduring influence on culture, the art industry and international political discourse." The unmasking raises questions about the commodification of anonymity itself in an art market where Banksy's identity-as-brand has functioned as both critique and commercial strategy. --- Arts and culture The cultural landscape this week is dominated by two contrasting tendencies: major studio releases that largely avoid engagement with the wars consuming the world, and smaller independent and arthouse works that grapple directly with questions of dispossession, historical memory, and social disintegration. *Project Hail Mary* opens nationwide The sci-fi adaptation of Andy Weir's novel, directed by Phil Lord and Christopher Miller and starring Ryan Gosling, opens wide this weekend with a score by Daniel Pemberton. The film, about a lone astronaut racing to save humanity, is the biggest wide release of the year so far. While the premise — one individual rescuing civilization through scientific ingenuity — captures a genuine public yearning for rational problem-solving in an era of political irrationality, it also reflects Hollywood's persistent retreat into individualist savior narratives. The social organization of science and the collective labor required to sustain it remain invisible in the Weir formula, as they were in *The Martian*. *Palestine 36* in limited release A far more consequential cinematic event is the limited release of Annemarie Jacir's *Palestine 36*, starring Hiam Abbass and Jeremy Irons with a score by Ben Frost. Jacir, one of the Arab world's most acclaimed filmmakers, sets her drama in the period of the 1936 Palestinian general strike — a six-month revolt against British colonial rule and Zionist settlement. The film's release amid an ongoing genocide in Gaza and the regional conflagration gives it an urgency that transcends its period setting. The 1936 revolt was itself a response to the dispossession that the Balfour Declaration and British Mandate had set in motion — the same historical trajectory whose consequences are playing out today in the killing of over 72,000 Palestinians. Arts roundup - **NYC Art House Cinema Week** (March 20–26): The first-ever citywide initiative offers 5,000 free tickets across nearly 30 independent theaters, with highlights including a Joel Coen and Frances McDormand-introduced screening and a Frederick Wiseman retrospective. The initiative, backed by the NYC Mayor's Office, represents a significant public investment in preserving independent cinema infrastructure under severe commercial pressure. Wiseman's inclusion is notable — his documentary method of sustained, unhurried observation of institutions (hospitals, welfare offices, public housing) remains the most powerful cinematic tool for revealing how class society actually functions. - **Berlinale short films:** The WSWS's Max Linhof and Verena Nees reviewed short films from the Berlinale that grapple with social disintegration, war, and catastrophe, examining how filmmakers are searching for solidarity and meaning in a turbulent world. - **Courtney Barnett returns:** The Australian indie rock artist released her long-awaited new album, her first in several years. --- Arts and culture The most significant cultural development of the weekend is the opening of *Project Hail Mary*, the Ryan Gosling-led adaptation of Andy Weir's novel, directed by Phil Lord and Christopher Miller. The film — a prestige sci-fi epic about an astronaut who must save Earth from an extinction-level threat — arrives as the Iran war dominates public consciousness, lending its themes of planetary catastrophe and isolated human resourcefulness a particular resonance. Weir's source novel, like his earlier *The Martian*, belongs to a genre of "competence fiction" that reflects both deep public anxiety about civilizational collapse and a faith in individual scientific ingenuity as the answer — a framework that, whatever its narrative satisfactions, sidesteps the social and political dimensions of existential crisis. The film competes head-to-head with *Ready or Not 2: Here I Come* for the top global box office spot, the pairing neatly illustrating Hollywood's current split between science-fiction earnestness and horror-comedy nihilism. On Broadway, the Olivier Award-winning play *GIANT* officially opened at the Music Box Theatre, with John Lithgow portraying children's author Roald Dahl alongside Aya Cash and Rachael Stirling. Directed by Nicholas Hytner, the production grapples with Dahl's complex and contradictory legacy — a writer of extraordinary imaginative gifts for children whose documented antisemitism poses uncomfortable questions about the relationship between artistic achievement and personal bigotry. That the play arrives at a moment of intensifying war against a predominantly Muslim nation, with antisemitism charges deployed as a political weapon against anti-war critics, makes its examination of these questions timely. **Additional developments:** - **The Forsytes** premiered on British television, an adaptation of John Galsworthy's *Forsyte Saga* novels with an original score from Oscar-winner Anne Dudley.
