--- Pseudo-left press review - [Jacobin / DSA](#jacobin--dsa) — frames the Iran war as a strategic miscalculation rather than imperialist aggression; promotes a "distinctive" socialist economic program that amounts to Keynesian redistribution within the Democratic Party orbit - [Left Voice](#left-voice) — most explicitly anti-imperialist line among the tendencies reviewed; correctly names the war as imperialist aggression and rejects reliance on Democrats, though organizational perspective remains limited to "mass movement" building - [Liberation News / PSL](#liberation-news--psl) — clear anti-imperialist opposition coupled with campist defense of Iranian sovereignty that blurs the line between opposing war and politically endorsing the bourgeois-clerical regime - [Socialist Alternative](#socialist-alternative) — correct on the war and ICE; risks popular-front dilution through "No Kings Day" coalition-building with liberal and Democratic-adjacent forces - [Socialist Worker / SWP (UK)](#socialist-worker--swp-uk) — consistent anti-war agitation but "Together Alliance" participation risks classic popular-frontism without a class-independent program - [Socialist Appeal / RCP (IMT)](#socialist-appeal--rcp-imt) — sharpest critique of liberal coalition politics among UK left; membership growth claims reflect genuine youth radicalization, but IMT's historic entryist orientation bears watching Jacobin / DSA The war dominates Jacobin's output but in revealing ways. **"Trump Wants a 'Video Game War' in Iran"** frames the conflict primarily as a *strategic miscalculation* by Trump rather than as imperialist aggression to be actively opposed — the analysis is pitched at a policy-wonk level with no demand to end the war and no solidarity with the Iranian or regional working class. **"A Post-Order World"** presents US imperial decline as a structural crisis of "consent" for hegemony rather than a crisis of capitalism itself, with no call for anti-imperialist mass action; class agency is symptomatically absent. **"Socialists Need a Distinctive Economic Policy Agenda"** leans on DSA/Mamdani electoral momentum to outline a "socialist" program that amounts to social-democratic Keynesianism — public options, redistribution — without any rupture from the capitalist state or challenge to the two-party system. The day's output reinforces Jacobin's function as an organ of the DSA's Democratic Party-adjacent reformism. The war is treated as a policy question to be debated within bourgeois institutional frameworks, not as an expression of capitalist imperialism requiring working-class political independence. The WSWS's polemic by Barry Grey against Eric Blanc's "Sectarianism Has Never Ended a War" directly addresses this political line.
Sources Jacobin Trump wants a "video game war" in Iran · Jacobin A post-order world · Jacobin Socialists need a distinctive economic policy agenda
Left Voice Left Voice maintains the most explicitly anti-imperialist line among the US pseudo-left tendencies. **"We Need a Mass Movement to Defeat Trump's Imperialist War on Iran"** names US-Israeli aggression directly, calls for independent working-class mobilization rather than reliance on the Democratic Party, and correctly distinguishes between opposing the war and supporting the Iranian theocratic regime. **"With Dwindling Interceptors and Degraded Radar, Israel and the US Enter Uncharted Territory"** provides military-strategic analysis aimed at puncturing US invincibility mythology for the anti-war movement. **"Anti-ICE Movement in Detroit Forces Police Chief's Hand"** highlights grassroots extra-institutional organizing as the decisive factor against ICE, consistent with Left Voice's line against reliance on the capitalist state. Left Voice's coverage is the most politically coherent on the war question among the tendencies reviewed, but its organizational perspective remains limited to calls for a "mass movement" without clearly articulating the need for a revolutionary party or addressing the historical lessons of the Fourth International on anti-war strategy.
Sources Left Voice We need a mass movement to defeat Trump's imperialist war on Iran · Left Voice With dwindling interceptors and degraded radar, Israel and the US enter uncharted territory

The film — about a lone astronaut who must save Earth from an extinction-level stellar phenomenon — arrives at a moment when its themes of international scientific cooperation and existential risk carry unavoidable political weight. With the real world consumed by a war that threatens global energy supplies and has already killed over a thousand Lebanese civilians, a narrative built on the premise that human survival depends on cross-species cooperation rather than military domination offers an implicit rebuke to the logic of imperialism, whether or not its creators intended it. Broadway is experiencing one of its most eventful weeks of the season. *The Rocky Horror Show* begins previews tonight at Studio 54 in a star-studded revival featuring Luke Evans, Stephanie Hsu, Juliette Lewis, Harvey Guillén, Rachel Dratch, and Michaela Jaé Rodriguez, directed by Sam Pinkleton. Richard O'Brien's 1973 creation — a transgressive celebration of sexual liberation set against the backdrop of Cold War paranoia — returns to a cultural landscape in which LGBTQ rights are once again under coordinated political assault from the far right. Whether this revival engages with that reality or retreats into nostalgic camp will determine its cultural significance. Also beginning Broadway previews is *Titaníque*, the Céline Dion-themed *Titanic* parody musical starring Jim Parsons and Deborah Cox, transferring from Off-Broadway to the St. James Theatre. A more substantive theatrical event is the upcoming revival of August Wilson's *Joe Turner's Come and Gone* (previews beginning March 30 at the Ethel Barrymore Theatre), starring Taraji P. Henson and Cedric the Entertainer, directed by Debbie Allen. Wilson's 1988 work — set in 1911 Pittsburgh and exploring the psychic wounds of slavery's aftermath on Black Americans seeking to reconstitute their identities — remains one of the most profound texts in the American dramatic canon. Its revival under a Black woman director represents a serious engagement with historical memory. The city-funded initiative represents a meaningful public investment in independent cinema infrastructure at a time when art house theaters face existential financial pressure from streaming platforms and rising real estate costs. Dafoe's selection is notable precisely because the Wooster Group represents the antithesis of the commercial theater machine: deconstructionist, non-narrative, politically confrontational. In a cultural moment dominated by franchise adaptations and jukebox musicals, the choice of Dafoe is a quiet rebuke to the commodification of the stage. Theater's position as the most immediately social of art forms — performed live, for a gathered audience, in shared physical space — gives it a unique role in periods of political crisis. The art form's capacity for direct engagement with contemporary reality stands in tension with the commercial pressures that increasingly reduce it to entertainment product. Three Broadway musicals launch previews simultaneously Three new Broadway productions began previews on March 27: *The Lost Boys* (an adaptation of the 1987 cult vampire film) at the Palace Theatre, *Beaches: A New Musical* at the Majestic Theatre, and a revival of Noël Coward's *Fallen Angels* starring Kelli O'Hara and Rose Byrne at the Todd Haimes Theatre. The simultaneous opening signals Broadway's peak spring season push ahead of Tony Award nominations. The programming choices are telling. *The Lost Boys* and *Beaches* represent the now-dominant tendency of adapting existing intellectual property for the stage — a process that treats theater as a subsidiary of the film industry rather than an independent art form. The Coward revival, by contrast, reconnects with the tradition of theatrical wit and social observation, though Coward's drawing-room comedies inevitably reflect the concerns and limitations of their upper-class milieu. The choice of subject matter — arms control negotiations at a moment of existential nuclear danger — resonates unmistakably with the present moment, as the US wages simultaneous wars and the risk of broader conflagration grows. Strait of Hormuz closure triggers largest oil supply disruption in history The effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz since March 2 has produced what IEA Executive Director Fatih Birol called "the largest supply disruption in the history of the global oil market." Tanker traffic through the strait has fallen to less than 10% of pre-crisis flows, taking an estimated 10 million barrels per day of Gulf oil production offline. On March 11, the IEA released an unprecedented 400 million barrels of emergency reserves — a measure that benefits OECD member states while leaving much of Africa, South Asia, and Southeast Asia exposed to unmitigated price shocks. The humanitarian consequences extend well beyond energy. Seventy percent of Gulf food imports have been disrupted, causing 40–120% price spikes in consumer staples across the UAE, Qatar, Kuwait, Bahrain, and Saudi Arabia. European gas storage stands at just 30% after a harsh winter, with the Dutch TTF gas benchmark nearly doubling to over €60/MWh. Pakistan brokered a limited deal allowing 20 Pakistani-flagged vessels to transit the strait — two ships per day — as a confidence-building measure, but this represents a fraction of normal traffic. Key facts: - Brent crude peaked at **$126/barrel**; currently ~$115/barrel, more than 55% above pre-war level - At least **40 energy assets across 9 countries** severely damaged - The Ras Laffan LNG facility in Qatar — the world's largest — has been offline since March 2 - First time oil exceeded $100/barrel in four years was March 8
Sources IEA Oil Market Report — March 2026 · CNBC Iran war energy impact: Oil, gas, Middle East · Al Jazeera Why the oil and gas price shock from the Iran war won't just fade away

--- Arts and culture The arts world this week is marked by three developments of genuine cultural significance: the 50th anniversary of South Africa's Market Theatre, a political testing ground during apartheid; the launch of *Saturday Night Live UK*, a transatlantic cultural export at a moment of acute political tension; and the continued reverberations of the 98th Academy Awards, where Paul Thomas Anderson's *One Battle After Another* dominated with six Oscars. Market Theatre celebrates 50 years as apartheid-era cultural landmark Johannesburg's Market Theatre is marking its 50th anniversary — a milestone for the institution that became one of the most consequential cultural spaces of the anti-apartheid struggle. Opened in an old fruit and vegetable market just three days after the 1976 Soweto uprising in which hundreds of protesting students were killed, the theater hosted work by Athol Fugard and Tony Award-winner John Kani at a time when multiracial audiences were considered subversive. Current artistic director Greg Homann recalled that "the theater was often raided. Actors were sometimes in some kind of danger" — apartheid censors would walk onstage during performances. The Market's history embodies the relationship between artistic expression and political resistance that the WSWS has consistently emphasized. Yet the celebration also invites sober reflection: South Africa's post-apartheid ANC government has presided over deepening inequality, mass unemployment, and the degradation of public services. The cultural space that once challenged state power now operates in a society where the promises of liberation remain unfulfilled for the working class. Issues of access to education, corruption, and gender-based violence are being tackled on its stage as the Market turns 50.

--- Arts and culture The death of Jürgen Habermas on March 14 at 96 and Gino Paoli on March 24 at 91 bookend a month that saw the passing of two major postwar European cultural figures — one in philosophy, one in music — whose lives illuminate the contradictions of intellectual and artistic production under capitalism in the Cold War and its aftermath. **Habermas (1929–2026)** was eulogized across the bourgeois press as a champion of democracy and rational discourse, "the last rationalist" per *Foreign Policy*. The WSWS's critical obituary by D. Szejnman and Steve Long offers the only published assessment from the standpoint of Marxist critique: Habermas systematically dismantled historical materialism — building his case on "Stalin's 1938 pamphlet" rather than engaging Lenin or Trotsky — and replaced it with a theory of communicative rationality that provided no basis for critiquing power structures rooted in economic domination. His support for NATO's Yugoslavia bombing, the Schröder welfare cuts, German rearmament, and dialogue with Cardinal Ratzinger trace the trajectory of a *staatstragender Denker* — a state-bearing thinker. The political lesson: Habermas drew the wrong conclusion from 1933, fearing working-class revolution rather than analyzing fascism's class origins. **Gino Paoli**, the Italian cantautore whose "Il cielo in una stanza" and "Sapore di sale" (often arranged by Ennio Morricone) redefined Italian popular music, died in Genoa surrounded by family. A leading figure of the Genoese school alongside Fabrizio De André and Luigi Tenco, Paoli emerged during Italy's rapid postwar industrialization, which created conditions for a new lyrical introspection displacing traditional bel canto forms. His 1963 suicide attempt — he shot himself in the chest and lived 62 more years with the bullet lodged in his pericardium — reflected the pressures of commodified fame during the economic boom. His later service as a parliamentary deputy for the Italian Communist Party (1987–1992) was characteristic of many postwar artists: an adaptation to existing political structures rather than a break toward genuine class struggle. - **LACMA David Geffen Galleries** open April 19 — Peter Zumthor's 110,000 sq. ft. structure spanning Wilshire Boulevard doubles the museum's gallery space. Named for David Geffen's $150 million gift, the $125 million County of LA–funded building completes a two-decade campus transformation. The opening installation spans 6,000 years of art history. - **NEA funding cuts continue to devastate arts organizations:** The Portland Mercury reports that nearly a year after the NEA cancelled hundreds of grants following the Trump administration's call to eliminate the agency, theaters, museums, and dance companies across the country are struggling. Oregon Contemporary's $30,000 grant for its 2026 Artists' Biennial (opening April 1) was cancelled. Executive Director Blake Shell stated: "the arts are under attack very clearly because of their political power." Eli Lilly's oral GLP-1 drug shows 11.2% weight loss in phase 3 trial Results published in the *New England Journal of Medicine* from the 72-week ATTAIN-1 phase 3 trial show that Eli Lilly's oral GLP-1 drug orforglipron, at its 36 mg daily dose, produced −11.2% mean body weight loss compared to −2.1% on placebo in non-diabetic adults with obesity. More than half (54.6%) of patients in the high-dose arm lost at least 10% of body weight. A companion *Lancet* paper (ATTAIN-2) showed similar results in patients with type 2 diabetes. Unlike injectable semaglutide (Ozempic/Wegovy), orforglipron is a once-daily pill — a potentially major access breakthrough that could transform obesity treatment by eliminating injection barriers. The development raises sharp questions about pricing and accessibility given the pharmaceutical industry's record of extracting monopoly profits from breakthrough therapies.

BSO dismissal of Andris Nelsons continues to provoke uproar The Boston Symphony Orchestra Board of Trustees' decision not to renew the contract of Grammy-winning music director Andris Nelsons — announced simultaneously to the press and public on March 6, leaving the 95-member orchestra to learn from media reports — continues to generate outrage. The full orchestra assembled on the steps of Symphony Hall in winter weather to demonstratively display solidarity with their conductor, and a public petition condemning the board's unilateral action has gathered significant support. Nelsons himself acknowledged the decision "was not related to artistic standards, performances, or achievements during my tenure." The BSO board cited $90 million in deferred maintenance costs and declining audiences as justification — a framing that reveals how capitalist mismanagement of cultural institutions is blamed on the artists rather than the administrators who allowed the infrastructure to decay. Reports indicate the board wants to hollow out classical offerings in favor of programming driven by market demographics rather than artistic integrity. The Nelsons affair illustrates a pattern visible across major American cultural institutions: boards dominated by financial elites treat orchestras, museums, and theaters as investment vehicles or branding opportunities, not as custodians of humanity's artistic heritage. The 13-year tenure of one of the world's leading conductors was ended by email.

Artemis II crew passes midpoint en route to first crewed lunar flyby since 1972 The Artemis II crew — Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover, Christina Koch (NASA), and Jeremy Hansen (CSA) — has passed the midpoint of humanity's first crewed mission beyond low Earth orbit since Apollo 17 in December 1972. The SLS/Orion spacecraft launched April 1 from Kennedy Space Center and is on track for a lunar flyby on Monday, April 6, when the crew will photograph areas of the Moon's far side never directly observed by human eyes. Hansen will become the first Canadian — and first non-American — to leave Earth orbit. The 10-day mission is a test of Orion's deep-space systems rather than a landing attempt. NASA released the crew's first high-resolution Earth images from mid-transit on April 4. Key facts: - Launch: April 1 at 6:35 p.m. EDT from Kennedy Space Center - Lunar flyby: Monday, April 6 - No landing — this tests Orion spacecraft deep-space life support, navigation, and communications - First crewed mission beyond low Earth orbit in 54 years

The film walks a tonal tightrope between dark comedy and psychological horror, with critics divided on whether its provocation amounts to genuine social commentary or calculated shock. At 78 percent on Rotten Tomatoes from 161 critics, the consensus praises the lead performances — particularly Pattinson's "incredibly witty and precise" disintegration — while noting the film's frustrating restraint in developing Zendaya's character. The more interesting cultural question is what the film's premise reveals about American social life: that mass violence has become so endemic that its potential exists as a dormant psychological feature even among the privileged classes. That the film locates this confession within the rituals of bourgeois marriage — the most private and financially consequential institution of middle-class life — gives it a sharper social edge than most critics acknowledge.

The lead article, **"Trump Is Robbing You to Pay for His Dumb War"** by Branko Marcetic, frames the $1.5 trillion military budget as a direct transfer from domestic programs to war spending, calling the war "dumb" — a word choice that trivializes the catastrophe as a policy error rather than an expression of imperialism's structural logic. The companion piece, **"The War on Iran Is More Expensive Than You Think,"** cites $2.1 billion per day in war costs, framing the issue primarily in terms of domestic fiscal impact rather than the devastation inflicted on Iran. Other notable pieces include **"Stop Asking If Israel Has a Right to Exist"** by Rawan Abhari, which correctly identifies the question as a rhetorical trap but approaches Palestinian self-determination through a liberal rights framework divorced from class analysis, and **"Crypto Is Flailing"** by Hadas Thier, which documents the sector's decline under Trump but treats it as a market curiosity rather than analyzing the class interests driving crypto deregulation. The overall orientation remains consistent: opposition to war framed in populist, taxpayer terms ("robbing you") designed to pressure Congress rather than mobilize the working class independently. The Democratic Party is absent from Jacobin's analysis as a co-architect of the war state — a silence that reflects the DSA's continued orientation toward pressuring Democrats from within.

Left Voice Left Voice published the sharpest material among the pseudo-left tendencies this cycle. **"Why Is Shawn Fain and the UAW Leadership Supporting Trump's Trade Policies?"** explicitly names the mechanism by which union bureaucracies tie workers to national capital against international solidarity: Fain's embrace of tariffs subordinates workers' internationalist interests to labor chauvinism and makes the UAW complicit in a protectionist program that will accelerate inflation and layoffs. A companion piece, **"Internationalism Has to Be Anti-imperialist: A Dialogue with Labor Notes,"** extends the critique to Labor Notes itself for insufficient challenge to the UAW's nationalist orientation. **"All Roads Lead to Stagflation"** analyzes Trump's tariff escalation as driving the US economy toward structural crisis, framing it as a feature of capitalism rather than a policy error. This is consistent with Left Voice's Trotskyist method of using economic conjuncture to argue for working-class political independence. Left Voice remains the most analytically rigorous of the pseudo-left tendencies on the trade question. However, its organizational orientation toward the Fraction of Trotskyists (FT/PTS) means these critiques serve an electoral and propaganda function in Latin America rather than building toward independent workers' organizations in the US. The absence of any engagement with the ICFI's perspective on the war or the Fourth International's analysis limits the political conclusions to a general call for "class independence" without the programmatic specificity to give it content.

US-Iran ceasefire takes hold but terms disputed and Lebanon excluded The two-week ceasefire between the United States and Iran — brokered by Pakistan after 40 days of US-Israeli strikes — took effect overnight, with Iran agreeing in principle to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, through which roughly 20 percent of the world's oil supply passes. But the terms remain sharply contested, and the ceasefire's durability is in serious doubt. Iran presented a modified 10-point plan that the White House immediately rejected. Washington's maximalist demands include ending uranium enrichment, eliminating ballistic missile capability, and full reopening of the Strait. VP JD Vance will lead the US negotiating team in Islamabad on Saturday, joined by Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner. Iran's Foreign Minister Araghchi responded: "The ball is in the U.S. court, and the world is watching whether it will act." The ceasefire's fragility was underscored by continued military action. Iran's Revolutionary Guards struck Saudi Arabia's Jubail petrochemical complex — one of the largest industrial cities in the world — even as talks proceeded. The King Fahd Causeway connecting Saudi Arabia and Bahrain was closed due to Iranian missile activity. Israel continued bombing Lebanon, which Netanyahu explicitly excluded from the truce. Iran accused the US of violating the ceasefire framework. A joint statement from Macron, Meloni, Merz, Starmer, Carney, and Takaichi declared: "Diplomacy must now replace military action." American freelance journalist Shelly Kittleson was freed after a week in detention by an Iran-backed Iraqi militia, and two US airmen were rescued from Iran. His 1982 track "Planet Rock" — which fused hip-hop with Kraftwerk-influenced electro-funk — was a landmark recording that helped define an entire genre and influenced generations of electronic and hip-hop artists. He founded the Universal Zulu Nation, originally conceived as a vehicle for channeling Bronx gang culture into artistic expression. His legacy was profoundly tarnished after multiple men accused him of sexually abusing them when they were boys during the 1980s and 1990s. The accusations confronted hip-hop culture with the contradiction between its origins as an art form of the oppressed and the predatory behavior of one of its founders — a contradiction the industry largely avoided reckoning with. His death will inevitably produce hagiographic retrospectives that elide the abuse; the fuller truth is that Bambaataa's story illustrates how cultural movements born from genuine social need can be deformed when individual power goes unchecked.

Gore Verbinski's *Good Luck, Have Fun, Don't Die* — David Walsh David Walsh reviews Verbinski's 2025 sci-fi black comedy as "a dreadful work" and "a libel against humanity." The film stars Sam Rockwell as a time traveler from a dystopian AI-ruined future who recruits present-day people to install safety software in an emergent AI. Walsh's central critique targets the film's message — "It's all your fault … everyone from your time. You're all equally complicit" — which he identifies as reactionary technological determinism. The real problem, Walsh argues, is not technology in the abstract but the capitalist organization of society. The film's portrait of youth as "hostile, ignorant, media-dominated zombies" ignores the mass protests organized via social media. Walsh concludes that technology properly understood is "a conquest of humanity" and "a basic requirement for the liberation of humanity," not an apocalyptic threat. The review is a useful example of the WSWS's method of connecting cultural criticism to fundamental questions of political economy.

US-Iran peace talks collapse in Islamabad after 21 hours with no deal The first direct US-Iran negotiations since the six-week war began collapsed Sunday morning in Islamabad with no agreement reached. US Vice President JD Vance led the American delegation alongside special envoy Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner. Iran's 70-member team was led by Parliamentary Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf and Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi. Iran demanded an end to Israeli attacks on Lebanon and Hezbollah, unfreezing of $6 billion in assets, guarantees around its nuclear program, and the right to charge ships passing through the Strait of Hormuz. The US demanded Iran commit to never developing nuclear weapons. The collapse pushes the existing two-week ceasefire — agreed April 8 — closer to expiration with no clear path to extension. As Kevin Reed noted on the WSWS, over 600 commercial vessels including approximately 400 oil tankers remain stalled in the Persian Gulf while only 22 ships passed through the Strait of Hormuz since the ceasefire began — indicating the blockade's economic stranglehold is largely intact. Key facts: - Vance: "The bad news is that we have not reached an agreement. And I think that's bad news for Iran much more than it's bad news for the U.S. ... they have chosen not to accept our terms" - Ghalibaf: "Our experience in negotiating with the Americans has always been met with failure and broken promises" - Trump declared on social media: "The only reason they are alive today is to negotiate!" - Pakistan pledged to continue mediating

Artemis II astronauts return to Earth after historic lunar mission NASA's Orion spacecraft splashed down in the Pacific Ocean off San Diego at 5:07 p.m. PDT on April 10, completing a 10-day, 695,081-mile journey around the Moon — the first crewed mission to travel to the lunar vicinity since Apollo 17 in December 1972, more than 53 years ago. The crew — Commander Reid Wiseman, Pilot Victor Glover, Mission Specialist Christina Koch (all NASA), and Mission Specialist Jeremy Hansen (Canadian Space Agency) — conducted a free-return trajectory with a close lunar flyby, passing within approximately 4,067 miles of the lunar surface at speeds reaching 23,864 mph during re-entry with heat shield temperatures of roughly 3,000°F. The mission sets the stage for Artemis III, which aims to land humans on the Moon. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries and Nancy Pelosi called for Swalwell's exit before any investigation was completed. Swalwell denied all allegations, calling them "false and politically motivated." --- Science, technology, and public health - [US measles cases surpass 1,714](#us-measles-cases-surpass-1714) — one of the two worst years since 2000, driven by kindergarten vaccination coverage falling from 95.2% to 92.5%; Utah's outbreak alone approaches 600 cases - [H5N1 bird flu entrenched in US dairy cattle and wildlife](#h5n1-bird-flu) — 71 human cases since February 2024, first confirmed H5N5 human infection recorded November 2025; no person-to-person transmission detected - [Alzheimer's early detection mechanism identified](#alzheimers-early-detection) — researchers discover immune cells actively destroy olfactory nerve fibers, explaining why smell loss precedes cognitive decline by years - [Anthropic's Claude Mythos identifies tens of thousands of software vulnerabilities](#claude-mythos-cybersecurity) — unreleased model reproduced working exploits in over 80% of cases; Anthropic commits $100 million for defensive cybersecurity - [US AI legislation accelerates to 25 new laws in 2026](#us-ai-legislation) — regulatory environment emerging faster than industry anticipated, with 27 more bills awaiting final signature US measles cases surpass 1,714 The CDC confirmed 1,714 measles cases across 33 US jurisdictions as of April 9, making 2026 one of the two worst years for measles since the disease was declared eliminated in 2000. Ninety-four percent of cases (1,609) are linked to outbreaks. Utah's outbreak — the largest still active — approaches 600 cases alone. The surge is driven in part by kindergarten vaccination coverage falling from 95.2% (2019–20) to 92.5% (2024–25), dropping below the 95% threshold needed for herd immunity. In a rare positive note, Florida's case count held at 144 for the week ending April 12 — the first week-over-week plateau in months. The Collier County outbreak centered on Ave Maria University has been stable at 106 cases since March 28, suggesting containment there may be succeeding. H5N1 bird flu: entrenched in wildlife, low immediate human risk The US has recorded 71 total human A(H5) bird flu cases since February 2024, with 94% classified as mild. November 2025 brought the first globally confirmed human infection with H5N5 — a distinct sub-variant. No person-to-person transmission has been detected. However, H5N1 is now entrenched in US dairy cattle, wild birds across six continents, and an expanding range of mammalian hosts, sustaining long-term pandemic concern. Alzheimer's early detection via smell loss mechanism Researchers have identified the cellular mechanism explaining why smell loss may precede other Alzheimer's symptoms by years. The study found that immune cells in the brain actively destroy olfactory (smell) nerve fibers after detecting abnormal surface signals. This opens a potential pathway for earlier biomarker detection through olfactory testing before cognitive decline is apparent — a significant development given Alzheimer's affects an estimated 6.9 million Americans. AI developments: cybersecurity, policy, and regulation Anthropic's unreleased Claude Mythos model, tested under Project Glasswing with Amazon, Microsoft, Apple, Google, and Nvidia, identified tens of thousands of vulnerabilities across operating systems and browsers, reproducing working exploits in over 80% of cases. Anthropic restricted access and committed $100 million in usage credits for defensive cybersecurity testing — marking the industry's first large-scale coordinated defensive deployment of an AI model. Separately, OpenAI released a 13-page policy paper arguing superintelligence is imminent and proposing a public wealth fund partly financed by AI companies, taxes on automated labor, and a four-day workweek incentive. Critics dismissed the proposals as "regulatory nihilism" designed to preempt tougher government oversight. The pace of US AI legislation is accelerating: since mid-March, the number of enacted AI laws has grown from 6 to 25, with another 27 bills having cleared both chambers. The House Foreign Affairs Committee unanimously passed a bill requiring location-verification chips on AI hardware eligible for export.

--- Arts and culture The death of Asha Bhosle, the Olivier Awards, and Coachella's first weekend dominate arts and culture news, while a WSWS review of two Berlin Film Festival entries offers a class analysis of migrant labor exploitation on screen. Asha Bhosle, legendary Indian playback singer, dies at 92 Asha Bhosle, one of the most prolific recording artists in world history with more than 12,000 songs across eight decades, died on April 12 in Mumbai from multiple organ failure. She was 92. Bhosle's career spanned the full arc of Indian cinema from the 1940s onward, and her extraordinary range — from classical and ghazal to pop, disco, and rock — defined the sound of Bollywood across successive generations. She received two National Film Awards, two Grammy nominations, and in 2011 was recognized by the Guinness Book of World Records for the most studio recordings in history. Her last rites are scheduled with full state honors at Shivaji Park on April 13. Bhosle's significance extends beyond entertainment: her voice was the soundtrack to post-independence India's self-image, and her artistic evolution tracked the country's social transformations over seven decades. In a period of Hindu nationalist cultural consolidation under the BJP, it is worth noting that Bhosle's repertoire crossed linguistic, religious, and regional boundaries in ways that nationalist cultural projects seek to foreclose. Olivier Awards: Paddington sweeps, Rosamund Pike and Rachel Zegler win The 2026 Laurence Olivier Awards, marking the ceremony's 50th anniversary, were held at the Royal Albert Hall on April 12. *Paddington the Musical* dominated with seven wins including Best New Musical — a commercially polished adaptation whose success reflects London's West End leaning ever more heavily on presold intellectual property. *Punch* won Best New Play. Rosamund Pike took Best Actress for *Inter Alia* at the National Theatre. Rachel Zegler won Best Actress in a Musical for her portrayal of Eva Perón in *Evita* — a revival that gains political resonance against the backdrop of rising global authoritarianism. Paapa Essiedu won Best Supporting Actor for *All My Sons*, Arthur Miller's indictment of wartime profiteering, whose themes carry obvious contemporary weight. Julie Hesmondhalgh won Best Supporting Actress for *Punch*. Coachella 2026: spectacle, controversy, and cultural commodity Coachella's first weekend (April 10–12) featured headliners Justin Bieber, Sabrina Carpenter, and Karol G, with passes for both weekends selling out in two days. The festival was marked by controversy when Sabrina Carpenter mistook a fan's zaghrouta — a traditional Arabic celebratory vocal expression — for yodelling and called it "weird" on stage, prompting backlash over cultural insensitivity. Carpenter later apologized on social media. Dance artist Anyma's closing set was canceled due to strong winds — one of several weather-related disruptions. Karol G warned fans about ICE enforcement activity in the region ahead of her performance, a reminder that the festival's curated escapism unfolds amid mass deportation campaigns. Bieber's minimalist, almost desultory set drew mixed reviews. Berlin Film Festival: exploitation and precarity on screen The WSWS reviewed two films from the 76th Berlin International Film Festival that examine extreme exploitation. *Enjoy Your Stay* (dir. Dominik Locher, Switzerland) follows Luz, an undocumented Filipino migrant hotel cleaner in Verbier with no legal protection or cathartic resolution. *I Understand Your Displeasure* (dir. Kilian Armando Friedrich, Germany) depicts a cleaning company manager ground down by the contradiction of maintaining profit margins while dealing ethically with workers. The reviewers note that the Davos elite met at a luxury resort four hours from Verbier — the structural irony is built into the geography.

This week in history: April 13–19 **25 years ago — April 18, 2001: Ethiopian Special Forces massacre 41 university students.** Ethiopian security forces opened fire on students at Addis Ababa University during a crackdown on pro-democracy demonstrations. The students had organized protests demanding democratic reforms, academic freedom, and an end to state repression. In addition to the 41 killed, approximately 15,000 political opponents were arrested across the country in the ensuing crackdown. Ethiopia at the time ranked 171 out of 174 countries on the UN Human Development Index. The massacre exemplified the willingness of African ruling elites, backed by Western governments, to use extreme violence against democratic movements. **50 years ago — April 15, 1976: India resumes full diplomatic relations with China.** After a 15-year rupture following the 1962 Sino-Indian border war, India and China restored full ambassadorial relations. The rapprochement reflected shifts in the Cold War balance — both nations sought to counterbalance Soviet influence in the region. The border dispute that triggered the 1962 conflict remained unresolved and continues to generate periodic military tensions to the present day, including deadly clashes in Ladakh in 2020. **75 years ago — April 18, 1951: Treaty of Paris establishes the European Coal and Steel Community.** Six nations — France, West Germany, Italy, Belgium, the Netherlands, and Luxembourg — signed the treaty creating the ECSC, the institutional precursor to the European Union. Proposed by French Foreign Minister Robert Schuman, the community placed coal and steel production under supranational authority, ostensibly to make war between France and Germany "not merely unthinkable, but materially impossible." The project served to integrate European capitalism under American hegemony during the Cold War and laid the foundation for the EU's current structures. **100 years ago — April 18, 1926: Martha Graham premieres first independent dances.** Martha Graham presented her first independent concert at the 48th Street Theater in New York, marking the beginning of modern dance as a distinct American art form. Graham rejected the conventions of classical ballet in favor of movement rooted in breathing, contraction, and emotional expression. Over the next seven decades, she created more than 180 works and trained generations of dancers who transformed global choreographic practice. National MMR coverage among kindergartners has dropped from 95.2 percent in 2019–20 to 92.5 percent in 2024–25 — below the 95 percent threshold generally required for herd immunity. On the Iran war itself, Jacobin's editorial line has been to criticize Trump's "recklessness" while implicitly endorsing the framework of US diplomacy over the Strait of Hormuz — an essentially liberal anti-war position indistinguishable from the Senate Democrats' failed war-powers resolution. **Assessment:** The publication continues to function as the magazine of Democratic Party left-liberalism. Its orientation today is to prepare its readership for the Democratic primaries as the "terrain of struggle" — a framework incompatible with a class-struggle response to the Iran war and militarization. On the Iran war, Left Voice has emphasized solidarity with Iranian workers — correct on its face — while obscuring the necessity of the defeat of the US-Israeli military campaign. **Assessment:** The tendency's pseudo-Trotskyist coloration continues to be used to insulate it from accountability for positions that effectively align with the US foreign-policy establishment on key questions. PSL's electoral work through the Green Party and its own independent campaigns remains oriented toward aggregating protest votes rather than building an independent working-class political alternative. **Assessment:** The "anti-imperialism" on offer is the anti-imperialism of the popular front, not of Lenin; it reproduces the Stalinist stages theory in contemporary form. Socialist Alternative / ISA Socialist Alternative's public materials this week have centered on a "tax the super-rich" campaign tied to the state-level response to Trump's budget cuts, and on "public takeover" demands around the energy-price shock. The demands stop systematically short of the expropriation question: the tendency asks for progressive taxation and public ownership of specific sectors, but not for the confiscation of billionaire wealth and the socialist transformation of the economy. **Assessment:** The CWI/ISA tradition of transitional-demand work has collapsed into minimum-program left-reformism; Socialist Alternative functions as pressure on the Democratic Party caucus from outside rather than as an independent working-class party. SWP (UK) / International Socialist Tendency *Socialist Worker* has continued its orientation to Stop the War Coalition mobilizations and its united-front appeals to Labour left MPs, particularly around the Gaza/Iran/Lebanon axis. Iran declares Strait of Hormuz open; US naval blockade remains Iran's Foreign Ministry announced on April 17 that the Strait of Hormuz was "completely open" to commercial shipping for the duration of the Israel-Lebanon ceasefire. The declaration sent oil prices tumbling 10–12 percent before they partially reversed as the conditional character of the opening became clear. Trump publicly thanked Tehran but stated the US naval blockade of Iranian ports "remains in effect." Parliamentary speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf responded that "with the continuation of the blockade, the Strait of Hormuz will not remain open." Ship-tracking firm Kpler confirmed that tankers attempting to transit were turned back because no approvals had been granted. The closure, now in its eighth week, has produced the largest global oil supply disruption since the 1970s. The International Energy Agency has called it "the greatest energy security threat in history": 13 million barrels of daily production disrupted and one-third of Persian Gulf energy infrastructure requiring two to five years to restore. As Alex Lantier noted on the WSWS, Iran reports 1,500 dead and 18,551 wounded, 3.2 million internally displaced, and 61,000 homes and 500 schools damaged — figures that likely undercount military casualties. Key facts: - Trump publicly thanked Iran but reiterated the US naval blockade is unchanged - Oil prices settled at roughly $93/barrel WTI, $96/barrel Brent, both off multi-week highs - Qatar and Kuwait GDPs projected to contract up to 14 percent; Saudi Arabia ~3 percent; UAE ~5 percent - Nearly 2.5 million migrant workers in Qatar's energy sector face mass unemployment with no social protection

The terms oblige Israel to suspend offensive operations while Lebanon's government commits to prevent Hezbollah attacks; the State Department announced that Washington will "facilitate the demarcation" of a permanent land boundary. Israel retains the right to "self-defense" against "planned, imminent, or ongoing attacks" — a clause that effectively preserves Israeli initiative throughout the truce period. The human cost during the seven weeks of fighting is staggering. Lebanese authorities report nearly 2,200 killed and 1.2 million internally displaced — roughly one in five Lebanese residents. Israeli forces occupy approximately 10 percent of Lebanese territory and show no sign of imminent withdrawal. A resident of southern Lebanon told Democracy Now: "Ten days? Either our land is fully returned, or we don't want the ceasefire." Key facts: - The ceasefire is formally linked to the US-Iran negotiations framework; collapse of one threatens the other - Israel's occupation of Lebanese territory remains unchallenged during the truce window - No provisions for Palestinian prisoners or reconstruction funding

5. IMF warns Iran war could push world into recession The IMF released its April 2026 *World Economic Outlook* on April 14, titled "Global Economy in the Shadow of War." The Fund cut global growth projections to 3.1 percent for 2026, down from pre-conflict estimates of 3.4 percent. Its "severe downside" scenario envisions growth falling to 2.0 percent — the IMF's own threshold for "a close call for a global recession." Strikingly, the report states that absent the Iran war the Fund would have *upgraded* 2026 global growth projections by 0.1 percentage points, citing the AI investment boom and easing monetary policy. The Iran war now ranks higher on the Fund's risk ledger than Trump's tariff policies. As Nick Beams wrote on the WSWS, the IMF's companion *Fiscal Monitor* report is the more politically revealing document: gross public debt reached 94 percent of global GDP in 2025 and is projected to hit 100 percent by 2029, while the Fund explicitly instructs governments to avoid "boosting spending to help populations affected by war." For the United States, the Fund prescribes cuts to Medicare and Medicaid; European governments are told to cut pensions and elderly care to fund military expansion. These are not technocratic observations but directives.

--- Arts and culture - [WSWS recommends six Iranian films as counterweight to war propaganda](#wsws-recommends-six-iranian-films) — Kiarostami and Farhadi works recovering a civilization the US war is trying to erase - [Viva Energy Geelong refinery fire destroys one of Australia's two remaining refineries](#viva-energy-geelong-refinery-fire) — a documentary-cinema moment in industrial collapse the WSWS fixes in its record of class violence WSWS recommends six Iranian films With the US-Iran war generating escalating anti-Iranian propaganda, Zac Corrigan's WSWS piece on April 18 recommends six films by Abbas Kiarostami and Asghar Farhadi as a counter: Kiarostami's *Close-up* (1990), a documentary-fiction hybrid about an impostor posing as filmmaker Mohsen Makhmalbaf; *Life, and Nothing More* (1992), tracing the survival of villagers after the 1990 Manjil–Rudbar earthquake; and *Through the Olive Trees* (1994), which examines social inequality in a community devastated by the same earthquake. From Farhadi: *A Separation* (2011), the first Iranian film to win the Oscar for Best Foreign Language Film, on class, gender, and the Iranian judicial system; *The Salesman* (2016), staged around a Tehran production of *Death of a Salesman*; and *A Hero* (2021), a moral portrait of a debtor-prisoner granted temporary leave. Corrigan's argument is that these works constitute evidence of "a complex and highly cultured society" whose dehumanization is now central to war propaganda. The films are not political cinema in a narrow sense; their strength is precisely their capacity to render Iranian social life with the density and particularity that propaganda must flatten. They span the post-revolutionary period's Third Cinema, neorealist, and chamber-drama traditions, and between them render women, children, laborers, students, bureaucrats, and the rural poor with the kind of sustained attention that bourgeois wartime discourse actively opposes. The article situates this cinema within a long Iranian tradition that predates the 1979 revolution and has survived both clerical censorship and sanctions — Kiarostami continued making films until his death in 2016, and Farhadi produced *A Hero* under conditions of severe restriction. Corrigan notes that both filmmakers have explicit anti-war records, and cites the broader Iranian diaspora cinema (Shirin Neshat, Jafar Panahi) as further evidence of a culture being systematically demonized in US and European media. Viva Energy Geelong refinery fire An explosion at Viva Energy's 70-year-old Geelong refinery — one of only two remaining oil refineries in Australia — took 13 hours to extinguish. All approximately 50 workers on site escaped unharmed; the AMWU's site organizer noted that a daytime incident "would've been a whole different outcome." Martin Scott's WSWS article documents the facility's history of safety failures (two 2017 hydrofluoric acid leaks, 11 WorkSafe charges in 2018, a 2020 oil spill, a dropped compressor in 2023) and indicts the trade union bureaucracy for simultaneously decrying conditions while defending the company against "competitive pressure." This is the texture of industrial dereliction under Australian capitalism, with 191 workplace fatalities annually — not an accident series but a system. The event is included in the arts-and-culture section here because the WSWS coverage of industrial collapse stands in the socialist documentary tradition: preserving, naming, and political-aesthetic accounting-for events that the bourgeois press reports as isolated incidents. It is precisely the function that the Iranian filmmakers above perform for the Iranian people and that is actively suppressed by wartime cultural discourse.
Sources WSWS 6 films from Iran that should be seen by workers in the US and around the world · WSWS Massive fire at 1 of Australia's 2 remaining oil refineries

Oral GLP-1 orforglipron delivers 11% weight loss in Phase 3 A Phase 3 trial (ATTAIN-1) published in the *New England Journal of Medicine* reports that once-daily oral orforglipron 36 mg produced a 11.2% mean body-weight reduction vs. 2% for placebo over 72 weeks in 3,127 adults with obesity without diabetes. In the top-dose arm, 54.6% of participants lost at least 10% of body weight. A companion *Lancet* trial (ATTAIN-2) confirmed efficacy in type 2 diabetes patients. This is the first oral small-molecule GLP-1 agonist to demonstrate efficacy on par with injectable agents (Ozempic, Wegovy). Access implications are substantial — if priced accessibly, an oral formulation could dramatically expand global reach; under the current pharmaceutical-capitalist model, the drug will be priced to extract maximum surplus from insurers and governments before generics arrive. Greenland's Prudhoe Dome fully melted 7,000 years ago Ice cores drilled from the Prudhoe Dome — a major high point of the Greenland Ice Sheet — show that the dome disappeared completely roughly 7,000 years ago during a Holocene warm period, then reformed. This is a direct challenge to the baseline sea-level-rise projections underpinning coastal-adaptation planning worldwide. The political point of the list is explicit: the function of imperial war is to dehumanize the population of the target country, and cinema is one of the principal means by which that dehumanization can be contested. Kiarostami's patient, contemplative realism — the Koker trilogy, *Close-Up*, *Taste of Cherry* — renders a living, breathing Iranian society of villagers, children, students, and workers, flatly incompatible with the abstracted "regime" that US war planners require the public to accept as a target. Farhadi's moral dramas — *About Elly*, *The Salesman*, *A Separation* — do the same work through urban middle-class Tehran. The piece is a modest intervention, but its method is correct. Against a sustained propaganda effort to reduce 88 million people to a single silhouette of Khamenei's successors, Corrigan offers the concrete humanity of the Iranian artistic tradition. Crosse situates the case within the rising ICFI campaign to demand the immediate release of all detained immigrant workers and the building of rank-and-file defense committees in the workplaces where detained workers' coworkers and family members remain. --- Pseudo-left press review - [Jacobin / DSA](#jacobin-dsa) — ambiguous "anti-war" posture that leaves open space for supporting Democratic presidential candidates in 2028 - [Left Voice](#left-voice) — correct identification of the Iran war as imperialist, wrapped in calls for a "mass workers' party" that in practice defers to existing union structures - [Liberation News / PSL](#liberation-news-psl) — opposition to Iran war framed through Third World nationalism rather than working-class internationalism - [Socialist Alternative](#socialist-alternative) — promotion of the May 1 general strike as building bloc for electoral project - [SWP UK / Socialist Worker](#swp-uk-socialist-worker) — framing of Sudan and Iran wars as separate "anti-imperialist" struggles without a coherent international program - [Socialist Appeal / RCP (IMT)](#socialist-appeal-rcp-imt) — calls for "communist" mass work within existing Labour Party and DSA structures Jacobin / DSA *Direct article-level access to Jacobin and DSA outlets was limited in this cycle; the assessment below is based on the tendency's known positions and its recent output pattern.* Jacobin's coverage of the Iran war continues to emphasize the incompetence and cruelty of the Trump administration rather than characterize the war as a structural expression of US imperialism requiring a revolutionary response. The tendency's overall orientation remains that of a reform-left current aligned with the progressive wing of the Democratic Party, with the Iran war acting — as with every prior imperialist war of the 21st century — as a stress test that Jacobin / DSA fails by refusing to call for an independent working-class political break. Its call for international working-class action against the war is correct as far as it goes. On the mega-layoffs and the May Day strike, Left Voice has positioned itself inside the organizing coalitions without raising the political content of the working class's required independence from the AFT/NEA/SEIU leaderships. On Sudan, PSL coverage has been notably thin, reflecting the tendency's difficulty with conflicts that do not fit a US-vs.-Third-World-government frame. The PSL's overall orientation — Stalinist campism wrapped around selective anti-imperialism — continues to place it outside the Marxist tradition's insistence on working-class political independence from all capitalist parties, including those opposing US imperialism in the current conjuncture. Socialist Alternative Socialist Alternative (US) has promoted the May 1 general strike as the central task of the moment, linking it to the broader anti-Trump mobilization and its own electoral project (the tendency continues to orient toward the Kshama Sawant-style council-seat model). The tendency's Iran-war coverage has emphasized the cost-of-living impact on US workers and the democratic threat of Trump's militarism, but without a consistent call for international working-class mobilization or a principled break with the existing union bureaucracy. Its framing of the May Day coalition embraces its progressive and liberal components — including AFT and NEA leaderships that have actively policed opposition to the Democratic Party — rather than orienting to independent rank-and-file committees. The tendency remains within the broad reformist-pressure-group tradition of the IST/CWI family. SWP UK / Socialist Worker Socialist Worker (UK, SWP) has covered the Iran war, Sudan, and the escalation of drone warfare as separate "anti-imperialist" struggles, without integrating them into a coherent international program against inter-imperialist war. Its coverage of Starmer's Labour government's complicity in the Iran war has been sharp on the specifics (arms exports, base facilities) but muted on the historical lesson — that Labour is a bourgeois workers' party whose governments invariably support imperialist war. The tendency's pattern of tailing specific "movements" (Stop the War, Palestine Solidarity Campaign) rather than building a revolutionary party remains its defining feature. On the mega-layoffs, Socialist Worker coverage has emphasized trade-union resistance and cross-union coordination rather than independent rank-and-file committees that challenge the bureaucracy itself. Socialist Appeal / RCP (IMT) The IMT's British section (now organized as the Revolutionary Communist Party in the UK, with parallel regroupments internationally) continues to call for "communists" to enter and transform existing organizations — the Labour Party in the UK, DSA in the US, similar reformist formations internationally — rather than building an independent revolutionary party on the ICFI model. The tendency's recent coverage of the Iran war, the mega-layoffs, and the IMF austerity offensive has been analytically sharp in places but politically disarming: the call to "communists" to work inside organizations whose leaderships have demonstrated through decades of practice that they will support imperialist war, discipline strikes, and enforce austerity is a recipe for demobilization. The tendency's orientation remains within the Grantite-Woods tradition of entrism, now repackaged with revolutionary-sounding rhetoric but unchanged in its programmatic content. **Overall assessment:** The pseudo-left press in this cycle has responded to the Iran war, the Gaza crisis, the mega-layoff offensive, and the May Day organizing with characteristic reformist adaptations — correct diagnoses paired with programs that in practice preserve the trade-union bureaucracy, the reformist parties, and the imperialist state institutions they claim to oppose. Trump threatens to destroy Iran's power plants and bridges as Hormuz blockade enters third week On day 51 of the US–Israeli war against Iran, and with a two-week ceasefire set to expire within 72 hours, Donald Trump posted on Truth Social threatening to "knock out every single Power Plant, and every single Bridge, in Iran." The threat followed the seizure by the USS Spruance of an Iranian-flagged cargo ship in the Gulf of Oman after Iran's Revolutionary Guard re-closed the Strait of Hormuz and fired on two India-flagged tankers. Iran's parliament speaker Mohammad Baqer Ghalibaf declared the strait would remain closed so long as Iranian vessels were themselves blocked by the US Navy, and Iran withdrew from the Islamabad negotiating track. As Andre Damon wrote on the WSWS, Trump's escalation expresses "a bipartisan ruling-class consensus." Former Biden adviser Amos Hochstein stated publicly that a Democratic administration "would also be bombing Iran," and a House War Powers Resolution to restrain the executive failed 213–214 — with only a single Democrat voting against the war. The Hormuz corridor carries roughly 20 million barrels of oil per day, about 20 percent of global seaborne oil trade. Twenty-five commercial vessels have been turned back under the blockade. Brent crude rebounded to $95 a barrel on the latest seizure, and major shipping companies have suspended operations in the Gulf. Key facts: - US intelligence reports China is preparing to deliver air defense systems to Iran within weeks, raising the prospect of a direct Great Power military confrontation in the theatre. - Documented casualties stand at 2,076–3,636 Iranian dead and 2,167 killed in Lebanon, including 172 children. - The background: US–Israeli strikes on Iran began February 28, 2026; Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei was assassinated; his son Mojtaba Khamenei has been named successor. - Trump told reporters, "We're offering a very fair and reasonable deal"; Iran's demand for 440 kg of enriched uranium rights and the US port blockade remain the critical sticking points. - 32 percent of Iran's crude oil revenue has been cut off since the blockade began, according to Treasury disclosures.

The Japan Meteorological Agency issued a three-metre (ten-foot) tsunami warning for Iwate, Hokkaido and Aomori prefectures and ordered the evacuation of 171,957 people across five prefectures. Sudan enters year four of civil war with 150,000 dead, 19 million facing acute hunger April 15 marked three years since the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) plunged Sudan into civil war. The country now enters year four with no resolution in sight. More than 150,000 people have been killed, more than 14 million displaced internally and externally — roughly a quarter of Sudan's 52 million population — and an estimated 19 million people face acute hunger. The SAF controls Khartoum and the eastern and central regions; the RSF holds Darfur and parts of Kordofan. The conflict has become an overt proxy war between regional capitalist states. Yale's Humanitarian Research Lab confirmed via satellite imagery that Ethiopia's military is supporting RSF operations and has allowed cross-border staging from an Ethiopian army base. The more serious critical question — which prestige entertainment journalism has largely avoided — is what it means for the culture industry to mount a $150-million celebration of a figure whose treatment by his own estate and record labels was itself an instance of capitalist exploitation of a child performer. The **Marvel Studios in-house visual development team** has been eliminated; future work will be outsourced to freelancers on project terms. - **Sony Pictures** — "A few hundred" positions cut globally; the **Pixomondo VFX studio**, founded in 2001 and Emmy-honored for its work on *Game of Thrones*, has been shuttered. - **Snapchat** — 1,000 jobs cut, **16% of workforce**, following pressure from **Irenic Capital Management** to slash over $500 million in annual expenses. - **Artnet** — post-merger with Artsy, **35% of editorial staff eliminated** in a declared shift to "AI tools." - **Condé Nast** — ceased publication of *Self* magazine and closed international editions, eliminating approximately 300 jobs. Disney's chief executive officer receives $45 million annually — roughly 900 times the median compensation of the creative workers being eliminated. This is not crisis management; it is the systematic destruction of the institutional knowledge and craft labor that make cultural production possible, on the bet that generative AI and freelance precarity can extract equivalent output at a fraction of the wage bill. The casualties include the VFX houses, artists, animators, designers and editors who built twentieth-century visual culture. Kennedy Center board includes Trump fixer Paolo Zampolli The elevation of **Paolo Zampolli** — the Milan-born modeling-industry operator who introduced Melania Knauss to Donald Trump in 1998 and was appointed US Special Envoy for Global Partnerships in March 2025 — to the **Kennedy Center board of trustees** marks another step in the absorption of US cultural infrastructure into Trump's patronage machine. Zampolli's ties to the Epstein network through his partner Amanda Ungaro, and to an alleged $5 million UN grant fraud scheme, are detailed in Marc Wells's WSWS investigation (see WSWS coverage section). The Kennedy Center, once nominally non-partisan, has been progressively restaffed since early 2025 with figures whose qualifications lie in proximity to Trump rather than artistic or administrative merit. The phenomenon is continuous with the broader pattern of "Mafioso-style" governance — cultural institutions transformed into instruments of personal loyalty rather than sites of collective creative production. Yasukuni offering accompanies Japan's rearmament Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's ritual offering to the **Yasukuni Shrine** — which enshrines more than 1,000 convicted WWII war criminals, including Class-A war criminals executed after the Tokyo Tribunal — was delivered the same week her cabinet lifted the 1967 ban on lethal weapons exports. The combination is not accidental. The historical memory that Yasukuni sanitizes — the crimes of Japanese imperialism in Korea, China and Southeast Asia — is precisely what must be rehabilitated to legitimize the revival of Japanese arms production. The cultural politics of militarism proceed in lockstep with the economic and military reconstruction of the same. Across the arts roundup, a consistent pattern emerges: creative labor treated as a cost center to be automated, cultural institutions subordinated to oligarchic networks, historical memory rewritten to serve rearmament. This is what the crisis of late capitalism looks like inside culture.
Sources WSWS Disney carries out "massive layoffs," while Sony, Snapchat, Artnet do their own job slashing · Al Jazeera Japan lifts ban on lethal weapons exports

David Walsh's analysis on the WSWS captures the breadth of opposition finding artistic expression at the 2026 festival. **The Strokes** projected an extended video montage of CIA regime-change operations, Israeli bombing in Gaza, and US strikes on Iran — with captions including "Over 30 universities destroyed in Iran" — standing before an illuminated mosque. **David Byrne** performed in an orange jumpsuit with ICE-chase footage projected behind him, telling the BBC that "a small group of maniacs decided to bomb Iran" without public endorsement. **Massive Attack** collaborated with **Tom Waits** on "Boots on the Ground," depicting soldiers as victims of ruling-class wars, with lyrics targeting "federal pricks" hiding in government. Walsh frames these performances as evidence that "the accumulating outrage and horror are inevitably finding expression in artistic circles" and that mass audiences are enthusiastically embracing anti-war, anti-ICE, anti-dictatorship messages. The sets represent an objective shift: Coachella is a corporate-sponsored festival, not a leftist gathering, and yet its headline acts have taken positions categorically opposed to the Trump administration, the Iran war, and the collaborationist posture of the Democratic Party. The response of the audience — videos circulating on social media show crowds cheering the anti-war and anti-ICE imagery — registers the same social polarization documented in polls showing two-thirds of Americans oppose the Iran war. Cultural context worth noting: - The political performances arrive against the background of intensified repression of pro-Palestinian speech at US universities throughout 2025-2026, mass ICE raids on students, and the detention of Chinese scientists documented elsewhere in this briefing. That artists at a high-profile commercial festival feel compelled — and commercially safe — to stage such material reflects a meaningful shift in popular consciousness. - The Strokes' explicit naming of CIA regime-change operations marks a departure from the generic "anti-war" iconography common to festival-stage politics. Specific historical reference — to coups in Iran (1953), Chile (1973), and subsequent operations — situates the current Iran war within the longer arc of US imperialism. - Byrne's orange jumpsuit performance reinstalls a decades-old Byrne motif (authoritarian cosplay, corporate critique from "Stop Making Sense" through "American Utopia") but directs it at the current administration's deportation regime. - Massive Attack's collaboration with Tom Waits reflects an older generation of politically engaged musicians continuing to produce anti-war material. Waits, at 76, has long been among the rare mainstream American artists willing to engage openly with class themes; the "federal pricks" lyric follows his pattern of excoriating American power from a specifically plebeian vantage point. Absent from the research material today are significant literary, theater, visual arts, or major film release developments. No significant cultural-figure deaths in the past 24 hours were flagged. The Coachella coverage dominates the cultural news cycle both because of the political content and because mainstream entertainment coverage has — uncharacteristically — been forced to engage with the substance of the performances rather than treating them as spectacle. The underlying pattern, as the WSWS has consistently argued, is that the contradictions driving the Trump administration — war, austerity, repression — cannot be fully contained within the cultural apparatus. US-Iran war: Iran seizes ships, peace talks collapse, oil surges past $100 The US-Iran war, now in its eighth week, escalated sharply on April 22–23 as Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps seized two foreign container ships in the Strait of Hormuz and fired on a third — just hours after President Trump had announced an indefinite extension of the shaky ceasefire. The seizures came as scheduled Islamabad peace talks were cancelled and the US naval blockade of Iran-linked vessels, begun April 13, entered its eleventh day. Trump told reporters on April 23 there is "no time frame" on the war, sending WTI crude above $94 and Brent briefly above $103 for a fourth consecutive day of gains. The Pentagon confirmed 13 US service members have been killed since fighting began February 28. Iranian authorities put the death toll inside Iran at 3,636, including 254 children. International Energy Agency chief Fatih Birol called the conflict "the worst energy crisis the world has ever faced." As Jordan Shilton wrote on the WSWS Perspective, "the material consequences of imperialist war fall most devastatingly not on those who launch or direct it, but on the international working class." Key facts: - Strait of Hormuz traffic has dropped far below the pre-war baseline of more than 100 ships per day; Iran declared the strait closed to US-linked vessels on April 18 - Iranian Foreign Minister **Abbas Araghchi** called the US blockade "an act of war"; President **Masoud Pezeshkian** said dialogue is "desired" but impossible under "blockade and threats" - Brent crude closed April 23 at **$103.38 (+1.44%)**; WTI at **$94.46 (+1.67%)** — a fourth straight up day driven by the ship seizures - The S&P 500 set its fifth all-time high in eight sessions on April 22 (Nasdaq also hit a fresh record at 24,657.57) before pulling back as the talks collapsed; **major oil corporations stand to gain more than $230 billion in additional 2026 profits from the war**, per figures cited on the WSWS - The Containerised Freight Index rose 10 percent within a month of the war's outbreak; UN Development Programme estimates the conflict could push 8.8 million additional people in 36 Asia-Pacific countries into poverty

Progressive Bulgaria wins absolute majority as GERB collapses Progressive Bulgaria — a coalition formed in March 2026 and formally unified on April 17 under President **Rumen Radev** — won 43.91% of the vote and 130 of 240 National Assembly seats in snap elections, enough to govern without coalition partners. El Gamal family released from Dilley after federal court order US District Judge Fred Biery ordered the immediate release of Hayam El Gamal and her five children from the CoreCivic-run Dilley family detention center in South Texas, where the family had been imprisoned since June 2025 without criminal charges. US measles cases reach 1,792 in 33 states The CDC's April 24 update reports **1,792 confirmed US measles cases across 33 states and jurisdictions**, with **22 active outbreaks**. **93% of cases (1,668)** are outbreak-associated. The largest cluster remains in Spartanburg County, South Carolina, which has functioned as a seed for cross-state spread since the 2025 outbreak there never fully resolved. The 2026 case count is running ahead of where 2025 stood at the equivalent point. The fundamental driver is sustained collapse of vaccination uptake; Trump-administration cuts to CDC outreach funding and HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.'s public skepticism of MMR vaccine schedules have not been reversed. H5N1: 71 US human cases, 2 deaths, third Cambodia case in 2026 The CDC reports **71 confirmed US human H5N1 cases** and **2 deaths** to date. In the past 30 days alone, H5N1 was confirmed in **85 poultry flocks** — 45 commercial and 40 backyard. A 3-year-old boy in Cambodia became that country's third human case of 2026 this week, per CIDRAP. The CDC has streamlined H5N1 surveillance reporting to monthly updates, citing reduced case volume — a shift critics say also reduces public visibility of the spread in dairy cattle and among farm workers. The agency continues to rate the public health risk "low" while acknowledging the persistent dairy-cattle reservoir. NEJM SERENA-6 trial: camizestrant nearly doubles progression-free survival The *New England Journal of Medicine* published the SERENA-6 results this week. Among **315 patients** with HR+/HER2- advanced breast cancer who developed ESR1 mutations during first-line aromatase inhibitor + CDK4/6 inhibitor therapy, switching to camizestrant produced **median progression-free survival of 16.0 months versus 9.2 months** for those who remained on the aromatase inhibitor (hazard ratio 0.44; p<0.0001). Time to deterioration in quality of life was delayed from 6.4 to **21.0 months**. The trial is potentially practice-changing — it establishes liquid-biopsy-guided treatment switching as a viable precision-oncology strategy, allowing therapy adjustment on molecular evidence of resistance before clinical progression. Geoffrey Hinton warns of "runaway AI" at UN Geneva conference Speaking April 23 at the UN Research Institute for Social Development's "AI for Social Development" conference in Geneva, Geoffrey Hinton compared AI to "a very fast car with no steering wheel," warning that superintelligent systems could outpace human control if global governance does not keep pace. He flagged that AI development capacity is concentrated in just a few economies — a concentration that, he argued, threatens to deepen global inequality even as it accelerates technical capability. The intervention came during a peak week of UN AI governance negotiations and adds moral weight to calls for binding international oversight, in direct tension with the Trump administration's federal-preemption push. **Other developments:** - **COVID-19:** The CDC rates national activity "very low" in wastewater and clinical surveillance; no notable variant or surge signal in this reporting window. - **Climate:** No major peer-reviewed climate publication in this window; the IMF April WEO underscores that the Iran war has, for now, displaced climate transition from policy primacy in major economies.

--- Arts and culture The week's most significant cultural event is the death of **Michael Tilson Thomas**, the American conductor and music educator, at age 81. Tilson Thomas — who led the San Francisco Symphony for 25 years (the longest tenure since the orchestra's 1911 founding), founded the New World Symphony academy for emerging musicians in 1987, and continued Leonard Bernstein's *Young People's Concerts* tradition through PBS's *Keeping Score* — represented a particular American synthesis: a conductor descended from Yiddish theater pioneers Boris and Bessie Thomashevsky, mentored for 22 years by Bernstein, who treated democratic access to classical music not as an outreach program but as the central political and pedagogical task of a working artist's life. He was diagnosed with glioblastoma in 2021 and gave his final performance in April 2025; his husband Joshua Robison, whom he married in 2014, had died only two months earlier. As Fred Mazelis writes on the WSWS, Tilson Thomas's career was unusual in mainstream American musical life precisely because of its sustained refusal to treat orchestral repertoire as an elite consumer product — a refusal informed by a leftward family inheritance and by Bernstein's own Popular Front-era cultural politics. The week's other major openings reflect a different set of pressures shaping the American stage and screen. - **August Wilson's *Joe Turner's Come and Gone* opens on Broadway.** A revival starring Taraji P. Henson, directed by Debbie Allen, opened April 25 at the Ethel Barrymore Theatre. Wilson's 1988 play — set in 1911 Pittsburgh among Black migrants from the Jim Crow South — remains the most rigorous treatment in modern American drama of the relation between historical memory, displacement, and the question of agency under capitalism. The casting choices have been received as significant for the play's continued life on the commercial stage. - ***Michael*** (Antoine Fuqua, dir.), the long-anticipated Michael Jackson biopic starring the singer's nephew Jaafar Jackson, opened nationwide April 24. The picture has drawn unusually heavy advance scrutiny because of the active involvement of the Jackson estate in the script and the unresolved historical record concerning Jackson's conduct toward children. The film's commercial scale and the estate's editorial control raise the standard problems of authorized biopics — celebrity hagiography under conditions of intellectual-property monopoly — though the role of Jackson's music in the working-class popular culture of the 1980s remains a genuine artistic subject regardless. - ***Mother Mary*** (David Lowery, dir.), a stylized psychological thriller starring Anne Hathaway and Michaela Coel, expanded to wide release April 24 after a limited run. Hathaway's performance has anchored awards-season buzz; the film engages, in displaced form, with the artist-muse relations of contemporary celebrity culture. - **YoungBoy Never Broke Again's *American YoungBoy* documentary** opened nationwide April 24 as an extension of his MASA tour, generating a "theater frenzy." Concert documentaries continue to be a viable commercial format in the wake of Taylor Swift's and Beyoncé's theatrical releases, though the YoungBoy picture also functions as legal-cultural rehabilitation for an artist who has spent much of the past decade entangled with the carceral system. - ***Beaches*** opened on Broadway April 23 — the stage adaptation of the 1988 Bette Midler film. The run will test whether nostalgia-driven IP can sustain commercial-musical economics in a saturated late-spring season. - **Michael Sheen returns to the West End in *Amadeus*** opposite Callum Scott Howells (*It's a Sin*). Sheen's return to one of the most demanding classical roles in modern English-language theater, and his pairing with Howells, has been received as one of the most anticipated London stage events of 2026.
