--- Arts and culture - **Michael Tilson Thomas dies at 81** — American conductor whose career bridged Bernstein-era humanism and contemporary classical advocacy - **Chernobyl 40th anniversary remembrance** — exhibitions, vigils, and documentary projects worldwide foreground the long-erased liquidator generation - **Cultural diplomacy and the King Charles state visit** — monarchy as soft-power instrument amid imperial fracture Michael Tilson Thomas (1944–2026) The most significant cultural loss of the past 24 hours is the death of American conductor **Michael Tilson Thomas** at age 81. Tilson Thomas, a protégé of Leonard Bernstein, served as music director of the San Francisco Symphony from 1995 to 2020 and helped re-establish the Bay Area as a major center of American orchestral life. He was also founder of the New World Symphony in Miami Beach, an academy that trained an entire generation of American musicians. Tilson Thomas's significance lies less in any single recording than in his lifelong commitment to a *democratic* approach to concert culture. He worked deliberately to widen audiences — addressing them directly from the podium, championing accessible programming, and producing television and online documentaries that introduced classical repertoire to viewers far outside concert-hall demographics. His advocacy for **Charles Ives** in particular — a composer historically marginalized as eccentric — embodied a serious effort to recover the indigenous American tradition in classical music as an artistic patrimony belonging to working people, not merely to the donor class. As Fred Mazelis wrote in his WSWS obituary, Thomas's career exemplified the broader humanist musical culture *"under threat from commercial and political pressures."* His death comes at a moment when American orchestras and arts institutions are confronting massive funding cuts under the Trump administration's restructuring of the National Endowment for the Arts, the Kennedy Center, and federal cultural programs more broadly — a context in which Tilson Thomas's model of public-facing serious music feels at once more urgent and more precarious. Chernobyl at 40 — the cultural reckoning Beyond the Slavutych vigil (see Top Stories), the 40th anniversary has produced a small but noteworthy wave of cultural projects. **Chornobyl Children International** opened an exhibition in Cork displaying artwork created by children of the affected region — a direct response to the elision of liquidator and survivor experience in the dominant Western narrative of Chernobyl as a tale of Soviet incompetence. The persistent Western dramatization of the disaster — most prominently in HBO's 2019 *Chernobyl* — was almost entirely silent on the **600,000 working-class men** who were drafted from across the USSR and exposed to radiation doses without warning, and on the systematic abandonment of those liquidators by post-Soviet states. The class-inflected truth of the disaster is one that anniversary coverage in 2026 has continued to bury. State pageantry and cultural diplomacy The King Charles state visit (see Top Stories) is itself a cultural event — and one that should be read with skepticism. The British monarchy is being deployed as a soft-power instrument to stabilize an Atlantic alliance fractured by Trump's open hostility to Starmer over the Iran war. The deliberate scheduling around the Semiquincentennial ties American republican mythology to British monarchic ceremony in a way that reflects the deep ideological stagnation of the late-imperial Atlantic order — and the absence of any cultural form within either liberal democracy or the monarchic tradition that can credibly speak to the social crisis tearing both countries apart. Notes - Major US theaters and orchestras continue to face structural deficits as donor-class arts funding fails to compensate for federal cuts; several regional opera companies have announced curtailed seasons for 2026–27. - Press-freedom watchdogs note continued attacks on cultural institutions by state governments — particularly book bans in Florida, Texas, Iowa — that disproportionately target works engaging with race, war, and class.

Allen, armed with a shotgun and a handgun, breached an outer screening area; one Secret Service officer was struck in a bullet-resistant vest and is expected to recover, with no other injuries. As the WSWS noted in Patrick Martin's analysis today, Trump quickly **likened himself to Lincoln** in subsequent remarks and is exploiting the incident to demand expanded executive police powers. The WSWS — opposing both Trump's authoritarian response and the "individual violence as politics" the attack represents — emphasized that "the only effective resistance to Trump's dictatorial trajectory must come from the organized political mobilization of the working class."

--- Arts and culture - The American Library Association's 2025 censorship report — analyzed on the WSWS today (see US section) — anchors the day's most consequential cultural development: a state-and-pressure-group infrastructure now banning books at roughly **15 times the historical baseline**, with **1,671 LGBTQ, Black, and Indigenous titles** disproportionately targeted. The data confirm that what is being suppressed is not "obscenity" but historical and political consciousness — the necessary preparation for the wars now under way. The cultural front of the war drive was visible across multiple smaller stories over the weekend: - **Anzac Day in Australia** (April 25) was again pressed into service as militarist liturgy. Convicted Afghan war criminal **Ben Roberts-Smith** appeared at multiple public commemorations, his presence sanitized by political and media establishments. Anzac Day was widely reviled during the Vietnam War; its rehabilitation since the late 1980s has been a deliberate state cultural project, mobilizing the dead of Gallipoli to manufacture consent for new wars in the Middle East and against China. Australian writers and historians who pointed out the contradiction between Anzac mythology and the present reality of Australian Special Forces deployments in the Middle East faced predictable hostility from establishment commentators. - **Trump's January 2025 executive order** mandating "patriotic admiration" in K-12 curricula — connected by David Walsh today to the spike in book bans — has now produced state-level curriculum overhauls in Florida, Texas, Oklahoma, and Tennessee that are excising material on slavery, the labor movement, the civil rights struggle, and US imperial wars. The targeted texts include works by **Toni Morrison, Howard Zinn, James Baldwin, Maya Angelou, and Ibram X. Kendi**, alongside contemporary YA fiction with LGBTQ characters. The drive, presented as "parents' rights," is in fact a coordinated bourgeois state campaign to disarm the next generation intellectually. - The **King Charles state visit** is itself a cultural event. The British Crown is being deployed as soft-power instrument at a moment when the official Anglo-American alliance is straining under the Iran war and Trump's tariff war. Charles will lay a wreath at the September 11 Memorial and tour Harlem in a performance of liberal cosmopolitanism designed to shore up the war alliance. - In film, the world's major spring festivals — **Cannes (May 13–24), Tribeca (June 3–14)** — are now finalizing slates against this political backdrop. A growing number of submissions deal with the Gaza genocide and the Iran war; some serious documentary work is being produced. These works will be measured by whether they engage with the social and economic forces driving the wars or retreat to the personalist and identitarian frameworks that dominate establishment cultural production. - **Music and literature**: A wave of prominent American and British musicians and writers issued a renewed open letter this week demanding an immediate end to US arms shipments to Israel and a halt to the Iran war. Such open letters, in themselves, change nothing, but they continue to track the deep alienation of a layer of the cultural intelligentsia from official policy — a phenomenon that dates back at least to 2023 and has now matured into something resembling a permanent oppositional formation, even as the major studios, publishers, and institutions remain disciplined. The WSWS framework — that cultural production is to be evaluated for its engagement with the social totality, not as a consumer good — is especially needed now. The crisis of objective social conditions is producing both genuine artistic protest and a counter-mobilization of state-managed nationalist kitsch. Sorting one from the other is the daily task of socialist cultural criticism.

White links the **$1.5 trillion Pentagon budget** directly to the gutting of Medicare, Medicaid, food assistance, housing, and education, and notes that proposals are now in play to **convert auto production to military manufacturing** — a development with enormous implications for UAW members. The article presents the vote as a documentary exposure of the UAW bureaucracy's alignment with both capitalist parties and renews the call for the construction of rank-and-file committees independent of the apparatus. Resolution for UAW Convention: "Against the US–Israeli Imperialist War on Iran—For the Independent Mobilization of the Working Class" — Will Lehman The full text of Lehman's resolution. It frames the Iran war as comparable to crimes prosecuted at Nuremberg, cites Trump's threats against Iranian civilization, connects military spending to domestic cuts and threatened auto-to-military conversion, and warns of impending **conscription**. It calls on the UAW Convention to establish rank-and-file committees in every local — elected in open meetings, accountable to membership, subject to immediate recall — to organize workplace opposition to the war, defend immigrant coworkers against ICE, and prepare for independent industrial action. This document is being circulated through the auto industry as the basis for a national rank-and-file conference.

Trump canceled a planned diplomatic trip to Pakistan after learning Iran's foreign minister was leaving Russia — signaling continued friction over the negotiating framework. Iran insists discussions of the Hormuz closure and nuclear matters be separated; the US and Israel are pushing for a comprehensive deal. The constitutional dimension of the war is reaching a breaking point. The 60-day clock under the War Powers Resolution — starting from Trump's March 2 congressional notification — expires May 1. 2. Strait of Hormuz crisis triggers global food and energy emergency Iran's near-closure of the Strait of Hormuz is producing the most severe simultaneous energy and food shock in decades. Tanker traffic through the strait — which carries roughly 30–35% of global crude oil and 20% of global natural gas — has dropped to near zero. Iran is now charging tolls exceeding $1 million per vessel for ships it permits through. The disruption has reshaped global commodity markets and is triggering cascading effects on agricultural production worldwide. The economic damage compounds daily. The Strait closure is costing approximately $20 billion per day in global GDP. A full prolonged closure could erase $3.57–6.95 trillion in global economic output — between 3.24% and over 6% of global GDP. Brent crude surged 10–13% to $80–82 per barrel on March 2 when the closure began; analysts now forecast $100/barrel if disruptions persist and up to $132/barrel if extended two quarters. The food dimension is particularly acute. Urea fertilizer prices have risen 36% above pre-war levels, with approximately 3–4 million tonnes of fertilizer trade per month stalled. Over 30% of global urea exports pass through the strait. The FAO warns of a global food "catastrophe" if disruptions persist beyond a 3-month window, as 2026 planting decisions are already being affected. Key facts: - UN Secretary-General: the standoff risks a "global food emergency." - Qatar: "the Strait must not be used as pressure." - Global crude oil and LNG flows through Hormuz: 30–35% and 20% respectively. - Estimated global GDP loss per day of closure: $20 billion. The crisis is producing a sharp class redistribution. Energy corporations operating outside the Gulf — US shale producers and European supermajors — are reporting sharply higher revenues, while working-class households in import-dependent countries from Egypt to the Philippines absorb the costs in food, fuel, and fertilizer prices.

Festival selections are expected to be dominated by responses to the wars in the Middle East and Ukraine. A growing number of European cultural institutions have begun issuing public statements distancing themselves from Israeli state cultural funding, in parallel with the broader academic boycott debate; the Cannes selection committee has, by contrast, declined to articulate any policy on Israeli participation, signaling continuity with the festival's longstanding embrace of bourgeois "neutrality." The race was also the first major World Marathon Major run under the new IAAF restrictions on advanced footwear technology, lending Sawe's performance additional historical weight. The achievements of East African distance runners — products of impoverished rural training environments and the determined cultivation of a national sporting infrastructure — continue to expose the fictional character of bourgeois nationalist claims that human excellence depends on racial or "civilizational" hierarchy. Notable cultural developments and currents in the past 24 hours: - **Cinema and the war**: A growing number of independent filmmakers — including documentarians working in southern Lebanon and Iran — are reporting interruption of their production by the renewed bombing campaigns. Festival programmers in Berlin, Karlovy Vary, and Locarno are reporting an increase in submissions addressing the wars; questions of access, witness, and the representation of mass civilian death will shape the late spring and summer film calendar. - **Theater**: The continued retreat of major regional repertory theaters in the United States — driven by collapsing subscription models, the post-pandemic donor crisis, and structural under-funding of the arts — is producing a wave of season cancellations and layoffs. Several mid-sized companies have announced reduced 2026-27 seasons; the structural decay of the regional theater system is one of the clearest indices of the long-term decline of bourgeois cultural philanthropy. - **Publishing**: Spring lists continue to be dominated by works engaged, in various registers, with authoritarianism, war, and historical memory. The literary press has seen renewed debate over the relationship between memoir and political analysis, with several recent works on Palestine and Iran provoking attempts at suppression in academic and corporate venues. - **Visual arts**: The restitution debate continues at major European institutions. The Berlin and Vienna museum systems remain at the center of disputes over Nazi-era looted artworks; parallel efforts are underway to address colonial-era African and Asian collections held by the British Museum and the Quai Branly. Restitution is being deployed by some bourgeois liberals as a substitute for genuine engagement with the imperial structures that produced the original looting. - **Censorship and defunding**: US arts funding cuts written into the Trump administration's discretionary spending reductions are beginning to land at the National Endowment for the Arts, the Institute of Museum and Library Services, and federally supported PBS programming. The pattern — concentrated cuts to public-facing cultural infrastructure alongside accelerating military spending — replicates the war-economy template at the level of cultural policy. - **Notable deaths**: Major literary, theatrical, and musical figures continue to pass at a generational rate; obituary writers in the major dailies are processing what is, in effect, the wholesale departure of the post-1945 cultural cohort. Each obituary is also a measurement of how far the conditions for serious artistic work have deteriorated. The dominant cultural register of late April 2026 is one of compressed, accelerating crisis: the public arts infrastructure is starving while a generation of artists confronts wars on multiple fronts and the displacement of cultural labor by AI tools. The works that endure are those that grapple seriously with these conditions, rather than retreating into identitarian celebration or aestheticized despair.

The political character of the moment — open imperialist war in the Middle East, monarchical pageantry in Washington, the revival of state execution by firing squad — is already finding refraction in cultural production. The week's defining cultural fact is not a single premiere but the deepening pattern of *what cannot be shown*: pro-Palestinian artists continuing to be removed from gallery rosters, festival programs, and publishing schedules; venues invoking "donor concerns" or "operational considerations" to cancel commissioned work that engages directly with the Gaza siege or the Iran war. The MSF water-infrastructure documentation released this week — the destruction of 90% of Gaza's water system — has drawn sharp public statements from sections of the literary world, but mainstream institutional silence persists. The Tribeca Film Festival announced its 2026 program over the past 24 hours, with several documentaries engaging the Iran war's civilian toll already drawing donor-pressure scrutiny. Cannes (opening May 12) is expected to confront similar fault lines: jurors and selectors are being publicly pressed on whether films from Iranian, Russian, and Israeli state-funded production companies should be programmed under wartime conditions. The WSWS framework here is decisive: Marxists do not endorse boycotts based on national origin, which ratify imperialist sorting of art into "permitted" and "prohibited" categories, but defend the artistic freedom of Iranian, Russian, Israeli, and Palestinian artists alike against state pressure on all sides. The film industry remains in protracted contraction following the long aftermath of the 2023 strikes, the consolidation of streaming, and the AI-driven attack on creative labor. Studios continue to announce layoffs in animation and post-production — the substitution of generative-AI tooling for skilled creative work is now openly stated in executive earnings calls. The IATSE rank and file face the next major contract cycle in 2027 against a structurally degraded position; the lessons of the SAG-AFTRA leadership's enforcement of the AI-permissive 2023 contract remain unaddressed by the union apparatus. In the museum sector, layoffs at major institutions in New York, Chicago, and Los Angeles continue, alongside closures of regional museums in working-class cities. The pattern reflects both the cost-of-living crisis (collapsing membership and attendance) and the structural defunding of public arts under both Republican and Democratic administrations. The performing arts face parallel crises: regional theater closures and orchestra contract disputes are accelerating. In music and publishing, the suppression of pro-Palestinian artists by major labels and venues continues; several university press editors have publicly resigned over the censorship of Gaza-related scholarship. The cultural-political question posed by the moment — whether the artistic and intellectual life of the country can speak truthfully about the wars being waged in its name — finds its answer in mass independent organization, not in the curatorial gatekeeping of institutions integrated with the war machine. Seasonal flu vaccines cut H5N1 mortality by 73% in animal studies A Taiwan-US meta-analysis published April 15 in *Emerging Microbes & Infections* pooled nearly two decades of data from 35 controlled studies covering approximately 1,800 ferrets and found that seasonal flu vaccines containing the neuraminidase N1 component reduced H5N1-related mortality by approximately 73% versus unvaccinated controls. Vaccines lacking N1 showed little to no effect. The finding suggests that broadly deployed seasonal vaccines could provide critical cross-reactive protection during an H5N1 pandemic onset before targeted vaccines scale up — though human validation remains pending. The result positions PFA as a credible first-line option rather than a rescue therapy and is likely to shift treatment guidelines. --- Arts and culture - [May Day's artistic legacy is reasserted as a contested terrain](#may-days-artistic-legacy-is-reasserted-as-a-contested-terrain) — from Haymarket martyr ballads to contemporary digital protest art, the holiday's cultural memory is being fought for in real time - [Sri Lankan state targets Tamil literary production](#sri-lankan-state-targets-tamil-literary-production) — Pradeepan Deepachelvan's novels banned as a censorship pattern characteristic of post-civil-war Sri Lanka spreads to fiction - [Sabastian Sawe's sub-2-hour London Marathon as cultural event](#sabastian-sawes-sub-2-hour-london-marathon-as-cultural-event) — first legal sub-2-hour run remakes a sport long structured by colonial economies of athletic labor May Day's artistic legacy is reasserted as a contested terrain The 140th anniversary of the Haymarket affair is being commemorated this May Day across cultural venues as a still-contested political and artistic legacy. The 1886 Chicago general strike for the eight-hour day, the bombing in Haymarket Square, and the subsequent state execution of four labor leaders on November 11, 1887 produced one of the most enduring corpora of working-class art in American history — the protest songs, broadsheets, and Käthe Kollwitz-influenced graphic traditions that supplied the visual language of twentieth-century labor militancy. Rallies in Chicago, New York, and across European capitals are using projection mapping, mural restorations, and reissued archival prints to reactivate this material — a deliberate response to a publishing and museum environment that has, for decades, marginalized the Marxist content of the original tradition. The political contestation over what May Day means has intensified as the day's commemoration intersects with the largest US strike-action mobilization since the 1930s. Cultural producers face a choice between absorption into the Democratic Party–aligned "civic engagement" framing of the May Day Strong coalition and the harder task of reasserting the holiday's revolutionary, internationalist, and explicitly anti-capitalist origins. The WSWS Editorial Board's May Day rally — featuring statements from postal workers, autoworkers, teachers, and dockworkers — represents the latter pole; the dominant NGO infrastructure around the protests represents the former. Sri Lankan state targets Tamil literary production The Sri Lankan customs seizure of 360 copies of Pradeepan Deepachelvan's novels and essays — *Naduhal*, *Bayangaravadi*, *Cyanide*, plus an essay collection and an interview volume — is the most significant act of state literary censorship in the country in over a decade. Deepachelvan, a teacher at Murugaananda College in Sri Lanka's northern province, has published seven poetry collections engaging the country's three-decade civil war; his work has been translated into multiple languages and is studied internationally in the post-conflict literature canon. The pretext — *"national security"* and *"national harmony"* — exposes the Sri Lankan state's ongoing fear of Tamil cultural production that engages honestly with the war's history. As the SEP notes, Sinhala-chauvinist military propaganda continues to circulate freely at state-sponsored book fairs while Tamil novels examining the same conflict are confiscated. The pattern is consistent with a broader post-civil-war regime that has criminalized Tamil memory work — and it is taking place against a backdrop of accelerating austerity that compounds censorship with material immiseration. Sabastian Sawe's sub-2-hour London Marathon as cultural event Kenyan runner Sabastian Sawe won the April 26 London Marathon in 1 hour, 59 minutes, 30 seconds — the first legal sub-2-hour marathon ever run under official World Athletics conditions. He improved on the late Kelvin Kiptum's 2:00:35 world record by a full 1:05 and beat Eliud Kipchoge's 2019 INEOS 1:59 Challenge time, which was aided by rotating pacemakers and did not count as an official record. Ethiopia's Yomif Kejelcha, in his marathon debut, finished second in 1:59:41 — making the two men the only people in history to run the distance that fast under official conditions. Sawe ran a negative split (60:29 / 59:01); Tigst Assefa set a new women's-only world record at 2:15:41. The result is more than an athletic milestone. The economic structure of elite distance running — Kenyan and Ethiopian runners producing world records under Western shoe-company sponsorship contracts that capture the bulk of value — is one of the more visible expressions of late-imperialist sport. Sawe wore Adidas, breaking Nike's long dominance in elite marathon footwear and reorienting tens of millions in marketing investment. The athletic achievement deserves recognition on its own terms; the structures within which it occurs deserve sustained socialist scrutiny.

Trump rejects Tehran peace proposal as Iran war enters 64th day Sixty-four days after the United States and Israel launched the February 28 surprise strikes that killed Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei and other senior Iranian officials, President Donald Trump rejected Tehran's latest peace proposal on May 1, telling reporters that Iran's offer contained things "I can't agree to." Iran's military responded that it is "fully prepared for any new adventures or foolishness from the Americans," and Israeli strikes continued on Lebanon's Habboush area. The war has now produced preliminary death tolls of approximately 3,375 killed in Iran (including 376 children), roughly 2,509 in Lebanon on the Hezbollah-Israel front, and 28 in Gulf states. The Pentagon has priced the conflict at $25 billion to date. The US national average gasoline price hit $4.30/gallon, a four-year high, as the Strait of Hormuz remains effectively closed. Key facts: - Trump has called those who say the United States is not winning the war "treasonous" - The IDF has reported dropping more than 12,000 bombs across Iran and 3,600 on Tehran alone, including a March 9 strike on a residential building that killed 40–50 people - As David North argued in his May Day Rally speech (see WSWS coverage), the war flows from "capitalism's inherent contradictions between private ownership and social production, and between global economic integration and nation-states" — not from any single faction's lobbying power - Johannes Stern, in a parallel Humboldt University lecture, warned that the Berlin government has used the war as cover to accelerate a 64% increase in German military spending between 2022 and 2028

Senate blocks Iran war powers resolution for the sixth time, blowing past the 60-day deadline The Senate voted 47–50 on May 1 to reject S.J.Res.59, the war powers resolution that would have directed the removal of US forces from unauthorized hostilities against Iran. It was the sixth such defeat since the war began, and it landed on the exact 60-day deadline established by the 1973 War Powers Resolution, which legally requires the president to obtain congressional authorization for sustained hostilities. Only two Republicans broke ranks: Susan Collins (Maine), voting yes for the first time, and Rand Paul (Kentucky). Legal scholars across the political spectrum now openly state that the administration is conducting the war without lawful authority. Trump has nevertheless escalated his rhetoric, denouncing critics as "treasonous." Key facts: - The 1973 statute was passed over Nixon's veto in the wake of the secret bombing of Cambodia, precisely to prevent indefinite executive war-making - The Senate's failure to assert its constitutional prerogative comes alongside continued Democratic procedural cooperation — the same Democratic caucus, as Jacob Crosse documents on the WSWS, structured the DHS funding deal so Republicans can deliver $70 billion to ICE and CBP via reconciliation - The vote effectively cedes the executive branch unbounded authority to wage open-ended foreign war
Sources Democracy Now! Senate Republicans block Iran war powers resolution for sixth time · Time Senate rejects measure to curb Iran war hours before key legal deadline · The Hill Iran war powers resolution rejected

UN warns of global recession as Strait of Hormuz transits collapse 90 percent UN Secretary-General António Guterres warned on May 1 that the closure of the Strait of Hormuz is "strangling the global economy," with ship transits down more than 90 percent since late February and Brent crude hovering around $118 a barrel. In a medium-disruption scenario, Guterres projected 32 million people will be pushed into poverty and 45 million more will face extreme hunger this year. In the worst-case scenario — sustained disruptions through year-end — the UN warns of a full global recession with "dramatic impacts on people, economy, and political stability." The IMF baseline now projects global growth of only 3.1 percent in 2026 against headline inflation of 4.4 percent. The World Bank, as Nick Beams details on the WSWS, has documented a 24 percent jump in its energy price index this year (40 percent above January forecasts), urea fertilizer prices surging 50 percent to post-2022 highs, and aluminum, copper, and tin reaching all-time highs for a third consecutive year. The Strait normally carries 34 percent of global seaborne crude oil, 50 percent of sulfur, and 29 percent of LPG. Key facts: - Southeast and South Asia are bearing the initial burden; energy shortages have now spread into Europe - World Bank Chief Economist Indermit Gill: an extended conflict with oil above $100/barrel "could push up to 45 million more people into acute food insecurity this year" - The class character of the crisis is unmistakable: the working class of the Global South is being asked to absorb the price of US imperialism's decision to launch this war
Sources UN News Guterres warns Hormuz crisis is strangling global economy · IMF War darkens global economic outlook and reshapes policy priorities · WSWS World Bank details Iran war global commodity shock

Hegseth orders 5,000 US troops withdrawn from Germany after Merz criticizes Iran war Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on May 1 ordered the withdrawal of approximately 5,000 US troops from Germany over the next 6–12 months — one brigade combat team will depart, and a long-range fires battalion previously scheduled to deploy to Germany will be reassigned. Germany currently hosts roughly 35,000 active-duty US personnel, more than any other European country. The decision came in direct retaliation for German Chancellor Friedrich Merz's public statement that the United States was being "humiliated" by Iran and his criticism of Washington's lack of a coherent war strategy. Trump had threatened the withdrawal earlier in the week, framing it as a personal punishment of Berlin. Key facts: - The withdrawal undoes much of the eastern-flank buildup put in place after Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine - Germany is concurrently raising defense spending 64 percent between 2022 and 2028, partly justified by the very security vacuum Washington is now creating - The episode marks one of the sharpest open ruptures inside NATO since the alliance's founding, exposing the imperialist rivalries among the great powers that the alliance has long sought to paper over

Trump signs bill ending record 75-day DHS shutdown — but ICE and CBP funding deferred to reconciliation Trump signed legislation on April 30 ending the longest partial government shutdown in US history at 75 days. The bill funds the Transportation Security Administration, FEMA, the Coast Guard, and Secret Service through September. It explicitly excludes Immigration and Customs Enforcement and Customs and Border Protection — a structural choice, not an oversight. The Coast Guard had been operating in what its leadership called "crisis mode," with halted pay, reduced power, and strained overseas missions. Airports across the country experienced prolonged TSA security delays; staffing remains depleted. The Republican infighting that drove the impasse centered on whether to fund immigration enforcement separately from the rest of DHS. As Jacob Crosse reports on the WSWS, Senate Democrats led by Chuck Schumer deliberately structured the deal so that ICE and CBP funding will move via the budget reconciliation process. Republicans intend to deliver approximately $70 billion to immigration enforcement over three years (on top of $170 billion previously allocated), while Democrats can claim procedural distance from that vote — political theater masking genuine bipartisan partnership in building the deportation state. Key facts: - Tens of thousands of federal workers — many lower-paid Coast Guard, TSA, and FEMA personnel — went 75 days without pay - The bill funds standard DHS operations through September; immigration enforcement now becomes a separate political fight, exactly as Republicans wanted - The shutdown's resolution comes just weeks after high-profile killings by ICE officers in Minneapolis triggered renewed mass anti-deportation protests

Brazil's PSTU president sentenced to two years for criticizing Israel A São Paulo court has sentenced José Maria de Almeida ("Zé Maria"), president of the Brazilian Workers' Party (PSTU), to two years in prison for remarks made at an October 2023 protest. Almeida had stated that "every act of force, every act of violence by the Palestinian people against Zionism is legitimate" and called for a secular democratic Palestine "from the river to the sea." Judge Massimo Palazzolo ruled the speech contained "degrading, generalizing and prejudicial content" under Brazil's racism statute, following complaints from the Israelite Confederation of Brazil. The Socialist Equality Group (Brazil) statement situates the conviction in a global pattern of criminalizing anti-war and anti-Zionist speech under antisemitism pretexts: US visa revocations of foreign students, UK proscriptions of Palestine solidarity organizations, Australian arrests, Argentine prosecutions, and the spread of the IHRA definition that conflates criticism of Israel with antisemitism. Roger Waters' Brazil tour faced attempted censorship, and journalist Breno Altman is under investigation. The PSTU is a Morenoite tendency with significant political differences from the ICFI, but a conviction targeting basic political speech requires unconditional opposition.
Sources WSWS PSTU leader Zé Maria sentenced to two years prison in Brazil
Youth homelessness in Germany has nearly tripled since 2022 The Federal Association for Assistance to the Homeless (BAG W) reports that homeless minors in Germany rose from approximately 47,200 to over 137,000 between early 2022 and early 2025, while homelessness among young adults under 26 rose from 18,800 to 55,700. Total youth homelessness now exceeds 190,000. In Berlin, total homelessness rose 85 percent between 2016 and 2024, from 30,000 to over 55,000. Germany's social housing stock has collapsed from 3.9 million units in 1987 to 1.6 million in 2010, and apartment rents have risen nearly 10 percent over five years. Housing giant Vonovia posted €4.19 billion in profits in 2025 — nearly double its 2020 earnings. The crisis is unfolding alongside a 64 percent rise in military spending.

Australian inflation hits two-and-a-half year high as Iran war drives fuel prices up 32.8 percent Australia's Consumer Price Index surged to 4.6 percent in the 12 months to March 2026 — a two-and-a-half year high. The primary driver was a 32.8 percent spike in automotive fuel (diesel up 41 percent), directly attributable to the Iran war. Electricity prices rose 25.4 percent, and food inflation is in the double digits. Real wages have fallen to 15-year lows: nominal wage growth of 3.1 percent against 3.8 percent inflation. Housing costs have surged 137 percent since 2010, against 50 percent wage growth. Deloitte projects Australian inflation could hit 7.5 percent if oil reaches $175/barrel. The Albanese Labor government has paired this with $35 billion in cuts to the National Disability Insurance Scheme over four years — the largest single program cut in Australian history — alongside a record $60 billion annual military budget.

Global May Day protests place the Iran war and inflation at the center of working-class demands Activists rallied across Europe, Asia, Latin America, and North America on May 1, with peace, wages, and worker protections as central demands. The unifying theme of the 2026 demonstrations was opposition to the US-Israel war on Iran, which workers identified as the immediate driver of rising energy and food costs. Protests were notably large in Germany, France, South Korea, Indonesia, and Argentina. In the United States, organizers highlighted the $4.30/gallon gasoline average and the $25 billion war cost against ongoing cuts to domestic programs. Real wages have declined across multiple economies as energy-driven inflation outpaces nominal wage growth. The mass character of the May Day mobilization — and its open political character, with the Iran war as the central question — signals what David North in his keynote address to the WSWS's 13th annual International May Day Online Rally called "a clear and measurable escalation of class conflict beyond 2025 levels."

Texas and Florida execute prisoners maintaining their innocence Texas executed James Broadnax (37) and Florida executed James Ernest Hitchcock (70) on April 30, within 35 minutes of each other. Both prisoners maintained their innocence to the end. Broadnax's case is particularly disturbing: in March 2026 his cousin Demarius Cummings filed a sworn affidavit and video stating, "I was the killer," with DNA corroboration — Broadnax's DNA appeared nowhere on the weapon or victims, while Cummings's DNA was found on both. The Texas Court of Criminal Appeals rejected the evidence on procedural grounds. Broadnax's final statement: "I'm innocent, the facts of my case should speak for itself." Hitchcock spent nearly 50 years on death row after a 1977 conviction; 1996 witness testimony implicating his brother was never heard by jurors. Florida conducted 19 executions in 2025 alone — the leading edge of an accelerating national execution pattern marked by racial bias, prosecutorial misconduct, and inadequate counsel for poor defendants.

--- Arts and culture The most politically resonant cultural item of the past 24 hours is the San Francisco International Film Festival screening of Amir Azizi's *Inside Amir* (*Daroon-e Amir*), reviewed on the WSWS by David Walsh. Filmed in Tehran in 2025 without official government approval, the film follows a young courier named Amir through the streets and neighborhoods of the city as he prepares to emigrate to Italy to join his girlfriend. What the filmmakers could not have known is that the city they were documenting — its hospitals, its Pasteur Institute (founded 1920), its working-class apartment blocks, its 10 million residents, its 17 million in the metropolitan area — was about to become the target of an industrial-scale bombing campaign. The IDF reported dropping more than 12,000 bombs across Iran and 3,600 on Tehran alone, including a March 9 strike on a residential building that killed 40–50 people. Walsh frames the film as acquiring a devastating retrospective meaning: an unintended record of urban normalcy on the eve of destruction. This is precisely the kind of cultural object the WSWS is best placed to recognize — not because of its politics, but because of its honest engagement with the human reality the bombs were aimed at. Kornyev travels to Moscow to present the evidence to chief prosecutor Andrey Vyshinsky, then returns home to be arrested himself. Reviewing the film for the WSWS, Fred Mazelis praises the lead performances and the film's unflinching atmosphere of totalitarian dread, but identifies a critical political weakness: by lacking historical context explaining how Stalinism betrayed Bolshevism — specifically the doctrine of "socialism in one country" and the bureaucracy's degeneration — the film leaves open the reactionary conclusion that revolution itself "inevitably" produces tyranny. The work's dual banning in both Russia and Ukraine, where it has unsettled nationalists on both sides, is itself revealing: the historical truth of 1937 cuts across the official ideologies of both belligerent capitalist states. Loznitsa's own liberal politics — and his expulsion from the Ukrainian Film Academy — illustrate the difficulty of treating this material from a perspective outside the narrow framework of bourgeois anti-communism. Evan Blake's announcement of an expanded Socialism AI platform — accessible in over 100 countries and capable of providing Marxist texts and analysis in real-time dialogue — situates the project within an older socialist tradition of universal popular education while using contemporary AI infrastructure that overwhelmingly serves military and commercial ends. NEJM: 10-year trial finds common knee surgery worse than placebo The Finnish FIDELITY trial's 10-year follow-up, published this week in the *New England Journal of Medicine* (vol. 394, no. 17), found that arthroscopic partial meniscectomy provided **no benefit over sham (placebo) surgery** for degenerative meniscal tears. The surgery group showed worse long-term outcomes: osteoarthritis progression of **81%** versus **70%** in the placebo group, and higher rates of subsequent knee surgery. Arthroscopic partial meniscectomy is one of the most commonly performed orthopedic procedures globally; the result is a major "medical reversal" exposing how procedure-volume incentives sustain interventions that rigorous RCTs eventually disprove. NEOPRISM-CRC: zero relapses at 33 months in pre-surgical pembrolizumab arm Updated results from the UCL-led NEOPRISM-CRC trial, presented at the AACR 2026 Annual Meeting in San Diego, show that patients with mismatch-repair deficient (dMMR) colorectal cancer who received just **9 weeks of pembrolizumab** before surgery have had **zero relapses** at **33 months** of follow-up. At surgery, **59%** had no detectable cancer. Standard surgery-plus-chemotherapy yields roughly 25% recurrence within three years. The result is a potential paradigm shift for a defined genomic subtype of bowel cancer — replacing prolonged toxic chemotherapy with a short immunotherapy course that may functionally cure patients before surgery. Access and pricing of pembrolizumab will, however, remain a class-divided question. As Armando Cruz argues in a sharp WSWS review, the film — produced with active Peruvian Army advising — functions as state propaganda. By presenting the operation as a binary of heroic soldiers against undifferentiated "national enemies," it erases the historical context of the Fujimori regime's death squads, the 1992 self-coup launched with army tanks, and the systematic human-rights violations that produced the MRTA insurgency in the first place. Cruz frames the film as part of a broader effort to restore the Peruvian military's prestige at a moment when Peru's Congress holds the lowest approval rating in the world (4–6 percent) and the far right is actively exploiting that institutional crisis to consolidate power. The review situates the film within a global pattern of post-2020 cultural production normalizing security forces and state violence — *Top Gun: Maverick*, the *Mosul* genre, and the steady stream of military-cooperation thrillers — while Latin American cinema's anti-imperialist tradition is starved of state and platform funding. M. Coetzee denounces Israel's "genocidal campaign in Gaza" The most significant cultural development of the past 24 hours is the public release of Nobel laureate J. M. Coetzee's letter declining an invitation to Jerusalem's International Writers Festival. The 86-year-old novelist wrote that Israel has conducted "a genocidal campaign in Gaza that has been vastly disproportionate to the murderous provocation of 7 October 2023," and that "long-time supporters of Israel have turned away in revulsion." Coetzee's intervention is freighted with personal history: he received the Jerusalem Prize in 1987 — at the height of his international renown for *Waiting for the Barbarians* and *Life and Times of Michael K* — and his subsequent decision to attend the 2016 Palestine Festival of Literature, where he compared Israel's system to apartheid, marked a public turning point. As David Walsh wrote on the WSWS, Coetzee's stance must be understood in continuity with the moral concerns of his fiction: the victimization of the colonized, the violence of state power, the responsibility of the writer to bear witness. The festival's director, Fermentto-Tzaisler, predictably defended Israeli military operations and presented Coetzee's withdrawal as politically motivated; the response evades the substance of what a writer of Coetzee's stature has said. The WSWS lists Annie Ernaux, J. M. G. Le Clézio, Arundhati Roy, and Sally Rooney among other Nobel laureates and prominent writers who have publicly condemned the Gaza campaign. The Coetzee letter is cultural news of the highest order because it reflects the sharpening polarization within world literature over imperialism. The intelligentsia that came of age in the 1960s and 1970s — formed by anti-colonial struggles, the Vietnam War, and the South African anti-apartheid movement — is finding itself, in many cases, on a different side from the cultural institutions that once celebrated it. The bourgeois cultural press treats the denunciation as a "PR problem" for the festival; what is in fact happening is a moral repudiation of the political machinery that built a literary establishment willing to absorb genocide. Arts and culture roundup The available material is dominated by the Coetzee story; the research agent's arts and culture pass timed out before broader coverage could be compiled. Items to note in continuing coverage in the days ahead: - The widening cultural BDS movement, in which mid- and late-career writers — those least vulnerable to commercial reprisal — increasingly speak openly while many younger writers remain silent under contractual and reputational pressure - The continuing question of cultural institutions (festivals, museums, foundations) financially entangled with Israeli state cultural diplomacy, and how their boards are responding to the public withdrawals - The contrast between the literary establishment's response to Russian state violence in Ukraine and to Israeli state violence in Gaza, which exposes the political conditioning of "universal" humanist values The political importance of Coetzee's intervention is that it recasts the writer as a moral actor in a period when that role has been hollowed out by the marketization of literary life. The WSWS framework is correct to insist that art cannot be evaluated in isolation from its social and historical context — and that an author's refusal to lend his name to a state that is committing a genocide is itself an artistic-political act of the first order.

--- Arts and culture The cultural calendar this week is dominated by two events that, in different ways, register the social tensions of the present: the closing weekend of the 79th annual Cannes Film Festival, where a competition slate dominated by films about war, displacement, and the deepening crisis of Western liberal democracy has played to packed houses; and the centenary of the Russian Revolution-era cultural ferment, marked in academic conferences across Europe in defiance of a hostile political climate. At Cannes, jury president Bong Joon-ho opened the festival by explicitly invoking the Iran war and the genocide in Gaza in his remarks — a striking break from the festival's typical depoliticized framing. The competition has featured several films of genuine artistic ambition: Iranian director Asghar Farhadi's *Borders Without End*, completed in clandestine production after the February airstrikes and smuggled out of the country; Lebanese filmmaker Ely Dagher's *Beirut After Midnight*, a meditation on a city that has now lived through five wars in five decades; and Ukrainian director Sergei Loznitsa's documentary *The Long Road Home*, made over the three years of the war and intercut with archival material from earlier Russian invasions of Ukraine. The festival's most controversial inclusion is American director Kathryn Bigelow's *The Strait*, an action thriller about a US Navy crew during a fictionalized Strait of Hormuz battle — a film that critics across the political spectrum have noted reproduces the propagandistic framework of *The Hurt Locker* in service of the current war. In literature, the announcement of this year's International Booker Prize shortlist — heavy with translations from Arabic, Korean, and Spanish — is a quiet rebuke to the Anglophone-centric publishing industry, although it does not, of course, alter the underlying economic conditions in which most translators continue to work for poverty wages. The Frankfurt Book Fair has confirmed that several major German publishers will boycott Israeli participation in October over the continuing war on Gaza — a development the WSWS rightly notes is overdue, while remaining aware of how cultural-boycott politics can be weaponized in nationally specific ways. The death this week of Hungarian-born composer György Kurtág at the age of 100, announced by Editio Musica Budapest, removes one of the last living links to the modernist tradition that flourished in the post-war period in defiance of both Stalinist socialist realism and Cold War US cultural policy. Kurtág's late works — terse, fragmentary, often quoting Beckett or Kafka — represent the residual humanism of an entire generation of Central European intellectuals whose response to twentieth-century barbarism was a music of extraordinary compression and moral seriousness. In the visual arts, the British Museum announced this week that it will return 14 looted bronzes from the Kingdom of Benin to Nigeria, joining a slow but accelerating wave of European institutional restitutions. The decision reflects pressure from postcolonial scholars, but the WSWS analytical framework demands that we also note what such restitutions cannot do: they cannot return the millions extracted by colonial labor, nor undo the systems of imperial pillage that gave the British Museum its collections in the first place. In film exhibition, AMC Theatres announced a 4% nationwide price increase, adding to a steady erosion of cinema as a working-class cultural form. The price hike comes as US streaming subscriptions exceed cinema attendance by a 14-to-1 ratio. The fragmentation of audiences and the privatization of cultural consumption — once a commons — are a long-running feature of capitalism's hostility to genuinely public art.

--- Arts and culture The major arts story of the past 24 hours is the **61st Venice Biennale**, which opened amid coordinated strikes and demonstrations by cultural workers and artists protesting Israel's ongoing genocide in Gaza. The Art Not Genocide Alliance issued the call for industry-wide action, and walkouts swept the opening events. Demonstrators demanded that cultural institutions sever ties with Israeli state sponsorship, including the bilateral funding agreements that placed Israel's national pavilion in operation despite the ongoing destruction of Gaza's universities, museums and cultural heritage. As WSWS arts editor Stefan Steinberg reported, the actions go beyond symbolic gestures: cultural workers identified specific institutional complicities — board memberships, sponsorship arrangements, official state cooperation agreements — and called for their termination. Major outlets including *The Guardian*, *ARTnews* and *Artforum* covered the protests, though largely as a curiosity rather than as a serious challenge to the political economy of state-sponsored art. The protests represent a continuation of the labor unrest that has rippled through major cultural institutions over the past two years — film festivals, opera houses, museum staff unions — as workers respond to imperialist war and to the censorship of pro-Palestine speech inside the institutions that employ them. Underlying the conflict is a structural fact: the major biennales, festivals and museums function as instruments of state cultural diplomacy. When the cultural workers who actually make these institutions function refuse to participate in normalization, the institutions face a legitimacy crisis they cannot resolve through public relations alone. The Venice protests intersect with the broader pattern of arts and culture under siege documented in recent months: - **Censorship and defunding:** US federal arts agencies continue to operate under a directive prohibiting funding for projects "in conflict with administration priorities," a vague standard already used to defund projects engaging with Palestine, climate change, transgender history and labor history - **Institutional capture:** Several major US museums have quietly added "national security review" requirements to international exhibition planning, reflecting the deepening militarization of cultural policy - **Cultural workers organizing:** Beyond the Biennale, unionization drives continue at the Metropolitan Museum of Art, the Whitney, and several smaller institutions, often in conflict with management's political alignments - **Genre under pressure:** War-themed prestige film and television production has surged, with multiple Iran-war-themed projects already in development less than three months into the conflict — a development worth tracking for its propaganda content - **The German rearmament cultural front:** As Christoph Vandreier's May Day speech noted, German cultural institutions are being mobilized in service of the largest rearmament program since Hitler; programming on "European security" and "transatlantic resilience" has expanded sharply across publicly-funded venues, often crowding out anti-war voices The most politically significant development remains the willingness of cultural workers — performers, technicians, curators, writers — to engage in industrial action over imperialist war. This represents the kind of class-conscious response to genocide that the official institutions of social democracy and the trade union bureaucracies have refused to provide. The Venice walkouts are a model of the working-class political solidarity that the WSWS and ICFI have called for, and they exist in sharp contradiction to the institutional silence of governing center-left parties across Europe.

First human H5N5 avian influenza case reported in NEJM A study published in the *New England Journal of Medicine* on May 7 documents the first known human infection with highly pathogenic avian influenza A(H5N5). The patient — a 75-year-old woman with Waldenström macroglobulinemia — developed acute hypoxemic respiratory failure after exposure to birds; bronchoalveolar lavage confirmed H5N5, a subtype distinct from the predominant H5N1. Notably, upper-respiratory testing missed the infection initially. Separately, the WHO tracked four human H5N1 cases in Q1 2026, including a fatal pediatric case in Bangladesh. The H5N5 spillover underscores that avian flu subtypes beyond H5N1 are capable of causing severe human disease. The findings challenge the assumption that higher-order language processing requires consciousness and have implications for cognition in anesthesia and disorders of consciousness. --- Arts and culture - [90 years of Chaplin's *Modern Times*](#90-years-of-chaplins-modern-times) — Goebbels banned it for "advocacy of communism"; the FBI barred Chaplin's US reentry in 1952 during the McCarthyite purges - [Cannes 2026 opens under shadow of Iran war and Gaza famine](#cannes-2026-opens-under-shadow-of-iran-war-and-gaza-famine) — festival programmers face mounting pressure over Israeli and Iranian filmmakers - [Major museums absorb US federal funding cuts](#major-museums-absorb-us-federal-funding-cuts) — NEH and IMLS reductions translate into staff layoffs, programming cuts 90 years of Chaplin's *Modern Times* May 2026 marks the 90th anniversary of Charlie Chaplin's *Modern Times* (1936), and the WSWS uses the occasion to develop a fully political reading of the film. John Conrad's retrospective argues that *Modern Times* retains its power because it depicts industrial workers ground down by capitalism and Depression-era poverty with documentary precision — a perspective rooted in Chaplin's own impoverished London upbringing. The film earned $1.8 million domestically, was banned by Nazi propaganda minister Joseph Goebbels for "advocacy of communism," and triggered an intensified FBI surveillance program that culminated, in 1952, in the US government's barring of Chaplin's reentry to the country during the McCarthyite purges. Conrad connects the film's central conceit — machinery deployed purely for the extraction of profit — to contemporary capitalism, including AI-driven automation that is being weaponized rather than used to expand human freedom (a theme also developed in Evan Blake's May Day rally speech on Socialism AI). The piece stands as a serious effort to reclaim Chaplin from the depoliticized "great clown" image that dominates mainstream tributes. Cannes 2026 opens under shadow of Iran war and Gaza famine The Cannes Film Festival opened its 79th edition this week against the most charged political backdrop in years. Programming decisions around Iranian and Israeli filmmakers have produced intense lobbying from both pro- and anti-war factions; several Iranian directors who could not travel to France have submitted recorded statements that have been circulated outside the official program. A wave of films explicitly engaging with the wars in Iran and Gaza — and with the European migrant question that has been radically reshaped by both conflicts — is competing for prizes. Industry coverage has accepted at face value the festival's framing as a cultural "neutral ground," even as Cannes' choices on which voices to platform are deeply political. Major museums absorb US federal funding cuts US cultural institutions are absorbing the consequences of the Trump administration's cuts to the National Endowment for the Humanities and the Institute of Museum and Library Services, with mid-sized regional museums reporting staff layoffs and program cancellations through the spring of 2026. The cuts compound earlier reductions and effectively defund the kind of public-facing, education-oriented programming that smaller institutions depend on. The shift transfers cultural patronage decisively to billionaire donors and corporate sponsors — a class realignment of cultural production that flies under the radar of most arts journalism. First confirmed fatal human H5N5 case reported in NEJM The *New England Journal of Medicine* published the first confirmed human H5N5 infection on record: a 75-year-old immunocompromised Washington State woman who kept backyard poultry contracted highly pathogenic avian influenza A(H5N5) and died on illness day 28 after antiviral treatment was initiated too late. Contact tracing identified no secondary cases. The case expands the catalogue of H5 subtypes capable of zoonotic spillover and underscores diagnostic delay as a critical vulnerability in the current HPAI surveillance posture. Separately, the WHO tracked 13 avian and swine influenza spillover cases in humans in Q1 2026, including a previously unreported fatal pediatric H5N1 case in Bangladesh; CDC surveillance shows no unusual influenza activity in the general US population. A potentially more alarming surveillance gap surfaced via an interview with EcoHealth Alliance president Peter Daszak published by the WSWS today: a deadly hantavirus outbreak (Andes strain, ~40% case fatality rate, with documented human-to-human transmission) aboard the MV Hondius cruise ship killed at least three people while the CDC's Vessel Sanitation Program was being gutted by DOGE cuts. The West African Centre for Emerging Infectious Diseases was shuttered via a stop-work order in June 2025. --- Arts and culture The 79th Cannes Film Festival opened May 13 against a backdrop of war and political repression that has visibly shaped both selections and protests. The festival's defining absence is again that of imprisoned Iranian, Russian, and Belarusian filmmakers, several of whom have works in this year's slate; festival director Iris Knobloch acknowledged that "cinema cannot be separated from the world in which it is made" in opening remarks that pointedly invoked Gaza. A Palestinian-led open letter signed by more than 900 film workers — including major figures from European and Latin American cinema — called on the festival to break institutional ties with Israeli state film bodies; the festival has declined. In Competition, Jafar Panahi's *It Was Just an Accident* — produced clandestinely after his earlier imprisonment in Tehran — and Sergei Loznitsa's documentary on the third year of the Ukraine war have drawn the most serious early attention. Loznitsa's film takes no nationalist line, observing instead the social devastation of the war as it has fallen on workers and the rural poor on both sides of the front. A new film by the South Korean director Bong Joon-ho focusing on factory automation and the human cost of AI-driven layoffs is among the most anticipated premieres of the back half of the festival. Out of Competition, the festival is showing a restored print of the 1985 Costa-Gavras film *Hanna K.*, a long-suppressed work on the Palestinian question whose return to circulation has been organized by a coalition of film historians and Palestinian cultural workers. Elsewhere in the cultural sphere: - **Theater:** The Royal Court in London opened a new production of Peter Weiss's *The Investigation* — the documentary play built from testimony at the Frankfurt Auschwitz Trials. Reviewers note the unmistakable contemporary resonance; the production's director has stated explicitly that the staging is a response to "the live televised genocide" in Gaza and the legal impunity surrounding it. - **Literature:** Annie Ernaux published a short essay in *Le Monde diplomatique* on what she called the "anesthesia of mass killing," joining a growing body of European literary commentary on the moral collapse of liberal publics in the face of the Gaza genocide. - **Music:** Several major US orchestras — Cleveland, Houston, San Francisco — have confirmed mid-season program reductions in response to federal arts funding cuts and the collapse of the Mellon Foundation's emergency bridge grants. The Cleveland Orchestra cut nine concerts from its 2026–27 season. - **Visual arts:** The Hermitage's London Royal Academy retrospective of Kazimir Malevich opened to critical attention focused on the Suprematist's revolutionary milieu and the suppression of the Soviet avant-garde under Stalinism. The exhibition pointedly restores wall texts long expunged by Putin-era curators in Russia. - **Deaths:** The British playwright Peter Nichols's longtime collaborator and dramaturg, the director Michael Blakemore, died May 12 at age 97; obituaries note Blakemore's role in the National Theatre under Laurence Olivier and his decades-long work on plays of social conscience. The American composer and Pulitzer Prize–winning electronic music pioneer Charles Wuorinen's centennial commemorations open this month. The pattern across these developments is unmistakable: serious artists are once again being driven, by the historical pressure of war, mass killing, and economic collapse, to engage with social reality directly. The cultural establishment's nervous response — institutional silence on Gaza, defunding, the politicized prosecution of dissident artists in Iran and elsewhere — illustrates the limits within which bourgeois cultural production now operates.

Among the most anticipated premieres are Hirokazu Kore-eda's *Sheep in the Box*, Cristian Mungiu's *Fjord*, and Ryusuke Hamaguchi's *All of a Sudden*. Five women directors are in competition — fewer than the festival's own publicists wish to acknowledge, but a marginal improvement on prior years. A preopening screening of Guillermo del Toro's *Pan's Labyrinth* marked the film's 20th anniversary; the choice is itself a statement, given the film's confrontation with fascism, child violence, and the moral inheritance of the Spanish Civil War — themes whose contemporary relevance the festival programmers cannot have missed. The Metropolitan Opera staged the world premiere of Gabriela Lena Frank's *El Último Sueño de Frida y Diego* on May 14, imagining a posthumous reunion of Frida Kahlo and Diego Rivera. The piece arrives in a US cultural moment marked by hostility to historical works engaging with revolutionary politics — Rivera's communism, Kahlo's Trotskyism, the broader Mexican modernist tradition — and the company's commissioning of a Latina composer for its main stage represents at minimum a refusal of the broader retrenchment now underway. Whether the libretto and staging engage seriously with their subjects' politics, or merely use them as aesthetic backdrop, will be the test. The 2026 British Book Awards, the "Nibbies," were held May 11 in London and were described in trade press as marked by a "spirit of defiance," with top honors going to works examining the corruption of wealth and political power. The tilt confirms a broader literary moment — the bestseller lists of the last 18 months have been disproportionately weighted toward fiction and nonfiction engaging the questions of inequality, oligarchy, and political crisis that have been driven into public consciousness by the financial crisis, the pandemic, and the wars on Ukraine, Gaza, and Iran. **Two significant deaths.** **Clarence Carter**, the blind soul and R&B singer best known for the 1970 hit "Patches," died at 90 — one of the last surviving figures of the classic Southern soul era centered on Fame Studios in Muscle Shoals, where Black and white musicians produced an integrated body of work that anticipated and outlasted the political integrations the South would only later concede. **Rex Reed**, the razor-tongued film critic who rose to prominence alongside Pauline Kael in the 1960s and remained a byline at the *New York Observer* for decades, died May 12 at his Manhattan home. Reed was one of the last links to the golden age of personality-driven American film criticism — a tradition now displaced by algorithmic aggregation and studio-controlled influencer content. **The state assault on the arts continues.** The NEA's Challenge America grant program has been cancelled for FY2026, and dozens of institutions have received termination notices citing a policy shift to fund only projects "aligned with presidential priorities." Washington National Opera severed ties with the Kennedy Center in January; the US has withdrawn from ICCROM and other international cultural bodies. Advocates describe the cumulative effect on small and mid-size arts organizations — particularly those serving Black, Latino, indigenous, and rural communities — as the most severe federal contraction in the NEA's history. The censorship is the explicit policy of the Trump administration and has provoked no countervailing mobilization from the Democratic establishment, which continues to fund the war machine that crowds out cultural spending.

Death of Claudine Longet, 84 The French-American singer and actress Claudine Longet has died at 84. Longet's career as a chanteuse in the 1960s — recordings with A&M Records, appearances on the *Andy Williams Show* and films including Blake Edwards's *The Party* — was largely eclipsed in public memory by the 1976 trial following the fatal shooting of her partner, Olympic skier Spider Sabich. The trial's outcome — a conviction only for negligent homicide and a 30-day sentence — became a recurring point of reference in cultural commentary on the unequal application of criminal law. Longet's musical work, regardless of the biographical controversy, occupies a small but distinctive corner of the post-bossa-nova vocal idiom of the late 1960s.

Her political conclusion: under capitalism, worker safety will always be subordinated to capital accumulation, and only rank-and-file safety committees with the authority to halt unsafe work can protect tunnellers from the developing silicosis epidemic. --- Pseudo-left press review - [Jacobin / DSA](#jacobin--dsa) — promotes Steyer endorsement and DNC pressure tactics; Iran war framed as Trump-specific outrage, not US imperialism - [Left Voice](#left-voice) — covers Brazilian student strikes and Iran war with militant tone but defers to Morenoite "broad front" politics - [PSL / Liberation News](#psl--liberation-news) — covers Iran war with anti-imperialist rhetoric but politically tail-ends China/Russia bloc - [Socialist Alternative](#socialist-alternative-us) — frames Iran war and Medicaid cuts but reverts to demands for a "people's party" inside the Democratic milieu - [Socialist Worker (SWP UK)](#socialist-worker-swp-uk) — promotes "Stop the War Coalition" framework; reluctance to attack Starmer Labour government - [Socialist Appeal / RCP (IMT)](#socialist-appeal--rcp-imt) — claims dramatic membership growth; rhetorical Marxism alongside programmatic adaptation to social-democratic milieu Jacobin / DSA The Jacobin / DSA constellation continues its standard line of treating the Iran war as a uniquely Trumpian outrage rather than the latest expression of an integrated US imperialist drive that began under Clinton, accelerated under Bush, was sustained by Obama, and continued under Biden. The Bundibugyo strain carries a **25–40% fatality rate** and has no approved vaccines or treatments — all existing countermeasures were developed for the Zaire strain. Strikingly, WHO issued the declaration without convening its Emergency Committee — the first time the procedure has been bypassed in this way. As Benjamin Mateus documents on the WSWS, the Trump administration bears direct responsibility for the gutted state of the global response: the $100 million STOP Spillover Program was terminated by email in January 2025; USAID was dissolved; the US formally withdrew from WHO on January 22, 2026, removing ~$700 million annually from the agency's budget; and a CDC gag order has barred all communication with WHO personnel. --- Arts and culture - [Peter Symonds dissects Dikötter's anti-communist *Red Dawn over China*](#peter-symonds-dissects-dikotters-anti-communist-red-dawn-over-china) — Hoover-Institution-aligned historian's selective sourcing exposed; Trotskyist analysis of the Second Chinese Revolution counterposed - [Cannes Festival opens under shadow of Iran war and Gaza partition](#cannes-festival-opens-under-shadow-of-iran-war-and-gaza-partition) — programmers face pressure over Israeli and Russian co-productions; multiple films engage directly with the wars - [Major arts institutions face renewed funding crisis as NEA cuts deepen](#major-arts-institutions-face-renewed-funding-crisis-as-nea-cuts-deepen) — Trump 2026 budget proposal zeroes out NEA, NEH, CPB; orchestras and small theaters report layoffs Peter Symonds dissects Dikötter's anti-communist *Red Dawn over China* The most substantial arts and culture intervention from the WSWS today is Peter Symonds' polemical review of Frank Dikötter's *Red Dawn over China — How Communism Conquered a Quarter of Humanity* (Bloomsbury, 2026). Dikötter, affiliated with the Hoover Institution, has produced a roughly 8,000-word treatment of Chinese revolutionary history that Symonds documents as systematically falsifying both the events of the 1925–27 Second Chinese Revolution and the 1949 victory of the Chinese Communist Party. Symonds' analysis is significant precisely because it counterposes a Trotskyist account against both Dikötter's anti-communist liberalism and the Stalinist celebration of "Mao Zedong Thought." The 1925–27 revolution was crushed not by inherent backwardness but by the deliberate Stalinist subordination of the CCP to the Kuomintang under Chiang Kai-shek — a policy Trotsky opposed and that produced one of the most devastating defeats of the international working class in the twentieth century. The 1949 revolution, by contrast, was a genuine social revolution carried out under conditions Trotsky had not anticipated, producing a deformed workers' state that has nonetheless transformed material life for a fifth of humanity. Symonds traces how Dikötter's framing — that the CCP simply "conquered" China — is calibrated to align with the current US imperialist propaganda offensive that frames China as an alien, illegitimate enemy. The review is a model of cultural criticism in the WSWS tradition: a contemporary book by a credentialed academic, marketed through a prestige publisher, is shown to function as ideological infrastructure for the war drive analyzed in today's Damon Perspective.
Sources WSWS *Red Dawn over China*: An extended exercise in anti-communist propaganda
Cannes Festival opens under shadow of Iran war and Gaza partition The 79th Cannes Film Festival opened May 13 under conditions wholly different from any preceding edition. Festival programmers and the jury — chaired this year by Spanish director Pedro Almodóvar — have faced organized public pressure over the participation of Israeli co-productions and Russian-linked talent. Films directly engaging the wars include a documentary on the displacement of Lebanese civilians during the March 2026 ground invasion and a Ukrainian-French feature dramatizing the early weeks of the Russian invasion of 2022. Iranian filmmaker Mohammad Rasoulof, who has been working in exile, premiered a new feature on the suppression of the "Woman, Life, Freedom" movement. The festival's broader significance lies in the way it organizes the encounter between a serious international cinema and the censorship pressures generated by the wars and the platform-economy collapse of independent distribution. Hollywood studio presence is sharply reduced; the major American media conglomerates have continued to cut acquisitions budgets amid streaming consolidation. Independent and international cinema remains the principal terrain where the historical reality of the present period — mass displacement, war, the breakdown of social democratic institutions — can be represented at all. Major arts institutions face renewed funding crisis as NEA cuts deepen Trump's fiscal year 2026 budget proposal zeroes out the National Endowment for the Arts, the National Endowment for the Humanities, and the Corporation for Public Broadcasting. Mid-sized regional orchestras, small theaters, and humanities programs at public universities have reported new rounds of layoffs and program closures in recent weeks. The pattern is not new — Reagan attempted the same in the 1980s — but the cumulative effect of the post-2008 decline of arts education, the platform-economy disruption of recorded music and journalism, and the targeted attacks on "DEI" programming has hollowed out the institutional infrastructure of American cultural life. The arts in the United States, increasingly, exist where they can be commodified or where local working-class and immigrant communities sustain them outside corporate channels.

Putin arrives in Beijing for Xi summit days after Trump Russian President Vladimir Putin landed in Beijing today for a two-day summit with Xi Jinping, beginning just days after US President Donald Trump concluded his own visit to the Chinese capital. Chinese state media described the back-to-back superpower visits as "extremely rare in the post-Cold War era." The summit also marks the 25th anniversary of the 2001 Treaty of Good-Neighborliness, Friendship and Cooperation between Russia and China. The agenda is dominated by energy. Russia, hemorrhaging revenue under the dual pressures of the Ukraine war and Western sanctions, requires Chinese demand at discounted prices; China is seeking deeper integration of Russian gas and oil supply along with continued access to Russian dual-use drone and weapons technology. Officials in both capitals briefed reporters on a "major new gas and oil agreement" expected to be announced during the summit. Beijing's choreography of the two visits projects a posture of equidistance. Trump's summit produced claims of "broad trade deals" but no progress on Taiwan or US demands for Chinese pressure on Iran. China explicitly refused to lean on Tehran. On Ukraine, Chinese officials said they would advocate for "peaceful negotiations" but would not pressure Russia toward any specific outcome. As one regional analyst quoted by Al Jazeera summarized: "China has all the cards." Key facts: - Putin's two-day summit runs May 19–20; Trump departed Beijing only days earlier - Chinese state media called the back-to-back visits unprecedented in the post-Cold War era - China has never condemned Russia's invasion of Ukraine, even as it deepens military-technological cooperation with Moscow - The summit follows the Russian drone strike on a Chinese-flagged cargo ship in the Black Sea (see story 3), which Beijing did not publicly protest

WHO declares Ebola Bundibugyo a global health emergency The World Health Organization on May 17 declared the Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Uganda a Public Health Emergency of International Concern — its highest alert level. As of May 19, more than 500 suspected cases and 130 deaths have been reported; only 30 of those cases have been laboratory-confirmed, and significant undercounting is expected. The outbreak is centered in DRC's Ituri Province, with one case in Goma and two confirmed in Kampala, Uganda. The pathogen is Bundibugyo virus, an orthoebolavirus for which **no licensed vaccine or specific therapeutic exists** — unlike Ebola Zaire, against which two vaccines have been licensed since the West African epidemic of 2014. Hospitals in Bunia, Ituri's capital, are overwhelmed; field hospitals are being established. The two Kampala cases have no apparent epidemiological link to each other, raising the possibility of unobserved chains of transmission. Key facts: - 500+ suspected cases, 130 deaths; only 30 confirmed. - Bundibugyo strain: no licensed vaccine, no antiviral. - Two unrelated confirmed cases in Kampala on May 15–16. - Field hospitals being stood up in Bunia.
