--- Arts and culture The political climate of war abroad and oligarchic consolidation at home has continued to shape the cultural moment. Two threads dominate the past 24 hours: a series of attempts by Hollywood and the streaming industry to engage with the Iran war and broader Middle East violence, often in evasive or jingoistic forms; and the unfolding crisis at the great cultural institutions, which are being squeezed simultaneously by Trump-era cultural decrees and by their own donor classes. The 79th Cannes Film Festival, which concluded last weekend, continues to reverberate through the trade press, with critics noting the unusual political weight of this year's selection — a Brazilian-Argentine-French co-production on the suppression of striker mobilizations during the 1973 Pinochet coup, an Iranian-French film smuggled out of Tehran during the war, and a Ukrainian documentary built from frontline footage. The jury's choice to award the Palme d'Or to the Iranian work was both a recognition of the courage of its makers and a tacit rebuke of the western military campaign now underway against the country in which it was filmed. That such a gesture is necessary at all is a measure of how thoroughly the broader film industry has abandoned political seriousness; the festival was otherwise dominated by big-budget franchise sequels, biopics of inoffensive figures and an unmistakable nostalgia for the Cold War period. Hollywood's relationship to the Iran war has been openly opportunistic. Within the past two months, multiple studios have green-lit projects framed around US naval operations in the Persian Gulf — variants of *Top Gun*-style militarist entertainment that present US strikes as inherently righteous and Iranian civilians as either invisible or as obstacles to be overcome. As the WSWS arts pages have observed repeatedly, this is the same cultural-industrial complex that gave us the genre of post-9/11 "war on terror" cinema two decades ago: militarist propaganda dressed as middlebrow drama. The current cycle is being accelerated by Pentagon technical-support agreements with major studios and by the integration of military-industrial-funded "consultants" into writers' rooms. In the institutional space, the Smithsonian continues to face direct political pressure under a Trump executive order requiring the removal of exhibitions deemed insufficiently celebratory of American history. Curators have reported the removal of materials on slavery, the labor movement and the civil rights struggle — even from museums founded specifically to document those histories. The Metropolitan Opera in New York has announced significant cuts to its 2026-27 season, citing donor losses; the New York City Ballet has reduced its corps positions. These institutional retrenchments are occurring in parallel with the cultural strangulation of public broadcasting, with PBS and NPR facing further congressional funding reductions in the reconciliation package now stuck in Senate negotiations. Among the deaths this week, the death of the Russian poet **Olga Sedakova**, 76, has been noted in literary publications worldwide. Sedakova — one of the major Russian-language religious poets of the late Soviet and post-Soviet period, a translator of Rilke and Dante, and a public opponent of the Putin government's war on Ukraine — wrote some of the most spiritually serious verse of her generation. Her death removes a distinct moral voice from the contemporary Russian literary scene. In book publishing, **Hisham Matar's** new novel on the Libyan revolution and its aftermath has received significant attention in the British and US press. Matar, whose previous work *The Return* won the Pulitzer Prize, continues to engage seriously with the legacy of imperialist intervention in North Africa.

--- Arts and culture Romanian director Cristian Mungiu won the Palme d'Or at the 79th Cannes Film Festival for *Fjord*, starring Sebastian Stan and Renate Reinsve. The film follows a mixed Romanian-Norwegian couple who relocate to a remote fjord village and collide with locals holding a "very different outlook on life" — widely described as a culture-war drama. Mungiu becomes only the 11th filmmaker to win the Palme twice, following *4 Months, 3 Weeks and 2 Days* (2007), his unsparing portrait of clandestine abortion under the Ceaușescu dictatorship. US distributor NEON claimed its seventh consecutive Palme d'Or. That a director who emerged from the Romanian New Wave — a movement rooted in honest reckoning with the Stalinist bureaucracy and its aftermath — should now win for a study of rural insularity and cultural friction is itself telling. The best of this tradition has insisted on examining ordinary people caught in the machinery of social crisis; the question for *Fjord* is whether it interrogates the reactionary "outlook" it depicts or merely stages it as spectacle. NEON's commercial dominance of the Cannes prize also illustrates how even the festival's gestures toward serious cinema are absorbed into a tightly controlled distribution market. The other major cultural event of the week was a monument to that same market logic. As David Walsh wrote on the WSWS, a single Christie's evening saw **$1.1 billion** in art sold, headlined by Jackson Pollock's *Number 7A, 1948* at $181.2 million — three times his previous record — and a new record for a Constantin Brancusi work, drawn from the estate of media billionaire S.I. Newhouse, whose widow explained she was "downsizing her life." Walsh invokes Marx and Diderot to argue that when monetary exchange dominates art's purpose, something essential to human creativity is destroyed. The global art market — $59.6 billion in 2025 — represents, in his words, capitalism's "extreme, parasitic decay," with masterworks that could enrich public museums locked away in private vaults. Roundup: - The juxtaposition of the two stories is instructive: at Cannes, art as a contested terrain of social meaning; at Christie's, art as a pure asset class for a parasitic financial aristocracy. Both are products of the same epoch of social polarization. - The concentration of cultural ownership — record sums for canvases by Pollock and Brancusi — mirrors the concentration of wealth that has driven equity markets to record highs even amid mass layoffs and falling living standards.

The causative agent is the Bundibugyo virus (Orthoebolavirus bundibugyoense), for which there are no approved vaccines or treatments. At least four healthcare workers have died, and the WHO warns that high positivity rates among initial samples and rising syndromic reporting suggest the true outbreak is much larger than detected. Key facts: - The PHEIC was declared May 17; the outbreak does not yet meet pandemic-emergency criteria - Response is severely hampered by ongoing armed conflict and displacement in eastern DRC, collapsed health infrastructure, and high urban mobility — conditions rooted in decades of imperialist resource competition over cobalt, coltan, and gold

Callais ruling A sweeping Republican campaign to redraw congressional maps across the American South is underway following the Supreme Court's April 29 ruling in *Louisiana v. Callais*. By a 6–3 vote, the Court struck down Louisiana's congressional map containing a second majority-Black district as an unconstitutional racial gerrymander — a decision that, in practice, has gutted what remained of the 1965 Voting Rights Act's protections for minority-majority districts. Within weeks, several Southern states moved to redraw maps, claiming their own VRA-mandated majority-minority districts were now unconstitutional. In his Perspective on the WSWS, Patrick Martin catalogs the scope: Tennessee Republicans have already eliminated the heavily Black Memphis district, carving it into three rural-anchored constituencies; Louisiana and Alabama are moving to eliminate second majority-Black districts; and the veteran districts of South Carolina's Jim Clyburn and Mississippi's Bennie Thompson face erasure. Martin calculates the number of majority-Black seats across the Deep South could fall to as few as seven, even though African Americans make up over 30 percent of the region's population. He frames the drive as "an attack on the democratic rights of the working class as a whole," and notes the Democrats pursue their own gerrymanders in California and Virginia.

The memo directs officers to weigh all factors case by case and emphasizes consular processing abroad as the default pathway, potentially forcing applicants to attend interviews in their home countries, where overstays can trigger three- to ten-year reentry bans. As Jacob Crosse reported on the WSWS, immigrant spouses of US citizens face the greatest impact — potentially becoming stranded in countries where the Trump administration restricts entry or where US consular services are suspended. Former Biden-era USCIS official Doug Rand warned that hundreds of thousands of cases could be affected. Immigration analysts note the memo's harsher framing came from an agency press statement rather than the operative guidance, but the chilling effect on family-based applicants is immediate.

--- Arts and culture The 79th Cannes Film Festival closed May 23, awarding the Palme d'Or to Romanian director Cristian Mungiu's *Fjord*, a culture-war drama set in Norway starring Sebastian Stan and Renate Reinsve. Mungiu becomes only the tenth director to win the Palme twice, having previously taken the prize for *4 Months, 3 Weeks and 2 Days* (2007), a harrowing account of clandestine abortion under Ceaușescu's police state. The recognition of Mungiu — one of the foremost living practitioners of social realism, whose work dissects the moral wreckage left by authoritarianism and the market — stands as an implicit rebuke to the spectacle-driven priorities of the commercial film industry. The Grand Prix went to Russian director Andrei Zvyagintsev's *Minotaur*; Zvyagintsev's earlier *Leviathan* offered one of the sharpest cinematic indictments of corruption and despair in post-Soviet Russia, and his presence in competition is notable given the cultural boycotts that have accompanied the Ukraine war. The jury was chaired by South Korean director Park Chan-wook. That a festival can honor both a Romanian chronicler of dictatorship and a Russian critic of his own society's decay points to a current in serious filmmaking that resists the nationalist and militarist pressures bearing down on cultural life. The challenge for these works is reaching audiences through a distribution apparatus increasingly geared toward franchise product and algorithmic streaming. --- Arts and culture The most substantive cultural intervention in the past 24 hours comes from the WSWS's review of Netflix's *Beef* Season 2, which doubles as a lens on the broader state of socially conscious television. Critic Matthew Brennan praises the season's performances — particularly veteran Korean actors Youn Yuh-jung and Song Kang-ho — and its central conceit: a California country club functioning as a metaphor for capitalist exclusion and class hierarchy, distilled in the line, "The people in charge have made it impossible for us." Yet Brennan faults the season for retreating into fatalistic pessimism. Rather than depicting resistance or an alternative, the struggling working-class couple Ashley and Austin end by absorbing the corruption of the wealthy elite. The ending is "cyclical," and Brennan argues the creators must pursue their social themes "with greater seriousness and historical awareness" if the work is to amount to more than a stylish portrait of despair. This pessimism is itself a symptom of the cultural moment. Across contemporary television and film, genuine class antagonism is increasingly acknowledged on screen — only to be resolved in resignation, individual collapse, or the substitution of identity for class. The WSWS framework insists that art be understood in its social and historical context: *Beef*'s instinct to name capitalist exclusion is a real artistic strength, but its inability to imagine a way out reflects the demoralization cultivated by decades of political reaction and the absence, until recently, of a visible working-class movement. The period also underscores the deepening assault on cultural and media workers as political actors. The Treasury Department's OFAC subpoenas targeting streamer and commentator Hasan Piker — one of the most-watched political broadcasters of his generation — alongside roughly 40 others over a humanitarian trip to Cuba represent a direct attempt to criminalize the work of independent media and cultural figures who dissent from imperialist policy. The targeting of a major streaming personality signals that the state increasingly regards the cultural sphere itself as a battleground, where commentary, journalism, and art that oppose war and blockade are to be policed as security threats. Roundup: - **Television:** *Beef* Season 2's class metaphor and its retreat into fatalism exemplify the limits of liberal social commentary that names inequality without imagining its overcoming. - **Media and free expression:** The OFAC probe into Hasan Piker and Medea Benjamin marks an escalation in the policing of cultural and journalistic figures, raising direct censorship implications for the broadcasting and documentary sphere. - **Cultural climate:** The convergence of war, austerity, and authoritarianism continues to shape artistic production, rewarding works that depict suffering while discouraging those that point toward collective struggle.

As of May 21, the CDC has confirmed 1,952 cases across 40 jurisdictions in 2026, with 93% outbreak-associated; Utah alone accounts for 400-plus cases, and a 600-case South Carolina outbreak was only recently declared over. Analysts now consider the US "highly likely" to lose the measles elimination status it has held since 2000, with summer travel expected to accelerate spread. Internationally, the catastrophe is far graver: as Wimal Perera reported on the WSWS, Bangladesh's outbreak has killed 555 children, roughly 80% of them under five, with 66,023 suspected cases — a disaster Perera attributes to skipped national vaccination campaigns and IMF-driven austerity, not natural causes. The most significant peer-reviewed study is a *Science Advances* analysis of more than 21,000 river systems from 1985–2023, which found nearly 80% have experienced declining dissolved oxygen at an average of −0.045 mg/L per decade, projected to accelerate sharply by century's end. Fish require 6–8 mg/L for health and die below 2 mg/L; some 200 million people depend on river fisheries for protein. As Philip Guelpa noted on the WSWS, global warming accounts for 62.7% of the deoxygenation and heatwaves for 22.7%. Roundup: - **H5N1:** WHO tracked 13 avian/swine flu cases in humans in Q1 2026, including a newly reported fatal H5N1 case in a child in Bangladesh; CDC reports no unusual US influenza activity, though the virus remains widespread in dairy cattle and wild birds - **COVID-19:** Activity is "low" nationally with wastewater at its lowest since spring 2021, but cases are "growing" in Georgia, Florida, and Louisiana; dominant variant is XFG.1.1 (32%); ~1,500 weekly hospital admissions forecast - **CERN:** Researchers at the Large Hadron Collider report the strongest hints yet of physics beyond the Standard Model — potentially pointing to new particles or forces if confirmed - **EU AI Act:** On May 7 legislators finalized the "AI Omnibus," lightening compliance burdens on SMEs, expanding regulatory sandboxes, and banning AI-generated non-consensual intimate imagery - **US AI policy:** The Trump administration is now weighing federal oversight of advanced AI models, driven by national-security concerns over Anthropic's cyber-capable "Mythos" model — a reversal of its prior deregulatory stance - **Vatican:** Pope Leo XIV's first encyclical, *Magnifica Humanitas*, frames AI regulation as a moral imperative; OpenAI's Sam Altman, speaking in Sydney, walked back his prior predictions of sweeping near-term white-collar job losses

--- Arts and culture The most significant cultural intervention reviewed by the WSWS over the past day is *Enough is Enough* (*Trop c'est trop*), Elisé Sawasawa's documentary on the catastrophe in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, reviewed by David Walsh and Joanne Laurier. The film documents a country ranked 171st of 193 on the Human Development Index, where roughly 120 armed groups operate in the east and the January 2025 fall of Goma to Rwandan-backed M23 rebels displaced millions — all while UN peacekeeping spent $1.5 billion annually over two decades to no protective effect. Walsh and Laurier use the documentary to insist that the crisis cannot be understood apart from imperialism's historical role, from King Leopold II's genocide through the present scramble for the DRC's cobalt (the world's largest supply), coltan (70% of global supply), and diamonds. The political conclusion — that the catastrophe demands international working-class resistance rather than NGO humanitarian management — exemplifies the WSWS approach of situating art in its full social and historical context rather than treating it as content. The day's cultural discourse was also marked by the Vatican's formal entry into the debate over technology and human life. Pope Leo XIV's inaugural encyclical, *Magnifica Humanitas*, frames artificial intelligence as a moral and civilizational question and calls for international governance structures — a significant ideological intervention by the Catholic hierarchy that simultaneously expresses real anxieties about technology's social effects and seeks to position the Church as moral arbiter over questions that are fundamentally ones of class and ownership. Roundup: - **Film:** Independent cinema continues to draw critical attention for offering an alternative to formulaic studio production; the broader trend reflects audiences and critics searching for work with genuine human content amid the dominance of franchise and algorithm-driven entertainment - **Cultural politics:** The persistent under-representation of catastrophes like the DRC, Sudan, and Bangladesh in mainstream cultural production — even as Ukraine and Gaza receive sustained treatment — reflects the same media hierarchy that ranks some lives as newsworthy and others as invisible, a question serious artists and critics increasingly confront - **Historical memory:** Renewed cultural attention to militarism and historical revisionism — including debate over the rehabilitation of war and nationalism in several countries — underscores the urgency of art that defends historical truth against official mythmaking The WSWS framework remains that genuine artistic achievement is recognized regardless of the artist's politics, while nationalist, militarist, and identitarian tendencies in cultural production are identified for what they are — adaptations to the demands of a ruling class preparing for war and austerity.
Sources WSWS Enough is Enough: Catastrophe in the Democratic Republic of the Congo · Tech Startups Pope Leo XIV issues first encyclical calling for AI regulation

--- Arts and culture The death of **Sonny Rollins**, the tenor saxophonist universally known as the "Saxophone Colossus," dominates the cultural week. Rollins died May 25 at his home in Woodstock, New York, at the age of **95**. With John Coltrane and Charlie Parker, he was among the most influential saxophonists of the twentieth century and one of the last surviving giants of the bebop and hard-bop eras. Born September 7, 1930, in New York City, Rollins grew up on Harlem's Sugar Hill, the "strivers' row" where many of the era's leading jazz musicians lived. His 1956 album *Saxophone Colossus* — and its defining track "St. Thomas," drawn from his Caribbean heritage — established him as a peerless improviser whose long, architecturally constructed solos rewrote the language of the instrument. His artistic seriousness was legendary: at the height of his fame in the late 1950s he **withdrew from public performance** for two years, practicing alone at night on the walkway of the **Williamsburg Bridge**; his 1962 return, the album *The Bridge*, was greeted as a cultural event. Rollins embodied the deep connection between jazz and the social struggles of the Black working class and the broader democratic movements of the mid-twentieth century — his 1958 *Freedom Suite* was one of the first explicit musical statements against racial oppression in the United States. His passing severs one of the last living links to a period in which a popular American art form reached extraordinary heights of collective and individual creativity. The tributes from the *Washington Post*, NPR, *Rolling Stone* and CNN reflect a recognition, even in the bourgeois press, that an irreplaceable artist has been lost. The month has been heavy with losses across the arts: - **Dennis Locorriere**, lead singer of Dr. Hook, died May 16 of kidney disease at 76; the group scored six US Top 10 hits including "Sylvia's Mother" - **Tom Kane**, the prolific voice actor (Professor Utonium in *The Powerpuff Girls*), died May 18 at 64 of complications from a stroke - **Grizz Chapman**, the actor known from *30 Rock*, died May 22 at 52 after years of illness and dialysis — a reminder of the toll of inadequate healthcare access - **Rob Base**, the hip-hop artist, died of cancer at 59 - **Claudine Longet**, French singer and actress, died May 15 at 84 On the festival circuit, the **Lanzarote International Film Festival** (May 13–23) spotlighted debut features from Romania, Bulgaria and Ukraine, while the Smithsonian's **IlluminAsia** festival continued in Washington. Such programming, foregrounding work from smaller national cinemas and immigrant communities, stands in contrast to the increasingly consolidated, franchise-driven output of the major studios — a tension between genuine artistic exploration and the commodification of culture that the WSWS arts coverage consistently examines.

US-Iran ceasefire extension stalls as Trump withholds approval US and Iranian negotiators reached a tentative agreement to extend the three-month-old ceasefire by 60 days and open fresh nuclear talks, but President Trump's Situation Room meeting on May 29 ended without a decision. Under the draft terms, Iran would clear all mines from the Strait of Hormuz within 30 days; in return, Washington would gradually lift its naval blockade on Iranian ports and relax sanctions to permit increased Iranian oil exports. The central obstacle remains Iran's stockpile of **440.9 kilograms of uranium enriched to 60 percent**. Trump opposes transferring the material to either China or Russia, and no third-party custodian has been agreed. Tehran further demands that any deal halt Israeli military operations against Hezbollah in Lebanon — a condition Washington has not accepted. Key facts: - Vice President JD Vance: *"It's hard to say exactly when or if the president's going to sign."* - Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, speaking at the Shangri-La Dialogue in Singapore on May 30, said the US is *"more than capable"* of resuming strikes. - An adviser to Iran's supreme leader accused Trump of *"betraying diplomacy for the third time"* by maintaining the blockade while negotiating. - Iranian forces fired ballistic missiles at Kuwait and launched drones toward the Strait on May 29, even as talks continued. The WSWS has tracked the US-Israel war on Iran since February as a calculated imperialist war drive, not a misadventure — the negotiation posture is a tactic within that drive, not a departure from it.

Phase 3 trial: bepirovirsen "functionally cures" 1-in-5 hepatitis B patients In the global B-Well Phase 3 trial (1,834 participants, 29 countries) published in the **NEJM**, **19–20 percent of patients** achieved a functional cure (sustained HBsAg loss plus undetectable viral DNA) after 24 weeks of the RNA-targeting drug bepirovirsen, versus **0 percent on placebo** and ~3 percent with the current decade-long standard of care. It is the first Phase 3 evidence that fixed-duration therapy can durably suppress hepatitis B, which chronically infects ~300 million people worldwide. An FDA priority-review decision is expected in Q3 2026. --- Arts and culture The **79th Festival de Cannes** closed with the Palme d'Or awarded to *Fjord*, a Norway-set drama by Cristian Mungiu (a previous Palme winner for *4 Months, 3 Weeks and 2 Days*), starring Sebastian Stan and Renate Reinsve. The choice of a director whose work has consistently dramatized the corrosive pressures of bureaucracy, poverty and moral compromise on ordinary people is significant at a moment of war and deepening social crisis — a counterweight to the festival's celebrity spectacle, which this year included honorary Palmes for Peter Jackson, John Travolta and Barbra Streisand. The jury, presided over by Park Chan-wook and including Demi Moore, Ruth Negga, Chloé Zhao and Stellan Skarsgård, distributed its major acting prizes in ways worth noting: - **Best Actor** went jointly to Valentin Campagne and Emmanuel Macchia in Lukas Dhont's *Coward*, continuing Dhont's preoccupation with masculinity, shame and adolescent vulnerability. - **Best Actress** was shared by Virginie Efira and Tao Okamoto for Ryusuke Hamaguchi's *All of a Sudden* — Hamaguchi again probing chance, intimacy and the fragility of bourgeois domestic life. - **Best Screenplay** went to Emmanuel Marre's *A Man of His Time*. The festival unfolds against the backdrop of an industry reshaped by streaming consolidation, AI anxieties and the political pressures of the present conjuncture. Cannes has historically been a venue where serious filmmaking — engaging war, class and historical memory — competes for attention against the marketing machinery of the culture industry. The honorary tributes to aging Hollywood and blockbuster figures reflect that tension: genuine artistic achievement (Mungiu, Hamaguchi, Dhont) sharing a stage with the nostalgia economy. Broader cultural notes: - The selection of European auteurs working in a humanist, socially attentive register — rather than the nationalist or militarist themes increasingly promoted in state-backed cultural production — is a welcome sign, though the festival remains an elite marketplace insulated from the conditions of working-class audiences priced out of cinema. - The continued prominence of films interrogating private life and moral failure (Hamaguchi, Dhont) points to a cinema reaching for psychological truth in the absence of a broader political vocabulary — a limitation, not merely a virtue, of much contemporary art-house work. The task for a Marxist criticism is to assess these works not as festival trophies or lifestyle content but in their social and historical context: what they reveal about consciousness under capitalism in crisis, and where they retreat from the great questions of war, inequality and historical reckoning that define the moment.

Iran halts US negotiations and vows to fully block the Strait of Hormuz Iran announced on June 1 that it is ending all communication with the United States through intermediaries and will move to completely seal the Strait of Hormuz, citing Israel's expanding military operations in Lebanon and continued ceasefire violations as the trigger. A tentative 60-day memorandum of understanding had reportedly been reached. Under its terms, Iran would remove all mines from the Strait within 30 days, guarantee "unrestricted" shipping, and commit to not pursuing a nuclear weapon, in exchange for US sanctions waivers permitting Iran to sell oil freely. The collapse confirms the WSWS analysis that the "negotiations" were never aimed at a stable settlement but at managing a war of imperialist plunder against Iran. US murder spree in Latin American waters moves beyond 200 killed — Andrea Lobo The Perspective documents the latest escalation of a US military campaign that began September 2, 2025 in the Caribbean, expanded to the Eastern Pacific in October, and has now killed more than 205 people across roughly 60 destroyed vessels. Lobo situates the campaign within three US imperial objectives: reasserting Monroe Doctrine dominance over Latin America after years of Chinese infrastructure investment; intimidating governments contemplating closer ties to Beijing; and targeting the corridor around Peru's Chancay port, a Chinese-developed Pacific hub. --- Pseudo-left press review - [Jacobin / DSA](#jacobin--dsa) — frames the crisis as "political capitalism" and rehabilitates the CPUSA, evading the question of working-class political independence. - [Left Voice](#left-voice) — sharply criticizes Mamdani from the left while still orienting workers toward defending the "Mamdani moment." - [Liberation News / PSL](#liberation-news--psl) — anti-imperialist phrasemongering coupled with uncritical promotion of bourgeois-nationalist regimes. - [Socialist Worker / SWP (UK)](#socialist-worker--swp-uk) — channels industrial militancy back into pressure on the Labour government and the union apparatus. - [Socialist Appeal / RCP (IMT)](#socialist-appeal--rcp-imt) — abstract "communist" propaganda detached from a concrete strategy in the unions. Jacobin / DSA Jacobin leads with **"The USA Is Living Under Political Capitalism,"** arguing that contemporary capitalism prioritizes wealth extraction through "political maneuvering" and monopoly rent rather than competitive markets. The framing of "political capitalism" as a distinct phase substitutes a moralizing critique of "rent-seeking" for an analysis of the capitalist mode of production itself — implying the problem is bad-faith manipulation rather than the profit system, and pointing toward regulatory reform rather than expropriation. **"American Communists Did a Lot Right and a Lot Wrong"** offers a soft rehabilitation of the CPUSA, treating its members as "more complicated than the stereotypes." Tellingly, the piece elides the central historical lesson — the CPUSA's Stalinist subordination of the working class to the Roosevelt Democrats and the Popular Front, the very orientation the DSA reproduces today. **"Emmanuel Macron Has Boosted France's Corporate Welfare State"** correctly skewers Macron's largesse to corporate "rentiers" but, consistent with Jacobin's house line, frames the remedy as a fairer distribution of state subsidies rather than a struggle against the capitalist state. *Assessment:* Jacobin's output reinforces its function as the theoretical workshop of the DSA's left-Democratic project — recasting the crisis of capitalism as a problem of policy capture, soluble within the existing order. Left Voice Left Voice continues its pointed criticism of Zohran Mamdani in **"Why Is Zohran Mamdani Endorsing Strikebreaker Kathy Hochul?"** and **"No, Zohran, Jessica Tisch Has Not Made New York Safer for the City's Working Class,"** attacking his endorsement of the governor and his retention of a billionaire police commissioner. These pieces are sharper than anything in the DSA press. Yet **"Fight the Attacks on Mamdani and All Immigrants with Mobilizations and Class Struggle"** reveals the contradiction: having exposed Mamdani's pro-capitalist trajectory, Left Voice still calls to defend him against the right, channeling workers back toward the "Mamdani moment" rather than toward a decisive political break with the Democratic Party. *Assessment:* Left Voice oscillates between trenchant criticism and a centrist refusal to draw the organizational conclusion — that the DSA's project is a trap, requiring an independent revolutionary party, not pressure on its left wing. Liberation News / PSL The PSL's recent output marks the 78th anniversary of the Nakba with a pledge to "intensify efforts to end U.S. aid to Israel," argues that capitalism is the cause of climate catastrophe, and issued a statement on Raúl Castro alongside reflections from a Pan-Africanism summit in Nairobi. The anti-imperialist rhetoric is consistent, but the PSL's method substitutes cheerleading for bourgeois-nationalist and Stalinist regimes for a perspective of independent working-class struggle — presenting capitalist states as anti-imperialist allies rather than as obstacles to the international unity of workers. *Assessment:* The PSL's campism leads it to subordinate the working class to one camp of bourgeois states against another, the opposite of an internationalist socialist strategy. Socialist Worker / SWP (UK) The SWP highlights **"College workers back national fight over pay and workloads,"** **"Labour's dystopian AI plan to clamp down on refugees,"** and **"Green council backs shoebox flats in Bristol housing scandal."** The reporting captures genuine working-class grievances and Labour's reactionary turn on immigration. But the SWP's perspective routinely terminates in calls for more militant pressure on the union leaders and the Labour "left," rather than in building an independent leadership against the bureaucracy that contains these struggles. *Assessment:* The SWP documents the militancy of the rank and file while leaving intact the apparatus that strangles it. --- Arts and culture The most significant cultural event of the day is the federal court ruling ordering Trump's name removed from the Kennedy Center. A judge held that the administration's addition of the president's name to the facade was unlawful because only Congress holds the authority to rename the federally chartered institution. The decision is a meaningful check on executive attempts to rebrand national cultural bodies as personal monuments — a tendency characteristic of authoritarian politics — and arrives amid a broader assault on public arts funding. That assault is most consequential in the NEA standoff. Following the administration's 2026 budget proposal to eliminate the National Endowment for the Arts, hundreds of previously awarded theater grants were abruptly rescinded, hitting organizations including the Drama League and Classical Theater of Harlem. In a partial counterweight, a separate federal judge permanently barred the cancellation of more than $100 million in humanities grants, ruling the move unconstitutional. The defunding represents the most significant restructuring of federal arts support in decades — a deliberate effort to strip working people of access to culture while channeling resources to militarism. The WSWS marked the day with Erik Schreiber's review of "Raphael: Sublime Poetry" at the Metropolitan Museum of Art (through June 28), the first comprehensive US exhibition of Raphael (1483–1546). Tracing his development from apprenticeship under Perugino through his Florentine absorption of Leonardo and Michelangelo to the Vatican frescoes "The School of Athens" and "The Parnassus," Schreiber argues that Raphael's achievement reflected the rising Renaissance bourgeoisie's genuine engagement with scientific and artistic progress — a capacity, he writes, that modern capitalism has "repudiated" in favor of "religious obscurantism, fascism, genocide and war." The finding intensifies debate over AI's role in clinical decision-making even as it lands amid record AI-driven layoffs, raising the question of whether such capabilities will expand access to care or be deployed to cut medical labor costs. --- Arts and culture The death of **Peabo Bryson** at 75, on June 2, marks the passing of one of the defining voices of late-20th-century American popular song. The two-time Grammy winner is best remembered for the soaring Disney duets "Beauty and the Beast" (with Céline Dion) and "A Whole New World" (with Regina Belle), both of which won Academy Awards for Best Original Song. Bryson's career, rooted in 1970s soul and R&B before crossing into the mainstream of the 1990s, embodied the trajectory of a Black American musical tradition shaped — and constrained — by the recording industry's commercial machinery. His finest work demonstrated a craftsmanship, vocal control and emotional sincerity increasingly squeezed out of a culture industry oriented toward algorithmic disposability and the fragmentation of audiences. The **79th Cannes Film Festival**, which concluded May 23, awarded the Palme d'Or to Romanian director Cristian Mungiu for *Fjord* — his second after *4 Months, 3 Weeks and 2 Days* (2007). Mungiu's cinema, formed in the Romanian New Wave, is distinguished by its unsentimental attention to ordinary people crushed by bureaucratic and social systems, a body of work attentive to questions of class, moral compromise and the long shadow of Stalinism's collapse in Eastern Europe. The jury, presided over by South Korea's Park Chan-wook, reflected a festival increasingly marked by the contradiction between serious world cinema and the commercial and political pressures bearing down on it. --- Arts and culture The most significant cultural event marked in the past day is the death of tenor saxophonist **Sonny Rollins**, one of the last and greatest figures of the bebop generation, reviewed at length on the WSWS by Jesse Thomas and John Andrews. Born September 7, 1930 in Harlem and dead at 95 on May 25, 2026 in Woodstock, New York from progressive pulmonary fibrosis, Rollins possessed what the authors describe as "an earthy, broad sound" that synthesized Coleman Hawkins, Lester Young and Charlie Parker into something wholly his own. His landmark recordings — *Saxophone Colossus* (1956), *Tenor Madness* (1956) and *Freedom Suite* (1958) — and his improvisations stretching past ten minutes helped define post-war jazz. The WSWS obituary is distinguished from most by its attention to Rollins's social formation. As a child he attended Camp Unity, described as "an interracial, antichauvinist, anticapitalist summer camp" run by Communist Party branches, and his aunt Mirium was a left-wing activist. *Freedom Suite*, recorded against the backdrop of the civil-rights struggle, stands as one of the era's most explicit fusions of musical innovation and social protest. Rollins's life also illustrates the toll of capitalist society on artists: he overcame heroin addiction in the early 1950s and took two extended sabbaticals (1959–1962 and 1968–1971) to study yoga and meditation, famously practicing alone on the Williamsburg Bridge. In a final, bitter irony, the September 11, 2001 attacks near his Manhattan apartment caused the pulmonary damage that ended his performing career; his last public performance came in 2012. His death severs another link to a generation of Black American musicians who forged a major art form under conditions of segregation and exploitation. Rollins's passing invites reflection on the present cultural moment, in which militarism and nationalism increasingly saturate official culture, and arts funding remains under sustained political pressure. Against that backdrop, the artistic seriousness and internationalist sensibility of figures like Rollins — formed in the milieu of the 1930s–40s left — stand as a reproach to the commodified, identity-segmented cultural product of today. Cultural roundup: - **Jazz legacy:** Tributes from across the music world underscore Rollins's influence on generations of saxophonists; his catalogue on Prestige, Blue Note and Riverside remains foundational to the post-war canon. - **Historical memory:** The WSWS framing — situating his art in the Communist-influenced cultural institutions of mid-century America — recovers a history of working-class and anti-racist cultural organizing that bourgeois obituaries routinely omit.

The framing presents imperialism as a policy error to be corrected by better leadership rather than the necessary external expression of capitalist crisis — leaving readers with moral indignation but no independent political perspective for the working class. The petrostate piece treats Canada's fossil-fuel economy as a moral failing of "the bankers" rather than a class question. Active outbreaks continue in Florida, Pennsylvania, Utah and Virginia; 93% of cases are outbreak-associated, 92% involve unvaccinated individuals, and 127 patients (6%) have been hospitalized. The US technically crossed the threshold for losing its measles elimination status (held since 2000) earlier this year; PAHO pushed its formal review to November, and CIDRAP analysts call loss of status "highly likely." MMR coverage in schoolchildren has slipped from 95.2% (2019–20) to 92.5% (2024–25). In a rare advance, the FDA approved ensitrelvir (Xocova) on June 1 as the first oral COVID-19 post-exposure prophylaxis for those 12 and older — a 5-day regimen that cut symptomatic infection by 67% when started within 72 hours of exposure. It arrives as the immune-evasive BA.3.2 "Cicada" variant, carrying over 70 new spike mutations, becomes the dominant US strain. CDC forecasts ~1,200 weekly hospital admissions — flat week-over-week, with COVID growing in just one state and declining in 41; severity is not elevated versus prior 2025 strains in healthy people. Roundup: - **H5N1:** WHO reported 13 avian/swine flu human cases in Q1 2026, including a previously unreported fatal H5N1 case in a child in Bangladesh. US dairy herds in multiple states remain infected; CDC sees no unusual human flu activity. Researchers continue to warn the animal-reservoir situation is "completely out of control." - **Australia diphtheria:** Nearly 260 cases since October 2025 — the largest outbreak since national reporting began in 1991 — with 95% among Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people, one death, and a third involving the respiratory form (10% fatality even with treatment). The WSWS ties it to over 50% household overcrowding and chronic under-funding of remote-community housing. - **Apple WWDC 2026:** Tim Cook's final keynote unveiled a rebuilt Siri powered by a custom 1.2-trillion-parameter Google Gemini model (~$1 billion/year), with ChatGPT and Claude as user-selectable alternatives — a historic admission that on-device AI alone can't differentiate Apple's products. - **AI and the military:** The DoD signed agreements with OpenAI, Oracle, AWS, SpaceX, Google, NVIDIA, Reflection and Microsoft to bring advanced AI to classified networks as part of an "AI-first fighting force." Anthropic separately warned its own models may soon be "too powerful to control." - **Attack on science:** Louisiana State Police forcibly removed five prominent diabetes researchers from the American Diabetes Association Scientific Sessions on June 5 as they distributed a peer-reviewed editorial criticizing NIH cuts; the WSWS documents an 89% drop in NIH funding notices and a ~66% fall in grant awards.

--- Arts and culture The most significant cultural story of the week is the institutional rupture at the Kennedy Center, addressed above as a top story. Below the headlines, the past 24 hours brought the 79th Tony Awards, the loss of two important artists, and continued fallout from the Trump administration's assault on arts education. The 79th Tony Awards at Radio City Music Hall crowned "Schmigadoon!" Best Musical — also winning score, book and orchestrations — while a revival of Arthur Miller's "Death of a Salesman" took the most trophies overall. The recognition of Miller's 1949 drama of a worn-out salesman discarded by a system that promised him everything remains strikingly relevant in an era of mass layoffs and collapsing living standards. "Ragtime," E.L. Doctorow's panorama of class, race and immigrant life at the turn of the 20th century, finally won Best Musical Revival after losing the top prize in its 1998 run, with Joshua Henry and Caissie Levy taking the lead acting awards — a belated recognition of a work that grapples seriously with American social history. The death of **Marjane Satrapi at 56** is a major loss. The Iranian-French author of *Persepolis* — the autobiographical graphic novel and Oscar-nominated animated film recounting a childhood under the Islamic Republic and exile in Europe — gave international readers one of the most humane and unsentimental portraits of life under repression. Her death is especially poignant as US and Israeli bombs fall on the country whose people she rendered with such care; her work stands as a rebuke to the dehumanization that accompanies war. The Élysée Palace called her "an artist devoted to freedom, whose work carried a universal message." Roundup: - **Peabo Bryson, 75:** The two-time Grammy winner who sang "Beauty and the Beast" and "A Whole New World" died June 2, his voice defining the sound of Disney's 1990s renaissance. - **Taylor Swift** released "I Knew It, I Knew You," co-written with Jack Antonoff, for Disney/Pixar's *Toy Story 5* — a further sign of the consolidation of dominant pop artists into the franchise machinery of the major studios. - **Arts education under threat:** A proposed Department of Education rule would revoke federal student-loan eligibility from programs whose graduates miss earnings benchmarks, explicitly targeting fine arts, music and studio arts and potentially cutting off more than 600,000 students from aid — the most structurally damaging blow to arts education in decades, threatening the pipeline for the next generation of artists.

Jacobin / DSA Jacobin's output centers on the June 23 New York Democratic primaries. "**NYC Socialists Are Trying to Expand Their Electoral Wins**" promotes a DSA slate of state-legislative and congressional candidates, riding momentum from Zohran Mamdani's election as mayor and AOC's endorsements of three challengers. A companion piece, "**We Need a Left-Labor Presidential Candidate**," argues the working class needs a standard-bearer inside the Democratic primaries, dovetailing with DSA's national-convention resolution to run a 2028 Democratic presidential candidate. The line is the consummate expression of the pseudo-left's strategic orientation: the subordination of working-class political independence to the Democratic Party — the very party that the same week voted 324–92 to continue the Iran war. By presenting electoral capture of Democratic ballot lines as "socialism," Jacobin demobilizes opposition to war and austerity and channels it back into the institutions responsible for both. Mamdani's mayoralty — which Jacobin itself describes as caught between "managing capitalism" and "overturning it" — is the demonstration in practice that administering the capitalist state means enforcing its priorities. Left Voice Left Voice's most prominent recent piece, "**The Left Must Defend the PSL and All of Those Facing State Repression**," correctly opposes state attacks on left organizations. But the framing — a defense of "the left" as an undifferentiated bloc — blurs precisely the political distinctions a Marxist must draw, lumping a Stalinist-influenced formation together with genuine revolutionary opposition and substituting movementist solidarity for a struggle over program. Left Voice's coverage of the Iran war continues to orient toward street mobilizations and the academic-left milieu rather than the independent political mobilization of the working class. PSL / Liberation News The PSL's statements — "**Stop Trump's War on Iran!**" and "Why Trump failed in his criminal war against Iran" — denounce the bombing but present the war as essentially Trump's personal crime, to be reversed by sustained "pressure." Absent is any reckoning with the bipartisan character of the war or with US imperialism as a systemic product of capitalism; the implicit horizon is a return to a more "rational," multilateral US foreign policy. The orientation tails Iranian and bourgeois-nationalist forces and frames the antiwar struggle as a single-issue campaign detached from the fight against the capitalist order. Socialist Alternative Socialist Alternative (ISA) continues to treat the Gaza genocide and the war on Iran as discrete questions, evading the reality of a single, escalating imperialist offensive across Lebanon, Gaza and Iran — a separation the WSWS specifically polemicized against in its April critique. Its coverage emphasizes building "mass movements" and pressure campaigns while avoiding a programmatic break with the union bureaucracy and the Democratic Party milieu it courts. The result is an adaptation to spontaneity that leaves the political leadership of struggles in reformist hands. SWP (UK) and IMT/RCP The British SWP frames the Iran war as fuel for protest-building, subordinating analysis to the next demonstration and its perennial front campaigns. The IMT/RCP, meanwhile, channels radicalizing youth toward parliamentary-reformist regroupment around figures such as Corbyn and Sultana — what the WSWS has identified as the substitution of left rhetoric for a genuine fight to build an independent revolutionary party. Both tendencies treat the danger of wider war as an organizing opportunity rather than as the central strategic question demanding the political independence of the working class.

--- Arts and culture The most significant cultural event of the day is the convergence of the **Metropolitan Opera's production of *El Último Sueño de Frida y Diego* (*The Last Dream of Frida and Diego*)** and MoMA's companion exhibition *Frida and Diego: The Last Dream*. The opera, with music by composer **Gabriela Lena Frank** — who has just won the 2026 Pulitzer Prize for her symphony *Picaflor: A Future Myth* — and a libretto by Nilo Cruz, draws strong notices for a score integrating Andean folk traditions, pre-Columbian percussion, and European classical music. Soprano Isabel Leonard (Frida), baritone Carlos Álvarez (Diego), and soprano Gabriella Reyes (La Catrina) are praised. The decisive point, as Fred Mazelis and Clare Hurley argue on the WSWS, is what the production omits. Both the opera and the exhibition almost entirely suppress the political lives of Rivera and Kahlo. There is no reckoning with Rivera's role in securing Trotsky's Mexican asylum in 1937, nor with the 1938 "Manifesto for an Independent Revolutionary Art," co-authored by Rivera, Trotsky, and André Breton — one of the central artistic-political documents of the 20th century. The libretto reduces this relationship to romantic biography and physical suffering. The reviewers attribute this to identity-politics frameworks that have turned Kahlo into a marketable brand and recast Rivera as a "bad boy," erasing both artists' revolutionary commitments and their tragic later reconciliation with Stalinism. The MoMA show is described as partly a "co-branded marketing opportunity," though it offers rare proximity to key works including *Self-Portrait on the Border Between Mexico and the United States* (1932). The death of historian **Gordon S. Wood** at 92 — struck by a car in a Rhode Island parking lot, weeks before the 250th anniversary of the Declaration of Independence — is also a major cultural loss. Wood's *The Radicalism of the American Revolution* (Pulitzer, 1993) and *The Creation of the American Republic* (Bancroft Prize) defended the Revolution as a genuinely transformative break with the monarchical Ancien régime. He collaborated with WSWS-published historians in opposing the New York Times' 1619 Project, demanding corrections to its racialist falsification of 1776. Roundup: - **Pope Leo XIV's Mass at the Sagrada Família** (covered above) marks the completion of one of the most ambitious works of architecture in the modern era, 140 years in construction - The papal and operatic spotlights alike point to a broader tendency: the institutional repackaging of radical or monumental cultural achievement as heritage spectacle, stripped of the social and revolutionary content that produced it

Jacobin / DSA Jacobin continues to frame the Iran war chiefly as a Trump policy failure. Its recent analyses — "[Why the US Is Losing the Iran War](https://jacobin.com/2026/05/us-empire-hegemony-war-trump)" and "[US, Israel Target Civilians as Iran Escalates War to Survive](https://jacobin.com/2026/03/iran-casualties-retaliation-war-us)" — characterize Trump as having "started an illegal and ill-planned war on Tehran" that he is "losing control of," emphasizing that the assassination campaign "did not cause the Islamic Republic to crumble." The political line treats imperialist war as a question of incompetent strategy and lost hegemony rather than the objective drive of US capitalism in crisis. By locating the problem in Trump's recklessness, Jacobin implicitly counterposes a more rational, managed imperialism — the standpoint of the Democratic Party wing it orbits. There is no call for the independent mobilization of the working class against both parties; the assumed agency remains electoral pressure and a restoration of "competent" foreign policy. Overall orientation: left cover for a section of the foreign-policy establishment dismayed at the war's mismanagement. Left Voice Left Voice's coverage — "[We Need a Mass Movement to Defeat Trump's Imperialist War on Iran](https://www.leftvoice.org/we-need-a-mass-movement-to-defeat-trumps-imperialist-war-on-iran/)" and "[Defend Iran, but Don't Support the Theocracy](https://www.leftvoice.org/defend-iran-but-dont-support-the-theocracy/)" — correctly identifies the war as imperialist and rooted in US decline and inter-imperialist rivalry, and formally calls for working-class independence. But its "defend Iran" defensism risks adapting to bourgeois-nationalist frameworks, and its parallel emphasis on "[Feminists Must Fight Imperialism in Iran](https://www.leftvoice.org/feminists-must-fight-imperialism-in-iran-without-supporting-the-theocratic-regime/)" channels the question into identity categories rather than the unified international class struggle. The Morenoite PTS tradition substitutes a stream of "mass movement" appeals and protest activism for the patient construction of a revolutionary party. Overall orientation: radical phraseology combined with an essentially propagandistic, movementist practice. Liberation News / PSL The PSL, through Liberation News and the ANSWER Coalition, has organized "Hands Off Iran!" protests in major cities (see "[PSL Statement: Stop Trump's War on Iran!](https://liberationnews.org/psl-statement-stop-trumps-war-on-iran/)" and "[Why Trump failed in his criminal war against Iran](https://liberationnews.org/psl-statement-why-trump-failed-in-his-criminal-war-against-iran-and-why-we-need-to-keep-up-the-pressure/)"). The line credits the war's stalling to "public pressure and the Iranian people's resistance," lending uncritical political support to the bourgeois Iranian regime and presenting the theocracy's survival as a victory for the oppressed. This campist orientation subordinates the Iranian and US working classes to one capitalist state against another. Overall orientation: anti-imperialism reduced to support for a rival bourgeois government, with protest pressure substituting for a revolutionary perspective. Socialist Worker / SWP (UK) The SWP's output remains organized around public meetings — "[Terror in Iran: Resisting imperialist war in the Middle East](https://socialistworker.co.uk/swp-meetings/terror-in-iran-resisting-imperialist-war-in-the-middle-east-3/)" and "[Will the war on Iran crash the world economy?](https://socialistworker.co.uk/swp-meetings/will-the-war-on-iran-crash-the-world-economy/)" — that correctly note Starmer's collusion in the war. --- Science, technology, and public health - [US measles cases hit 2,030 across 40 jurisdictions](#science-section) — worst year in decades as kindergarten MMR coverage falls to 92.5% - [H5N1 spreads in poultry across 12 states](#science-section) — over 100 million birds culled cumulatively; 71 US human cases since 2024 - [Three journals simultaneously expand finerenone to non-diabetic kidney disease](#science-section) — NEJM, JAMA and Lancet studies could add millions of eligible patients - [AI policy clash](#science-section) — Anthropic's CEO demands government blocking authority days after a deregulatory White House order **Measles and H5N1.** The CDC confirmed 2,030 measles cases this year across 40 jurisdictions as of June 4, with 30 active outbreaks accounting for ~93% of cases — putting the US on pace for its worst measles year in decades. Kindergarten MMR coverage has fallen to 92.5% for the 2024-25 school year, below the 95% herd-immunity threshold. Separately, the USDA confirmed active H5N1 detections in commercial poultry across 12 states, triggering depopulations that have surpassed 100 million birds cumulatively this cycle. The CDC reports 71 total US human cases since February 2024; NIOSH has relaunched its dairy-worker safety campaign targeting roughly 500,000 agricultural workers at elevated occupational risk. **Finerenone studies.** Three studies published simultaneously the week of June 5 in the *New England Journal of Medicine*, *JAMA* and *The Lancet* — presented at the 2026 European Renal Association Congress in Glasgow — show that finerenone, a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist previously approved only for diabetic chronic kidney disease, significantly protects the hearts and kidneys of patients with non-diabetic CKD, including glomerular disease. It is the most concentrated simultaneous release of finerenone evidence to date and could expand the eligible patient population by millions globally. Roundup: - **AI regulation clash:** In a June 10 essay, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei argued voluntary transparency is no longer sufficient and that governments should have standing legal authority — with revenue-based civil penalties — to block AI deployments that fail mandatory third-party safety testing. Ensemble models forecast ~1,000 new hospital admissions for the week ending June 13; COVID ED visits are at ~0.087% of all visits, down from 0.11% the prior week — a low summer baseline with no surge underway.

--- Arts and culture The most significant cultural news of the day was the loss, confirmed earlier this month, of **Marjane Satrapi**, the Iranian-French cartoonist and filmmaker, who died June 4 at age 56. Satrapi won worldwide acclaim for *Persepolis*, her graphic-novel bildungsroman of growing up during and after the 1979 Iranian Revolution and the Iran-Iraq war, later adapted into an Oscar-nominated 2007 animated film. Her death lands with particular weight as the US-Israel war devastates the Iranian population: *Persepolis* remains one of the most humane and widely read accounts of how ordinary Iranians lived through revolution, theocratic repression and imperialist-fueled conflict — a corrective to the dehumanizing war propaganda now saturating Western media. Satrapi's work insisted on the universality of the Iranian people's experience against both the clerical regime and Western militarism. In literature, novelist **Dave Eggers** discussed his new novel *Contrapposto*, a project he says has been on his mind for nearly two decades. Eggers's fiction has long engaged questions of surveillance, technology and the alienating structures of corporate capitalism (*The Circle*), and the new work continues his interest in the social pressures bearing on the individual. Roundup: - **Documentary:** *American Pachuco: The Legend of Luiz Valdez*, David Alvarado's film on the Chicano theater pioneer, screened June 11 as part of a Latino Arts Festival collaboration after winning the 2026 Sundance Audience Award for US Documentary. Luis Valdez's El Teatro Campesino emerged directly from the 1965 Delano grape strike and farmworker organizing — a reminder of the historical bond between cultural production and the labor movement. - **Music obituaries:** Avant-garde guitarist **James Blood Ulmer** died June 3 at 86; his "harmolodic" fusion of jazz, funk and blues, developed in collaboration with Ornette Coleman, was among the most original American musical voices of the late 20th century. R&B vocalist **Peabo Bryson**, a two-time Grammy winner, died June 2 at 75. - **Stage and screen:** Actor **Anthony Head**, known to a generation for *Buffy the Vampire Slayer* and *Ted Lasso*, died June 1 at 72. British character actor **Patrick Godfrey** died June 4 at 93. - **History:** **Gordon S. Wood**, the influential historian of the American Revolution, died June 7 at 92 after being struck by a car; his scholarship reshaped understanding of the social forces behind the founding of the United States. The concentration of deaths of older artists and intellectuals is a reminder of a generation formed in the postwar decades now passing — figures whose work, at its best, treated art as a means of grappling with history and society rather than as disposable content.

US-Iran war: Pakistan says "final agreed" peace text reached as strikes continue Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif announced on June 12 that "a final, agreed upon text of the peace deal has been reached," declaring that "peace has never been as close as it is now." Iran's foreign ministry pointedly declined to confirm any agreement, saying only that "final internal deliberations" were underway. A sign-off from Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei remains the last missing piece, and Iranian officials publicly called Trump "deceitful," insisting nothing has been finalized. The diplomatic maneuvering unfolds against continued military operations. Trump canceled a fresh wave of strikes on June 11 after having warned Iran it would be hit "very hard tonight." The war, now in its fourth month, began February 28 when Trump announced "major combat operations" with massive joint US-Israeli strikes; Iran retaliated against US embassies, Gulf military installations, and Strait of Hormuz shipping. As Andre Damon noted on the WSWS, the threats have escalated to Trump menacing Iran with "civilizational destruction" and proposing the seizure of Iranian oil infrastructure — exposing the colonial-plunder logic driving the war. The human toll is staggering. Iran's Health Ministry reports at least 3,468 killed and more than 26,500 injured since February 28, including at least 1,621 children. The conflict has produced what the IEA called "the largest supply disruption in the history of the global oil market," with traffic through the Strait of Hormuz down more than 90 percent. Key facts: - US equipment losses are estimated at $5.14 billion; at least 13–15 US personnel have been killed in action. - Cross-theater deaths are estimated at 8,336–17,685 across all sides. - Gulf states face a "grocery supply emergency," with 70 percent of food imports disrupted and consumer prices spiking 40–120 percent. - There is near-total bipartisan support in Washington for the war despite the civilian death toll receiving minimal US prime-time coverage.

--- Arts and culture The death of historian **Gordon Wood** at 92 — struck and killed by a motorist on June 8 — removes one of the most influential American historians of his generation. Wood won the 1993 Pulitzer Prize for History for *The Radicalism of the American Revolution*, which argued that the Revolution was a genuinely transformative social upheaval that dissolved the hierarchical, monarchical order of colonial society. His passing lands amid a renewed contest over the meaning of the Revolution's 250th anniversary. The WSWS this week took up that contest directly, with Paul Mitchell sharply criticizing the BBC documentary *Lucy Worsley Investigates: The American Revolution* for substituting celebrity-presenter superficiality and personality-driven narrative for any class analysis of the revolutionary period's causes and contradictions — treating one of the most decisive events in world history as costume drama. Wood's scholarship, whatever its limitations from a Marxist standpoint, at least grasped the Revolution as a real social transformation rather than a pageant of great men. The death of psychiatrist and author **Robert Coles** on June 7, a Pulitzer winner whose *Children of Crisis* series documented the inner lives of poor and segregated children through the civil-rights era, marks the loss of a writer who insisted that the testimony of the oppressed belonged at the center of American letters. Roundup: - **Questlove's documentary on Earth, Wind & Fire** — exploring the band's utopian, cosmically themed fusion of soul, funk, and jazz — is now streaming on HBO, the latest in the director's project of treating Black popular music as serious cultural history rather than nostalgia. - The **45th anniversary of *Raiders of the Lost Ark*** (June 12) prompted retrospectives on the Spielberg-Lucas blockbuster that, for better and worse, helped define the modern franchise-driven Hollywood economy now dominated by intellectual-property recycling. - New US releases dated June 12 — including *Scary Movie 6* and an untitled film from the Daniels (the *Everything Everywhere All at Once* duo) — illustrate the industry's bifurcation between exhausted parody franchises and the occasional auteur project squeezed into the summer calendar. - In the orchestral repertory, programs this week paired Copland's *Lincoln Portrait* — a wartime work built on Lincoln's own words about democracy and union — with Gershwin and Barber, a reminder of how mid-century American composers wrestled openly with national identity at a moment when that question is again politically charged. The throughline across these items is the struggle over historical memory: who controls the narrative of the American Revolution, of the civil-rights era, of national identity itself. As the WSWS framework insists, cultural production is never neutral entertainment — it is a terrain on which class forces contend over how a society understands its own past and possibilities.
Sources PBS NewsHour Gordon Wood, historian of the American Revolution, dies at 92 · WSWS Lucy Worsley Investigates: The American Revolution

--- Arts and culture The weekend's dominant cultural events are inseparable from the political crisis. Trump's "UFC Freedom 250" and the accompanying Zac Brown Band concert on the White House lawn, and the Democrats' rival $330-a-ticket "Rise Up, Sing Out" benefit concert, represent two faces of the instrumentalization of mass culture by a decaying ruling order. The first marshals combat sport and country music into a fascistic personality-cult spectacle of "the American fighting spirit"; the second deploys celebrity performance to channel genuine popular hostility to authoritarianism back into the safe harbor of the Democratic Party and "inclusive patriotism." In both, culture is conscripted as a political instrument, and in both the working-class audience is treated as a passive mass to be mobilized rather than addressed. The World Cup opening ceremonies offered a parallel case. Bollywood star Nora Fatehi's headline performance and the lavish staging in Canada were widely shared, but the spectacle played out before stadiums pocked with empty seats despite full ticket allocations — a telling image of mega-event culture organized around corporate sponsorship and inflated pricing rather than genuine popular access. That the host nation simultaneously bars Iranian fans from its soil exposes how thoroughly geopolitics has colonized what is nominally a festival of international sport. Against this backdrop, a genuinely valuable cultural recovery comes from Britain, where a rediscovered documentary, *The 1926 General Strike: A Revolution Betrayed*, has resurfaced on the centenary horizon of the strike. The film's framing — that the nine-day general strike of three million workers was betrayed by the Trades Union Congress leadership — speaks directly to the present, when union bureaucracies across the postal, auto, education and steel sectors are again suppressing rank-and-file struggles. Historical memory of working-class militancy and its betrayals is precisely the kind of cultural work that serves, rather than diverts, the working class. Other developments worth noting: - The ninth anniversary of the Grenfell Tower fire was marked in Britain this weekend, a continuing indictment of the social murder of 72 working-class residents and the impunity of landlords, contractors and government — a subject of ongoing artistic and documentary treatment. - Coverage of combat sports as a cultural form is increasingly preoccupied with its capture by tech billionaires and Gulf sovereign wealth — the White House octagon being the logical endpoint of that consolidation of mass spectacle in oligarchic hands. Recognizing genuine artistic achievement regardless of an artist's politics remains essential; so does naming the militarist, nationalist and commercial tendencies that increasingly shape what is produced and promoted.

US and Iran reach framework deal to end war and reopen Strait of Hormuz The United States and Iran announced a 60-day ceasefire on Sunday, June 14, suspending a war that began February 28, 2026, with US-Israeli strikes that killed Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei and two senior IRGC commanders. --- Arts and culture The two dueling spectacles of June 14 — Trump's UFC cage match on the White House lawn and a Democratic celebrity fundraiser in Manhattan — together offer a portrait of cultural life under a decaying social order. The "Rise Up, Sing Out: A Concert for the First Amendment" in New York, featuring Jane Fonda and Julia Roberts with tickets over $330, was staged as the liberal counterpoint to the gladiatorial brutalism downtown. As Barry Grey argued on the WSWS, both events express "the collapse of American democracy and the depravity of American capitalism in its death agony" — each party performing for its own constituency while workers have no political representation. The contrast is itself a cultural document: mass entertainment reduced to either sanctioned violence or self-congratulatory philanthropy, neither speaking to the social crisis engulfing the population. The most substantive cultural criticism of the day came in Erik Schreiber's WSWS review of the 2024 Spanish film **_Rich Flu_**, directed by Galder Gaztelu-Urrutia (_The Platform_). In the film, a mysterious disease begins killing the wealthy, forcing a media executive and her family through the dehumanizing conditions normally reserved for migrants and the dispossessed. Schreiber praises the film's "unblinking" social commentary and Buñuel-esque absurdism — a genuine artistic engagement with class inequality — while faulting its attribution of inequality to individual "greed" rather than the structural logic of capitalism, and its utopian resolution in "small, self-sufficient, sustainable settlements," which he reads as a regression from collective social organization. The review's verdict is characteristic of the WSWS approach: the film reflects authentic mass opposition to injustice finding artistic form, even as its conclusions remain trapped within the horizon of bourgeois social thought. Beyond these, the cultural sphere remains marked by the pressure of war and repression: - The destruction of the **Dormition Cathedral roof** at the Kyiv-Pechersk Lavra (see Top stories) is a cultural-heritage atrocity as much as a war crime — an 11th-century UNESCO monument set ablaze, drawing comparisons to Notre Dame and underscoring how imperialist war consumes the accumulated cultural inheritance of humanity. - In Britain, the legal **ban on Palestine Action** — upheld this week and contested by its co-founder — continues a pattern of state criminalization of political art and protest, a question with direct implications for cultural and democratic rights (covered below in the pseudo-left review and coverage suggestions). - The reduction of major broadcast and streaming infrastructure to instruments of a billionaire-allied political project — Paramount+'s livestream of the White House cage match — illustrates the subordination of mass culture to oligarchic interests. These developments confirm the WSWS framework: culture is not a neutral leisure category but a contested terrain in which the social crisis, the drive to war, and the concentration of wealth find expression — and against which genuine artistic truth-telling, as in _Rich Flu_, retains a critical charge.

As Andrea Lobo writes, "the beautiful game" has fallen into "the grip of Trump and financial oligarchy." The other dominant cultural story is structural: the DOJ's clearance of the $111 billion Paramount–Warner Bros. merger (covered above) consolidates an enormous share of American film, television and news production under the Ellison family. The reorganization of the culture industry along oligarchic lines has direct implications for artistic freedom, the diversity of cultural output, and the independence of journalism. A single politically connected family now controls two major studios, two streaming platforms, and the CNN and CBS newsrooms — a degree of concentration that subordinates cultural and journalistic production to the immediate interests of a layer tied directly to the Trump administration. --- Arts and culture The day's most substantial cultural intervention came from the WSWS itself: David Walsh's review of Steven Soderbergh's new film *The Christophers*. Walsh argues that the film — centered on a fictional artist, Julian Sklar, who declares he has produced "nothing but shit in 30 years. Nothing at all in 20" — is stylish but fundamentally shallow, itself guilty of the same fashionable cleverness it gestures at. Drawing on the 19th-century Russian critic N.A. Dobrolyubov's argument that subject matter matters more than raw talent, Walsh contends that Soderbergh's generation abandoned its radical instincts under the reaction of the 1980s and 1990s and retreated into irony, producing work that cannot grip mass audiences because it lacks genuine commitment to meaningful social themes. Critics praise it, Walsh writes, because "they are not difficult to impress." The review is a useful entry point for the broader question of why a technically accomplished American cinema remains so politically and emotionally evasive in a period of war and social crisis. The art world continues to absorb the loss of **David Hockney**, who died June 11 at age 88. One of the most important British painters of the postwar era, Hockney moved across pop art, the California swimming-pool canvases, photo-collage, opera design, and late-period iPad works such as the 90-metre digital frieze *A Year in Normandie*. The Tate has confirmed two posthumous projects for next year: a major Tate Britain retrospective spanning seven decades and a Turbine Hall multimedia installation of his opera designs. Hockney's restless reinvention and his insistence on the direct observation of life and landscape stand as a rebuke to the ironic detachment Walsh criticizes in Soderbergh — a genuine artistic achievement rooted in sustained engagement with the visible world. Other developments: - **Gene Shalit**, the *Today* show's longtime, mustachioed movie and book critic, died June 12 at age 100. A mainstay of American morning television from 1970 until his 2010 retirement, his career traced the transformation of cultural criticism into mass-media personality. - **Anthony Head**, the actor known for *Buffy the Vampire Slayer* and *Ted Lasso*, died at 72. - Hockney tribute exhibitions and retrospectives across London — at the Tate and Serpentine — point to the enduring public hunger for serious visual art even as arts institutions face funding pressure and commercialization.

US-Iran deal on verge of collapse 48 hours after Versailles signing A 14-point memorandum of understanding signed by Donald Trump and Iranian representatives at a dinner in the Palace of Versailles on June 17 — formally ending the war that began with US-Israeli airstrikes on February 28, 2026 — was on the verge of breakdown within 48 hours. Israel, which refused to participate in the agreement, struck more than 80 targets in southern Lebanon on June 18, killing at least 47 people, following a Hezbollah ambush that killed four Israeli soldiers. --- Science, technology, and public health - [Whole-genome newborn screening study detects disorders missed by standard tests](#science-technology-and-public-health) — a cohort of nearly 10,000 Chinese newborns found 19 confirmed disorders, 8 missed by traditional screening - Fabricated citations in biomedical literature up 12-fold in two years - USAID dismantlement linked to over 600,000 preventable deaths as the Ebola response is starved of funds The most significant peer-reviewed development is a prospective cohort study of nearly 10,000 newborns in China, published in Nature Health, which found that whole-genome sequencing (WGS) identified 19 clinically confirmed disorders — eight of which were missed by traditional newborn screening — suggesting WGS detects monogenic conditions more effectively than standard methods. The finding has significant implications for screening policy, though it also raises questions about access, cost, and the commercial control of genomic data under a privatized health system. A second Nature Health analysis of government-led cash assistance for pregnant women in India found a 7.4% absolute reduction in low birth weight and increased maternal weight gain — concrete evidence that direct material support, not behavioral intervention, drives improvements in maternal and infant health. The finding bears directly on debates over whether poverty-related health outcomes are best addressed through income transfers or through means-tested, conditional programs of the kind being expanded across the imperialist centers. Separately, a Retraction Watch analysis found that roughly one in 277 PubMed-indexed papers in early 2026 cited fabricated references, a 12-fold increase in two years, reflecting the corrosion of scientific integrity under pressure from AI-generated text and publish-or-perish incentives.
