--- Arts and culture The death of David Hockney, who died June 11 at his London home at age 88, is the most culturally significant event of the period, and the WSWS published a substantial assessment by Paul Mitchell. Mitchell traces Hockney's career from his Bradford working-class roots through his Royal College of Art years, the Californian pool paintings (*A Bigger Splash*; *Portrait of an Artist (Pool with Two Figures)*), the revolutionary 1980s "joiners" (composite photographic works challenging single-point perspective), the controversial *Secret Knowledge* thesis that Old Masters used optical projection devices, the Yorkshire landscapes (*Garrowby Hill*; *Bigger Trees Near Warter*), and the lockdown-era *A Year in Normandie* (100+ iPad paintings). Mitchell credits Hockney's exceptional draftsmanship and his sustained inquiry into visual perception — recognizing genuine artistic achievement — while arguing that his "anarchistic individualism" accepted self-imposed limitations of content. Hockney examined the visible world with extraordinary intensity but deliberately excluded deindustrialization, class conflict, war, neoliberal restructuring, and widening inequality from his frame. The essay closes by calling on subsequent generations to widen their "visual scope, reintegrating beauty and history within unified frames" toward the "worldly comprehension that Hockney, despite his considerable gifts, deliberately declined to pursue." The mainstream obituaries (Washington Post, Guardian) emphasized his reinvention through technology and his status as an LGBTQ icon, but did not engage the social limits of his apolitical aesthetic. Mitchell's distinction — between recognizing Hockney's real contribution to the study of perception and identifying what his individualism excluded — exemplifies the WSWS approach to culture: artistic achievement is assessed seriously and on its own terms, while the social content of a body of work, including what it refuses to see, is subjected to historical criticism. Other developments: - **Film festivals:** The 25th Tribeca Festival (June 3–14, New York) awarded its Founders Award for Best US Narrative Feature to *Cotton Fever*, directed by Daniel Blake Schwartz. The New Media Film Festival's Grand Prize went to *Ish Meets A Mermaid*, by Ojibwe artist Jonathan Thunder, and the imagineNATIVE festival distributed $75,500 across 17 categories — a concentration of significant Indigenous-led work, though much of it filtered through the awards-circuit economy - **Literature:** American poet Sasha Debevec-McKenney won the 2026 Swansea University Dylan Thomas Prize, the largest literary prize for writers under 40 - **Photography:** British photographer Rene Matić won the £30,000 Deutsche Börse Photography Foundation Prize - **Sport and culture:** Jacobin reported on FIFA's complicity with the Trump administration's harassment of players and fans and the exclusion of Palestinian participation — a reminder of how international sport is being subordinated to militarist and nationalist agendas The breadth of festival and prize activity stands in contrast to the broader assault on arts funding amid austerity; genuine artistic achievement continues to emerge even as the institutions that sustain it face defunding.

On June 18, Mack Trucks worker Will Lehman received a presidential nomination at the UAW's 39th Constitutional Convention in Detroit, running as an openly socialist candidate on a platform of dismantling the union's top-down bureaucracy and returning power to the shop floor. This is his second campaign; his 2022 run exposed the limits of the UAW's "reform" experiment, when only about 10% of members participated in the first direct vote for international officers. Hall sets the nomination against the convention itself: incumbent president Shawn Fain received a $30,000 salary increase, strike-fund thresholds were altered to keep dues elevated while limiting strike support, a resolution to abolish immigration enforcement was rejected, and only a minimal divestment from Israeli investments was approved. Tree built a substantial following through a knowing, ironic synthesis of pop, alternative rock and internet-era performance art — a persona that both satirized and depended on the viral mechanics of the streaming economy. The consistent line is the subordination of socialist politics to the Democratic Party's electoral apparatus — the mechanism by which every insurgent movement in US history has been absorbed and neutralized. The death of British painter **David Hockney** at 88, on June 11, removes one of the most vital figures to emerge from mid-20th-century pop art. Hockney's California swimming-pool paintings, double portraits, photo-collages and opera designs spanned six decades; his restless experimentation — from Polaroid joiners to iPad drawing — reflected an artist who refused to treat any medium as beneath serious art. Whatever the commercial mythology built around him, Hockney's best work testifies to a sustained effort to render perception, light and intimacy with fresh eyes, against the grain of art-market cynicism. Starmer resigns as UK prime minister and Labour leader Keir Starmer resigned on June 22 as British prime minister and leader of the Labour Party, less than two years after leading Labour to one of the largest general election victories in UK history. His resignation was triggered by catastrophic local election losses in May, collapsing poll ratings, and the rapid rise of Nigel Farage's far-right Reform UK. Starmer will remain as caretaker prime minister until a successor is chosen; nominations open July 9 and close July 16, with a new leader expected before Parliament returns in September. Greater Manchester Mayor Andy Burnham — who has just won the Makerfield by-election and entered Parliament — is the clear frontrunner. Britain will have its **seventh prime minister in ten years**, a measure of the depth of the country's political and economic crisis. As Chris Marsden wrote in the WSWS Perspective, the resignation "was not driven by popular pressure from below but was demanded by the British ruling class" to preserve Labour as an instrument of austerity and war once Starmer himself had become a liability. The ruling class had turned to Labour in 2024 precisely because the Conservatives had become ungovernable; but its majority rested on the thinnest foundation, and Starmer proved unable to deliver on his assigned tasks — stabilizing British capitalism, restoring the US-UK relationship under Trump, prosecuting the NATO war in Ukraine, and suppressing working-class resistance. Trump delivered a parting humiliation, posting that Starmer "failed badly on two very important subjects — IMMIGRATION AND ENERGY." Key facts: - Starmer is the UK's sixth PM since Cameron, following May, Johnson, Truss and Sunak; Labour's 2024 majority rested on "the lowest share of the vote of any majority government in British history." - His appointment of Peter Mandelson as US ambassador entangled the government in the Epstein scandal; he failed to secure a meaningful trade deal with Washington while alienating European allies. - He repeatedly flinched before demands to cut welfare and to raise military spending to 3.5% of GDP by 2035; senior military officers publicly attacked him over insufficient rearmament. - Cabinet collapse preceded the fall: Health Secretary Wes Streeting and Defence Secretary John Healey resigned in the weeks before; Streeting immediately stood aside for Burnham. - Burnham has already abandoned his "end 40 years of neoliberalism" rhetoric, declaring himself "not squeamish" about welfare cuts and telling the BBC: "I do agree with what Farage is saying." - Jeremy Corbyn's "Your Party," which drew 800,000 initial supporters, has been demobilized to near-irrelevance; John McDonnell has urged Burnham to readmit Corbyn to Labour.

7. Alan Greenspan dies at 100 Former Federal Reserve Chair **Alan Greenspan died Monday at 100** from complications of Parkinson's disease. He led the Fed from **1987 to 2006**, navigating the 1987 stock-market crash, the 1997-98 Asian financial crisis and the LTCM collapse, and was celebrated during his tenure as "the Maestro." His legacy has since been substantially reassessed: critics blame his light-touch regulatory philosophy and low interest-rate policy — the so-called "Greenspan put" that socialized risk while privatizing gains — for fueling the subprime mortgage bubble that detonated in 2008. After the crash, Greenspan acknowledged "a flaw" in his ideological framework — his belief that banks' self-interest would protect shareholders — in testimony before Congress. It was a rare moment in which a ruling-class technocrat conceded that the theory underpinning decades of deregulation was wrong, even as the working class bore the cost of that error in foreclosures, unemployment and pension losses. Germany establishes permanent combat brigade in Lithuania German Defence Minister Boris Pistorius visited Lithuania to observe the first exercise of the Bundeswehr's **Armoured Brigade 45** — Germany's first permanently deployed combat brigade on foreign soil since World War II. Pistorius pledged the brigade will be fully operational with **4,800 soldiers by the end of 2027**, based at Rudninkai near the border with Belarus, and warned that not all deployed soldiers will be volunteers: Germany is prepared to **conscript** troops for the deployment if necessary. The "Freedom Shield 2026" exercise assembled around 2,900 soldiers — roughly 2,400 of them German — and some 800 vehicles from eight NATO states at the Pabradė training ground. The visit fell on the **85th anniversary of Operation Barbarossa**, the June 22, 1941 Nazi invasion of the Soviet Union that killed at least 27 million Soviet citizens. As Johannes Stern wrote in the WSWS, the choice of date is not incidental but exemplifies the inversion of "Never again" into its opposite, with German militarism once again massing forces on Russia's borders. Stern reports that Lithuanian authorities have reportedly threatened a memorial to Jewish partisans at the Bundeswehr site.

H5N1 avian influenza spread continues The global panzootic of highly pathogenic avian influenza H5N1 (clade 2.3.4.4b) continues to spread through wild birds, poultry and mammals across multiple continents. Recent surveillance reviews underscore the danger: a Lancet-cited review found that **human H5N1 infections can be asymptomatic** and that limited human-to-human transmission may already be occurring, exposing a critical gap in systems that monitor only symptomatic illness. In a recent reference period, public-health authorities logged hundreds of H5 detections in birds across two dozen European countries and 20 human infections — including four deaths — across six countries (Bangladesh, Cambodia, China, India, Mexico, Vietnam). Experts continue to warn that the virus is a leading candidate to drive the next human pandemic, while US surveillance has been weakened by federal staffing and funding cuts that leave the population dangerously exposed. --- Arts and culture The day's most politically revealing cultural item is HBO's release of Josh Fox's documentary *The Welcome Table*, profiled by Jacobin. Fox — best known for *Gasland* — argues that the climate crisis cannot be separated from empire and capitalism, advancing a case for universal freedom of movement for the hundreds of millions who will be displaced this century. The film's strength lies in connecting ecological catastrophe to the social order that produces it; its weakness, characteristic of the milieu around it, is a tendency to substitute moral appeal for any analysis of the working class as the agency capable of reorganizing production. Still, in a cultural landscape saturated with disaster spectacle that treats climate change as fate, a work insisting on its man-made, profit-driven character deserves serious engagement. Literature offers a quieter but significant moment in the Canadian launch of Maggie O'Farrell's new novel *Land*, among the most anticipated books of 2026. O'Farrell, whose *Hamnet* — adapted into the TIFF People's Choice-winning film she co-wrote — demonstrated a rare capacity to render historical grief and the texture of vanished lives, continues a body of work concerned with memory, loss and the persistence of ordinary people beneath the official record. At its best, such historical fiction restores the inner lives that "great man" history erases. Roundup: - **Repertory and restoration:** TIFF Lightbox screened a new 4K restoration of James Bidgood's *Pink Narcissus* (1971) for its 55th anniversary — a reminder of the value of preserving independent and avant-garde cinema against the streaming era's disposability — alongside a 20th-anniversary screening of *She's the Man* (2006). - **The Greenspan obituaries as culture war:** Jacobin's appraisal of the late Fed chair as "a faithful servant of the ruling class" stands against the hagiographic obituaries dominating the mainstream press, underscoring how the framing of a public figure's death is itself a political battleground. - **Cultural deaths of the month:** The wider toll of June 2026 included actor Anthony Head (*Buffy the Vampire Slayer*, *Ted Lasso*) at 72 and longtime *Today* film critic Gene Shalit at 100 — figures whose careers spanned the postwar consolidation and subsequent corporate hollowing-out of broadcast culture. The throughline across these items is the contest over historical memory and the social meaning of art — whether culture serves to illuminate the forces shaping human life or to anaesthetize against them. The genuine artistic achievements worth defending are those that, regardless of their makers' politics, insist on the reality of the social world.

Iran ceasefire frays as Tehran rejects new Hormuz shipping routes The fragile ceasefire ending the 2026 Iran war (Operation Epic Fury, Feb. 28–June 17) came under severe strain on June 25 as Iran declared newly proposed Strait of Hormuz shipping routes "unacceptable and dangerous," warning vessels against transiting without Iranian clearance. The declaration directly contradicts the US interpretation of the June 17 Islamabad Memorandum, signed by Trump at Versailles following the G7 and countersigned by Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian in Tehran. The 60-day window to negotiate a final settlement is now less than a month from expiry, and the dispute over who controls passage through the world's most important oil chokepoint has become the central flashpoint that could reignite open war. The standoff over Hormuz — through which roughly a fifth of global oil trade passes — has direct consequences for global energy markets and, through them, for working people facing surging fuel and food prices worldwide. Iran closed the strait on June 20, citing Israeli truce violations; some 150 freight vessels were stalled during earlier blockades. On June 24, Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz signed an order designating the Central Bank of Iran a terrorist organization, a provocative measure that further inflamed an already brittle truce. The interlocking of the US-Iran ceasefire with the unresolved Israel-Lebanon war means that continued Israeli operations in Lebanon are the specific violations Iran invokes — making a durable settlement in one theater impossible without the other. Key facts: - The war killed an estimated 3,468–6,000 Iranian military personnel, 39 Israelis, 3,912 Lebanese, and 16 US soldiers; Arab states incurred roughly $120 billion in damages, and Iran faces an estimated $1 trillion in economic losses. - US military costs reached $40 billion by June 21; Trump has requested an additional $87 billion from Congress, pushing the projected total above $127 billion in roughly four months. - The IAEA inspections dispute (see International developments) is a parallel obstacle, as US hawks demand verified denuclearization before any sanctions relief. The WSWS has covered the war throughout as a US-Israeli imperialist war over regional dominance and control of oil transit routes, in which the enormous human and financial costs are borne by workers in Iran, the Arab states, and the imperialist powers alike, while the oil and defense interests that drove the conflict reap the gains.

Justice Sonia Sotomayor delivered an oral dissent from the bench, stating that the ruling "regrettably and tragically extinguishes the light of the torch of the Statue of Liberty." The decision overturned lower-court orders that had blocked the administration's cap on daily asylum appointments — a metering practice that originated under the Obama administration and was expanded under Trump. The court issued a second immigration ruling the same day, blocking recipients of Temporary Protected Status (TPS) from seeking judicial relief — removing judicial oversight of executive detention and deportation decisions. The two rulings together effectively nullify asylum rights for tens of thousands fleeing conditions created or worsened by decades of US intervention, while weaponizing the legal fiction of non-arrival against the most vulnerable layers of the working class.

--- Arts and culture The intersection of art and the politics of war and historical memory dominates the cultural calendar this week. At the Australian War Memorial's reopening — analyzed in the WSWS coverage section below — the state's embrace of an alleged war criminal as a guest of honor underscored how official culture is being mobilized to sanitize imperial violence. A counterpoint emerges in documentary cinema: Academy Award winner Alex Gibney's *Knife: The Attempted Murder of Salman Rushdie*, inspired by the novelist's memoir of the 2022 stabbing that cost him an eye, confronts the long shadow of religious-reactionary violence against artistic freedom and the fatwa that has hung over Rushdie since 1989. The film's premiere this year keeps in view a question the cultural establishment prefers to bury: the defense of free expression against both theocratic and state repression. Festival season is at its height across the United States. The 23rd Rochester International Jazz Festival (June 19–27) is presenting more than 300 shows with over 1,750 artists, including Gladys Knight on June 26 and the Count Basie Orchestra on June 27 — a living link to the Black American musical tradition that arose out of the Great Migration and the social struggles of the 20th century. The 25th-anniversary Tribeca Festival has showcased work from both established and first-time filmmakers, while regional festivals from Utah to upstate New York continue to provide some of the few remaining venues for independent and working artists outside the streaming conglomerates. Roundup: - **Documentary:** Gibney's *Knife* situates the Rushdie attack within decades of clerical incitement and the failure of liberal institutions to defend writers under threat — a theme of renewed urgency amid rising censorship. - **Music:** The persistence of large free and low-cost jazz festivals reflects genuine popular demand for live communal art even as recorded-music revenue is captured by a handful of platforms; performers like Gladys Knight carry a repertoire forged in the civil-rights era. - **Visual arts and memory:** The reopening of national war memorials across the Anglosphere is increasingly an exercise in militarist myth-making, recasting colonial and imperial wars as occasions for solemn national pride. - **Cultural economy:** The contrast between SpaceX's $75 billion IPO and the defunding of public cultural and postal infrastructure exemplifies the diversion of social wealth from the commons to private capital — a pressure felt acutely by museums, libraries and performing-arts institutions facing budget cuts. The throughline is the deepening conflict between art as a vehicle for truth-telling about war, repression and social life, and the drive of the ruling class to subordinate culture to nationalism, spectacle and the market. Genuine artistic achievement — whether in Rushdie's literary defiance or in the jazz tradition's improvisational humanism — retains its force precisely because it resists that subordination.

US-Iran war escalates as both sides strike military bases The war between the United States and Iran sharply escalated over the weekend as both powers traded direct strikes on military installations, effectively ending a one-week-old ceasefire. On June 26, US Central Command struck Iranian missile and drone storage facilities and coastal radar sites near the port of Sirik in the Strait of Hormuz — the third US strike on Iran in three weeks — citing an Iranian drone attack on the cargo ship *Ever Lovely*. On June 27, Iran's Revolutionary Guard (IRGC) retaliated with drones and missiles against the Ali Al-Salem Air Base in Kuwait and the US Navy's Fifth Fleet base in Bahrain. No US casualties have been confirmed. The proximate trigger is Iran's demand that all commercial vessels transiting the Strait of Hormuz use an Iranian-designated northern route and obtain Iranian permission — a de facto blockade of a waterway carrying roughly 20% of global oil trade. Washington has rejected the demand. As Kevin Reed noted on the WSWS, the ceasefire's ambiguous language about Iran making "best efforts" on safe passage was "political theater from the outset," and Iranian parliamentary official Ebrahim Azizi accused the US of "attacking in the middle of negotiations once again." Key facts: - Trump warned Tehran: "There may come a point when we are no longer able to be reasonable," threatening to "complete the job"; Vice President Vance said "violence will be met with violence." - Iran declared it had "neutralized" the US strikes and pledged further retaliation. - Trump accused Iran of a "foolish violation" of the ceasefire after the *Ever Lovely* strike. - The Hormuz standoff represents a potential chokepoint crisis unseen since the 1980s tanker wars. The escalation marks the unraveling of a ceasefire that Washington itself had presented, only weeks ago, as a diplomatic triumph. The war the Trump administration launched in late February has already killed more than 3,000 Iranians by most estimates and triggered a global food and energy shock. Each cycle of strike and counter-strike now draws the Gulf monarchies — host to the very US bases Iran is targeting — deeper into a conflict their populations overwhelmingly oppose, while the danger of a miscalculation that pulls in additional powers grows. The targeting of US installations in Kuwait and Bahrain, even without casualties, represents a qualitative widening of the war beyond Iranian and Israeli territory and onto the soil of nominally neutral states.

National kindergarten MMR coverage has fallen to 92.5%, below the 95% herd-immunity threshold, and the US could lose the measles elimination status it has held since 2000 when authorities conduct a formal review in November. The resurgence tracks the collapse of childhood vaccination rates amplified by official anti-vaccine rhetoric and the gutting of public-health infrastructure — a preventable epidemic that falls hardest on poor and rural communities with the least access to care. Three measles deaths have already been recorded this year, the first US measles fatalities in nearly a decade. **Novel avian flu subtype infects a human for the first time.** The *New England Journal of Medicine* published a case report documenting the first human infection with highly pathogenic avian influenza A(H5N5), a subtype never previously reported in humans. Viral load was substantially higher in lower-respiratory-tract specimens than in upper-respiratory ones, complicating early detection. Separately, a University of Pittsburgh study explained why H5N1-infected dairy cows shed heavily in milk with few respiratory symptoms: the virus's preferred cell-surface receptors are concentrated in bovine mammary tissue rather than lung tissue — a finding with immediate implications for farm biosecurity and spillover risk to farmworkers. Roundup: - **COVID-19:** SARS-CoV-2 wastewater concentration is "very low," test positivity ~0.76%, with COVID declining or stable in 46 of 50 states; the CDC flags early uptick signals in the South and Midwest heading into summer travel. ([The Sick Times](https://thesicktimes.org/2026/06/16/national-covid-19-trends-june-16/)) - **Metabolism:** A new study found glucose strongly suppresses hunger-promoting hypothalamic neurons in mice while fructose suppresses them far more weakly despite identical calories — a possible neurological basis for fructose-driven overeating. Separately, researchers identified stem cells appearing in aging tissue that dramatically accelerate visceral fat formation, a candidate target against middle-age metabolic disease. - **AI policy:** As of June 26, 78 AI chatbot bills are active across 27 states. Rhode Island signed a chatbot-therapy ban into law; Arizona's governor vetoed three AI bills; California passed a ban on AI teachers in public schools (pending signature). The regulatory fragmentation intensifies pressure for federal legislation even as the "Magnificent Seven" market correction signals investor skepticism about AI capital-expenditure returns.

--- Arts and culture The most politically charged cultural development of the day is the Trump administration's "Great American State Fair," analyzed by David Walsh on the WSWS as empty patriotic spectacle — state pavilions offering shallow "sensory experiences" in place of genuine cultural expression. Walsh uses the fair as a lens onto the administration's broader assault on arts funding: the attempted elimination of the National Endowment for the Arts ($207 million in 2026), the National Endowment for the Humanities, and the Institute of Museum and Library Services, with Congress preserving funding only at 2025 levels under threat. Walsh calculates that the NEA's budget is 4,879 times smaller than military spending and notes that even funded arts organizations now self-censor under threat of defunding. Invoking Eisenhower's 1953 warning that arms spending diverts resources from education and culture, he argues the spectacle reflects capitalism's "ruthless and barbaric character" in a period of war and austerity. The episode is emblematic of a wider pattern in which the cultural superstructure is increasingly subordinated to militarism and nationalism. As the United States approaches the 250th anniversary of the Declaration of Independence, the official commemorations promise pageantry stripped of the revolutionary-democratic content the WSWS insists must be reclaimed by the working class rather than ceded to a ruling class busy dismantling democratic rights. The contrast is instructive: while the state mounts hollow festivals celebrating national greatness, the genuine cultural institutions that serve working people — libraries, museums, community arts programs, public-broadcasting affiliates — are starved of the modest sums that sustain them. The Institute of Museum and Library Services alone underwrites library services in thousands of communities that have no commercial alternative. The targeting of these bodies, whose combined budgets are a rounding error against the Pentagon's, reveals that the aim is not fiscal savings but the deliberate impoverishment of independent cultural and intellectual life. Roundup: - **Defunding as cultural policy:** The NEA/NEH/IMLS threats function less as a budgetary measure — the sums are trivial against the federal budget — than as a disciplining mechanism over independent cultural institutions, museums, and libraries. - **Self-censorship:** Walsh's reporting that even funded organizations preemptively soften programming illustrates how the threat of defunding produces a chilling effect well beyond the institutions directly targeted. - **Historical memory:** The contest over the meaning of 1776 — and the parallel polemic against the 1619 Project's framing of the Revolution as a counter-revolution for slavery — is itself a cultural-political struggle over how the past is mobilized in the present. For ICFI readers, the through-line is the WSWS framework: art and culture are not entertainment commodities or lifestyle content but expressions of definite social relations. The defunding of public arts, the nationalist repackaging of history, and the criminalization of dissent (see the Ulm 5 and Prairieland cases below) are facets of a single process — a ruling class stripping society of both material resources and critical cultural memory as it prepares for war abroad and class conflict at home.
Sources WSWS The Great American State Fair and the war on arts and culture in the US

Left Voice Left Voice has maintained a vocal anti-imperialist line on the US-Iran war, denouncing the strikes and Washington's regional aggression. Its coverage correctly identifies the conflict as imperialist, but the political conclusion it draws orients readers toward pressure on the existing protest movement and broad "anti-war" mobilization rather than toward the construction of a revolutionary party rooted in the working class. --- Arts and culture The WSWS marked a significant career retrospective this week with Kevin Reed's survey of **Peter Gabriel**, "From progressive rock to world music and beyond." The piece traces Gabriel's trajectory from his years fronting Genesis, through the commercial peak of *So* (1986), his founding of the WOMAD festival and Real World label, and up to his forthcoming eleventh studio album, *o/i*, due throughout 2026. Following the model of 2023's *I/O*, each track receives both "Bright-Side" and "Dark-Side" mixes released in step with the lunar cycle; the first single, "Been Undone," appeared on the January "wolf moon." Reed foregrounds Gabriel's political engagement — the 1980 anti-apartheid anthem "Biko," his human-rights activism, and his recent public condemnation of "Israel's genocidal violence in Gaza." Gabriel's career offers a case study in the WSWS's approach to culture: the impulse toward internationalism and social conscience in his best work (the collaborations across African, Middle Eastern and South Asian traditions on WOMAD stages) stands as a rebuke to the nationalism and provincialism now being cultivated across official culture. That an artist of Gabriel's stature has publicly named the Gaza genocide — at a moment when many cultural figures maintain silence for fear of blacklisting — is itself notable. Roundup: - **Cultural censorship in Texas:** The State Board of Education's mandate of Bible stories and its simultaneous purge of global-history content (covered above) belongs equally to the cultural sphere — part of a broader assault that includes more than 22,000 book challenges in Texas since 2021. This is the systematic narrowing of what may be taught, read and imagined. - **Historiography:** The WSWS published a letter from historian Steven Mintz praising a recent WSWS webinar's characterization of the American Revolution as a bourgeois revolution, contrasting the Marxist method favorably with academic historiography's turn toward discourse and identity. The exchange points to a live struggle over historical memory — whether the revolutionary content of the past is preserved or dissolved into fragmented "narratives." - **Music-industry note:** Gabriel's lunar-cycle release strategy — bypassing conventional album-cycle marketing — reflects both the creative possibilities and the commercial pressures of a streaming economy in which even established artists must engineer novelty to hold attention. The through-line across these items is the contest over culture as a terrain of political struggle: the ruling class works to impose religious and nationalist orthodoxy on public education while independent artists who engage honestly with war and oppression face marginalization.
Sources WSWS Peter Gabriel: From progressive rock to world music and beyond · Rolling Stone Peter Gabriel has a new album, but he needs to start thinking bigger

This week in history: the 1929-1930 miners' lockout John Harris and Peter Symonds recount the 15-month lockout of roughly 10,000 New South Wales coal miners beginning in 1929, a defining experience of the Australian working class. Mine owners, backed by the Bruce-Page conservative government, sought to slash wages and impose the "dilution" of labor. When miners resisted, they were locked out. On December 16, 1929, police opened fire on miners at the Rothbury colliery, killing 29-year-old Norman Brown and wounding many others. Trump disclosure shows income tripling to $2.2 billion Donald Trump's annual financial disclosure, filed with the Office of Government Ethics in a 927-page document, shows his reported income roughly tripling in a single year — from $622 million in 2024 to about $2.2 billion in 2025, the first year of his second term. The figures were reported across the financial press, with Bloomberg, NBC News, ABC News and CNBC all confirming that cryptocurrency was the dominant driver. The WSWS Perspective by Barry Grey frames the disclosure not as an ethics story but as evidence that the presidency has been converted into a "wealth-extraction machine." Grey renders the sum in class terms: $2.2 billion is "equivalent to the incomes of 37,931 US autoworkers," or roughly $251,000 per hour. Key facts: - About **$1.4 billion** of the total came from crypto, including roughly $636 million from a licensing deal tied to the $TRUMP memecoin and about $580 million connected to World Liberty Financial, which issues the WLFI token and USD1 stablecoin. - The wider Trump family's collective wealth has roughly doubled to about **$10 billion** since the November 2024 election; Eric Trump's net worth rose tenfold to $400 million. - Real estate added gains — Mar-a-Lago revenue rose to $77 million, Trump National Doral to $122 million — alongside more than $14 million in Saudi and Qatari licensing deals. - Trump refused to sign the standard ethics pledge, rescinded Biden-era ethics rules, and left the Office of Government Ethics leaderless after firing its director. - Asked about the figures, Trump claimed outside managers "run my money." Grey notes labor's share of national income fell to a record-low 53.8 percent in the third quarter of 2025, down from 70 percent in 1947, and concludes that "this entire class must be expropriated."

--- Arts and culture The most politically significant cultural development of the day is the detention of Turkish comedian **Deniz Göktaş** at Istanbul airport over political satire. As Ulaş Sevinç reports on the WSWS, the arrest is part of a widening crackdown by the Erdoğan government on artists, comedians and journalists whose work criticizes the state. The targeting of satire — historically among the sharpest weapons of the oppressed against arbitrary power — reflects the regime's fear of any independent voice as economic crisis and political instability deepen in Turkey. On the WSWS arts pages, **Clara Weiss** reviews the late historian Alexander Rabinowitch's fourth volume, *The Bolsheviks Survive: Petrograd 1919*. The book documents the Bolsheviks' rule during the civil war's most difficult year — fuel shortages, British intelligence infiltration by agents such as Paul Dukes, and Finnish counterrevolutionary conspiracies. It emphasizes Leon Trotsky's decisive intervention against General Yudenich's October 1919 assault on Petrograd, when Trotsky arrived by armored train and mobilized both the Red Army and the city's working class to prevent occupation. Rabinowitch also examines the March 1919 Eighth Party Congress, where the Stalin-backed Military Opposition challenged Trotsky's disciplined, centralized Red Army model — a conflict Lenin resolved in Trotsky's favor. Weiss praises the archival scholarship while noting the volume's neglect of the international context, above all the founding of the Communist International in 1919. Roundup: - **Victor Willis**, the original lead singer of the Village People and co-writer of "Y.M.C.A.," "In the Navy" and "Macho Man," died June 30 at 74. --- Science, technology, and public health - [Deadly heat wave drives a mounting public health emergency](#deadly-heat-wave-drives-a-mounting-public-health-emergency) — 185 million exposed to extreme heat with no federal occupational standard - [H5N1 bird flu continues low-level global spread](#h5n1-bird-flu-continues-low-level-global-spread) — 12 human cases outside the US from Aug 2025–June 2026, with three deaths - [New studies link climate change to health and social breakdown](#new-studies-link-climate-change-to-health-and-social-breakdown) — Nature research warns of conflated drivers in health projections Deadly heat wave drives a mounting public health emergency The heat wave gripping the United States is fundamentally a public health emergency as well as a labor one. Heat indexes reaching 115°F across a region home to more than 185 million people put the elderly, the chronically ill, and outdoor workers at acute risk of heat stroke and cardiovascular collapse. Emergency departments across the affected regions reported spikes in heat-related admissions. Public health experts note that the absence of a federal occupational heat standard — 50 years after OSHA's creation — leaves the workforce without enforceable protections, even as climate change makes such events more frequent and severe. The roughly 3,700 heat-related deaths recorded across Europe during comparable events underscore the scale of preventable mortality. H5N1 bird flu continues low-level global spread The CDC's latest global summary reports 12 human infections with avian influenza A(H5N1) outside the United States between August 2025 and June 2026, reported by Bangladesh, Cambodia and India, with three deaths (one in Bangladesh, two in Cambodia). No person-to-person spread was identified, and the CDC continues to assess the risk to the US public as low. Within the US, H5N1 remains widespread in wild birds and continues to cause outbreaks in commercial poultry across several states and in dairy cattle, with sporadic human infections among dairy and poultry workers. The ongoing circulation keeps alive the risk of viral reassortment. New studies link climate change to health and social breakdown - A study in **Nature Human Behaviour** found that "social health" — the ability to access and maintain meaningful human relationships — is a critical determinant of population health and climate resilience, and that climate change disrupts housing stability and community cohesion while social disconnection undermines collective capacity to respond. - Research in **Nature Medicine** warned that many climate-health projections conflate three distinct drivers of future risk: changes in climate hazards, population growth, and the underlying vulnerability of exposed populations — with implications for how mortality estimates are interpreted. Other developments: - **Measles:** The US continues to log confirmed cases across multiple states in 2026, with Florida among the states reporting the most cases (21 confirmed) — sustaining the trend of resurgent vaccine-preventable disease amid declining immunization rates and public health funding cuts. - **Technology/AI:** The expanding role of Palantir in the British state — including an NHS data contract now reportedly under review — highlights the fusion of AI surveillance infrastructure with the state apparatus, a development with far-reaching implications for democratic rights.

US measles cases near full-year 2025 total As of July 2, 2026, the US has recorded 2,170 confirmed measles cases across 41 jurisdictions, with 31 new outbreaks in 2026 and 93% of cases (2,019 of 2,170) outbreak-associated; 138 people (6%) have been hospitalized, with no deaths reported so far this year. Case counts are already approaching the full-year 2025 total with six months still to go, driven by kindergarten MMR vaccination coverage falling to 92.5% nationally — below the 95% herd-immunity threshold — leaving an estimated 286,000 kindergartners unprotected. The resurgence is the direct product of the anti-vaccine agenda now entrenched in federal public-health leadership.
Sources Global Biodefense US measles cases in 2026 nearly match full-year 2025 toll · CDC Measles data and research
H5N1 surveillance updated; udder-tropism mystery solved Between August 4, 2025 and June 10, 2026, 12 human H5N1 infections were reported outside the US (Bangladesh: 3, Cambodia: 8, India: 1), including 3 deaths, all linked to sick or dead poultry exposure with no evidence of human-to-human transmission. The CDC and WHO maintain that public-health risk remains low, but continued mammalian spillover keeps surveillance a priority. Separately, researchers explained why H5N1 behaves differently in dairy cattle: the receptors the virus needs are abundant throughout udder tissue but nearly absent in airway tissue, explaining why it concentrates in milk rather than causing respiratory disease. One hundred dairy herds across 18 states remain in USDA's voluntary monitoring program as field trials of a cattle vaccine continue.
Sources CDC H5N1 global summary · ScienceDaily Why H5N1 behaves differently in dairy cattle

As Kevin Reed argued on the WSWS, the spectacle functions as modern "bread and circuses" — a lavish celebrity distraction unfolding in the same city where hundreds of thousands live in poverty, and timed suspiciously close to the Independence Day festivities. The event, and the wall-to-wall entertainment-press coverage it commanded, epitomizes a culture industry that recycles extreme private wealth as mass entertainment while the social crisis deepens. That such extravagance is presented as aspirational, rather than obscene, is itself a measure of the ideological role assigned to celebrity culture. The week also underscored how sections of the media establishment are actively cultivating the far right. In Australia, TV host Karl Stefanovic launched a podcast featuring far-right figures including Pauline Hanson and British agitator Tommy Robinson before it was pulled following public backlash. The WSWS analysis situates this not as an isolated misjudgment but as part of a broader strategy by media elites to channel genuine social alienation toward reactionary, nationalist politics rather than allow it to find left-wing expression — a warning about the mainstreaming of fascistic voices under the guise of "anti-establishment" edginess. Roundup: - **Independence Day cultural programming:** The federal "Freedom 250" commemoration drove a wave of official 250th-anniversary cultural events, museum exhibitions, and media retrospectives — overwhelmingly framed in nationalist and celebratory terms that suppress the revolutionary, egalitarian content of 1776 and its unfinished character. - **Music and visual art:** The RCP/IMT's own arts coverage this week (see pseudo-left review) surveyed jazz titan Sonny Rollins, painter Hurvin Anderson, and the exhibition "Stitching the Intifada" — a reminder that Palestinian solidarity continues to surface in gallery and textile art even amid institutional pressure and the political climate around Gaza. - **Publishing loss in Kyiv:** The Russian strike that destroyed roughly 800,000 books at a Kyiv publishing warehouse (see Top stories) is also a cultural atrocity — the physical destruction of literature and the material basis of Ukrainian intellectual life, a dimension of the war that deserves recognition alongside the human toll. Across these developments a common thread runs: culture under conditions of war, austerity, and oligarchy is increasingly pressed into service either as distraction from the social crisis or as a vehicle for reactionary politics — even as genuine artistic engagement with war and oppression persists at the margins.

Russia launches its largest air assault of the year on Kyiv Russian missiles and drones struck the Ukrainian capital in the early hours of July 6, killing at least 12 people and wounding some 60 more, according to President Volodymyr Zelensky. Emergency crews combed rubble at residential high-rises in two districts that took direct hits. Ukraine's air force said Russia fired 351 drones and 68 missiles overnight, and that all 29 ballistic missiles launched struck their targets — a sign of the widening gap in Ukrainian air defenses after months of attrition and dwindling Western interceptor supplies. Russia's Defense Ministry described the bombardment as retaliation for Ukrainian long-range strikes that have inflicted severe fuel shortages inside Russia. The Kyiv attack follows a Russian strike days earlier that killed 31 people in the capital — the deadliest single assault on Kyiv this year. Key facts: - Ukrainian strikes cut power across occupied Crimea; the Moscow-appointed head of Sevastopol reported blackouts later restored via backup equipment - Two people were wounded and more than 70 Ukrainian drones downed over Yaroslavl, Russia - Trump is scheduled to meet Zelensky and Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa on the sidelines of a NATO summit in Turkey this week

Heat dome kills at least 25 in the US as European toll nears 20,400 A multi-day heat dome over the central and eastern United States killed at least 25 people over the July 4 weekend, with New Jersey accounting for 22 of the confirmed deaths. Officials said many victims were found in homes without air conditioning; others were discovered on the street or in parked cars. Atlantic City hit 106°F on July 4 and Newark reached 105°F for the first time since 2001. Key facts: - Spain and Portugal approached 44°C (111°F); France recorded its hottest June day on record at 43.3°C (110°F) - The World Weather Attribution initiative found fossil-fuel emissions have sharply intensified European heat waves within a few decades - Cooling demand across parts of Europe hit its highest level in at least 45 years

PECO utility workers strike for the first time in 145 years More than 1,600 unionized workers at Philadelphia Electric Company (PECO) walked off the job just after midnight July 4 — the first strike in the utility's 145-year history — after contract negotiations collapsed amid a lethal heat wave. IBEW Local 614 members across automation, engineering, customer service, facilities and line work struck over wages, benefit tiers and pensions. --- Arts and culture Christopher Nolan's **The Odyssey** premieres in London today, July 6, ahead of a July 17 wide release by Universal in IMAX and premium formats. Adapted from Homer's epic, the film follows Odysseus's perilous return from the Trojan War through encounters with the Cyclops, the Sirens and Calypso. It carries an unusually large ensemble — Matt Damon as Odysseus, Anne Hathaway as Penelope, Tom Holland as Telemachus, Zendaya as Athena, Robert Pattinson as Antinous and Charlize Theron as Circe — and was shot on location across Italy, Iceland, Greece, Morocco and Scotland. That a major studio is mounting a mass-audience adaptation of one of the foundational works of world literature — a narrative of war, exile, endurance and homecoming — is itself notable in an industry dominated by franchise product; the reception will test whether serious engagement with the classical inheritance can still command a broad public. The premiere arrives against the backdrop of the US "semiquincentennial," a commemoration the Trump administration has sought to bend toward nationalist and militarist spectacle — the Mount Rushmore address and fireworks being the clearest example. The tension between the democratic and revolutionary content of 1776 and its reactionary appropriation is a live cultural battleground, one the pseudo-left is also contesting (see below). Roundup: - **Deaths:** **Victor Willis**, the original lead singer of the Village People and co-writer of "Y.M.C.A." and "Macho Man," died June 30 at 74 following a short, aggressive illness. Willis, the group's "cop," spent years in litigation reclaiming rights to songs that became inescapable fixtures of popular culture — a reminder of how the music industry's structures dispossess the artists who create its most enduring work - **Documentary:** *The Last Picture Shows*, Rustin Thompson's documentary chronicling 10,825 miles of travel to film 123 movie theaters in small American towns, was released July 5 — an elegy for communal cultural spaces hollowed out by economic decline and consolidation - **Festivals:** The Tribeca and Provincetown festivals wound down amid a summer calendar; industry press continues to track the concentration of distribution in a handful of streaming platforms

--- Arts and culture The WSWS published two significant cultural pieces in the past 24 hours, both engaging directly with the relationship between artistic production and social crisis. **David Walsh's critique of the New York Times' list of "definitive" films about America** takes aim at the newspaper's selections as historically shallow and evasive. The WSWS argues that the *Times*' curatorial framework — bound up with the outlook of an affluent upper-middle-class layer — is incapable of honestly reckoning with the great questions of American history: slavery, war, class exploitation and revolution. Walsh's essay defends the principle that film, like all art, must be judged by its capacity to illuminate objective social reality rather than flatter contemporary prejudices. The WSWS treats such works seriously: not as protest branding, but as expressions, however partial, of a radicalizing mood among artists and audiences responding to a world in crisis. Trump tears up Iran truce and reopens war President Trump declared the 60-day US-Iran truce reached June 17 to be dead, telling reporters alongside NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte, "As far as I'm concerned, it's over," and warning the US would "very probably" attack Iran "hard again tonight." US Central Command said American forces struck roughly 90 targets across southern Iran to "degrade" Iran's ability to threaten navigation in the Strait of Hormuz; Iranian authorities reported eight military personnel killed. Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps answered with drone and missile fire at US targets, and Iran struck US bases in Kuwait and Bahrain, warning other Gulf states against facilitating American aggression. The immediate pretext was an attack on three commercial tankers transiting the Strait of Hormuz on Tuesday, which Washington and Gulf governments blamed on Tehran without direct Iranian claim of responsibility. The deeper trigger, as the WSWS Perspective by Keith Jones details, was the US cancellation of an oil-sanctions waiver Tuesday, followed within hours by air strikes on more than 80 targets. Trump threatened to reimpose a naval blockade and to "take over" Kharg Island, Iran's main oil export terminal, and boasted of having ordered the strike that killed Supreme Leader Ayatollah Khamenei at the war's outset, calling Iran's leaders "scum." Key facts: - Trump: "I don't want to deal with them anymore… as far as I'm concerned, it's over." - The truce was signed with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian after the US failed to achieve regime change or eliminate Iran's nuclear and missile programs. - Since July 4, millions have joined six days of funeral observances for Khamenei and family members, including his 14-month-old granddaughter killed in the February 28 decapitation strike. - Democratic criticism came from the right: Senator Adam Schiff called the earlier truce "a thorough capitulation"; Senator Chris Murphy termed it "essentially a surrender to Iran." The first was a migratory brown skua found in Cape Le Grand National Park; the NSW case was a giant petrel near Hawks Nest. Officials report no mass mortality, no poultry infection, and low human risk to date. Australia was the last continent without local transmission of the panzootic strain. As Gary Alvernia reported on the WSWS, more than 280 million birds have been culled worldwide and at least 10 human deaths recorded since 2021. The WSWS criticizes Australia's $113 million response as underfunded — only $22 million allocated for vaccination and PPE — reflecting the same neglect of public-health infrastructure that has characterized the ruling-class response to COVID-19. mRNA vaccine and gene-editing advances - **Nipah vaccine:** A phase 1 study in *Nature Medicine* found that an mRNA vaccine (mRNA-1215) encoding the Nipah virus Malaysian-strain protein was safe and induced elevated immune responses at one year — a notable step against a pathogen whose case-fatality rate can exceed 70 percent. - **In-vivo base editing:** A phase 1 trial in six patients reported that lipid-nanoparticle base editing targeting PCSK9 in liver cells reduced LDL cholesterol without serious adverse events, advancing one-time genetic therapies for cardiovascular disease. - **Antimicrobial resistance:** An evaluation across 193 countries for the 2026 Global Action Plan update found that states with strong multisectoral governance achieved measurable reductions in antimicrobial resistance — underscoring that AMR is fundamentally a question of public investment and coordination. - **Infrastructure and disease:** The Sri Lankan prison catastrophe and Michigan carbon-monoxide deaths (above) are, in the final analysis, public-health failures rooted in overcrowding and grid neglect — reminders that "science" questions are inseparable from the allocation of social resources.

--- Arts and culture The most pointed cultural intervention of the past day came from the WSWS, where David Walsh dissected the *New York Times*' feature ranking the "definitive" movies about America. Walsh's critique goes beyond quibbling over a list: he argues the panel's omission of works like *Citizen Kane* and *The Grapes of Wrath* — films that confront class, poverty, and the concentration of wealth and power — in favor of more fashionable choices reflects the *Times*' abandonment of any class-based, historical understanding of American life. The exercise, he contends, substitutes identity-inflected and market-driven criteria for a serious reckoning with the social truths great cinema has captured. It is a useful illustration of how a leading organ of upper-middle-class opinion approaches culture: as a curation of taste divorced from the objective realities of American society. Against this backdrop, the summer's release calendar leans heavily on nostalgia and the recycling of the pop-cultural past rather than new work grappling with the present crisis: - **Music documentaries:** *Sia: Nostalgic for the Present*, a 75-minute concert film, gets a limited release July 23; *Wham! 10 Days in China*, the 1986 record of the duo's George Michael–led tour, returns to theaters July 28. Both trade on the packaging of earlier decades — a symptom of an industry with diminishing confidence in the contemporary. - **Theater revival:** A new *Death Note* stage musical is being revived for a 2026 London run, part of the broader mining of established franchises for the West End. - **Cultural losses of 2026:** The year has already claimed Canadian vocalist David Clayton-Thomas of Blood, Sweat & Tears, whose brass-driven, socially conscious late-1960s hits reflected a period of ferment, and Alan Osmond of the Osmonds — figures whose careers spanned the commercialization of postwar popular music. The WSWS framework insists that cultural production be read as a register of social contradictions. In a period defined by war, mass strikes, and the drive toward authoritarian rule, the retreat into nostalgia and franchise revival — and the *Times*' aestheticized, class-blind canon-making — reveal an artistic establishment increasingly detached from the great questions confronting humanity. The genuine artistic achievements of earlier eras, whether the muckraking realism of *The Grapes of Wrath* or the formal daring of *Citizen Kane*, remain a standard against which the thinness of much current output is measured.

The festival remains a venue where serious international cinema — including work from Eastern Europe, the Balkans and the Global South — reaches audiences outside the commercial Hollywood circuit, at a moment when war and militarism increasingly shape both funding and content across the film world. Looming over the summer release calendar is Christopher Nolan's **The Odyssey**, opening July 17 in the United States. Adapted from Homer's epic and featuring Matt Damon, Tom Holland, Zendaya, Robert Pattinson and Anne Hathaway, the film represents another large-scale attempt to return ancient epic to mass audiences. Homer's poem — a meditation on war, homecoming, exile and the human cost of a decade-long conflict — carries obvious resonance in an era of open imperialist war; whether Nolan's spectacle engages that content critically or reduces it to visual grandeur will be the test. In the visual arts, two major exhibitions center women artists of the twentieth century: - **Alice Neel, "Beautifully Imperfect,"** opens July 16 at the Serralves Foundation in Porto. The through-line across these developments is the pull of war, exile and class on serious culture — and the countervailing pressure of institutions to defang that content. Genuine artistic achievement, from Neel's portraits to Klimov's cinema, retains its power precisely because it refuses to look away.

The New Zealand actor, who died "suddenly and unexpectedly" in Sydney, built a five-decade career spanning independent art cinema, international blockbusters and television. Best known globally as Dr. Alan Grant in *Jurassic Park*, Neill's finest work lay in more textured roles — from Jane Campion's *The Piano* to the menacing performances in *Possession* and *In the Mouth of Madness* — that revealed a subtle, intelligent screen presence. His passing marks the loss of an actor whose career bridged the New Zealand and Australian new waves with the Hollywood studio system, and who repeatedly chose challenging material over easy stardom. Elsewhere, the machinery of state intervention in culture is advancing on multiple fronts: - **Trump's assault on the Smithsonian.** The administration is moving to impose what the WSWS terms a "fascistic version of US history" on the Smithsonian museums, purging exhibitions on slavery, racism and class struggle in favor of a triumphalist national narrative (see WSWS coverage below). The effort to rewrite historical memory from above is a hallmark of authoritarian regimes and a direct attack on the scientific study of history. - **Booker Prize.** The 2026 Booker Prize longlist — the "Booker Dozen" — will be announced Tuesday, July 28, focusing attention on the year's literary fiction and the ongoing pressures of consolidation and commercialization in publishing. - **Film.** The expanded Fraenkel Film Festival opened in early July, with Christian Marclay programming Brian De Palma's *Carrie*. Documentarian Ross McElwee's new film *Remake* — a somber meditation generated by the death of his son — arrives in theaters this month, alongside a 40th-anniversary re-release of his landmark *Sherman's March*. Rustin Thompson's documentary *The Last Picture Shows*, traveling 10,825 miles to record 123 small-town movie theaters, chronicles the slow extinction of communal cinema-going under the pressures of streaming monopolies and economic decline. - **Visual arts.** The Galway International Arts Festival 2026 features Sean Henry's lifelike figurative sculptures — part of a broader resurgence of representational public art engaging directly with the human figure. These developments unfold against a backdrop of tightening political control over cultural institutions, from museum defundings to the intimidation of the press. The WSWS framework insists that art be understood in its social and historical context: works like *The Last Picture Shows* and McElwee's autobiographical documentaries speak to real processes of social atomization and loss, while the state's drive to rewrite history at the Smithsonian is an ideological weapon of a ruling class preparing for war and repression.

US resumes bombing of Iran and reimposes Strait of Hormuz blockade The United States has entered a renewed and far more dangerous phase of its war against Iran, three weeks after the June 17 ceasefire collapsed. After Iran fired on a commercial ship transiting the Strait of Hormuz over the weekend and declared the waterway "closed until further notice," US Central Command launched three consecutive nights of strikes. Iran said it struck two tankers; the US said it hit scores of targets — coastal surveillance systems, drone and missile sites — and Iran fired toward Jordan, Qatar, Kuwait and Oman. Trump then reimposed a naval blockade of Iranian ports, set to resume at 4 p.m. ET Tuesday, and announced via Truth Social that Washington would provide protection for shipping through Hormuz "at the rate of 20% on all cargo shipped." He told a radio host, "We're going to hit them very hard tonight... and there's not a damn thing they can do about it." Crossings through the strait have fallen by more than half week-on-week. As Andre Damon wrote in the WSWS Perspective, a blockade is "inherently an act of war whose logic points toward invasion," vindicating a June 15 warning that the 2026 ceasefire "will pave the way for the war that follows." No faction of the political establishment opposes the war's predatory aims — only its results. Key facts: - US forces struck **300+ targets** across Iran over three nights; two carrier strike groups, two amphibious groups and ~**50,000 troops** are massed in the region - Trump threatens to seize **Kharg Island**, through which ~90% of Iran's oil exports flow, and to destroy power/desalination plants serving 90 million people - The war, launched in February, has failed after **136 days** to topple Tehran, dismantle its nuclear program or seize Hormuz - Democratic complicity: Schumer called the June deal the "art of surrender"; Pence (WSJ op-ed) called it "appeasement" and urged Trump to "let the armed forces finish the job"

--- Arts and culture - [Sam Neill dies at 78](#sam-neill-dies-at-78) — the New Zealand actor of *Jurassic Park*, *The Piano* and *Possession* died in Sydney, "sudden and unexpected" - [Court rejects Trump bid to keep his name on DC arts venue](#court-rejects-trump-bid-to-keep-his-name-on-dc-arts-institution) — DC Circuit denies all arguments against removal Sam Neill dies at 78 Sam Neill, the New Zealand actor whose career spanned four decades, died in Sydney on Monday, July 13, at 78. His family called the loss "sudden and unexpected," noting he had announced in April he was cancer-free after years of treatment for blood cancer. Neill achieved international recognition as paleontologist Dr. Alan Grant in Steven Spielberg's *Jurassic Park* (1993), a role he reprised across the franchise. But the enduring measure of Neill's artistry lies in more demanding work. In Jane Campion's *The Piano* (1993) he played the repressed colonial husband Alisdair Stewart, and in Andrzej Żuławski's *Possession* (1981) he gave one of the era's most harrowing portrayals of psychological disintegration. He anchored the Australian miniseries *The Dismissal* and brought a wry humanism to television and independent films alike. A serious, self-effacing craftsman who spent much of his later life running a vineyard in Central Otago, Neill embodied a generation of actors formed by the flowering of Australian and New Zealand cinema in the 1970s–80s — a national film culture built with public investment now being eroded across the Anglophone world. --- Science, technology, and public health - [Record cyclosporiasis outbreak sickens nearly 7,000](#science-technology-and-public-health) — 34 states affected, Michigan hardest hit with 3,309 cases, exceeding the 2019 record with six weeks left in the season. - [H5N1 bird flu remains widespread with sporadic human cases](#science-technology-and-public-health) — 71 US human cases and 2 deaths since 2024; 12 additional cases abroad since August 2025, with 3 deaths. - [Lancet Countdown warns of surging European heat deaths](#science-technology-and-public-health) — 99.6% of monitored European regions saw more heat-attributable deaths in 2015–24 than in 1991–2000. - [DRC Ebola outbreak triggers new US travel restrictions](#science-technology-and-public-health) — US now requires travelers from Congo to spend 21 days elsewhere before entry. A record cyclosporiasis outbreak has sickened nearly 7,000 people across 34 states, with Michigan the hardest hit at 3,309 cases — already exceeding the 2019 record with six weeks left in the season. As Evan Blake reports on the WSWS, the surge follows Trump–Kennedy administration cuts that gutted federal foodborne-disease surveillance, eliminating some 3,500 FDA and 2,400 CDC jobs. The outbreak, driven by contaminated fresh produce, is a direct consequence of dismantling public-health infrastructure in the interests of agribusiness profit; the WSWS calls for socialized public health and the expropriation of the agribusiness monopolies. Disease surveillance: - **H5N1 avian influenza:** The CDC reports 71 human cases and 2 deaths in the US from 2024 to May 2026, with no confirmed person-to-person spread; globally, 12 additional human cases (3 fatal, in Bangladesh and Cambodia) were reported from August 2025 to June 2026 across Bangladesh, Cambodia, and India. The virus remains widespread in wild birds, US poultry, and dairy cattle. - **Measles:** The US recorded 164 confirmed cases in 2025 across nine states, with continued clusters driven by declining vaccination rates and the erosion of federal public-health capacity. - **Ebola (DRC):** US health officials now require citizens who have traveled in the Democratic Republic of Congo to spend 21 days in a third location before entering the US amid a growing outbreak — a punitive measure that does nothing to address the underfunded state of Congo's war-ravaged health system. Climate and environment: - The **2026 Europe report of the Lancet Countdown** on health and climate change finds that nearly all monitored European regions (823, or 99.6 percent) saw increased heat-attributable deaths in 2015–24 compared with 1991–2000, warning of a "narrowing window for decisive health action." - New analyses in **Nature Climate Change** document multidimensional intensification of global heat stress since 1950 and show, across more than 5,100 species, that climate change has caused more frequent local extinctions among temperate than tropical species. The convergence of these findings — accelerating heat mortality, spreading zoonotic disease, and the deliberate defunding of surveillance — underscores the WSWS argument that the response to biological and climatic threats is being sacrificed to austerity and private profit.

--- Arts and culture The death of **Sam Neill**, the New Zealand actor, dominated cultural news. Neill died in Sydney aged 78, in a passing described as "sudden and unexpected," months after he said in April that he remained cancer-free following treatment for stage-three blood cancer. Neill's five-decade career resists the reduction of screen acting to blockbuster spectacle. Though best known internationally as Dr. Alan Grant in *Jurassic Park*, he built a body of work rooted in the independent and art cinema of Australia and New Zealand — from Gillian Armstrong's *My Brilliant Career* (1979), a landmark of the Australian film revival engaging questions of women's independence and colonial society, to Jane Campion's *The Piano* (1993). His willingness to embody menace and moral ambiguity, in films from *Possession* to *Dead Calm*, reflected a serious craftsman's temperament increasingly rare in an industry dominated by franchise product. His obituaries have rightly stressed the substance of his work over its box-office scale. In new releases, **Christopher Nolan's *The Odyssey*** — an adaptation of Homer starring Matt Damon, Tom Holland, Anne Hathaway, Robert Pattinson, Zendaya, Charlize Theron, and Lupita Nyong'o — anchors the summer film calendar. A large-scale studio treatment of one of the founding works of Western literature carries the potential to bring the epic's themes of war, exile, and homecoming to a mass audience, though it also raises the perennial question of whether the spectacle apparatus of contemporary Hollywood can do justice to the poem's tragic and humanist depths. Roundup: - **The Odyssey (film):** Nolan's ensemble adaptation of Homer arrives as the season's most anticipated release, testing whether classical literature can survive translation into franchise-scale cinema. - **Booker Prize:** The 2026 "Booker Dozen" longlist will be announced July 28 — an occasion to assess the state of literary fiction against the pressures of a concentrated publishing industry. - **Fraenkel Film Festival:** The expanded 2026 edition opens with artist Christian Marclay's choice, Brian De Palma's *Carrie*, and marks the 40th anniversary re-release of Ross McElwee's *Sherman's March*, a foundational work of personal documentary cinema. - **Repertory and revival culture** — the festival re-releases and artist-curated screenings — point to a continued appetite for cinema history that runs counter to the streaming platforms' erasure of the film heritage. These developments should be understood against the broader assault on culture — defunding, censorship of anti-war and pro-Palestinian expression, and the subordination of artistic production to corporate concentration — that the WSWS has documented, and against which genuine artistic achievement, wherever it appears, must be defended.

--- WSWS coverage — last 24 hours **Perspective published:** "A revealing comment from former IMF chief economist" by Nick Beams — read in full on wsws.org Beams takes as his point of departure a *New York Times* op-ed by Pierre-Olivier Gourinchas, who stepped down in June as the IMF's chief economist and, freed from institutional constraints, offered an unusually candid diagnosis of the crisis of world capitalism. Beams' central argument is that Gourinchas's framing of the world economy as caught between two opposing "forces" — the destruction of war and the supposedly countervailing boost of AI investment — is fundamentally misleading: AI under capitalism does not offset the logic of war and fragmentation but intensifies the same contradictions, being deployed to destroy jobs and raise profit rates. The two "forces" are two expressions of a single crisis of the profit system. Beams treats Gourinchas's own words as significant admissions from within bourgeois orthodoxy. Gourinchas warned of "a dangerous feedback loop" as "countries seek to insulate themselves from perceived risks" and "risk fragmenting the global economy further still," and observed that "the world's superpowers are searching for strategic advantages, identifying choke points, adopting inward-looking policies and increasing military expenditures." Most strikingly, Beams highlights Gourinchas's explicit analogy to the pre-1914 period: "We have seen such dynamics before... What followed was a period of intense deglobalization, coinciding with rising nationalism and militarization — and two world wars." Beams reads this as an unintentional concession that global capitalism is retracing the slide into inter-imperialist war. Gourinchas, he concludes, "could offer no solution" beyond a "vacuous appeal" to IMF cooperation; the only answer is "the perspective of socialist revolution." Jacobin / DSA Jacobin's coverage of the Iran war, **"Unable to Accept Defeat, Donald Trump Presses On in Iran,"** frames the escalation as Trump's stubborn refusal to accept a strategic defeat, emphasizing Iran's leverage over the Strait of Hormuz. The anti-imperialist framing is directed at Trump's personal recklessness and US militarism, but it does not call for the independent mobilization of the working class against the war — leaving the "solution" implicitly with a more rational bourgeois foreign policy. This is made explicit in **"The Left Needs Its Own Foreign Policy,"** which argues the US left lacks a coherent program and implies that foreign policy is a domestic prize to be won through electoral coalitions — a national-reformist conception that substitutes influence over the American state for international class struggle. A third piece, **"Why the French Revolution Matters,"** offers competent popular-Marxist history of 1789 as a bourgeois revolution, disconnected from present tasks. *Assessment:* Jacobin channels genuine anti-war sentiment into pressure for a reformed imperialist policy administered by the Democratic Party, never breaking from the framework of the American nation-state. Left Voice Left Voice reports the **UAW's divestment of $400,000 in Israel bonds** as a rank-and-file victory forced onto the convention agenda by UAWD pressure, correctly crediting pressure from below rather than the leadership. **"Promises, Promises: AOC, Israel, and the DSA"** criticizes AOC and the DSA from the left for illusions in the Democratic Party, consistent with the group's "no confidence in the Democrats" line, while **"General Strike to Shut Down the Shutdown"** calls for independent mass action rather than Democratic maneuvering. *Assessment:* Left Voice remains the pseudo-left tendency closest to a class-independent posture, but its "from below" activism is not anchored in a struggle to build a revolutionary party, leaving its militant calls without a strategic road forward. The **"Solidarity Statement with the Communist Party of Turkey (TKP) on the anti-NATO protests"** exemplifies PSL's campism — solidarity organized around opposition to NATO rather than an independent working-class internationalism, aligning the group with state and party actors positioned against Washington. *Assessment:* PSL's campist orientation subordinates the working class to a geopolitical bloc politics, obscuring the class character of the regimes and forces it defends. Socialist Alternative **"ICE Murders Again—Build The Fightback From Houston To Maine!"** calls for an organized mass fightback against the ICE killings, converging with the SEP's factual account but framing the response around movement-building rather than a political struggle against the capitalist state. **"The Democrats Won't Save Us—The Case For A New Party"** explicitly rejects reliance on the Democrats and argues for a new workers' party, while **"Middle East War: Capitalism Offers No Way Out"** blames US-Israeli aggression for 10,000+ dead and calls for international working-class opposition. *Assessment:* Socialist Alternative's break from the Democrats is welcome, but its "new party" remains a broad-left electoral vehicle rather than a Marxist revolutionary party, and its perspective stops at protest. US widens war on Iran with fifth day of strikes and reimposed naval blockade The United States carried out a fifth consecutive day of airstrikes on Iran this week and reimposed a naval blockade of Iranian ports, sharply escalating a war launched on February 28 to topple the Tehran government and seize control of the Strait of Hormuz. CENTCOM announced it had disabled an empty oil tanker sailing toward Kharg Island — Iran's main crude-export terminal — the first vessel struck since the blockade was restored. US officials described the latest wave of strikes as intended to degrade Iran's ability to target shipping in the strait. Iranian officials said overnight strikes hit an army barracks and other sites, killing at least seven soldiers and wounding roughly 260 people across the country. Government spokesperson Fatemeh Mohajerani said strikes on southern Iran killed more than 30 civilians. Tehran said it retaliated against US military infrastructure in Kuwait, Bahrain and Jordan. More than four months after the war began, the government still stands and the strait remains contested, pushing Washington toward open discussion of a ground invasion. Trump told Fox News, "Sometimes you need a ground campaign." As Andre Damon wrote in the WSWS Perspective, the war abroad and the police-state buildup at home are "two fronts of the same war." He cited a former Pentagon official's estimate that securing the strait would require tens of thousands of troops at "very high costs," and noted that a Reuters/Ipsos poll found only 37 percent of Americans backed resuming the bombing. Key facts: - Pentagon acknowledges 14 US dead and 414 wounded as of Monday; WSWS calls the figure systematically understated. - Internal Pentagon cost estimate runs up to $100 billion (NBC News); Harvard's Linda Bilmes projects long-run costs above $1 trillion, including $200–300 billion to repair 228 damaged US military sites. - Strait shipping traffic collapsed to roughly 6 vessel crossings in a recent 24-hour window versus 18–22 per day normally.

US measles cases near 2,300, threatening elimination status The CDC reported 2,231 confirmed measles cases in the United States as of July 9 — just 58 short of the 2,289 recorded for all of 2025, with six months of the year remaining. There have been 32 outbreaks, and 93 percent of cases are outbreak-associated, spanning more than 40 states and the District of Columbia. Officials attribute the surge chiefly to falling vaccination coverage: MMR coverage among kindergartners dropped from 95.2 percent in 2019–2020 to 92.5 percent in 2024–2025, below the 95 percent threshold needed for herd immunity. The CDC warned that summer travel will likely drive further cases, and authorities will formally review whether the US retains its measles elimination status in November.

H5N1 now confirmed on every continent The dominant H5N1 strain (clade 2.3.4.4b) is now circulating in wild birds, poultry and a growing list of mammals across all six inhabited continents plus Antarctica, the CDC's mid-2026 global summary reports.
