--- Science, technology, and public health - [US measles cases hit a 33-year high](#us-measles-cases-hit-a-33-year-high) — 2,318 confirmed cases surpass the full-year 2025 total with five months remaining; MMR coverage down to 92.5 percent - [H5N1 spreads to a sixth continent](#h5n1-spreads-to-a-sixth-continent) — Australia records first detections; nearly half the world's breeding female southern elephant seals may already be dead - [Study: greenhouse warming intensifies El Niño's grip on the Indian monsoon](#study-greenhouse-warming-intensifies-el-niños-grip-on-the-indian-monsoon) — projected to increase rainfall-deficit risk for a population of 1.4 billion - [Record heat dome bakes the US West](#record-heat-dome-bakes-the-us-west) — Lake Mead and Lake Powell at a combined historic low US measles cases hit a 33-year high The CDC reported 2,318 confirmed measles cases for 2026 as of July 23, and by July 30 the year's total had surpassed the 2,289 recorded for all of 2025 — the highest annual count since 1991, with five months of the year remaining. Cases have been reported by 45 jurisdictions, plus 16 among international visitors. There have been 35 new outbreaks this year, and 93 percent of confirmed cases (2,153 of 2,318) are outbreak-associated. Utah has recorded more than 500 cases; Virginia has gone from six cases in 2025 to 176 in 2026. Some 138 people — 6 percent of cases — have been hospitalised; no deaths have been recorded. The overwhelming majority of those infected are under 20 and either unvaccinated or of unknown vaccination status. National MMR coverage among kindergarteners has fallen from 95.2 percent in 2019–20 to 92.5 percent in 2024–25, below the roughly 95 percent threshold required for community immunity. The United States' measles elimination status, certified in 2000, is now openly in question. H5N1 spreads to a sixth continent Highly pathogenic avian influenza H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b is now circulating in wild birds, poultry and an expanding list of mammal species across six continents, with Australia confirming its first-ever detections in June. More than 180 million poultry birds have been affected since the outbreak began, and over 1,000 dairy herds across multiple US states have reported infections — a host jump virologists regard as unprecedented. Mass die-offs have struck South American sea lions, and on the Antarctic coast researchers estimate that close to half the world's breeding female southern elephant seal population may already have been killed. From 2024 to May 2026, 71 human cases were identified in the United States, all linked to direct animal exposure, with no confirmed person-to-person transmission; CDC continues to assess general population risk as low. Study: greenhouse warming intensifies El Niño's grip on the Indian monsoon Research published July 31 finds that greenhouse warming has already strengthened the influence of El Niño on the Indian summer monsoon in the historical record, and projects further intensification — raising the risk of severe rainfall deficits and consequent food insecurity across South Asia. The finding matters because monsoon variability in India is not a meteorological abstraction: it determines the incomes of hundreds of millions of agricultural labourers and small cultivators, the same social layers whose children are now protesting unemployment in Delhi. Record heat dome bakes the US West A record-challenging heat dome settled over the western United States at the end of July, delivering the summer's highest temperatures so far. Meteorologists warn the heat will accelerate soil desiccation and wildfire risk, and increase evaporative loss from reservoirs. The combined water level of Lake Mead and Lake Powell stands at a historic low. --- Arts and culture The most significant cultural news of the day is the WSWS's obituary for **Sam Neill**, who died on July 13 in Sydney at the age of 78. Neill had been diagnosed in 2023 with angioimmunoblastic T-cell lymphoma, a rare non-Hodgkin lymphoma, and had announced in April that he was clear of the disease; his death came suddenly. Richard Phillips's appreciation places Neill where he belongs — not primarily as Dr. Alan Grant in *Jurassic Park*, the role by which most obituaries identified him, but as a formative figure in the Australian and New Zealand new wave of the late 1970s and 1980s. Neill's first major role, in Roger Donaldson's *Sleeping Dogs* (1977), was in a film about an apolitical man swept into a fictional New Zealand under martial law — a work made in the immediate aftermath of the 1975 dismissal crisis in Australia and the intensification of state powers across the Antipodes. Gillian Armstrong's *My Brilliant Career* (1979) and later Jane Campion's *The Piano* (1993) situated him in a cinema attempting to work through questions of colonial settlement, class and sexual repression with genuine seriousness. That this cohort of filmmakers largely dispersed into international commercial production by the 1990s is itself a comment on what happened to national film cultures under the pressures of globalised entertainment capital. Neill's own range — from Campion and Armstrong to Spielberg franchise work — traces that arc. **Venice unveils a war-heavy 83rd edition.** The Venice Film Festival, running September 2–12, has announced a competition and sidebar lineup organised around war, the climate crisis, migration and family breakdown. Several selections warrant attention: - Alina Marazzi's *La Ragazza Con La Leica* opens the Horizons section, on Gerda Taro — the first woman photojournalist killed covering a war, at Brunete during the Spanish Civil War, and Robert Capa's collaborator. That a film about the anti-fascist photographic record of 1937 opens a major festival in 2026 is not incidental. - Two documentaries on the Gaza war: Amos Gitai's *The Road to Jericho* and Ahmed Hassouna's *Citizen Osama*. - Shinya Tsukamoto's *Mr. Nelson, Did You Kill People?*, drawn from the experiences of an African American veteran of the Vietnam War — a continuation of the anti-war line Tsukamoto pursued in *Fires on the Plain*. - More conventional star vehicles fill the competition, including a Robert Pattinson feature, *Primetime*, and an Oasis documentary — the festival's now-routine accommodation to streaming-era publicity requirements. **Elsewhere:** - *Spider-Man: Brand New Day* opened wide over the weekend of July 31, the franchise's latest continuity reset. The recourse to narrative erasure as a commercial mechanism — wiping a character's accumulated history so the property can be sold again — is the studio system's answer to creative exhaustion. - The touring production of *Come From Away*, the Tony-winning musical about the Newfoundland town that hosted stranded air passengers after September 11, continues its national run. Its enduring popularity rests on a sentimental humanism deliberately detached from what the September 11 attacks were used to justify — a quarter-century of war whose latest phase is being fought over Iran this week. - Live music this weekend included Nile Rodgers and CHIC at the Pacific Amphitheatre and Violent Femmes in Los Angeles — both acts now four decades into careers sustained largely by the nostalgia circuit, a reflection of a music industry in which catalogue exploitation has displaced the development of new work.

--- Arts and culture **Vincent Pastore, 1946–2026.** The actor was found dead Saturday afternoon at his home in the Bronx, aged 80, apparently of natural causes. Pastore played Salvatore "Big Pussy" Bonpensiero on *The Sopranos*, and his character's arc — an aging, financially squeezed soldier who becomes an FBI informant and is executed by his closest friends — was among the series' most sustained explorations of loyalty, betrayal and the disintegration of a social milieu. Pastore came to acting late, after years running a New Rochelle nightclub, and brought to the role a lived familiarity with the world David Chase was dissecting. *The Sopranos* remains the most serious American television treatment of the decay of postwar working- and middle-class life in the New Jersey suburbs, and Pastore's performance was central to it. His subsequent typecasting in a long series of mob roles is its own comment on how the industry processes talent. **Sam Neill, 1947–2026.** The WSWS published Richard Phillips's obituary of the New Zealand actor, who died aged 78. Phillips situates Neill as a key figure in the Australian and New Zealand new wave — a body of work including *Sleeping Dogs*, *My Brilliant Career* and later *The Piano* that emerged from a period of state film funding and genuine social questioning in both countries. Neill's international career, from *The Hunt for Red October* to *Jurassic Park* to *Peaky Blinders*, made him a familiar face, but the more substantial achievement lies in the earlier films. Tributes came from Toni Collette ("You legend. You sweetheart."), Karl Urban and Alan Cumming. **Locarno opens Wednesday.** The 79th Locarno Film Festival runs August 5–15 with 233 films from 69 countries and 103 world premieres, including new work by Hong Sangsoo, Denis Côté, Maria Back, Ann Oren and Basil Da Cunha. The Piazza Grande opener is Fanny Liatard and Jérémy Trouilh's *The Green Eyes*. Locarno remains one of the few major festivals still oriented toward formally serious and non-commercial filmmaking rather than awards-season positioning. **Venice unveils its 83rd edition.** The festival runs September 2–12 under a jury led by Maggie Gyllenhaal, opening with Danny Boyle's *Ink*. The selection includes new films from Lee Chang-dong, Tsai Ming-liang, Lav Diaz, Werner Herzog, Julia Loktev, Luca Guadagnino, Nanni Moretti, Martin McDonagh, Mariano Llinás, and documentarians Laura Poitras and Robert Greene — an unusually strong concentration of directors whose work engages historical and social material seriously. Lee Chang-dong's return after eight years and a new Lav Diaz are the most significant entries for anyone concerned with cinema that treats history as something other than backdrop. Also of note: - Jacobin published Abel Prieto's "The Cuban Revolution Was a Revolution in Art and Culture," an official-Havana account of the revolution's cultural policy that suppresses the record of censorship, the Padilla affair, and the persecution of writers and artists under the Castro bureaucracy - Artforum's August music picks and continued coverage of institutional funding pressures reflect an arts sector operating under sustained fiscal contraction as public money is redirected toward armaments across the US and Europe

--- Arts and culture **A record box office weekend built on a single franchise.** North American cinemas took roughly $430 million over the August 2 weekend — the largest collective weekend in box office history — driven almost entirely by *Spider-Man: Brand New Day*, which opened to $355 million domestically and $927 million globally. It is the second-biggest domestic opening ever recorded, behind only *Avengers: Endgame*. Christopher Nolan's *The Odyssey* added $50 million in its continuing run and is tracking toward a $1.4 billion global finish. Year-to-date domestic grosses have passed $6 billion. The numbers are less a sign of cultural vitality than of consolidation. A theatrical market that once sustained hundreds of mid-budget releases now depends on two or three corporate tentpoles a year to generate the revenue that keeps exhibition chains solvent. That *The Odyssey* — an adaptation of Homer produced at enormous scale — is the closest thing to a "serious" work in the top tier says a good deal about the narrowing of what the studios will finance. Its commercial success does at least indicate an audience appetite for material drawn from the deep well of world literature, an appetite the industry has spent two decades insisting does not exist. **The Booker longlist.** The 2026 Booker Prize longlist, announced July 28, comprises 13 novels selected from 163 submissions by a panel chaired by classicist Mary Beard and including poet Raymond Antrobus, musician and writer Jarvis Cocker, editor Rebecca Liu and novelist Patricia Lockwood. Previous winners Douglas Stuart (*Shuggie Bain*, 2020) and Marlon James (*A Brief History of Seven Killings*, 2015) return; Elizabeth Strout is longlisted a third time for *The Things We Never Say*; three debut novelists are included. The list spans dystopian science fiction, Dublin gangland romance, medieval court intrigue and a campus satire set entirely inside a black bag. The shortlist follows September 22, with the winner announced November 9. The generic spread is notable chiefly for what is largely absent: the wars in the Middle East and Ukraine, five years of pandemic mass death, and the deepening social crisis in Britain itself register only obliquely across the selection. The retreat of serious contemporary fiction from these questions — into speculative allegory, historical costume, and campus interiority — is itself a social fact worth registering. --- Arts and culture **Record box office weekend underscores the concentration of film capital.** The weekend of July 31–August 2 produced roughly $430 million in North American ticket sales — the largest collective weekend in box office history — driven by *Spider-Man: Brand New Day* and Christopher Nolan's *The Odyssey*, and achieved without the Chinese market. Nolan's adaptation of Homer took $50 million domestically in its second weekend and is tracking toward a $1.4 billion global total. The result deserves more than industry-page treatment. That the single largest weekend on record was produced by a superhero franchise instalment and an adaptation of the founding epic of Western literature says something about the present state of cinema: the studio system now sustains itself almost entirely on pre-sold intellectual property and event-scale spectacle, while mid-budget filmmaking about contemporary social life has been effectively liquidated. Nolan's film is a genuine attempt at serious material on a scale the industry rarely permits — the *Odyssey* is, after all, a poem about a soldier's decade-long inability to come home from a war, and about what the war did to everyone who waited. Whether the adaptation engages that content or merely renders it as spectacle is the question worth asking of it. The commercial verdict is unambiguous: audiences will turn out in enormous numbers when offered work of ambition, contradicting a decade of studio insistence that the theatrical audience has evaporated. **Museum censorship intensifies under conditions of federal defunding.** The American Alliance of Museums, which represents 35,000 institutions, published new guidance on August 3 on how museums can resist censorship — an unusual step for a trade body, and an index of how severe the pressure has become. The AAM's own recent report documents that US museums have been hit hard by Trump-ordered funding cuts. The pattern of the past year: Amy Sherald's cancellation of her *American Sublime* exhibition at the Smithsonian's National Portrait Gallery over the removal of LGBTQ content; the Art Museum of the Americas in Washington cancelling *Nature's Wild With Andil Gosine* weeks before opening without explanation. The *Art Newspaper* has separately documented that a growing number of US artists are now expected to fundraise for their own museum exhibitions as institutional budgets shrink — the combination of federal and state defunding, legislative attacks on diversity programming, and housing costs in cultural centres producing conditions in which, as the paper puts it, artists' material needs have become indistinguishable from their artistic needs. This is not merely a question of "culture war" targets. The defunding of public art institutions and the proletarianization of artists proceed from the same source as the destruction of public education and health care, and the artistic response so far has been fragmented and largely confined to liberal-institutional appeals. **Deaths.** Vincent Pastore, the American character actor best known as Salvatore "Big Pussy" Bonpensiero in HBO's *The Sopranos*, died August 1. Pastore came to acting late, after years running a nightclub in New Rochelle, and brought to the role a lived familiarity with the milieu that gave the series its documentary weight — a naturalism largely absent from the prestige television that followed it. Japanese actor and impressionist Ryotaro Shimizu died August 1 at 37. Horse trainer and author Monty Roberts, who popularized non-coercive "natural horsemanship" methods against a century of orthodoxy, also died August 1.

None referenced the ICFI or WSWS directly. The common thread — from Jacobin's Democratic organizing through Socialist Alternative's independent candidacies to the RCP's abstract revolutionary appeals — is the absence of any orientation to the actual industrial struggles now under way, and silence on the union apparatuses' role in them.

--- Arts and culture Nolan's *The Odyssey* becomes a mass cultural phenomenon Christopher Nolan's adaptation of Homer's *Odyssey* has been seen by **more than 60 million viewers worldwide** in its initial release, recouping its estimated **$250 million** budget several times over within weeks. Writing on the WSWS, David Walsh treats the response as the significant fact: a "sincere, serious" film drawing enormous audiences indicates a hunger for substantive art against the prevailing banality of commercial cinema. He calls it "without question an important social and cultural phenomenon, perhaps a barometer." Walsh's assessment is not uncritical. He finds the drama artificially earnest and dependent on Hollywood conventions; the guilt-ridden Odysseus Nolan constructs becomes incoherent when he massacres the suitors; the film lacks Homer's "delight in physical existence" and its exuberant sensuousness; and Nolan avoids any meaningful confrontation with ancient slavery, the social foundation on which the *Odyssey*'s world rests. That an epic centrally concerned with return, exile and the destruction wrought by a decade of war should find a mass audience in 2026 is itself a comment on the period. Notably, the IMT's *communist.red* has published its own reading of the film as "an anti-war epic" — a more straightforwardly celebratory treatment that reads Nolan's ambivalence as a settled political position. --- Arts and culture Bayreuth's AI-generated *Ring* booed at the festival's 150th anniversary The most significant cultural event of the week is the Bayreuth Festival's new production of Wagner's *Der Ring des Nibelungen*, titled *Ring 10010110*, staged for the 150th anniversary of the cycle's premiere at the Festspielhaus. Curator Marcus Lobbes, working with Nils Corte and dramaturge Andri Hardmeier, fed roughly 1,000 images drawn from the fifteen previous Bayreuth *Ring* productions into a generative model, which then produced a continuous stream of associative imagery as the cycle's visual environment. Singers appeared as floating sculptural figures in costumes by Pia Maria Mackert. The audience booed. Lobbes and his design team were met with whistles at the curtain call, while conductor Christian Thielemann and the cast received a warm reception. Critical reaction identified the central failure precisely: the software could assemble images but could not construct drama. Reviewers described *Das Rheingold* as "stiff and dramatically inert," with the performers only gradually reclaiming human presence over the course of the four evenings. The episode deserves attention beyond the opera world. The *Ring* is, among other things, a work about the corrupting power of accumulated wealth and the destruction of the natural and social world by those who seize it — themes that have never been more directly relevant. To reduce its staging to a recombinant collage of prior stagings is to substitute a statistical average of the past for an artistic engagement with the present. Generative models can only interpolate within what has already been made; they cannot pose a question. The boos at Bayreuth were, in this sense, an audience defending art against its liquidation into content. Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan sign trilateral mutual-defense pact Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan and Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif signed the "Mecca Joint Defence Agreement" on August 7, declaring that an armed attack on any one of the three states constitutes an attack on all. The agreement builds on the bilateral Saudi-Pakistani defense pact concluded in September 2025 and was signed directly in the shadow of the US-Israeli war on Iran that began in February and the Houthi missile and drone campaign now reaching into Saudi territory. The practical content of the pact is the extension of nuclear-armed Pakistan's deterrent over the Arabian Peninsula — the first time a nuclear weapons state has formally extended such a guarantee to an Arab government. It represents a significant realignment of regional military blocs, driven by the perception among the Gulf bourgeoisie that Washington's security guarantees have become unreliable, and by Ankara's drive to establish itself as an independent regional power. Key facts: - The pact was signed in Mecca by the three heads of government on August 7, 2026. - It commits all three signatories to treat an attack on one as an attack on all, on the NATO Article 5 model. - Pakistan possesses an estimated 170-plus nuclear warheads; Saudi Arabia has repeatedly stated it would seek nuclear parity with Iran. - Turkey and Saudi Arabia have been on opposing sides of multiple regional conflicts over the past decade, including Qatar, Libya and Syria — the pact papers over rather than resolves those antagonisms. - Neither the United States nor Israel was consulted in advance, according to regional reporting.

Neuroimaging foundation model trained on 5.24 million scans beats frontier AI Researchers publishing in *Nature Medicine* trained "NeuroVFM," a three-dimensional visual foundation model, on 5.24 million CT and MRI volumes drawn from 566,915 studies accumulated over two decades of routine clinical care at Michigan Medicine. Iran sets six conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz Iran's Supreme National Security Council, headed by Mohammad Bagher Zolghadr, published a six-point list of conditions the United States must meet before Tehran will permit the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, closed since the outbreak of the US-Israeli war on Iran on February 28. The announcement came as Iranian and Omani negotiators signalled they were close to a separate technical agreement on managing traffic through the waterway — an agreement which, Iranian officials stressed, would not by itself reopen the strait. President Masoud Pezeshkian publicly backed a deal, telling state media that "now is the best time for an agreement" and arguing that Iran negotiates from a position of strength: "There is cohesion, strength, and unity in the country, and as far as I know, Iran is considered victorious and powerful in this war." The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps confirmed that reopening remains contingent on US acceptance of the six conditions and is formally separate from the Oman track. Key facts: - The six conditions: an end to US threats and "insults to national and religious values"; a permanent halt to attacks on Iran and its allies in Lebanon, Palestine, Yemen and Iraq; lifting of the US naval blockade and withdrawal of US forces; compensation for damage from "two imposed wars"; lifting of sanctions; and release of frozen Iranian assets. - These terms go substantially beyond the June 17 US-Iran memorandum, which envisaged phased reciprocal steps. Tehran now presents them as preconditions. - An unnamed US official said the naval blockade would be lifted only once "commercial shipping through Hormuz was restored without impediments" — an explicitly conditional formulation that inverts Iran's sequencing. - The UAE reported that a commercial vessel was targeted in the same period, underscoring that the waterway remains effectively closed to normal traffic. - Roughly a fifth of world seaborne oil normally transits Hormuz; Brent closed the week at about $83.55/bbl.
Sources Al Jazeera Iran issues new demands as Pezeshkian seeks deal · CNN Iran demands concessions from US as it nears Strait of Hormuz deal with Oman · US News / Reuters Iran says deal on Strait of Hormuz is close but is not enough to open the waterway

US Senate passes sweeping Russia-Iran sanctions bill 86-11 The Senate approved sweeping new sanctions legislation targeting Russia and Iran by 86 votes to 11, the largest bipartisan war measure of the year. Republicans voted 49-1, with Rand Paul of Kentucky the sole GOP dissenter and three absent. Democrats split 37-10. The bill, originally authored by the late Senator Lindsey Graham and Senator Richard Blumenthal (D-Connecticut), extends Iran sanctions for five years and authorises measures against Russia's "shadow fleet" of oil tankers — a provision carrying the direct risk of naval interdiction of Russian-linked shipping. Blumenthal framed the vote as a message to Moscow: "Today we say to Vladimir Putin: You will not conquer Ukraine." Patrick Martin's WSWS Perspective column dissected the Democratic minority's position, noting that "not one of them opposed the sanctions. Their objection was to the tariff provision" attached to the bill. When an amendment to strip the tariff language came to the floor it failed 32-64, with sixteen Democrats joining forty-eight Republicans to defeat it. Martin's conclusion: "twenty of them registered a toothless protest and then voted for the war." Key facts: - Bernie Sanders was among the ten Democratic "no" votes; none of the ten based their opposition on the sanctions or the war. - The shadow-fleet provisions authorise action against tankers carrying Russian crude, raising the prospect of physical interception at sea by US or NATO vessels. - The five-year Iran sanctions extension arrives while the US is in active military confrontation with Tehran over Hormuz. - Martin situates the legislation within the WSWS's standing analysis that "the purpose of the US-NATO war in Ukraine ... is to prepare the conquest and dismemberment of Russia itself by the imperialist powers."

US payrolls fall 23,000 in July, first decline since February The Bureau of Labor Statistics reported Friday that nonfarm payrolls fell by 23,000 in July against a consensus forecast of a gain of 83,000 — the first monthly decline since February 2026. --- Science, technology, and public health - [US measles cases near 35-year high with elimination status under review](#us-measles-cases-near-35-year-high-with-elimination-status-under-review) — 2,465 confirmed cases as of August 6, already above all of 2025; 93% unvaccinated or unknown - [COVID "Nimbus" variant dominant, growing in 43 states](#covid-nimbus-variant-dominant-growing-in-43-states) — hospital admissions projected to rise from ~1,200 to ~1,600 per week; declining in no state - [H5N1 reaches Australian seabirds in first mass-mortality event](#h5n1-reaches-australian-seabirds-in-first-mass-mortality-event) — 49 dead and 35 sick terns off Adelaide; Victoria logs 53 positives across 37 investigations - [Study finds exercise guidelines drastically understate the dose needed](#study-finds-exercise-guidelines-drastically-understate-the-dose-needed) — 150 min/week yields only 8-9% cardiovascular risk reduction; 560-610 min/week needed for >30% - [EU AI Act enforcement begins](#eu-ai-act-enforcement-begins) — fines up to €15 million or 3% of global turnover US measles cases near 35-year high with elimination status under review The CDC reported 2,465 confirmed measles cases in the United States as of August 6, 2026 — already exceeding the 2,289 recorded in all of 2025 and approaching levels not seen since the early 1990s. Some 94 percent of cases (2,309 of 2,465) are outbreak-associated; two-thirds are in people aged 19 and under; and 93 percent of patients were unvaccinated or of unknown vaccination status. A national verification committee meets in mid-August to determine whether the United States has lost the measles elimination status it has held since 2000. Loss of that status would be a formal admission that the destruction of public health infrastructure, the gutting of vaccination programmes and the promotion of anti-vaccine ideology at cabinet level have reversed one of the signal public health achievements of the twentieth century. COVID "Nimbus" variant dominant, growing in 43 states The NB.1.8.1 "Nimbus" Omicron subvariant is now the dominant strain nationwide. As of August 5, COVID-19 infections were growing or likely growing in 43 states and declining in none. CDC forecasting projected weekly hospital admissions climbing from roughly 1,200 to 1,600 by early August. Severity appears unchanged from prior strains, but the late-summer surge is straining a respiratory surveillance system that has been progressively defunded. H5N1 reaches Australian seabirds in first mass-mortality event Australia confirmed H5N1 in a mass-mortality event involving 49 dead and 35 sick terns off Adelaide — the country's first major wild-bird die-off from the panzootic, which had until now largely spared the continent. Victoria has logged 53 positive cases across 37 investigations as of August 8. In the United States, CDC surveillance showed no unusual human influenza activity as of August 7, though the virus remains widespread in wild birds and continues to circulate in dairy cattle herds. Study finds exercise guidelines drastically understate the dose needed An observational study published in the *British Journal of Sports Medicine*, following participants for an average of 7.8 years and recording 1,233 cardiovascular events including 156 heart attacks and 92 strokes, found that meeting the standard 150 minutes per week of physical activity was associated with only an 8-9 percent reduction in cardiovascular risk. Substantial protection — greater than 30 percent risk reduction — required 560 to 610 minutes per week, a level achieved by only 12 percent of participants. The findings suggest current guidelines require major revision toward higher and more individualised targets. They also underline a class question: 9 to 10 hours of weekly exercise is not available to workers on twelve-hour shifts or holding multiple jobs. EU AI Act enforcement begins As of August 2, 2026, the EU AI Office and national authorities began enforcing the AI Act. Article 50 transparency obligations — including labelling of AI-generated content — are now in force, and high-risk system obligations covering credit scoring and insurance pricing are legally binding for any company operating in the EU, including the major US AI firms. Non-compliance can trigger fines up to €15 million or 3 percent of global annual turnover, whichever is higher. Enforcement capacity remains the open question: the AI Office is small relative to the firms it regulates, and the framework accepts the private ownership of the technology as given.

--- Arts and culture **William Orbit (1956-2026).** The death of the English producer and musician William Orbit at 69, announced this week after he died at home on July 23, removes one of the more genuinely inventive figures in late-twentieth-century popular music. Born William Wainwright in Hackney to a working-class London family, Orbit came out of the early-1980s independent scene and spent a decade making ambient and electronic records under the name Strange Cargo before his production work on Madonna's *Ray of Light* (1998) won three Grammys, including Best Pop Album. His achievement there was not commercial packaging but the opposite: he brought the textures of British ambient techno — long decaying reverbs, filtered analogue synthesis, an unhurried sense of space — into the centre of American mass-market pop, and in doing so gave a performer then widely written off as a spent commercial force the most artistically serious record of her career. His work on Blur's *13* (1999) served a similar function, opening up the band's guitar music to electronic dissolution at the moment Britpop's nationalist self-congratulation was collapsing. He also produced Beth Orton's debut and reworked Barber and Vivaldi on *Pieces in a Modern Style*. Orbit's career is a reminder that the most durable popular art of the period came from figures working at the margins of the industry rather than its promotional centre. **Kanye West in Portugal and the politics of the concert boycott.** Roughly 34,000 people attended a Kanye West concert at the Algarve Stadium on Saturday, after Israel's ambassador to Portugal publicly called for its cancellation over West's antisemitic statements. West's descent into open Hitler apologetics is a genuine cultural disgrace, and the WSWS has consistently identified the promotion of such material as a symptom of the political putrefaction of a layer of the wealthy celebrity milieu. But the intervention of the Israeli state — a government prosecuting a genocide in Gaza — to demand the cancellation of a concert is not an anti-fascist act. It is an assertion of the state's right to determine what may be performed, deployed by a government that has spent two years suppressing artistic and journalistic speech about Palestine. Opposition to antisemitism cannot be delegated to the censors; it requires a political movement of the working class against the social conditions that produce racialist demagogy in the first place. **Roundup:** - **Locarno.** The 79th Locarno Film Festival runs August 5-15, with 233 films across 11 sections and 103 world premieres selected from a record 7,759 submissions. The International Competition includes new work from Hong Sang-soo, Basil Da Cunha, Gurvinder Singh and Denis Côté; the festival opened with *The Green Eyes* by Fanny Liatard and Jérémy Trouilh, with Belgian director Fabrice Du Welz presiding over the main jury. The volume of submissions — a record in a period of collapsing independent film financing — indicates an enormous reservoir of unabsorbed creative work. - **Venice.** The 2026 Venice lineup, announced for September 2-12, opens with Danny Boyle's *Ink* and includes world premieres of Florian Zeller's *Bunker*, Martin McDonagh's *Wild Horse Nine* and Lee Chang-dong's *Possible Love* — the latter the first feature in some years from one of the most serious living directors of social realism. - **Paris.** Nearly 100,000 people have signed a petition opposing a proposed new pavilion for the National Assembly, an argument over public architecture and the cost of parliamentary self-aggrandisement at a moment of austerity budgeting. - **Rome.** Archaeologists uncovered an ancient Roman building with mosaics and frescoes beneath a restoration site on the Caelian Hill. - **Edinburgh Fringe.** Amanda Knox has brought her own account of her prosecution to the Fringe — a case that remains a study in how prosecutorial misconduct and tabloid misogyny can construct a criminal narrative out of nothing.

German interior minister exploits Berlin Pride attack to demand police-state expansion — Marianne Arens Arens establishes a documented chain of state failure. --- Pseudo-left press review - [Jacobin / DSA](#jacobin--dsa) — combines a correct anti-imperialist line on Cuba with a technocratic regulatory programme on inequality that never leaves the framework of capitalist reform - [Left Voice](#left-voice) — the sharpest formal case against the "dirty break," but reduces class independence to an electoral-organisational question - [Liberation News / PSL](#liberation-news--psl) — celebrates a Democratic primary result as an anti-Zionist victory, channelling opposition to genocide back into the party prosecuting it - [Socialist Alternative](#socialist-alternative) — anti-Democratic in form, reformist in programme; police "accountability" demands framed within the capitalist state - [Socialist Worker / SWP (UK)](#socialist-worker--swp-uk) — pressures the new Burnham Labour government to spend differently rather than opposing Labour as a party of British imperialism - [Socialist Appeal / RCP (IMT)](#socialist-appeal--rcp-imt) — revolutionary phraseology on the British state combined with an inter-tendency polemic against the SWP that avoids programmatic questions Jacobin / DSA **"After Blocking Fuel, the US Turns to Cuba's Food Supply"** develops an anti-imperialist critique of the blockade, adopting the "silent Gaza" framing. The article is factually useful and its opposition to the blockade is unambiguous. Its limitation is structural: Jacobin criticises US foreign policy in the abstract while its entire domestic orientation is toward the Democratic Party, which has administered the blockade through every presidency including Obama's and Biden's. No call is made for industrial action, and no conclusion is drawn about the party Jacobin's political milieu works within. **"Don't Just Tax the Rich — Attack Inequality at the Root"** argues that taxation alone cannot resolve inequality and that structural regulation of markets and finance is required. This is a technocratic social-democratic programme: the "root" of inequality is located in insufficiently regulated market design rather than in the private ownership of the means of production. There is no call for independent working-class action; the implied agent is a reforming legislature. **"The Fight for Abortion Rights Was Won in the Streets"** credits mass mobilisation, mutual aid and telehealth networks rather than electoral channels for preserving abortion access post-*Roe*. This is the more left-sounding pole of Jacobin's output, but the "streets" here are invoked as pressure on Democratic legislators, not as the basis of an independent political movement. *Assessment:* Jacobin's output continues to combine correct criticisms of imperialism and inequality with a programme that presupposes the Democratic Party as the vehicle. The function is to keep radicalising layers of workers and youth oriented toward that party. Left Voice **"Kshama Sawant's Third-Place Finish Shows the Space for a Party of Our Own"** treats Sawant's independent run as evidence for the viability of a workers' party outside the Democratic ballot line. **"August Primaries: Progressive Challengers Continue to Threaten Democratic Party Establishment"** argues the "dirty break" strategy fails because the Democratic Party absorbs and neutralises its progressive wing. **"SOUTHCOM Announces New Military Campaign, Expanding Land Operations in Latin America"** correctly identifies the narco-terrorism pretext as cover for building regional repressive capacity. Left Voice's formal opposition to work inside the Democratic Party is the clearest on the American pseudo-left. The problem lies in what class independence is taken to consist of: an electoral and organisational break, rather than a struggle over programme and historical perspective. The Morenoite tradition Left Voice descends from has repeatedly constructed "broad" parties on precisely this basis — the FIT-U in Argentina being the operative model — that then function as left pressure on bourgeois governments. Nothing in this output addresses the theoretical questions on which the Fourth International split. *Assessment:* Correct on the immediate electoral question, unserious on the programmatic foundations that would make an independent party a revolutionary one. Liberation News / PSL **"Michigan primary: A huge defeat for AIPAC and the Israel Lobby"** presents a Democratic primary victory over an AIPAC-backed candidate as a strategic blow against Zionism. This is the clearest instance in the day's scan of channelling mass opposition to genocide back into the party that armed and funded it. The framing also carries an analytical error the WSWS has repeatedly identified: locating the source of US Middle East policy in a "lobby" rather than in the strategic interests of American imperialism, which displaces class analysis with a conspiracy of influence. **"PSL Statement: Defend our Haitian neighbors! We've stopped ICE before and can do it again!"** calls for mass direct action in defence of Haitian TPS holders and demands ICE's abolition — a genuinely mobilising orientation. **"One month after Lorenzo's murder, the fight for justice continues"** covers organising around an ICE killing in Houston. *Assessment:* PSL combines real street mobilisation with an electoral orientation that consistently returns to Democratic primaries. The two are not in tension for the PSL because it has no conception of political independence as a matter of programme. Socialist Alternative **"Support Left Independent Candidates—Build An Alternative To The Two Corporate Parties"** rejects both capitalist parties and backs Sawant's independent campaign. --- Arts and culture **Venice opens ticket sales for a festival tilted away from Hollywood.** The 83rd Venice International Film Festival (September 2–12) put its public screening schedule online on Friday and opened online ticket sales this afternoon. The programme is notable for the near-absence of major studio product and a corresponding weight of auteur and independent work: new films from Martin McDonagh, Florian Zeller, Werner Herzog and Danny Boyle, whose *Ink* opens the festival on September 2. The documentary strand includes Alex Gibney's film on Elon Musk and a chronicle of the Oasis reunion tour. The retreat of the studios from Venice is itself a social fact. As the streaming conglomerates consolidate and strip out mid-budget filmmaking, the festival circuit becomes the residual venue in which serious dramatic work can still find an audience — while the same films struggle to reach beyond a metropolitan art-house public. Whether this year's competition produces anything that seriously confronts a world in its sixth month of a US-Iran war remains to be seen; recent editions have tended toward interiority and historical costume. **Palestinian culture at the Edinburgh Fringe.** The 2026 Fringe (August 7–31) hosts "Welcome to the Fringe, Palestine," organised by an independent group of Scotland-based writers, dancers, theatre-makers and publishers. A play will be streamed live by satellite from Gaza to Edinburgh audiences on **August 17**, alongside a full day of storytelling, poetry, stand-up, dance and theatre — including Al-Harah Theatre's *Shakespeare's Sisters* — plus Palestinian short films, discussions and a photography exhibition. The organisers state explicitly that the initiative exists to circumvent the censorship Palestinian artists face in established British cultural institutions. On August 2, pro-Palestinian protesters interrupted an event with Scottish First Minister John Swinney at the Stand Comedy Club, demanding he use the word "genocide." **The Booker longlist and the state of the novel.** The 2026 Booker Prize longlist, announced late last month, runs to 13 titles judged by a panel chaired by Mary Beard and including Raymond Antrobus, Jarvis Cocker, Rebecca Liu and Patricia Lockwood. It mixes previous laureates — Douglas Stuart (*John of John*), Marlon James (*The Disappearers*) — with Elizabeth Strout, Gwendoline Riley, Emma Cline, M. John Harrison and several debuts. The shortlist arrives September 22, the winner November 9. The selection's range across thriller, dystopia and domestic realism reflects a literary culture in which the dystopian mode has become the default form for registering social crisis, generally at the cost of any concrete social analysis. **Attacks on cultural institutions.** The White House review of the Smithsonian, launched under an executive order titled "Restore Truth and Sanity to American History," continues to press the museums to purge "divisive" or "ideologically driven language" — that is, any critical treatment of slavery, racism or class. The administration's budget excluded funding for the National Museum of the American Latino and the Anacostia Community Museum, and the House Oversight Committee summoned Smithsonian executive director Anthea M. Hartig on July 21 to a hearing titled "Rewriting American History." NEA grants have been cancelled en masse and the agency's priorities redirected toward "skilled trade jobs," "AI competency" and support for "the military and veterans" — the open subordination of federal arts funding to militarism and workforce discipline. **Deaths.** Austrian novelist **Monika Helfer**, 78, whose autofictional Vorarlberg trilogy (*Die Bagage*, *Vati*, *Löwenherz*) reconstructed rural poverty and the wreckage of two wars in a family chronicle, died August 2. Dutch singer **Jerney Kaagman**, 79, lead vocalist of Earth and Fire, died August 6 of complications of Parkinson's disease. Dutch-Surinamese rapper **Tony Scott**, 54, a pioneer of hip house, died August 6 of complications of multiple sclerosis. American actor and politician **Ben Jones**, 84, died August 9. Texas steel guitarist and producer **Tommy Detamore**, 70, a central figure in the preservation of Western swing, died August 5.

The Editorial Board states flatly that "the record of the case contains no act of treason—no espionage, no sabotage, no collaboration." The prosecution rested entirely on his writing: state experts examined 14 texts, seven were indicted, one charge was dropped after the court's own forensic commission found nothing criminal in it, and he was convicted on the basis of **six articles published on the World Socialist Web Site**. The court's stated objections were explicitly political: Syrotiuk's "non-recognition of Ukraine's legitimately elected political leadership," his "comparisons with fascists and Nazis," his critical assessments of the Armed Forces' performance, and his "reinterpretation of national heroes." On the first, the Board notes that Zelensky's term expired in **May 2024** and he "remains in power more than two years past his legal mandate, ruling by decree under a state of permanent martial law" — Syrotiuk is being imprisoned for stating a fact. The "national heroes" in question are Stepan Bandera and other OUN Nazi collaborators rehabilitated by the Ukrainian state. The court disregarded a 65-page defence criminology report finding no material amounting to propaganda for Russian aggression. The Board situates the case in a systematic campaign: communist parties and symbols banned under the 2015 "decommunization" laws; eleven opposition parties suspended in 2022 and the largest banned outright; roughly **20,000 criminal cases** opened under treason and collaboration statutes; the WSWS itself banned in Ukraine since June 6, 2024. Crosse's central political argument concerns the Democratic Party's role: by agreeing to separate ICE funding from broader appropriations, Democrats preserved the ability to vote against symbolic measures while allowing the money for the repressive apparatus to flow uninterrupted. The devices are designed for close-quarters application to restrained individuals — their function is not crowd control but the infliction of pain on people already in custody. White concludes that workers must build rank-and-file committees rather than appeal to court officers. --- Pseudo-left press review - **[Jacobin](#jacobin-and-dsa)** — three articles, two of them on a single Democratic primary, treating a near-miss on the Democratic ballot line as proof the "socialist electoral project" has room to grow - **[Left Voice](#left-voice)** — reports the same primary cycle as a "progressive sweep" while running a genuinely useful exposé on privatized surveillance infrastructure - **[Liberation News / PSL](#liberation-news-psl)** — sharpest rhetoric against the Democratic establishment, yet frames anti-Zionist and anti-ICE sentiment entirely through Democratic primary outcomes - **[Socialist Alternative](#socialist-alternative)** — the only US tendency explicitly rejecting both parties, but channels this into "left independent" electoralism - **[Socialist Worker, SWP UK](#socialist-worker-swp-uk)** — from-below framing of South Asian uprisings; skeptical of Unite's re-elected leadership - **[Socialist Appeal / RCP](#socialist-appeal-and-the-rcp-imt)** — British capitalism in terminal decline, with no illusions in Labour but no strategy beyond propaganda Jacobin and DSA Jacobin devoted two of its three notable pieces to the Wisconsin Democratic primary defeat of Francesca Hong. **"The Socialist Electoral Project Still Hasn't Hit Its Ceiling"** presents the loss as evidence of expanding left strength, measured by vote share within a Democratic primary. **"Five Takeaways From Francesca Hong's Near-Win in Wisconsin"** extracts tactical lessons on the same terrain — canvassing operations, endorsement dynamics, the role of the state party. The unexamined premise of both is that the vehicle for socialist advance is the Democratic ballot line, and the measure of progress is how close a DSA-aligned candidate came to defeating the machine. Neither article poses the question of what a Hong victory would have obligated her to — the Wisconsin Democratic caucus, the party's national fundraising apparatus, its unbroken support for the Gaza and Iran wars. The "ceiling" metaphor is itself revealing: it treats the Democratic Party as a container that can be filled from below rather than a state-integrated institution designed to absorb and dissipate exactly this energy. **"John Deere Is Testing Its Workers' Resolve"** is stronger, covering the UAW contract fight with genuine sympathy for the shop floor. But it treats the UAW apparatus as a neutral or merely inadequate instrument rather than as management's partner, and offers no perspective for workers beyond hoping the union negotiates harder. **Assessment:** A day's output almost entirely absorbed in the internal metrics of Democratic Party primaries — the clearest possible expression of the DSA's function as a left flank of the party it claims to be transforming. Left Voice **"Sanders-Backed Flanagan Wins Minnesota Senate Primary, Continuing Progressive Sweep"** reports a Sanders-aligned candidate's victory as part of a broader wave. The framing — a "sweep" of progressive candidates within Democratic primaries — sits uneasily with Left Voice's own stated Trotskyist opposition to class collaboration. The article does not draw the conclusion its politics would require: that a Sanders endorsement is precisely the mechanism by which anti-establishment sentiment is recaptured for the Democratic Party. **"How Flock Is Building America's Private Surveillance Infrastructure"** is the more valuable piece — a documented account of how the automated license-plate-reader company has built a national surveillance network sold to municipalities, arguing correctly that privatization is not the problem and municipal ownership is not the solution, since the class function of the apparatus is unchanged. **Assessment:** Capable investigative work coexisting with an electoral commentary that reports Democratic primary results in the vocabulary of the milieu it formally criticizes. Liberation News (PSL) **"Desperate Democratic Establishment Narrowly Defeats Hong in Wisconsin"** is the most class-antagonistic treatment of the primary, naming Governor Evers and the "big-business" Democrats as the opponent and advancing concrete demands — minimum wage increases, healthcare, repeal of the anti-union Act 10. **"Flanagan Wins Big in Primary as Minnesotans Reject AIPAC and ICE"** reads a Democratic primary result as a popular referendum against AIPAC and immigration raids. The contradiction is structural: the PSL denounces the Democratic Party as an instrument of capital, then reports its primaries as the arena where mass consciousness registers itself. Treating a Sanders- and Warren-backed candidate's win as a mass anti-Zionist verdict inflates an electoral datum into a political mandate and obscures that the winner will caucus with the party funding the war. **Assessment:** Militant tone, national-reformist content — a program of demands to be won from the existing state, with no perspective of independent working-class power. Socialist Alternative With no output in the immediate window, the most recent significant pieces are **"Support Left Independent Candidates—Build An Alternative To The Two Corporate Parties,"** which rejects both parties by name and cites ICE killings and US backing for the Gaza and Iran wars, and **"South Africa: Xenophobia & The Street War Against Black Immigrants,"** which traces anti-immigrant violence to mass unemployment and indicts the ANC's post-1994 neoliberal turn. The South Africa piece is a serious class analysis of a national liberation party's integration into capitalist rule. The electoral piece, however, substitutes "left independent" campaigns — the Sawant model — for the construction of a revolutionary party, offering municipal-reform electoralism outside the Democratic Party rather than a break with electoralism as strategy. **Assessment:** Correct on the party question, reformist on the programmatic one. Socialist Worker (SWP UK) **"Revolt Spreads in India and Pakistan"** celebrates spontaneous mass uprisings across South Asia, paired with anti-monarchist commentary on the Mountbatten-Windsor funeral. **"Sharon Graham Wins After Poor Choice in Unite Union Leadership Race"** applies the classic SWP rank-and-file line — skepticism toward Graham and the Unite machine, a call for shop-floor organization independent of officials. The limitation is the same one the SWP has carried for six decades: mass struggle is celebrated as self-sufficient, with the party reduced to an auxiliary that encourages spontaneity rather than fighting for a program. "Rank-and-file organization" without a struggle for political leadership leaves the bureaucracy in place. **Assessment:** Genuine internationalist instinct, no theory of the party. Socialist Appeal and the RCP (IMT) **"Burnham and British Capitalism – Bouncing Into an Abyss"** argues Labour's post-Burnham polling recovery is illusory given the underlying crisis of British capitalism. **"UK Foreign Office Decimated: Britain's 'Soft' Power Gets Even Softer"** reads Foreign Office austerity as symptomatic of British imperialism's terminal decline rather than as underfunded diplomacy. Both avoid the reformist illusions in Labour that characterized this tendency's earlier entrism, and the imperialist-decline framing is analytically closer to Marxism than most of what appears elsewhere in this survey. What is absent is any programmatic conclusion — the pieces describe capitalist crisis as spectacle, with the revolutionary party appearing only as an assertion at the end. **Assessment:** Sound diagnosis, propagandistic prescription. **Cross-tendency notes:** Three US outlets led with the same Wisconsin primary and none broke toward independent working-class politics outside the Democratic ballot line. Strikingly, no article across any of the six tendencies in this window took a stated position on an ongoing imperialist war — Gaza, Iran or Ukraine appeared only obliquely. No direct polemics against the ICFI or Trotskyism appeared in the window scanned.

Firefighters working near Khiam were forced to retreat this week when a drone struck close to their position as they fought a blaze ignited by Israeli-dropped flares. The Israeli military did not respond to requests for comment on specific incidents, though it has previously argued that Hezbollah uses wooded areas for cover. The burning of agricultural land in a region whose population depends on olive, tobacco and fruit cultivation constitutes a systematic attack on the economic basis of civilian life — the same method now documented in Gaza and the West Bank.

Western Europe records its hottest summer ever June and July 2026 were the hottest such months ever recorded in Western Europe, Copernicus confirmed, with a combined average of 21.62°C — 2.79°C above the 1991–2020 norm and almost half a degree above the previous record set in 2022. June alone ran 3.06°C above the historical mean. Wildfires have burned more than 1.23 million acres, mainly in Spain, France and Italy, displacing hundreds of thousands. - Germany recorded roughly **12,500 heat-related deaths** between the start of April and the end of July; France documented over **5,700**. - The WHO estimates approximately **200,000 heat-related deaths across Europe over the past four years**. - Portugal, Spain, France, Italy and Greece experienced major wildfires; Spain declared a state of emergency in July for the first time. - The Gironde region near Bordeaux suffered its largest forest fire since 1949, destroying **42,000 hectares**. - Low water levels on the Rhine and Danube disrupted industrial production and forced temporary shutdowns of nuclear power stations in several countries. The deaths are overwhelmingly concentrated among the elderly, the poor and workers in unairconditioned housing and outdoor employment — a class distribution that no European government has moved to address through the mass public investment required.

--- Arts and culture Nolan's *The Odyssey* passes $1 billion, drawing an audience "starved for challenging material" Christopher Nolan's adaptation of Homer's *Odyssey* has crossed $1.008 billion worldwide — $429.65 million domestic, $578.8 million international — in three weeks, his first film since *The Dark Knight Rises* (2012) to reach the mark and shortly to become his highest-grossing release. Its $264.1 million global opening was the largest of Nolan's career. It passed *Oppenheimer*'s entire domestic run of $330 million in thirteen days. The exhibition figures are as striking as the grosses: the BFI IMAX Southbank sold out 173 showings, running screenings around the clock; Milwaukee's Oriental Theatre drew 3,600 attendees in its opening days. Over 100 million people have now seen the film. Writing on the WSWS, David Walsh treats the phenomenon seriously rather than dismissively. He acknowledges that earlier WSWS reviewers judged Nolan's work harshly, but argues that *Oppenheimer* and *The Odyssey* represent "a considerable jump" — "substantial and complex films about issues that matter." Walsh locates the appeal in the material: "the horrors of war, the foul role of a usering and cruel aristocracy," themes that resonate against present conditions. His central formulation is worth noting for editorial discussion: "Life-and-death themes embodied in a classic, treated seriously and generously, have encountered a sizeable global viewing public clearly starved for challenging material." That is the significant fact. The commercial success of a three-hour adaptation of an ancient epic, in a period when studio output is dominated by franchise product, indicates an audience whose appetite for serious art has been systematically underestimated and underserved by an industry organized around risk-minimization. The figure of Odysseus — resourceful, enduring, returning to a household seized by parasites — has evident contemporary purchase. Deaths - **Benjamin Alire Sáenz**, poet and novelist, died at 71. Raised on a farm outside Las Cruces, New Mexico, and long resident in El Paso, he became in 2013 the first Latino writer to win the PEN/Faulkner Award for Fiction, for *Everything Begins and Ends at the Kentucky Club*. His young adult novel *Aristotle and Dante Discover the Secrets of the Universe* brought international readership. Sáenz used the US-Mexico border not as exotic backdrop but as the concrete social terrain on which questions of love, humiliation, redemption and survival were posed — writing that gains rather than loses force as the border becomes the site of mass detention and militarized policing. - **Plas Johnson**, tenor saxophonist, died July 15 in Granada Hills, Los Angeles, at 94. Best known for the solo on Henry Mancini's "The Pink Panther Theme," Johnson was one of the most recorded session musicians in American popular music, a fixture of the Los Angeles studio scene whose playing appears on hundreds of records by artists who never learned his name. His career is a reminder that the actual labor of American popular music was performed largely by anonymous, mostly Black instrumentalists working for scale. Roundup - The **2026 Whitney Biennial**, which opened in March against the backdrop of the administration's assault on arts funding and DEI programs, continues to draw divided criticism. Fifty-six artists are included, among them three Palestinian visual artists and one born in Baghdad. Reviewers have described it as politically charged but evasive about the specific character of the present American crisis — *Frieze* called it "an underwhelming show for overwhelming times." The tension between an institution dependent on the same financial elite it gestures at criticizing, and artists attempting to address war and repression, remains unresolved. - Regional opera and theater continue to operate under acute funding pressure. The West Coast premiere of *American Apollo* — an opera on the painter John Singer Sargent and his model Thomas Eugene McKeller — was staged in Oakland on August 13, one of a number of new works being produced by smaller companies as major houses retrench.

Jacobin / DSA **"Socialist David Morales Wants to Be Providence's Next Mayor"** is a sympathetic profile of a DSA-aligned mayoral candidate who argues explicitly that socialists should contest Democratic Party primaries, and who criticizes his own local DSA chapter for declining to do so. The article presents this as strategic realism. It is the clearest statement of Democratic Party electoralism in the week's output: there is no conception of class independence, only "engagement within Democratic primaries" as a permanent method. **"Don't Back Down on Medicare for All"** urges the left to resist Democratic-sponsored "public option" dilutions of single-payer. The content of the appeal is defensive and legislative: the strategic horizon is winning or protecting a bill inside the capitalist state, addressed to Democratic legislators as the agency of change. The class question — that the insurance and hospital corporations are represented in both parties and will not be legislated out of existence — is not posed. **"John Deere Is Testing Its Workers' Resolve"** reports on the UAW-Deere contract vote scheduled for August 23. The article treats the formal bargaining process as the terrain of struggle and does not address the role of the UAW apparatus, which has imposed successive concessionary agreements at Deere. Workers are positioned as an audience for the union's negotiating performance rather than as an independent force. **Assessment:** Jacobin's output this week is consistently oriented toward the Democratic Party as the vehicle and the legislature as the arena. The absence of Gaza coverage over an extended period is itself a political fact, reflecting the tendency's integration into a Democratic milieu for which the question is an electoral liability. Left Voice **"A New Political Moment? Trumpism's Crisis, the Midterms, and Shifts to the Left in the U.S."** rejects the channeling of radicalized layers into Democratic campaigns, characterizing the party as "a graveyard for social movements," and argues for an independent socialist alternative. **"Sanders-Backed Flanagan Wins Minnesota Senate Primary"** covers a Democratic primary result while stating flatly that the party "is capitalist, imperialist, and Zionist to its core, and cannot be reformed." **"The Democratic Party Establishment Punches Back"** argues that the contradictions the Democrats face over Israel cannot be resolved within a capitalist party and calls for the construction of an independent working-class party. **Assessment:** On the question of the Democratic Party, Left Voice's formulations this week are the most consistent of the six outlets. The unresolved question — which the WSWS has addressed at length in relation to the Morenoite tradition — is what independent organization means concretely: the calls for a "workers' party" remain programmatically undefined, and the tendency's orientation to the existing union apparatus and to protest movements has repeatedly cut across the class independence its articles assert. Liberation News (PSL) **"Desperate Democratic establishment narrowly defeats Hong in Wisconsin"** calls the Democratic Party "a party of big business and empire" — but the practice being reported and defended, a socialist running on the Democratic ballot line, is electoral fusion with that party. The rhetorical denunciation coexists with the tactic it denounces. **"Flanagan wins big in primary as Minnesotans reject AIPAC and ICE"** goes further, favorably contrasting one Democratic primary candidate against another over AIPAC funding. This lends relative political credibility to a faction inside a bourgeois party rather than maintaining independence from the contest as a whole. **"A year of federal occupation in D.C. shows what's at stake in our struggle"** describes Trump's DC takeover as "soft-launch martial law," rejects electoralism and calls for revolutionary class organizing — the strongest of the three pieces, and directly at odds in method with the primary coverage. **Assessment:** The PSL's line remains internally divided between anti-Democratic rhetoric and practical intervention in Democratic primaries. The underlying orientation is toward a radicalized milieu whose activity is defined by whatever electoral or protest vehicle is available. --- Arts and culture Kennedy Center board votes a second time to close the complex — and restore Trump's name The Trump-appointed board of the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts voted Thursday for the second time to close the Washington complex's main campus for two years for a **$250 million renovation**, three months after a federal judge temporarily blocked an identical decision. The board simultaneously voted to reinscribe the president's name at the entrance, designating the building "Restored and Renovated by President Donald J. Trump." The main building would reopen in summer 2028; the REACH pavilion, a 2019 addition, remains open for limited programming and as a memorial to the assassinated president. The project includes structural repairs, new marble floors, nearly **$12 million** in "acoustical improvements," and the temporary removal of the eight-foot bronze bust of Kennedy that stands in the main foyer. The scale of the political intervention is unusual even by the standards of this administration. Representative Joyce Beatty, an ex-officio board member, sued in December to reverse the renaming and halt the renovation; eight architecture and cultural preservation organizations filed a separate suit in March. Shutting the country's flagship performing arts institution for two years destroys the livelihoods of hundreds of musicians, stagehands, technicians and box-office workers, and eliminates the programming — the National Symphony Orchestra, the Washington National Opera, touring theatre — that constitutes the institution's actual social purpose. The renaming converts a national cultural institution into a monument to the sitting president, in the manner of a personalist regime. "The Brink of War": Reykjavik 1986 as historical costume drama Among Friday's US theatrical releases is **The Brink of War**, a dramatization of the October 1986 Reykjavik summit between Ronald Reagan and Mikhail Gorbachev, at which discussions on human rights, the Strategic Defense Initiative and the elimination of nuclear arsenals collapsed over SDI. The subject matter is genuinely significant: Reykjavik was one of the closest approaches to nuclear disarmament in history, and its failure prefigured the Stalinist bureaucracy's capitulation and the dissolution of the USSR. Early critical response has been unfavourable — one reviewer called it "a stage play adaptation gone horribly wrong" — and the film reportedly reduces the summit to a chamber drama of personal negotiation. The historical problem is that Gorbachev arrived at Reykjavik not as a peace envoy but as the representative of a privileged bureaucratic caste preparing the restoration of capitalism. A film that treats the summit as a contest of two statesmen's characters cannot address why the promise of disarmament evaporated — a question with obvious contemporary weight as the nuclear powers rearm and Washington wages open war on Iran. Also released Friday: **The End of Oak Street**, written and directed by David Robert Mitchell (*It Follows*), with Anne Hathaway and Ewan McGregor as a couple in an early-1980s suburb torn out of space and deposited in a landscape of predatory dinosaurs — a genre hybrid whose premise of a middle-class neighbourhood stripped of its securities has evident allegorical potential. **The Rivals of Amziah King** stars Matthew McConaughey as a rural Oklahoma beekeeper reunited with an estranged foster daughter under threat from competitors. Israeli airstrikes kill 11 in southern Lebanon Israeli warplanes struck villages across southern Lebanon on Saturday, killing at least 11 people, in the deadliest single day of attacks since the June 20 arrangement that nominally reduced hostilities between Israel and Hezbollah. Lebanon's Health Ministry reported seven killed when a house in the village of Ansar was hit, and four more killed in a strike on Deir El Zahrani. Nineteen people were wounded. The Israeli military said the attacks were retaliation for a Hezbollah operation against its troops in southern Lebanon and confirmed that it had killed Ali Samir Al-Haj Hassan, described as a commander in Hezbollah's Radwan Force, near Ansar. Hezbollah said the strikes would be "met with what they deserve." The escalation comes as Israeli forces remain in occupied positions inside Lebanese territory and as the Gaza "ceasefire" enters its eleventh month with a continuing death toll. Key facts: - Among the seven killed in Ansar were three children and two women, according to the Lebanese Health Ministry. - This was the most substantial escalation since mid-June and the deadliest attack since the June 20 agreement took effect. - In Gaza, 1,259 Palestinians have been killed and 4,146 wounded by Israeli attacks between the October 10, 2025 ceasefire and August 11, 2026, according to UN figures; roughly 160 were killed in July alone. - At least 300 children in Gaza have been killed in the 300 days since the ceasefire nominally began, the UN reported this month. - The Palestinian National Committee for the Administration of Gaza, the technocratic body created to oversee reconstruction, has still not been permitted to enter the territory.

DR Congo Ebola epidemic becomes largest ever recorded The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo has become the largest ever recorded in that country and is expanding faster than any previous Ebola epidemic anywhere. As of August 12, the World Health Organization reported 4,665 confirmed cases in the DRC, with 2,184 deaths — a crude case fatality ratio of 46.8 percent. Twenty cases have been reported in Uganda and one in France. WHO also disclosed this week that the outbreak began in February, well before it was formally declared, with early cases misattributed to malaria and typhoid — a delay directly traceable to the collapsed state of public health infrastructure in eastern Congo, a region shattered by decades of imperialist plunder and proxy war. The strain involved is Bundibugyo ebolavirus, for which there is no licensed vaccine and no specific treatment; WHO is urging a trial of the Ervebo vaccine, developed against the Zaire strain. Key facts: - The outbreak has spread from a single health zone in Ituri Province to 54 health zones across six provinces: Ituri, North Kivu, South Kivu, Haut-Uélé, Tshopo and Bas-Uélé. - WHO describes the epidemic as being in "a phase of intense transmission." - A new treatment centre opened at the epicentre in early August, reported by UN News, months into uncontrolled spread. - Cases topped 4,000 on August 7, meaning several hundred additional confirmed infections in under a week.

--- Arts and culture **Benjamin Alire Sáenz, 1954-2026.** The El Paso poet and novelist died at 71 after a long illness. Born in Old Picacho, New Mexico, a farming community near Las Cruces, into a family of agricultural workers, Sáenz became the first Latino writer to win the PEN/Faulkner Award, for *Everything Begins and Ends at the Kentucky Club* (2013), a collection of stories set along the Ciudad Juárez-El Paso border at the height of the cartel war. His young-adult novel *Aristotle and Dante Discover the Secrets of the Universe* reached an international audience and was named by Time among the 100 best YA novels ever written. Sáenz's best work is rooted in a specific social reality: the border as a place of labor, poverty, migration and state violence, not as metaphor. A former Catholic priest who left the priesthood, he wrote about masculinity, class and the interior lives of working-class Mexican-American youth with a directness rare in contemporary American fiction. At his request, the El Paso Community Foundation has established a literary fund to found a book festival in the city and support regional writers. **Venice unveils a competition weighted toward auteur cinema.** The 83rd Venice International Film Festival (September 2-12) has announced a 20-film competition notably lighter on studio and streaming product than in recent years. Lee Chang-dong returns with *Possible Love*, his first feature since *Burning* (2018); Hirokazu Kore-eda presents *Look Back*; Werner Herzog, Martin McDonagh (*Wild Horse Nine*), Florian Zeller (*Bunker*) and Andrea Pallaoro (*The Echo Chamber*, with Alicia Vikander and Susan Sarandon) also compete. Casey Affleck debuts as director with *Company*. Danny Boyle's *Ink* opens the festival, and a documentary on the Oasis reunion tour features in the out-of-competition slate. Only one of the 20 competition films, Danish-Egyptian director May el-Toukhy's *Woman Unknown*, is directed by a woman — a fact that will dominate festival commentary and largely displace discussion of the films themselves. The more substantive question is what this selection says about the retreat of serious cinema from the industrial center: Venice's turn away from studio and streamer product reflects the collapse of the middle of the film industry, not a resurgence of artistic ambition within it. **Roundup:** - **Edinburgh.** The Edinburgh Art Festival is running Catherine Opie's *To Be Seen* at the Royal Scottish Academy, the first major UK museum survey of the American photographer's work, alongside Del LaGrace Volcano's *Love Bites Back* — a documentary record of underground communities in the 1980s and 90s. Both were the subject of a joint artist talk with the International Book Festival on August 15. The Royal Botanic Garden's *Earth Matters*, marking the 300th anniversary of James Hutton's birth, brings together more than 30 artists on the theme of soil. - **Box office and the biography industry.** The Michael Jackson biopic *Michael* arrives on streaming this month having passed $1 billion worldwide, surpassing *Oppenheimer* as the highest-grossing biographical film in history — a commercial fact that says more about the studios' retreat into pre-sold intellectual property, including the intellectual property of dead celebrities, than about any revival of the biographical film as a form. - **Coyote vs. Acme** finally reaches theatres after being shelved by Warner Bros. as a tax write-off, an episode that remains one of the clearest illustrations of the subordination of completed artistic work to accounting maneuvers. - **Yeon Sang-ho**, director of *Train to Busan*, returns to the genre with a South Korean thriller centred on an unemployed former professor surviving a mutating virus released at a biotech conference — one of the few new releases engaging directly, if allegorically, with the pandemic and with mass unemployment among the educated.

US-Iran deal deadline expires as Trump threatens Oman The 60-day deadline established by the 14-point Memorandum of Understanding signed by Donald Trump and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian on June 17 expired Monday with no permanent agreement, leaving the United States and Iran deadlocked over the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, the US naval blockade, and the disposition of frozen Iranian funds. Trump had already declared the MOU "over" on July 8. On Monday he said he was "not in a hurry" to conclude a deal and threatened to "bomb" Oman, which has served as the principal intermediary in the talks. The economic consequences were immediate. Brent crude settled near $91 per barrel, its highest level of the year, as vessel traffic through the Strait fell to near a standstill. At least one cargo ship was struck, reportedly resulting in a crew casualty and engine-room damage. Key facts: - Tehran and Washington had committed in the June MOU to reach a "final deal in maximum 60 days." No concrete framework for ending the war was announced as the window closed. - Trump ruled out extending the shipping ceasefire covering the Strait of Hormuz and threatened Iran with "economic isolation." - The conflict has now run nearly six months. Higher oil prices have fed directly into inflation expectations, cutting the market-implied probability of a September Fed rate cut to roughly 30 percent from about 50 percent a week earlier. - Iran's foreign minister separately condemned a drone attack on the office of Iraqi Kurdistan Region Prime Minister Masrour Barzani, a sign of how the conflict continues to metastasize across the region.

Ebola outbreak in DR Congo becomes deadliest in the country's history The World Health Organization confirmed Monday that the Ebola Bundibugyo outbreak in the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo has become the deadliest in the country's history, with 2,325 deaths recorded — surpassing the 2,299 deaths of the 2018-2020 outbreak. There are 4,945 confirmed cases. The outbreak is the fastest-growing on record. The speed is without precedent. Deaths reached 2,000 within three months; by comparison, the 2014-16 West Africa epidemic took five months to reach 1,000 deaths. UN officials describe the outbreak as killing approximately one person every 30 minutes. Key facts: - The outbreak is spreading roughly five times faster than previous Ebola epidemics, according to WHO comparisons. - Only the 2014-2016 West Africa outbreak (28,616 cases, 11,310 deaths) remains larger in absolute terms — but the current outbreak's fatality rate per unit time far exceeds it. - The epidemic is unfolding in Ituri and surrounding provinces, regions devastated by decades of armed conflict, mass displacement, and the collapse of health infrastructure. - The Bundibugyo strain has no licensed vaccine equivalent to the Ervebo product used against Zaire ebolavirus, a critical gap in the response. The scale of this catastrophe — over 2,300 dead in an outbreak that has received a fraction of the attention devoted to far smaller events in the imperialist centres — is a direct index of the subordination of global public health to the profit system and the collapse of international coordination since the COVID-19 pandemic.
