Following a 30-day waiting period, the union can be certified as the collective bargaining representative for Uber and Lyft drivers — potentially the largest union of gig workers anywhere, covering roughly 800,000 people. The critical fact is what the enabling law, AB 1340, does not do. Drivers remain classified as independent contractors. They gain a right to sectoral bargaining over wages and conditions while being denied employee status, minimum wage protections, overtime, unemployment insurance and workers' compensation. Delivery drivers for DoorDash and similar platforms are excluded entirely. The arrangement — negotiated between the Newsom administration, SEIU, and the platform companies themselves — institutionalises a second-tier legal category for a mass of low-paid workers, with a dues-collecting apparatus attached.

Ninety-four percent of cases are outbreak-associated. Utah's outbreak leads with 514 cases. This is the highest annual US count since before the country's 2000 elimination declaration and confirms the accelerating collapse of elimination status — the predictable outcome of a public health apparatus gutted by budget cuts and headed by an administration hostile to vaccination. H5N1 hits 20 more commercial poultry operations USDA APHIS confirmed at least 20 new H5N1 outbreaks at commercial poultry facilities in the past week, including a 3.2-million-bird layer facility in Hyde County, North Carolina. Over the past 30 days, 67 flocks and 11.54 million birds have been affected. The CDC continues to rate general public health risk as low, but the scale of culling maintains pressure on egg prices and on surveillance for mammalian spillover. The concentration of the industry — single facilities holding millions of birds — is itself the epidemiological risk factor. COVID rising in all 50 states as BA.3.2 "Cicada" variant spreads As of August 12-14, COVID-19 cases are rising in all 50 states, though national activity remains classified as "low." Roughly 15 percent of cases are attributed to the new BA.3.2 lineage, nicknamed "Cicada." Weekly test positivity is near 4 percent, down from over 9 percent at the same point last year. The comparison is a function of collapsed testing volume as much as reduced transmission; wastewater surveillance remains the only reliable indicator and is itself being defunded. A 10-cent digoxin pill cuts heart-failure hospitalizations by 25 percent Research led by cardiologists at University Medical Center Groningen found that low-dose digoxin — costing under 10 cents per day — reduces heart-failure hospitalisations by approximately 25 percent. Patients who discontinued the drug deteriorated significantly within six weeks. Digoxin is derived from foxglove and has been in clinical use since the 18th century. That a generic costing pennies delivers outcomes comparable to drugs priced at hundreds of dollars monthly is an indictment of a pharmaceutical research system organised around patentability rather than therapeutic value. **Also this week:** - **Alzheimer's:** ETH Zurich researchers led by Ursula Quitterer report that an experimental molecule, "Compound 10," stabilises the protein GRK2 and prevents it from clumping on mitochondria, slowing nerve-cell death and extending survival in mouse models. --- Arts and culture Salzburg Festival remains without an artistic director after political purge The Salzburg Festival — the most prestigious classical music and theatre festival in Europe — has completed its 2026 season under an interim director, seven months after the abrupt removal of Markus Hinterhäuser. The board announced in March that Hinterhäuser would leave "effective immediately," citing "irreconcilable differences of opinion," and placed him on paid leave until his contract expired at the end of September. Karin Bergmann has served as interim artistic director since. The official account is a contract dispute: Hinterhäuser was initially offered a third term running from October 2026 to 2031, then presented with a one-year extension he declined to accept before the board's deadline. As Verena Nees reports on the WSWS, that account obscures years of political pressure over Hinterhäuser's refusal to blacklist Russian artists — above all the conductor Teodor Currentzis and soprano Anna Netrebko — and his removal followed shortly after a *Der Spiegel* article questioning his conduct. Several sponsors withdrew funding over the dismissal, and a group of businesspeople and politicians sent a letter of solidarity to the board. Whatever the internal politics, the outcome is unambiguous: the leading festival of the German-speaking world has been decapitated, and the principle that artists are to be judged by their work rather than their passport has been abandoned. Nees draws the parallel to the Nazi *Gleichschaltung* of Austrian cultural life after 1938 — a comparison that will be attacked, but which accurately identifies the mechanism at work: cultural institutions being brought into line with a war drive. Tupac Shakur murder trial opens 30 years on Opening statements began Monday in Las Vegas in the trial of Duane "Keffe D" Davis, 63, charged with murder with a deadly weapon in the September 7, 1996 killing of Tupac Shakur. Prosecutors do not allege Davis fired the shots; they describe him as the "shot caller" who supplied the weapon in a plot to avenge the beating of his nephew by Shakur and members of his entourage at the MGM Grand. Davis faces life imprisonment; the trial is expected to run a month and, as NPR noted, will likely never establish who pulled the trigger. The prosecution's case rests substantially on Davis's own memoir and interviews — leading defence attorneys to frame the trial as a dispute over "truth or fiction," and to argue that a man is being tried on the basis of self-promotional storytelling. Shakur's death at 25 remains one of the most significant cultural events of the 1990s. His best work registered, with real artistic power, the social devastation of American inner cities under Reagan and Clinton — mass incarceration, the destruction of industrial employment, police violence — even as it was distorted by the commercial machinery that packaged that devastation for sale. **Roundup:** - **Deaths:** Actress **Hayden Panettiere**, known for *Heroes* and *Nashville*, died August 16 in Greenville, South Carolina at 36. Director and actor **Mark Rydell** — who made *On Golden Pond* and *The Rose*, and who studied under Sanford Meisner — died August 13 in Los Angeles at 97. Ugandan playwright **Alex Mukulu**, a major figure in East African political theatre, died August 15 at 72. - **Edinburgh Festival Fringe** continues through August 31 with 3,649 shows across 258 venues from 71 countries — 53,884 performances. Programmers identify artificial intelligence, the "manosphere," social class, and "the state of the world" among dominant themes, an indication of how deeply the present crisis has penetrated even the most commercialised arts marketplace. - **Booker Prize:** the 2026 longlist of 13 novels, chaired by classicist Mary Beard, includes previous winners Douglas Stuart and Marlon James, Elizabeth Strout for *The Things We Never Say*, and three debut novelists.

--- Pseudo-left press review - [Jacobin / DSA](#jacobin-dsa) — advises the Democratic Party on how to recapture defecting Trump voters through "economic populism," treating the party as the vehicle for working-class politics - [Left Voice](#left-voice) — presents Bolivian "self-organization" as the international model against the far right while orienting to the US "shift to the left" inside Democratic primaries - [Liberation News / PSL](#liberation-news-psl) — frames Democratic primary results as evidence of "the rise of socialism," measuring political progress by ballot-box outcomes within the ruling party - [Socialist Alternative](#socialist-alternative) — combines calls for "left independent candidates" with sustained orientation to DSA-aligned Democratic campaigns and to the union apparatus - [Socialist Worker / SWP (UK)](#socialist-worker-swp-uk) — building support for the new Corbyn-Sultana left party while covering strikes as pressure on that project - [The Communist / RCP (IMT)](#the-communist-rcp-imt) — abstract propagandism for "world revolution" alongside identity-framed campaigning, with no orientation to the actual struggles of the day --- Jacobin / DSA **"Donald Trump's Coalition Is Coming Apart"** (August 17) presents polling data showing Trump "waverers" rising from 20 percent in February to over 25 percent in July, with poor, non-white and young voters defecting fastest. The decisive finding is buried: fewer than 5 percent of 2024 Trump voters have switched to the Democrats; 56 percent of waverers remain unsure and 22 percent favour independents. Jacobin's own data thus documents a mass of workers breaking from both capitalist parties. The article's conclusion is nonetheless a strategy memo for the Democrats — that they can recapture these voters by "demonstrating commitment to economic populism and fighting corruption." The class content is explicit: Jacobin functions as a policy consultancy for a wing of the Democratic Party, and the independent political movement its own polling implies is precisely what it exists to prevent. **"The Trump Administration Has Been Spying on Labor Unions"** reports DHS infiltration of meetings of the CWA and SEIU in Minnesota — genuinely important factual reporting. But the framing treats state surveillance as a Trump-specific aberration rather than the continuation of an apparatus built under Obama and Biden, and the implied remedy is electoral: replace the administration. **"Capitalism Is Killing Summer"** applies a similar method to public pools and municipal recreation — real austerity, described without any conclusion beyond restored public spending. **Assessment:** Jacobin's output today is oriented entirely toward the 2026 midterms and the internal problems of the Democratic Party. The word "socialism" functions as a brand for a redistributive programme to be enacted by that party. Left Voice **"Self Organization in Bolivia Shows How to Fight the Far Right Internationally"** and **"The Next Chapter in the Bolivian Struggle"** (both August 16) advance the Morenoite method: the elevation of spontaneous mass organisation — councils, blockades, neighbourhood committees — into a strategy in itself, without the construction of a revolutionary party contesting for power. Bolivia is presented as a "model," which evades the historical record of exactly how the MAS and the union bureaucracy demobilised these same structures in 2005-06 and again in 2019-20. **"A New Political Moment? Trumpism's Crisis, the Midterms, and Shifts to the Left in the U.S."** (August 13) locates the "shift to the left" in Democratic Party primary results — the same framework as Jacobin, with a more radical vocabulary. **"Sanders-Backed Flanagan Wins Minnesota Senate Primary, Continuing Progressive Sweep"** (August 12) treats a Sanders-endorsed Democratic primary victory as a datum of working-class radicalisation. Left Voice formally criticises the Democratic Party while treating its internal contests as the arena where the class struggle is measured. **Assessment:** Radical phraseology attached to an orientation indistinguishable in practice from the DSA milieu. Liberation News / PSL **"Flanagan wins big in primary as Minnesotans reject AIPAC and ICE"** and **"Desperate Democratic establishment narrowly defeats Hong in Wisconsin – but it won't stop the rise of socialism"** (both August 12) construct an entire political perspective out of Democratic primary arithmetic. A Democratic candidate's victory becomes a popular rejection of ICE; a Democratic candidate's defeat becomes proof that socialism is rising. The PSL, which formally maintains a Marxist-Leninist self-description and runs its own presidential tickets, functions in practice as a left auxiliary of the Democratic Party's progressive wing at the local level. **"A year of federal occupation in D.C. shows what's at stake in our struggle"** (August 11) documents the federal deployment in Washington but poses the alternative as "the movement" and street mobilisation, never as the political independence of the working class or the fight for power. **Assessment:** Militant on the streets, adaptive at the ballot box — a combination that channels genuine anger back into the Democratic Party. Socialist Alternative **"Democratic Socialist Francesca Hong Concedes In Wisconsin—What Way Forward?"** (August 15) draws the lesson that a defeated DSA-backed Democratic primary campaign points toward "left independent candidates," a conclusion also advanced in **"Support Left Independent Candidates—Build An Alternative To The Two Corporate Parties"** (August 2). The formulation is significant for what it omits: no party, no programme, no international perspective — only better candidates. **"Interview: Union Nurse In Maine On Organizing Against ICE Brutality"** (August 17) presents the existing union structures as the natural vehicle for resistance, with no examination of the union apparatus's integration into the Democratic Party and the state. **Assessment:** Perpetual oscillation between running inside the Democratic Party and calling for independents, with the trade union bureaucracy treated throughout as an ally. Socialist Worker / SWP (UK) **"Speaking out for the new left party"** develops the SWP's orientation to the Corbyn-Sultana formation — a left-reformist parliamentary project that the SWP joins while offering tactical advice, reproducing the pattern of its Respect and Left Unity interventions. **"Strikers fighting for their safety against climate catastrophe"** and coverage of the indefinite strike begun August 10 by Institute of Cancer Research workers provide useful strike reporting, but the strikes are consistently framed as pressure to be applied on Labour and the union leaderships rather than as the basis for organising independently of them. **Assessment:** Movementist agitation subordinated to a parliamentary regroupment project. The Communist / RCP (IMT) **"Jason Arday: Killed by the racist establishment media"** (August 17) frames the death of the Cambridge academic through the category of racism as an autonomous force, a formulation that substitutes racial for class analysis. **"Air 'con': Climate culture war heats up as temperatures rise"** (August 17) and **"Artificial intelligence or artificial scarcity?"** (August 14) offer general propaganda against capitalism without any concrete programme for the workers involved. **"Defend the Cuban revolution! Defeat US imperialism!"** (August 13) uncritically defends the Cuban state apparatus, abandoning any Marxist analysis of the Stalinist bureaucracy's role. **Assessment:** The RCP's recruitment-oriented propagandism combines abstract calls for "world revolution" with adaptation to identity politics and to Castroism. **No direct attacks on the ICFI or WSWS were noted in the past 24 hours.** The most significant convergence with the bourgeois press remains the shared treatment of Democratic Party primaries as the measure of American political radicalisation — a framework Jacobin, Left Voice, PSL and Socialist Alternative all share with the *New York Times*.

US national debt crosses $40 trillion as 30-year yields hit highest since 2007 The US national debt has crossed the $40 trillion threshold — up from under $6 trillion at the turn of the millennium, doubled in the past decade, and with roughly $3 trillion added in the last year alone. The government must borrow at least another $2 trillion this year. Annual interest payments now exceed $1 trillion, surpassing the entire military budget and consuming close to one dollar in five of federal revenue, even as the administration drives military spending toward $1.5 trillion. The 30-year Treasury yield touched roughly 5.32 percent this week, its highest level since 2007, before Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent intervened by doubling government buybacks of long-dated debt, pulling the yield back more than 10 basis points to 5.184 percent. In today's WSWS Perspective, Nick Beams argues the intervention is itself an admission that the American state can no longer rely on ordinary market mechanisms to finance itself, and that the Treasury market has entered a self-reinforcing "debt spiral" in which borrowing increasingly serves only to pay interest on debt already accumulated. Key facts: - Marc Goldwein of the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget: "The scariest thing... is how we're starting to see the debt spiral begin." - Hedge funds doubled their Treasury exposure between 2023 and 2025 through leveraged "basis trades" and now hold 8.5 percent of the market — more than Japan, China and Saudi Arabia combined. - The *Financial Times*' Robin Wigglesworth is cited describing the Treasury market as "arguably a source of peril"; Ambrose Evans-Pritchard characterised recent Treasury interventions as behaviour that "screams desperation." - The S&P 500 fell earlier in the week under pressure from surging sovereign yields worldwide, despite having hit an all-time high earlier in August. 2026 has already seen eight weeks in which the gap between the best- and worst-performing S&P sectors hit double digits — a frequency last matched in 2000, 2001 and 2009.

Communist (RCP, IMT) - **"Mau Mau Uprising — how the British mutilated Kenya"** is a substantive historical exposure of British colonial atrocities, and the strongest material published by any of these tendencies today. - **"Air 'con': Climate culture war heats up as temperatures rise"** argues that capitalists exploit climate debates by "pitting climate activists against ordinary people." The framing accepts the premise that environmental measures are experienced as an imposition on workers, adapting to right-wing populist agitation instead of advancing a socialist program for the rational reorganization of energy and production. - **"AI, data centres, and the quiet hum of revolution"** catalogues environmental damage and unemployment from AI expansion, but the conclusion — "revolutionary responses" in the abstract — is unconnected to any concrete intervention in struggles like the Hyundai strike, where AI displacement is the actual bargaining issue. *Assessment:* Strong historical material coexists with a present-day perspective built around national-populist framing and recruitment appeals in place of a program for the working class. Left Voice - Coverage of the cancellation of Temporary Protected Status, which places 300,000 additional immigrant workers at risk of deportation, centers on a resolution passed by NYC Teamsters Local 804. Left Voice presents resolutions passed by union bodies as the substance of the fight, without addressing that the Teamsters' national leadership under Sean O'Brien has openly aligned itself with the Trump administration. - Coverage of the Bolivian uprising emphasizes assemblies and roadblocks as expressions of "Latin American resistance to Trump and the international Far Right" — a framing that subordinates the independent class movement of Bolivian workers to a continental anti-Trump front. *Assessment:* Left Voice registers militant struggles more accurately than most of these tendencies, but its perspective consistently stops at the boundary of the existing union apparatus. International Socialist Alternative - ISA's report on its International School, held July 25-30 in Kiel, Germany, with over 100 participants, features a World Perspectives plenary titled **"Trump's reactionary offensive deepens capitalist crises — class battles incoming."** The formulation is characteristic: struggles are always impending, never present, and no organizational conclusion — above all no break with the trade union bureaucracy or the parties of the "broad left" — is drawn. - The report devotes prominent space to a €42,218 finance appeal. *Assessment:* An organization whose international gathering produces perspectives documents anticipating battles rather than intervening in the ones underway at Hyundai, Tyson and across the Victorian health system.

Newly identified immune organ in skull bone marrow Researchers at Washington University report in *Nature* the identification of lymph-node-like structures within skull bone marrow that function as first responders to brain disease. These structures use channels linking the skull to the dura mater to detect brain-derived signals before distant lymph nodes can respond. Disrupting them accelerated glioblastoma growth and shortened survival in mice, while local immune stimulation improved tumor control. Analogous structures were identified in human skull marrow. The finding effectively describes a previously unrecognized immune organ dedicated to the central nervous system, with implications for glioblastoma, Alzheimer's and Parkinson's disease. --- Arts and culture - [Venice opens with a film about Rupert Murdoch](#venice-opens-with-a-film-about-rupert-murdoch) — Danny Boyle's *Ink* premieres as the 83rd festival hands Clooney its first lifetime achievement Golden Lion - [Museums under financial and political siege](#museums-under-financial-and-political-siege) — the Philadelphia Museum of Art faces a roughly $10 million operating deficit amid a broader federal assault on arts funding - [Deaths](#deaths) — the Romanian soprano Ileana Cotrubaș and the American actor Michael Wright Venice opens with a film about Rupert Murdoch The 83rd Venice International Film Festival, running September 2-12, will open with Danny Boyle's *Ink*, a dramatization of Rupert Murdoch's early career and his acquisition of *The Sun*, with Guy Pearce as Murdoch and Jack O'Connell as editor Larry Lamb. That the festival should open with a study of the man who did more than almost any other individual to degrade mass journalism into an instrument of reaction is not without significance — though whether Boyle treats Murdoch as a social phenomenon or as a picaresque anti-hero remains to be seen. The competition includes new work from Martin McDonagh, Werner Herzog and Florian Zeller, Casey Affleck's directorial effort *Company*, and — most notably — South Korean director Lee Chang-dong's *Possible Love*, his first feature since *Burning* (2018). Lee remains one of the few working filmmakers whose work seriously examines the psychic damage inflicted by South Korean capitalism on ordinary people. Maggie Gyllenhaal serves as jury president. George Clooney will receive the festival's first Golden Lion for Lifetime Achievement — a decision that says more about the industry's need to honor a reliable liberal establishment figure than about any body of work commensurate with the award. Museums under financial and political siege The Philadelphia Museum of Art is confronting a roughly $10 million operating deficit as new leadership attempts a turnaround — a crisis emblematic of institutions squeezed between collapsing public subsidy and dependence on donor whim. The broader context is the systematic defunding and political policing of American cultural institutions documented in a recent timeline of federal actions against the arts: the gutting of the NEA and NEH, purges at the Kennedy Center and Smithsonian, and content directives imposed on federally supported exhibitions. Roundup: - Stolen works by Cézanne, Renoir and Matisse valued at $10 million were recovered in a cardboard box, months after a three-minute museum heist - The Metropolitan Museum of Art has placed on view one of the oldest surviving copies of the *Odyssey* — a papyrus fragment containing three lines absent from standard modern translations, a reminder that the Homeric text is a living historical document rather than a fixed monument - The Speed Art Museum repatriated 24 artifacts to the Cheyenne and Arapaho Tribes - Five Philadelphia-area cultural organizations each received $100,000 in unrestricted funding through Etsy and the Center for Craft — private philanthropy filling, minimally, the void left by the destruction of public arts funding - Telfair Museums named Caitlín Doherty as director following a leadership shakeup Deaths **Ileana Cotrubaș**, 87, the Romanian soprano, died August 20. Trained in Bucharest under the Ceaușescu regime and later a fixture at Covent Garden, La Scala and the Vienna State Opera, Cotrubaș was among the great lyric sopranos of the postwar era. Her Violetta, Mimì and Gilda were distinguished not by vocal display but by an unusual dramatic intelligence and an ability to convey the vulnerability of women crushed by social circumstance — precisely the element in Verdi and Puccini that a great deal of contemporary opera production works to obscure. **Michael Wright**, 70, the American actor, died August 21. Wright emerged from David Rabe's *Streamers* — both on stage and in Robert Altman's 1983 film — and gave his most memorable performance as Eddie King in *The Five Heartbeats* (1991), a portrait of talent destroyed by the music industry. He later appeared in HBO's *Oz*. His career, marked by long stretches without work, illustrated the narrow range of parts made available to Black actors of his generation. Also reported: Romanian-born opera figures aside, the Sri Lankan singer **Nanda Malini**, whose protest songs were banned during periods of state repression, died August 20; Indian film actress **Sowcar Janaki**, 94, died August 21.

Australia had been the last inhabited continent free of the H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b panzootic that has killed hundreds of millions of birds and spread into mammals across every other continent, including Antarctica. Its arrival threatens endemic species with no evolved resistance and creates new reservoirs for reassortment. In the United States, CDC influenza surveillance as of August 7 showed no indicators of unusual activity in people, including avian influenza A(H5). From 2024 through May 2026, 71 human cases of highly pathogenic avian influenza were identified in the US, concentrated among dairy and poultry workers, and the CDC's public risk assessment remained "low." That assessment rests on a surveillance apparatus that has been substantially defunded — a point of continuing WSWS criticism. JWST finds early galaxies three to four times more massive than believed Astronomers using the James Webb Space Telescope have found that massive early galaxies contain far more small, faint stars than models predicted. The hidden low-mass population may make some of these galaxies three to four times more massive than previously estimated — a finding that compounds the existing tension between JWST observations of the early universe and standard models of galaxy assembly, which struggle to explain how so much mass accumulated so quickly after the Big Bang. Separately, astronomers reported observations of stars repeatedly approaching supermassive black holes and surviving the encounters, producing repeating light bursts that unexpectedly dim with each return — a class of repeating partial tidal disruption events whose fading mechanism remains unexplained. Medical and biological research roundup - **Multilingualism and brain aging:** people speaking four languages showed brains appearing approximately 13 years younger than monolingual counterparts on imaging-based biological age measures — evidence for cognitive reserve, though the finding is confounded by the class distribution of multilingualism. - **Alcohol withdrawal and relapse:** mice showed more than double the activity in a brain region associated with stress and addiction following alcohol withdrawal, with the neural signature appearing *before* relapse behavior — a possible predictive biomarker. - **Peppermint oil and hypertension:** adults with mildly elevated blood pressure taking a small dose twice daily for 20 days saw systolic pressure fall by an average of 8.5 mmHg. - **Exercise and weight:** exercise proved substantially more effective at preventing weight regain than at producing initial weight loss, through muscle preservation and metabolic support — a direct rebuttal of the moralizing framework used to justify withholding obesity treatment. - **Immunotherapy:** a yeast-based food supplement restored immune capacity to fight cancer in mice, a low-cost candidate adjunct. - **Greenland sharks:** the 400-year-old species maintains healthy retinal tissue and specialized proteins for Arctic vision with no age-related decline — a model system for studying vertebrate longevity. - **Photonics:** freezing the liquid core of an optical fiber produced an environment in which light and sound interact more than 1,000 times more strongly than in ordinary fibers, with implications for sensing and signal processing. - **Materials:** Tokyo Metropolitan University researchers derived theoretical design rules for new thermoelectric materials, relevant to waste-heat recovery. Chinese humanoid robot runs 100 metres in 9.32 seconds A Chinese humanoid robot, "Lightning," ran 100 metres in 9.32 seconds — faster than Usain Bolt's world record of 9.58 seconds. The achievement is a demonstration of actuator power density, balance control and thermal management rather than a like-for-like athletic comparison, but it marks a real inflection point in bipedal robotics. --- Arts and culture The 83rd Venice International Film Festival opens September 2 with a lineup that reflects, in fractured form, the crisis of the present moment. The opening film is Danny Boyle's *Ink*, on the early days of Rupert Murdoch's acquisition of *The Sun*, with Guy Pearce as Murdoch and Jack O'Connell as editor Larry Lamb — a subject of some consequence given the role the Murdoch press has played over fifty years in poisoning political life in Britain, Australia and the United States. Whether Boyle, whose *Slumdog Millionaire* and 2012 Olympics ceremony represented a certain liberal Britishness, can produce a serious anatomy of that machinery rather than a stylized origin story remains to be seen. Martin McDonagh's *Wild Horse Nine*, a CIA story set shortly before the September 1973 coup in Chile, is among the more significant entries. The overthrow of Allende and the murder of thousands of Chilean workers is one of the decisive experiences of the twentieth century, and any serious treatment of the American role bears directly on questions the working class confronts today. The competition also includes new work from Lee Chang-dong, Tsai Ming-liang, Lav Diaz, Hirokazu Kore-eda, Wim Wenders, Werner Herzog, Paul Schrader, Nanni Moretti, Julia Loktev, Laura Poitras and Shinya Tsukamoto — a jury led by Maggie Gyllenhaal will decide among them. The Spotlight sidebar is described as unusually political this year. **The politics of cultural memory.** Two archaeological reports this week bear on how societies remember catastrophe. Excavators at Pompeii uncovered 15th- and 16th-century artifacts indicating that the buried city retained a continuous cultural presence long after Vesuvius, contradicting the assumption of total abandonment. In Budapest, a Wehrmacht motorcycle was recovered from the Danube containing the remains of two German soldiers — physical residue of the 1944–45 siege, surfacing in a country whose government has spent fifteen years rehabilitating the Horthy regime that made that siege possible. **Culture and war.** Ukrainian authorities restricted the children's cartoon *Masha and the Bear* on grounds of Russian propaganda content — a small item that illustrates the wartime logic by which cultural production is subordinated to the nation-state, the same logic that produced the court order to destroy Bogdan Syrotiuk's socialist library. Actor Liev Schreiber, serving as a UNITED24 ambassador, sheltered during Russian strikes in Kyiv and called for expanded air defense, an example of the direct enlistment of cultural figures into the NATO war effort. **Roundup:** - Johannes Vermeer's *Girl with a Pearl Earring* left the Netherlands for its first international exhibition in more than a decade, on view in Osaka for five weeks — a loan that raises again the question of whether the world's most fragile paintings should travel for institutional revenue. - **Violet Hensley died at 109.** A fiddler and fiddle-maker from Arkansas, she was among the last living links to a rural American string-band tradition rooted in the labor and social life of the Ozarks, and built instruments by hand for more than eighty years. - **Hayden Panettiere died at 36** on August 16, found unresponsive in a South Carolina apartment. Best known for *Heroes* and *Nashville*, she had spoken publicly about addiction and postpartum depression; her death at that age is another instance of the toll the entertainment industry exacts on performers who enter it as children. - Puerto Rican reggaeton artist Wisin announced a "University of Perreo" devoted to documenting the genre's history — a genuine impulse toward preserving a working-class musical form, packaged in the commercial idiom of the industry that commodified it. - The FCC's campaign against ABC's broadcast licenses, detailed above, remains the sharpest live threat to artistic and journalistic expression in the United States.

Himalayan glacier collapse kills more than 350 in Nepal and Tibet A catastrophic glacial collapse on the Nepal–Tibet border on August 26 has killed more than 350 people and left over 1,300 missing, including foreign trekkers and pilgrims travelling the Kathmandu–Kerung corridor. Satellite imagery analyzed by glaciologists shows that a substantial section of the lower tongue of a glacier detached at roughly 5,200 metres elevation and fell some 1,200 metres onto the valley floor, gathering rock and sediment as it descended and striking the Lhende river about 20 km northeast of the Nepal–China border crossing. The debris dammed the river; when the natural dam failed, it released a wall of water, mud and rock several stories high through the Lhende Khola valley. More than 5,000 Nepalese army and police personnel are engaged in search and recovery. Helicopters are supplying tents and food to villages cut off by destroyed roads. Officials expect the toll to climb sharply as crews reach areas still buried under meters of mud. Key facts: - Water levels in the valley rose approximately 27 feet in 30 minutes, according to survivor accounts and hydrological reconstruction - Nepal has lost close to one-third of its total ice volume over the past three decades; the Hindu Kush–Himalaya region is warming faster than the global average - Nepalese authorities reported 157 bodies recovered and 54 people rescued in the first 24 hours; Anadolu put the confirmed toll at 160 with 680 missing on Thursday morning before it climbed further - This is the worst disaster in the region since the 2015 earthquake, and follows the 2024 Thame flood and the 2025 Uttarakhand flash flood in the same glacial-lake-outburst pattern - No functioning early-warning system existed on the Lhende; glacial-lake and ice-collapse monitoring in the region remains almost entirely dependent on episodic international grant funding

--- Arts and culture **Péter Nádas, 1942–2026.** The Hungarian novelist died at his home in Gombosszeg on the morning of August 26, aged 83. Nádas began as a photojournalist and reporter under the Kádár regime and turned to fiction after the censors made journalism impossible for him. *A Book of Memories* (1986), written over eleven years and withheld from publication by Hungarian censorship, interleaves three narrative strands to reconstruct the psychic texture of life under Stalinist rule; Susan Sontag called it "the greatest novel written in our time, and one of the great books of the century." *Parallel Stories* (2005), a 1,200-page work spanning from 1939 Berlin to post-1989 Budapest, is among the most ambitious attempts in postwar European literature to render the twentieth century's catastrophes — fascism, the Holocaust, Stalinism, and the restoration of capitalism — as they were registered in individual bodies and consciousnesses. Nádas refused both the nationalist mythology promoted by the Orbán government and the liberal triumphalism of 1989. He was a perennial Nobel contender who never received the prize. **Dolly Parton, 1946–2026.** The country singer and songwriter died in Nashville on August 25 at 80, after what her publicist described as a brief battle with cancer following admission to Vanderbilt University Medical Center with kidney and autoimmune complications. Parton was the fourth of twelve children born into rural poverty in Sevier County, Tennessee, and her strongest work drew directly on that material: "Coat of Many Colors," "In the Good Old Days (When Times Were Bad)," and "9 to 5," which remains one of the few genuinely popular songs in the American canon organized entirely around the experience of wage labor and the resentment of the boss. Her later career was substantially given over to the Dollywood enterprise and to a carefully maintained apolitical public persona, which the music industry rewarded and which flattened the class content of her best songwriting. The recorded work from 1967 through the mid-1970s is nonetheless a significant body of American vernacular art. **Tim Curry, 1945–2026.** The English actor died at his Los Angeles home on August 25 at 80. Curry trained in repertory and came to prominence in the original 1973 London stage production of *The Rocky Horror Show*, whose 1975 film adaptation made him a permanent fixture of a subculture built around the film's midnight screenings. His range — from the sinister precision of *Clue* to the malevolence of *It* — was consistently underused by an industry that could not classify him. A stroke in 2012 confined him largely to voice work; his memoir *Vagabond* appeared last year. **Roundup:** - The 83rd **Venice International Film Festival** opens September 2 with Danny Boyle's *Ink*. --- Arts and culture The death of **Yayoi Kusama** at 97, announced by the David Zwirner gallery on August 26 (she died August 14 in a Tokyo hospital of multiple organ failure), closes one of the most singular careers in postwar art. Kusama's seven decades of work — the obliterating polka dots, the infinity rooms, the accumulation sculptures — grew from a genuinely modernist impulse to represent the dissolution of the isolated individual into a larger material world, an impulse rooted in her wartime childhood in militarist Japan and her subsequent decades of voluntary residence in a psychiatric institution. Her New York years in the 1960s placed her at the center of an avant-garde that included anti-Vietnam War "happenings." That her late work was absorbed into the luxury-branding apparatus of the art market — Louis Vuitton collaborations, ticketed selfie rooms — is a comment on that market, not on the work. Hungarian novelist **Péter Nádas** died on August 26 at 83. Nádas belonged to the generation of Central European writers formed by the Stalinist suppression of the 1956 Hungarian revolution and the long stagnation that followed. *A Book of Memories* (1986) and the vast *Parallel Stories* (2005) attempted, through an exhaustive attention to bodily and psychological experience, to render the interior life of people living under a regime that falsified everything. Nádas's achievement was to insist that the historical catastrophes of the twentieth century are lived in individual nervous systems and not merely in documents. **Dolly Parton** died on August 26 at 80. Whatever the layers of commercial packaging accumulated over six decades, Parton emerged from genuine rural poverty in East Tennessee and wrote a body of songs — "Coat of Many Colors," "Jolene," "9 to 5" — that gave direct voice to the experience of working-class women in the American South. "9 to 5," written for a film about a workplace rebellion, remains one of the very few genuinely popular songs about the exploitation of labor. --- Science, technology, and public health - [NASA launches the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope](#nasa-launches-the-nancy-grace-roman-space-telescope) — an 18,000-pound observatory with Hubble's sharpness and 100 times its field of view, built from a repurposed spy telescope - [Measles kills two in Pennsylvania as US cases hit a 30-year high](#measles-kills-two-in-pennsylvania-as-us-cases-hit-a-30-year-high) — 2,777 confirmed cases nationally, 94 percent outbreak-associated; the CDC's August 28 data update was delayed - [Research and technology roundup](#research-and-technology-roundup) — micro-awakenings linked to Alzheimer's genetic risk; all 212 UK plant-based meat products tested carried fungal toxins; AI deepfakes of late-night hosts spread unchecked NASA launches the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope lifted off at 7:26 a.m. ET Sunday from Kennedy Space Center aboard a SpaceX Falcon Heavy, beginning a million-mile journey to the second Sun-Earth Lagrange point (L2), where the James Webb telescope also orbits. The 18,000-pound spacecraft, roughly the size of a tour bus, will take more than three months to reach L2, followed by calibration. Roman has Hubble's optical sharpness with a field of view at least 100 times larger, allowing it to survey enormous swaths of sky at once. Its central missions are the mapping of dark matter through weak gravitational lensing — measuring how gravity bends light across cosmological distances — and the characterization of dark energy through a vastly expanded catalogue of Type Ia supernovae, the "standard candles" used to measure cosmic expansion. The instrument's origin is itself instructive: it was initially built as a spy telescope for the National Reconnaissance Office and donated to NASA. The observatory carries the name of NASA's first chief astronomer, known as the "Mother of Hubble," who died in 2018. "It's basically like our time to kick the tires," said NASA integration and test scientist Jeremy Perkins.

--- Arts and culture **The Paramount-Warner merger and the destruction of film employment.** A 118-page report submitted to the Los Angeles County Board of Supervisors on August 18 by the Department of Economic Opportunity assesses the consequences of Paramount Skydance's proposed $110 billion acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery — a merger that would unite two of the six remaining major Hollywood studios under a structure dominated by the Ellison family fortune and $82 billion in gross debt. The projected damage: 10,360 job-years at risk in Los Angeles County, a further 14,000 corporate job-years of consolidation globally through 2030, $1.26 billion in lost wages, $2.79 billion in economic value, $4.06 billion in business output and $547 million in tax revenue. These follow directly from management's stated plans, including CEO David Ellison's pledge to extract $6 billion in annual "synergies." The baseline is more damning than the projections. Los Angeles County motion-picture employment averaged 93,263 jobs in 2025 — a record low, 35.7 percent below the 2022 peak. California has lost 52,016 film and television jobs since 2022, with 99.6 percent of those losses in Los Angeles County. Major US film and television releases fell from 2,122 in 2022 to 1,629 in 2025; cable series, historically the foundation of recurring employment, collapsed from 992 releases in 2019 to 579 in 2025. Paramount Skydance plans to finance the deal with $54-57.5 billion in bridge loans, with Larry Ellison guaranteeing up to $45.7 billion in equity from Oracle holdings — leverage approaching seven times earnings. As Marc Wells writes on the WSWS, the county report "reads, in its cool bureaucratic language, like an autopsy of a still-living body." **Venice opens Wednesday.** The 83rd Venice International Film Festival runs September 2-12. Danny Boyle's *Ink* opens the festival and competes for the Golden Lion, in a competition of 20 films that includes new work by Lee Chang-dong, Martin McDonagh, Werner Herzog and Lance Oppenheim. Only one competition entry, May el-Toukhy's *Woman Unknown*, is directed by a woman. Maggie Gyllenhaal presides over a jury that includes Kaouther Ben Hania, director of *The Voice of Hind Rajab*, composer Daniel Blumberg, film theorist Francesco Casetti, and directors Xavier Giannoli, Shahrbanoo Sadat and Johnnie To. Lifetime Achievement Golden Lions go to George Clooney and Ellen Burstyn. **Roundup** - **Dolly Parton (1946-2026).** Coverage of the singer's death continues to widen, with reporting on the extraordinary reach of her work across Africa. Parton's best songs — "Coat of Many Colors," "Nine to Five," "Jolene" — drew directly on the poverty of her east Tennessee childhood and on the experience of working women, and were written with a formal economy that concealed considerable craft. That an artist who never disguised her origins should be claimed simultaneously by every political tendency in America says more about the vacuum in contemporary popular culture than about her. - **Vienna museum heist.** Two unmasked men bought tickets to the Museum of Applied Arts (MAK), shattered a display case with a hammer during opening hours Thursday and made off with a 200-carat platinum necklace set with 673 diamonds, made in 1939 for Queen Nazli of Egypt and on loan to the museum. It is the latest in a series of smash-and-grab thefts from European cultural institutions whose collections have been steadily devalued as public assets and revalued as collateral. - **Deaths.** Franco Fontana, the Italian photographer whose saturated, near-abstract colour landscapes reshaped postwar European photography, died August 29 at 92. Antonino Fogliani, the Italian conductor and a leading interpreter of Rossini, died the same day at 50.

Report to the Ninth Congress of the SEP: The global eruption of the class struggle and the rebellion against the union bureaucracies — Tom Hall The WSWS published Tom Hall's report to the Ninth Congress of the Socialist Equality Party (US), held August 2-7, introducing the fourth resolution, "On the international class struggle and the building of the IWA-RFC," adopted unanimously. The report is the most important document in today's output and the one Evan should read in full. Its empirical core: the Armed Conflict Location and Event Data Project recorded more than 148,000 distinct demonstrations across 197 countries in 2025, with demonstrations rising globally for a third consecutive year. Allianz Commercial's 2026 political-violence report ranks civil unrest as the second-greatest political-violence concern facing corporations, tracking roughly 250 large strike, riot and civil-commotion events over five years and identifying cost-of-living pressure as the driver. Verisk Maplecroft's global Civil Unrest Index reached a six-year high in the second quarter of 2026, citing energy costs, inequality, poverty and austerity. On the conflict with the apparatus, Hall reports a conservative review of publicly reported contract votes in the US and Canada over five years identifying at least 103 union-backed agreements voted down by the membership — 17 in auto parts, nine in rail, eight each in food processing and healthcare, seven in airlines. The report affirms the assessment of the 2026 International May Day Rally that the first months of the year "mark the point at which the resistance of the working class has emerged as a global force, contending against the offensive of the oligarchy on a scale that places the fundamental questions of the epoch — war or peace, dictatorship or democracy, socialism or barbarism — directly on the historical agenda." Its conclusion: the next stage requires expansion of the rank-and-file committees and, above all, the recruitment into the party of workers who, as the Will Lehman campaign demonstrated, introduce socialist consciousness into the class struggle.
Sources WSWS The global eruption of the class struggle and the rebellion against the union bureaucracies
John-Paul Himka, leading historian of Ukraine, condemns prosecution of Bogdan Syrotiuk Dr. John-Paul Himka, Professor Emeritus of History at the University of Alberta, has sent a letter to the Pervomaisk City District Court condemning the imprisonment of Bogdan Syrotiuk, the 27-year-old Ukrainian Trotskyist sentenced on August 10 to 15 years for "high treason" under martial law. The letter was copied to the WSWS and published in full. Himka is among the world's foremost historians of modern Ukraine, author of *Ukrainian Nationalists and the Holocaust: OUN and UPA's Participation in the Destruction of Ukrainian Jewry, 1941-1944* (2021), *Socialism in Galicia* (1983), *Galician Villagers and the Ukrainian National Movement in the Nineteenth Century* (1988) and *Religion and Nationality in Western Ukraine* (1999), and a former Wisen Fellow at the US Holocaust Memorial Museum. He denounces the Ukrainian regime's "official cult of Holocaust perpetrators and ethnic cleansers." The political significance is considerable: Himka supports Ukraine in the present NATO-backed war and states plainly that his standpoint differs from that of the WSWS and of Syrotiuk. His intervention indicates that the defense campaign is winning support from serious academic figures on the basis of elementary democratic principle, independent of agreement with the ICFI's program. It should be used in approaches to other scholars and civil-liberties bodies.
Sources WSWS John-Paul Himka, leading historian of Ukraine, condemns prosecution of Bogdan Syrotiuk
Postal worker Russell Scruggs Jr.'s ex-wife speaks out, backs call for rank-and-file inquiry into postal deaths — Kathleen Martin Barbara Scruggs, ex-wife of Russell Scruggs Jr. and mother of three of his children, has publicly backed the IWA-RFC's independent inquiry into deaths at the USPS Palmetto Processing and Distribution Center in Georgia and is urging his coworkers to come forward. Scruggs, 44, died on November 15, 2025, weeks after starting the job; coworkers told the WSWS he suffered a head injury after falling onto machinery, and that he had complained earlier that day of feeling unwell and was denied a request to go home. His was one of four deaths at Palmetto since 2024; Demarcus Little died at the same facility this June. Workers report the facility has no cell phone service, leaving them dependent on management to summon help, and that supervisors called security before calling an ambulance. Scruggs died one week after Detroit postal worker Nick Acker was killed in a mail sorting machine. The inquiry is being conducted by the Postal Workers Rank-and-File Committee — by workers themselves, rather than by USPS management or the American Postal Workers Union. "Workers have to stand up and do something about this," Barbara Scruggs said, insisting that workers are "humans, not machines."
Sources WSWS Postal worker Russell Scruggs Jr.'s ex-wife speaks out, backs call for rank-and-file inquiry into postal deaths
Moving tribute to Oscar Robayo, Montreal airport worker crushed to death amid safety violations by subcontractor Oscar Robayo, a 39-year-old ground handling worker at Montréal-Trudeau International Airport, was crushed to death Monday during a routine aircraft pushback. The WSWS reports that in the absence of an extension cable, Robayo was forced to stand near the front wheel of the jet while it was towed by a tractor, and was run over as the driver manoeuvred the plane away from a remote port. A coworker detailed a litany of violated safety procedures, broken equipment and corner-cutting by the subcontractor Samsic, a French-based multinational that has played a major role in driving down conditions in airport ground operations across North America. The article carries a photomontage tribute assembled by his coworkers. The case is a direct parallel to the postal deaths inquiry: outsourcing to low-cost subcontractors as the mechanism of industrial homicide.
Sources WSWS Moving tribute to Oscar Robayo, Montreal airport worker crushed to death
How to combat the far-right AfD — Peter Schwarz Days before the September 6 state election in Saxony-Anhalt, the AfD leads with 42 percent in the latest Infratest dimap poll, ahead of the CDU on 22 percent, the Left Party on 11 percent and the SPD on 8 percent. For the first time since 1945, a far-right politician — AfD lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund — could become premier of a German federal state. Whether he does depends on how many parties fall below the 5 percent threshold and whether other parliamentary groups back him; the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance has already signalled willingness to cooperate. Schwarz's argument targets the establishment's staged opposition. *Der Spiegel* ran an August 14 cover calling Siegmund "Germany's most dangerous man." CDU premier Sven Schulze and Chancellor Merz insist on the "firewall." The Left Party is prepared to vote for a CDU premier to block the AfD. The campaign group Campact is spending more than €600,000 urging tactical second votes for the SPD or Greens. Schwarz: the fascist danger does not originate in the person of a 36-year-old businessman but in a ruling class turning to authoritarian methods amid war and austerity — and the parties presenting themselves as the alternative are implementing that program.
Sources WSWS How to combat the far-right AfD
What lessons must be drawn from Mélenchon's warnings of a French neofascist presidency? — Alex Lantier At La France Insoumise's summer school, Jean-Luc Mélenchon warned that the 2027 presidential contest will likely be between himself and the Rassemblement National, and compared the situation to the 1930s: "The Republic is on fire and is breaking apart… We see the great conversion of the right wing and the center parties to a unified ideological bloc with the National Rally. They are already there, all of them lined up… those who, seeing us advancing towards victory, are already starting to say: rather Hitler than the Popular Front." Lantier grants that the historical comparison is not exaggerated — the RN leads every poll, sustained by favourable media coverage, while France and the other major European states pour tens and hundreds of billions into war spending amid unsustainable debt and impose austerity rejected by the overwhelming majority. But he draws the opposite conclusion from Mélenchon's: the 1936 experience demonstrates precisely why workers cannot entrust the struggle against dictatorship to a pro-capitalist politician whose program is the electoral defence of the Fifth Republic.
Sources WSWS What lessons must be drawn from Mélenchon's warnings of a French neofascist presidency?
US strikes on border and resignation of Sinaloa governor expose logic of Sheinbaum's endless concessions to Trump — Andrea Lobo US Northern Command announced Thursday that an Army Multipurpose High Energy Laser shot down three drones in the Rio Grande Valley late Tuesday and early Wednesday — reportedly the first use of a high-energy laser against aircraft the US military attributes to Mexican cartels. The military would not say where the drones were downed, which cartels they allegedly belonged to, or whether the shots crossed into Mexican airspace. Lobo notes that in February the same class of system shot down a US Customs and Border Protection drone by mistake, closing airspace around El Paso airport. The claims parallel those made about the fishing vessels bombed in the Caribbean and eastern Pacific, where no evidence of trafficking has been produced. What is being established, she argues, is a precedent that US forces may fire across the border. The strikes coincided with the removal of Sinaloa's Morena governor Rubén Rocha Moya, indicted April 29 by the US Attorney for the Southern District of New York along with nine other state officials, including Senator Enrique Inzunza Cázarez, for allegedly conspiring with "Los Chapitos." Rocha took leave, was defended by Sheinbaum and the entire Morena leadership as a victim of foreign interference, announced his return by tweet on August 21 without informing the presidency — and was gone again 33 hours later.
Sources WSWS US strikes on border and resignation of Sinaloa governor expose logic of Sheinbaum's endless concessions to Trump
Sri Lankan government bans railway workers from using social media — Sujeewa Amaranath On August 26, Sri Lanka Railways General Manager Ravindra Pathmapriya issued a circular prohibiting all railway workers from commenting on social media during "duty hours" on railway operational matters, internal decisions, official documents or "institutionally sensitive information," declaring that only the General Manager and the Information Officer may provide information externally. Violators face "maximum disciplinary action." The circular followed Facebook posts by Kasun Chamara, secretary of the Railway Station Masters' Union, about repeated locomotive technical failures; the administration demanded an "explanation." The measure is the JVP/NPP government's response to rising discontent among railway workers and passengers over austerity and pro-business restructuring, and effectively bars workers from publicly raising safety issues.

Rodent infestations in Chile's collapsed schools: A powder keg in the making — Mauricio Saavedra A week after Carabineros ordered two secondary students to strip inside a classroom at the Rayen Mapu Lyceum in Quellón, Chiloé, Saavedra examines the conditions in the school system that produced the confrontation. In May 2026, 11 schools across the Los Lagos Region — the Rayen Mapu Lyceum among them — had classes suspended or were barred from operating because of rodents, pigeons and bats. In the Coquimbo Region, a survey of 32 schools by the La Serena Teachers Association found 70 percent presented serious health risks including "plagues of rats and pigeon feces." In Santiago, students at the Augusto D'Halmar Lyceum in Ñuñoa — the only municipal school ranked among the country's top 100 on the university entrance exam — voted by 89.1 percent for an indefinite strike in August, demanding among other things an end to a recurring rat infestation. Saavedra traces this to the Pinochet constitution's "subsidiary state," which devolves education to municipalities with radically unequal tax bases or to private operators extracting profit from per-pupil subsidies.

Australian government pledges a miserable $5 million for Nepal-China flood victims — Oscar Grenfell Grenfell contrasts Foreign Minister Penny Wong's declaration that the "scale of the destruction is devastating" with the size of the Australian pledge, noting that the average Sydney house price is roughly $1.73 million — meaning the entire national contribution to one of the region's worst disasters in decades amounts to under three houses. Workers Struggles: Asia, Australia and the Pacific The weekly compilation documents a wave of labor action almost entirely absent from Western reporting: - **India:** The United Forum of Bank Unions, representing seven bank employee and officer unions, has called a one-day national strike for September 11, a three-day walkout September 28-30 and an indefinite strike from October 26 if demands are unmet — centrally, implementation of the five-day banking week agreed with the Indian Banks' Association in the March 2024 settlement but still awaiting government approval, and opposition to a revised performance-linked incentive scheme for senior officers. - **Chennai:** Around 80 sanitation workers organised by Uzhaippor Urimai Iyakkam continued protests at the Tondiarpet zonal office on August 23, a fourth consecutive day, demanding permanent jobs, a daily wage increase to 832 rupees ($8.72), paid weekly leave, maternity benefits and basic workplace facilities, plus reinstatement of 13 workers excluded from a group of 1,400 the Greater Chennai Corporation had agreed to take back. --- Pseudo-left press review - [Jacobin / DSA](#jacobin--dsa) — frames the UAW election as a referendum on Fain's "reform" project and endorses a consumer boycott at Starbucks in place of industrial action - [Left Voice](#left-voice) — published a defense of Bogdan Syrotiuk calling for an "international united front," while continuing to orient toward pressuring DSA and its elected officials - [Liberation News / PSL](#liberation-news--psl) — reports the Tyson layoffs and Dolly Parton's death, but its electoral line remains support for "socialist" Democratic primary candidates - [Socialist Alternative](#socialist-alternative) — advances "left independent candidates" for the midterms while presenting the Iran war through Financial Times framing - [Socialist Worker / SWP (UK)](#socialist-worker--swp-uk) — covers NHS and cancer-research strikes militantly but subordinates them to the existing union apparatus - [Communist / RCP (IMT)](#communist--rcp-imt) — correctly identifies Burnham's Ukraine trip as imperialist, then locates the alternative in party-building abstractions rather than the international unity of the working class Jacobin / DSA Jacobin's most significant piece is **"The United Auto Workers Are Voting for Their Top Leadership"** (Luis Feliz Leon and Jane Slaughter, August 27), which presents the election as "a referendum on President Shawn Fain's attempts to reform the UAW since 2023." The framing is the whole political line: the union apparatus is treated as an institution capable of reform from above by a better leadership, and the members' role is reduced to ratifying or rejecting that leadership. The article does not address the collapse of the 2023 contract's promised gains, the wave of plant closures, or the systematic exclusion of rank-and-file opposition — nor does it mention Will Lehman's campaign or the demand for abolition of the apparatus. **"Starbucks Workers Are Calling for a Nationwide Boycott"** (Jenny Brown, August 29) reports the union's turn to a consumer boycott without asking why, five years on, no contract exists. A boycott shifts the arena from the workplace to the market, substituting the goodwill of consumers for the collective power of workers — the logic of an apparatus that has ruled out the industrial mobilization that would be required. Jacobin also ran **"Dolly Parton Used Her Voice to Tell Working-Class Stories."** Its cultural writing remains its strongest material, but the political function is to reduce class to a demographic identity to be represented rather than a social force to be organized. *Assessment:* Jacobin's orientation remains the reform of the trade union bureaucracy and the Democratic Party from within, with the DSA's electoral operation as the vehicle. Left Voice Left Voice published **"Free Bogdan Syrotiuk: Defend a Socialist Imprisoned for Opposing Imperialist War"** (August 28), stating that "Syrotiuk's case demonstrates the urgent need for an international united front against political repression." This is the second occasion on which the Morenoite PTS's US affiliate has taken up a case initiated and sustained by the ICFI. The defense of Syrotiuk is unconditionally correct, and the growth of support is welcome. But the "united front against political repression" formula detaches the case from what it is actually about — Syrotiuk was prosecuted for building the Fourth International's section in Ukraine and for opposing both Zelensky's regime and Putin's — and converts it into a generic civil-liberties campaign in which the political questions can be evaded. **"AOC and Mamdani Should Apologize for Their Anti-Black Comments"** (August 27) is the purest expression of the tendency's method: a demand for apologies from two Democratic Party officeholders framed as a "teachable moment" for "Black Puerto Ricans and other Afro/Black Latinx people." The category "working class" does not appear; the political relationship to the Democratic Party is not raised at all. **"What Does It Mean to Engage in Mass Politics? A Response to Eric Blanc"** (August 27) polemicizes against Blanc's adaptation of DSA to "what elected officials can defend inside the Democratic Party" — an accurate criticism whose limits are set by Left Voice's own orientation toward the DSA milieu as the audience. *Assessment:* Left Voice combines formal opposition to the Democratic Party with a practical political life conducted entirely within DSA's orbit and within the framework of racial and identity categories. Liberation News / PSL **"Workers in Joslin, IL are fighting back against Tyson's mass layoffs"** (August 28) covers the August 13 announcement of over 2,500 layoffs at the Joslin plant, delivered without notice to workers with more than 15 years' service. The reporting is concrete; the political conclusion is confined to community protest and pressure on the company. Liberation also published **"In Memoriam: Dolly Parton."** Its recent electoral coverage — celebrating Peggy Flanagan's Minnesota primary win as a rejection of "AIPAC and ICE," and framing Francesca Hong's narrow Wisconsin defeat as evidence that the Democratic establishment "won't stop the rise of socialism" — remains the tendency's decisive weakness: the promotion of Democratic primary candidates as socialist advances, alongside nominal calls for "an independent political movement." *Assessment:* PSL continues to fuse militant-sounding rhetoric with de facto support for the left wing of the Democratic Party. Socialist Alternative **"Support Left Independent Candidates — Build An Alternative To The Two Corporate Parties"** (August 2) sets the midterm line: not the construction of a revolutionary party, but electoral support for an assortment of independents whose programs are not specified. **"Trump's DHS Goes After Left Groups & Unions: We Won't Be Intimidated"** (August 19) documents real repression, but its perspective is the defense of existing organizations rather than the political mobilization of the working class against the drive to dictatorship. On the war, **"The 'New' Middle East — Continued War Crisis"** opens by quoting the Financial Times' formulation that "Trump [is] caught between more war or a deal on Iran's terms" — adopting the framing of a leading organ of British finance capital as its own analytical starting point. *Assessment:* Electoralist and defensive, with the analysis of imperialist war borrowed from the bourgeois press. Socialist Worker / SWP (UK) **"NHS strikers say, 'We don't do it for the money, but goodwill doesn't pay the bills'"** and **"Cancer research strikers make their voices heard outside talks with management"** (both August 28) report walkouts by operating theatre staff, clinical support workers, housekeepers and nurses across Greater Manchester, and an indefinite strike at the Institute of Cancer Research that has already forced concessions. The reporting is sympathetic and detailed. The conclusion in every case is to press the union leaderships to call more action — the apparatus is criticized for insufficient militancy, never identified as an instrument of the state. **"Ukrainian AI system could be used to suppress dissent"** (August 28) notes correctly that Burnham handed over Storm Shadow blueprints and that British police may acquire Ukrainian AI surveillance technology. **"US bosses rake in record profits while workers suffer"** reports US corporate pre-tax earnings at $4.8 trillion in the second quarter alongside a historic low in labour's share. *Assessment:* Trade-union militancy without a break from the bureaucracy; opposition to war framed as a moral objection to Labour policy rather than a struggle against the British state. Communist / RCP (IMT) **"Buying time with Ukrainian blood: Burnham recommits to the slaughter"** (August 28) is the sharpest piece from any of these tendencies today, identifying Britain and the European powers as "cynically prolonging this bloodshed for their own imperialist interests." **"UK prison overcrowding: Burnham grapples with the crisis of the British state"** treats the prison crisis as "intractable under capitalism." **"Dolly Parton (1946-2026)"** is a substantial appreciation. The uniform limitation is the conclusion: every article ends by advertising the RCP as the solution, without any concrete perspective for the intervention of the working class — no rank-and-file organization, no independent international strategy. The correct anti-imperialist phrase substitutes for a program. *Assessment:* Verbal orthodoxy on war and the state combined with propagandistic party-building detached from the actual class struggle. --- What the WSWS should cover today 1.
